titles.en: The Woman Who Sets the Price

synopsis.title: Synopsis
synopsis.content:
On the night of her father’s birthday, in front of two hundred guests, Aurelia Song’s mother raises a glass and announces that her daughter’s jewellery boutique is losing four million a year and will close in January. Aurelia walks out onto the balcony in gold silk, shaking, doing sums in her head. A stranger at the far end gives her his coat.

Six weeks later, the stranger walks into her boutique and asks to rent it. His name is Chen Si. He runs the Syndicate. He wants her shop for his business. She sets a price instead: a seat at his table.

Then she proposes. Eleven pages, in red ink, with terms. Clause nine is about the bedroom. Clause ten is a single word.

Between them stand a mother who loves only winners, a vice-minister who framed his father, a poisoned glass of wine on New Year’s Eve, a traitor at the table, and a woman who has never once in her life been loved without having to win.

The Woman Who Sets the Price is a sharp, glamorous, power-couple romance about a queen who refuses to be a title, and a man who never once asks her to win.

The main story is told across four volumes and is complete. Side stories at the end can be read any time. Aurelia and Chen Si first appear in Every Flower in the Shop and Proof by Induction, but this book stands on its own.

contentWarn.title: Content Warning
contentWarn.content:
21+ · For adult readers. Mature themes and heated love scenes.

This book has some dark moments:

• A parent who humiliates her daughter in public, and emotional coercion within a family

• Organised crime, with threats and violence mostly off the page, and a car attack (A Snake in the Syndicate)

• A poisoning, intensive care and a long recovery (Volume Three)

• A panic attack and its aftermath, and therapy (The Word Is Milan)

• Memories of a parent’s wrongful arrest and death in custody, and of a riot and a stabbing in a juvenile detention centre (The Sewer, Nineteen Years Ago)

• Consensual power-play love scenes between a married couple, with a contract, orders, blindfolds, silk ties and a safe word. They are sensual but not explicit

authorNote.title: Author Note
authorNote.content:
Aurelia Song was the rival in Every Flower in the Shop: gold, sunglasses, a slap in the rain, a running score. I wanted to know who she was at two in the morning, when nobody was watching her walk. This is her book.

The crime is kept at the level of a story; nothing here is a how-to. The jewellery is as real as I could make it: piercing saws, gravers, box links soldered one at a time, rouge on the wheel for the last pass.

Thank you for reading. Second is just the first of the ones who kept going.

glossary.title: Names & Terms
glossary.content:
AURELIA — Aurelia’s jewellery boutique on Harbour Road.
The Syndicate — The organisation Chen Si runs. Thirty years old, and older than him.
The terms — Aurelia’s price for laundering money through her shop: a share, real pieces, the books, no lies, a seat at the table.
The marriage agreement — Eleven clauses, renewable after ten years, when the Wife may rewrite every one. At the renewal, he adds a twelfth and a thirteenth.
Clause twelve — The Wife is not the Husband’s queen.
The word — The safe word written into the agreement. It is “Milan.”
Numero Uno — The necklace she named at two in the morning, after a phone call with her mother.
The Jade Hall — A restaurant on Temple Street with a round table for twelve. It has belonged to the Syndicate for thirty years.
The house on the Peak — Her parents’ house, where the party for her father’s fifty-seventh birthday was held.
The Song Group — Her father’s company.
The Pearl — The restaurant booked for New Year’s Eve, same as always.
Tesoro — Her father’s name for her, from before Vienna.

chapters.title: The Balcony Where He Lent Her His Coat
chapters.desc: Her father’s birthday. Her mother’s toast. The worst night of her life, and a stranger who didn’t try to fix it.
chapters.epigraph: “The world is obsessed with your shine. I’m more interested in what you do in the dark.”
chapters.content:
The toast came at ten o’clock, between the lobster and the cake, and Aurelia Song had known for three days that it would be bad.

She had known since Tuesday, when her mother had walked into the boutique on Harbour Road without calling first, in a white coat and dark glasses, and stood in the middle of the shop floor for four minutes without saying anything. She had looked at the cases. The rings on their velvet. The necklace in the window that Aurelia had designed at two in the morning with a pencil and a cup of cold coffee and a feeling, for the first time in her life, of making something that was entirely hers.

Then Vittoria Song had taken off her glasses and said, in Italian, “How much did you lose last quarter?”

And Aurelia had told her. Because you did not lie to Vittoria Song. Nobody did. It was like lying to the weather.

Her mother had nodded once and put her glasses back on and left.

✦ ✦ ✦

The party was for her father’s fifty-seventh birthday, at the house on the Peak, and two hundred people had come, because two hundred people always came when Song Weiren invited them. Bankers and developers and a deputy minister. The woman who owned the biggest television channel in the province. Three ambassadors. The man who designed the new opera house, who was drunk.

Aurelia wore gold.

She always wore gold. Gold silk, cut on the bias, that moved like liquid when she walked and made every head in a room turn the way a compass needle turns north. She had designed the earrings herself. Long, thin, articulated drops of yellow gold that caught the light and threw it. She had put on her mother’s red lipstick and her own fig perfume and walked down the staircase at seven o’clock with her chin up and her heart going like a hammer, and two hundred people had looked at her, and she had let them.

She was twenty-two. She had been Number One at everything she had ever been allowed to compete in, except once. She was not going to let her mother see that she was afraid.

She smiled through the champagne. She smiled through the lobster. She smiled at the deputy minister, who looked at her necklace and said, “Your father’s work?” and she said, “Mine,” and he laughed as if she had told a joke.

At ten o’clock, her mother stood up and tapped a glass.

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria Song gave toasts the way other people gave injections. Quickly, precisely, and in a place you would feel for days.

She stood at the head of the long table in black silk, with diamonds at her throat that had belonged to her grandmother in Milan, and she raised her glass to her husband, and said lovely things about him in two languages, and the room laughed in the right places. She talked about the Song Group. About the new department store over the border. About the bridge her husband was going to build across the harbour, Harbour Bridge Two, the biggest project in the city’s history, if the right people said yes, and the deputy minister at the end of the table smiled into his wine.

Then she turned and looked down the table at her elder daughter.

“And of course,” said Vittoria Song, “I must say something about our girls.”

Aurelia’s hand tightened on the stem of her glass.

“Our younger daughter, Serafina, cannot be with us tonight,” said her mother pleasantly. “She is, I believe, under a car somewhere in the industrial district, covered in oil. We wish her well with that.” A ripple of uncertain laughter. Everybody knew. Serafina had walked out of an engagement dinner two years ago at nineteen, and out of the house, and nobody had said her name in it since. “And our elder daughter, Aurelia, has a little shop.”

The room turned to look at her.

Aurelia smiled. She had been trained to smile. She had been trained to smile through anything since she was four years old, in Milan, at the side of runways and in the front rows of shows, with her mother’s hand on the back of her neck.

“A jewellery shop,” said Vittoria. “On Harbour Road. She designs everything herself. Isn’t that charming?” She smiled. It was a beautiful smile. It had been on the cover of Italian Vogue twice. “It lost four million last year. Weiren and I have agreed to close it in January. We’re so proud of her for trying.” She lifted her glass a little higher. “In this family, we have always believed that second place is just the first of the losers. But it is very important for children to learn that for themselves.”

She drank.

The room, after a beat, drank with her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia did not run.

She had decided that before she was even out of her chair. She would not run. She would not cry. She would not give two hundred people the story they wanted to tell at breakfast. The Song girl burst into tears at her father’s party. She would walk.

So she put her glass down, and she smiled at the deputy minister, who had the grace to look embarrassed, and she said “Excuse me” to the developer on her other side, and she stood up, and she walked. Not fast. Not slow. With her shoulders back and her chin up and the gold silk moving like water, the way her mother had taught her to walk down a runway at eleven, through the long dining room and the drawing room and the music room, past the waiters and the ice sculpture and the string quartet, to the glass doors at the end, and out onto the balcony, and she closed the doors behind her very gently.

Then she put both hands flat on the cold stone balustrade and held on, because her legs had stopped working.

The city was below her. All of it. The Peak fell away into the dark, and under it the harbour spread out silver and black and gold, with the ships moving slowly across it and the lights of the towers on the far side going all the way up into the clouds. It was October and the wind off the water was cold. She was in gold silk with no sleeves.

She didn’t feel it.

Four million. She had known. Of course she had known. She had sat up every night for a month with the accounts, and she had known. She had not known her mother would say it out loud, in front of the deputy minister, between the lobster and the cake.

In January.

She had not known that at all.

She stood on the balcony and looked at the city and did not cry. She did not cry because there was a part of her, very deep down, cold and clear and furious, that was already working out the numbers. That was already thinking: four million, but the second half of the year was better, the necklace in the window has had three enquiries, if I could just get a single serious buyer, if I could just—

She was so busy not crying that it took her a moment to understand that she was not alone.

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a man at the far end of the balcony.

He was standing in the shadow where the light from the music room didn’t reach, with his back against the wall of the house. He had clearly been there before she came out. He was not smoking, or drinking, or on his phone. He was simply standing, very still, in a grey suit and a long camel coat, holding a cup of coffee that she could see from here he had not touched, and looking at the harbour.

He did not look at her.

That was the first thing she noticed. Two hundred people in that house had looked at her tonight. They had looked at her dress and her earrings and her face and her mother’s face and back at hers, all through the toast. This man, alone on a balcony with her, did not look at her at all.

“I’m sorry,” said Aurelia. Her voice came out perfectly steady, which was a small miracle. “I didn’t know anyone was out here.”

“I came out before the lobster,” said the man. His voice was quiet. Mild. Educated, with an accent she couldn’t place. “I don’t like lobster. I don’t like toasts either. I thought I would miss both.”

“You missed a very good toast.”

“I heard it,” said the man. “The doors are glass.”

Aurelia closed her eyes. Of course they were.

✦ ✦ ✦

She waited for him to say something.

People always said something. Your mother didn’t mean it. I’m sure the shop will be fine. You look beautiful tonight, don’t let her get to you. Something kind and useless that would make her want to push them off the balcony.

He didn’t say anything.

He stood at the far end of the balcony with his untouched coffee and looked at the harbour, and let her stand at her end with her hands on the stone, and the silence went on, and on, and it was not uncomfortable. That was the strange thing. It was the first silence in that house all evening that did not feel like a test.

After a while, he put the coffee cup down on the balustrade.

He took off his coat.

He walked down the balcony toward her, not quickly, and stopped a little way off, and held it out. Not around her shoulders. Out. In his hand. So that she could take it or not.

She looked at the coat. Camel cashmere. Very good. Very plain. No label showing.

“I’m not cold,” she said.

“You’re shaking,” said the man.

“I’m angry.”

“Yes,” he said. “I can see that. You can be angry in a coat.”

She looked at him then, properly, for the first time. He was perhaps twenty-four or twenty-five. Not tall. Slight, and very contained, with a calm, handsome face and dark eyes that were looking straight into hers with an expression she didn’t recognise at all.

It wasn’t pity. She had seen pity all night.

It was interest.

She took the coat.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was warm from him. It smelled of cedar and rain and something faintly bitter, like the coffee he hadn’t drunk. She put it on over the gold silk and it was too big in the shoulders and came down to her knees and she pulled it closed with both hands and was so grateful she could have screamed.

“Thank you,” she said, through her teeth.

“You’re welcome.”

He went back to the far end of the balcony. He picked up his coffee. He looked at the harbour.

She stood in his coat and looked at it too.

“Aren’t you going to tell me she didn’t mean it?” said Aurelia, after a while.

“She meant it,” said the man.

Aurelia laughed. It came out of her before she could stop it, short and sharp and astonished, like a bark.

“Aren’t you going to tell me the shop will be fine?”

“I have no idea if the shop will be fine,” said the man. “I haven’t seen the accounts.” He tilted his head slightly. “I’ve seen the window, though. The necklace. The one with the broken chain that isn’t broken.”

She went very still.

The necklace in the window. The one she had designed at two in the morning. A heavy collar of yellow gold that looked, at first glance, as if it had been snapped and mended, the links twisted apart and then soldered back together with tiny bright seams of white gold, so that the break was the most beautiful part of it.

Nobody had understood it. Three enquiries in four months, and all three had asked if it could be made without the break.

“You’ve seen it,” she said.

“I walk down Harbour Road every morning,” said the man. “I’ve looked at it every morning for six weeks.” He paused. “I thought whoever made it must know something about breaking.”

Aurelia didn’t say anything.

“Your mother,” said the man, “is obsessed with your shine.” He looked down at his coffee. “Everyone in that room is. The dress. The earrings. The way you walked out. Two hundred people watched you walk out of that room, and every one of them was thinking about how well you did it.” He was quiet for a moment. “I’m more interested in what you do in the dark. At two in the morning. When nobody’s watching you walk.”

She stood on her father’s balcony in a stranger’s coat and felt something happen in her chest that she had no name for.

“Who are you?” she said.

He finally smiled. It was very small. It went nowhere near his mouth. It lived entirely in his eyes.

“Someone who doesn’t like lobster,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The glass doors opened behind her.

Light and noise spilled out onto the balcony. The quartet. Laughter. And a man in a dinner jacket, one of her father’s assistants, looking flustered.

“Miss Song, your mother is asking for you. The cake—” He stopped. He saw the coat. He saw the man at the end of the balcony. Something went across his face very quickly, something that looked almost like fear. “Mr. Chen. I’m sorry. I didn’t—the minister was looking for you.”

“Tell the minister I’ll be in shortly,” said the man mildly.

The assistant fled.

Aurelia turned and looked at the man at the end of the balcony.

Mr. Chen.

She had heard the name. Everybody had heard the name, in the way you hear about weather systems out at sea. Her father had said it once at dinner, very quietly, and then changed the subject. Her mother had said it once on the phone, in Italian, in a tone Aurelia had never heard her use before, which on anyone else she would have called afraid.

“Chen Si,” said Aurelia slowly.

He inclined his head, very slightly.

She looked down at the coat she was wearing. The camel cashmere. The coat of a man her father would not do business with. The coat of a man the newspapers did not name, because the newspapers were not stupid.

She should take it off. She knew she should. She should take it off and hand it back and walk back into that room and eat the cake and smile.

She pulled it tighter.

“I’m keeping this,” she said. “For now. Until I go in.”

“Keep it as long as you like,” said Chen Si.

He picked up his coffee cup. He walked past her, toward the glass doors. At the doors, he stopped, and looked back at her, standing at the balustrade in his coat with the city behind her and her mother’s red lipstick and her chin up.

He looked for longer than a stranger should. Not at the dress. At her face, and her mouth, and her hands holding his coat closed, as if he were learning them by heart and did not intend to forget any of it.

“The necklace,” he said. “Don’t let them talk you into taking out the break.”

He went inside.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed on the balcony for another twenty minutes, in his coat.

She did not go back in for the cake. She went down the side stairs to the garden and out of the gate and called a car, and went to the boutique on Harbour Road at midnight in a gold dress and a camel coat, and let herself in with her key, and turned on one light, and sat down at the bench in the back with a pencil and a sheet of paper.

She did not cry.

She drew until four in the morning.

When she finally went home, she hung the coat on the back of her bedroom door. It hung there for a week. Every morning she looked at it.

On the eighth day, a letter arrived at the boutique.

It was on thick cream paper with no letterhead. It said that a client would like to discuss a commercial arrangement concerning the premises at 18 Harbour Road. It was signed with two initials.

C.S.

She read it three times.

Then she went home and took the coat off the back of her door, and put it over her arm, and went to find out what the most dangerous man in the city wanted with her little shop.

chapters.title: The Man Who Wanted to Rent Her Shop
chapters.desc: He came to use her boutique. He offered a very generous fee. She sent him back a counter-offer in red ink.
chapters.epigraph: “You want my shop. I want a seat at your table. Those are the terms.”
chapters.content:
He came at eleven on a Tuesday, when the shop was empty, exactly as the letter had said he would.

She had spent the morning getting it ready. Not for him. For herself. She had polished every case. She had changed the flowers. She had put on black, for once, a narrow black dress with long sleeves and no jewellery at all except one ring, because she had decided at six that morning that she was not going to dazzle Chen Si. She was going to make him look at the work.

His coat was folded over the back of a chair by the counter. Dry-cleaned. On a hanger. With a note pinned to the collar in her handwriting: Thank you. — A.

The bell rang at 10:59.

He came in alone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in grey again. A different grey. He had a cup of coffee in his hand from the café across the road, the lid still on, and he walked into the boutique and stopped just inside the door and looked around it, slowly, the way she had seen buyers from the big houses look around a showroom in Milan. Not at the jewellery. At the room. The cases, the lights, the angle of the windows, the door to the workshop at the back, the safe.

Then he looked at her.

“Miss Song.”

“Mr. Chen.” She came round the counter. She did not offer her hand. “Your coat.”

He looked at it on its hanger with its little note.

“You had it cleaned.”

“It smelled of my father’s house.”

Something moved at the corner of his mouth. He put his coffee down on her counter, carefully, on a folded napkin, which she noticed, and took the coat off the chair and put it over his arm.

“Thank you,” he said.

“Thank you.” She folded her arms. “Your letter said a commercial arrangement concerning the premises. I assume you didn’t walk down Harbour Road for six weeks because you wanted to buy a ring.”

“No,” said Chen Si. “Although I did think about it.”

She raised her eyebrows.

“The broken necklace,” he said. “I thought about buying it. Then I thought you would sell it to me and I would never see it in the window again.” He looked at the window, where it still lay on its black velvet throat. “I like walking past it.”

She didn’t know what to say to that, so she said nothing.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her what he wanted standing at the counter, in a low, even voice, as if he were describing a train timetable.

He wanted to use the shop.

Not to buy it. To use it. He had, he said, associates abroad who needed to move value from one place to another, quietly, in a form that didn’t pass through banks. High jewellery was very good for that. Stones were small. Gold was gold everywhere. A necklace sold in Milan for one price and bought back in this city for another, on paper, could carry a great deal of value with it across a border, and a real boutique with a real designer and real customers and a real workshop was the best possible place for that to happen.

“That’s the shape of it,” he said, when she opened her mouth. “I won’t bore you with the mechanics. You would be paid a fee. A very generous fee. Enough to cover last year’s four million and next year’s, and the year after. Your mother would not close the shop in January. Nobody would ever know.” He paused. “You would keep designing. You wouldn’t have to do anything except sign certain invoices and not ask about certain customers.”

Aurelia looked at him across her own counter.

“You want to wash your money through my shop,” she said.

“Yes.”

“And in return you’ll pay me to look the other way.”

“Yes.”

“That’s what you came here to say. After six weeks of looking at my necklace.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “I’m sorry. I find it’s best to be clear.”

She let him wait.

Then she smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was not her mother’s smile. It was the smile she had worn at sixteen, in a school library, reading a boy’s private notebook out loud. The one that had made a whole school step back.

“No,” she said.

He didn’t look surprised. He picked up his coffee. He did not drink it.

“May I ask why?”

“You can ask.” She walked round the end of the counter to the cases. She ran her fingers along the top of one, the one with the rings in it, emeralds and white gold. “You came here thinking I was a socialite with a hobby. A rich girl with a little shop, who lost four million and got humiliated at her father’s party and would be so grateful to anyone who rescued her that she would sign whatever they put in front of her.” She looked at him over her shoulder. “That’s what you thought, isn’t it? On the balcony. You thought, she’s desperate.”

“I thought you were angry,” said Chen Si. “I still think so.”

“I’m furious,” said Aurelia. “But I’m not desperate. And I’m not for hire.”

She went to the back of the shop, to the workshop door, and came back with a single sheet of paper. She put it down on the counter in front of him.

He looked at it.

It was his own letter. A client would like to discuss a commercial arrangement concerning the premises at 18 Harbour Road. Thick cream paper, no letterhead, two initials.

She had written all over it in red ink.

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it without picking it up. She watched him read. He read slowly, the way she imagined he did everything, and his face did not change at all, except that at the third line his eyebrows went up by a millimetre, and at the eighth they stayed there.

COUNTER-OFFER, it said at the top, in red capitals.

1. No fee. I don’t want your money. I want a share. Twenty per cent of the value of every piece that passes through this shop for your associates, paid into an account in my name, which you will not touch.

2. Every piece that passes through this shop will be a real piece. Designed by me. Made in my workshop, by my jeweller. If your associates want to move value through AURELIA, they will move it as AURELIA. If I am going to be a front, I am going to be the best front in Asia.

3. I see the books. All of them. The ones for this shop and the ones for whatever this shop is connected to. I will not sign anything I have not read.

4. I am not to be lied to. Ever. About anything.

5. A seat at your table. Not as your laundress. As your partner. When decisions are made about the money that passes through my hands, I will be in the room.

6. You will never again stand on a balcony and decide I am desperate.

Signed,

A. Song

He finished reading.

He looked at it.

Then he looked up at her, and his face was doing something it clearly did not often do, and she realised, with a jolt that went all the way down to her shoes, that the most dangerous man in the city was trying very hard not to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Number six,” he said.

“Is non-negotiable.”

“I gathered.” He put his coffee down. He picked up the paper, finally, and held it, and read it again. “Twenty per cent.”

“The going rate for a fee is five,” said Aurelia. “I asked. Discreetly. A man who used to buy watches for my father. You were going to offer me eight, because I’m young and you think I don’t know. I want twenty, because without me you have a shop with a window and no designer, and the customs people in Milan know my mother’s name and would never look twice at a crate with mine on it.”

He was looking at her now with the same expression as on the balcony. The one that wasn’t pity. Only now there was heat under it, plain and steady, and he did not trouble to hide it, and she felt it on her skin like the sun through the window.

“Who told you I was going to offer eight?”

“Nobody. I guessed. You just told me.”

There was a silence in the boutique on Harbour Road.

Then Chen Si laughed.

It was very quiet. It came out of him as if he had forgotten it was there: a short, low, startled sound, and he put his hand over his mouth, and looked away, and looked back at her, and his eyes were bright.

“Miss Song,” he said. “I have negotiated with ministers. I have negotiated with men who were holding guns. I have negotiated with my own brother, who doesn’t speak.” He set the paper down on the counter very gently. “Nobody has ever made me tell them my own number in under four minutes.”

“Then you’ve been negotiating with the wrong people.”

“Evidently.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say yes.

He picked up his coat and put it on and picked up his coffee, which he still had not drunk, and folded her counter-offer in half and put it in his inside pocket, next to his heart, which she noticed, and went to the door.

At the door, he stopped.

“Number five,” he said, without turning round. “A seat at the table. You understand what table it is?”

“I understand what the newspapers don’t say about you,” said Aurelia. “I was Number One in my year at school for two years running. I can read.”

“Two years,” said Chen Si. “What happened the third year?”

She went cold.

He turned and looked at her across the shop.

“Someone else came first,” said Aurelia. Her voice was perfectly flat. “She didn’t even try.”

He looked at her face. She didn’t know what he saw in it. She didn’t want to know.

“I’ll think about it,” he said. “The counter-offer. All six points.”

“How long?”

“A week.”

“You have three days,” said Aurelia. “After that, I’ll find someone else to laugh at my terms.”

He opened the door. The bell rang. The noise of Harbour Road came in: traffic, a tram, a man selling chestnuts on the corner.

“Miss Song,” said Chen Si. “Nobody else will laugh at them.”

“Why not?”

“Because nobody else in this city,” he said, “will understand that you mean every word.”

He went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She watched him walk away down Harbour Road through the window, past the broken necklace on its velvet throat, in his camel coat, with his coffee.

He stopped outside the window. He looked at the necklace for a moment, the way he said he did every morning.

Then he looked up, through the glass, at her. Standing behind the counter in black with one ring on, with her arms folded.

He lifted his coffee cup to her, very slightly. A toast.

Then he walked on.

She stayed behind the counter after he had gone, and did not move until the next tram went past.

Then she went into the workshop, where Maestro Enzo Bellini, sixty-three, formerly of Valenza, the finest bench jeweller she had ever met and the only person in the city who had followed her from Milan, was sitting at his bench pretending he had not been listening at the door.

“Well?” said Enzo, in Italian, not looking up from the ring he was setting.

“He laughed,” said Aurelia.

Enzo stopped. He put down his tweezers. He looked at her over the top of his magnifying glasses, his old brown face very still.

“Chen Si laughed,” he said.

She nodded.

“Cara,” he said finally, “I have lived in this city for seven years, and I have heard many things about that man. I have never heard that he laughs.” He picked his tweezers back up. “Either you are going to be very rich, or we are both going to be at the bottom of the harbour.”

“Which do you think?”

Enzo set the stone.

“I think,” he said, “that you should start designing something with a lot of gold in it. Just in case.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the evening of the third day, at six o’clock, a courier came to the boutique.

He brought a flat envelope. Inside was her own counter-offer, in her red ink, on his cream paper.

Under each of her six points, in black ink, in a small, precise hand, there was one word.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

Agreed.

And under number six:

Agreed. With pleasure.

At the bottom of the page, he had added a seventh point of his own.

7. Dinner. Thursday. To discuss the books. You choose the restaurant, because I would like to see what you choose. — C.S.

She read it standing at the counter, in the evening light, with the necklace in the window behind her.

Then she picked up her red pen, and under number seven, she wrote:

Agreed. Not lobster.

chapters.title: Aurelia Negotiates a Don Into a Corner
chapters.desc: She chooses a basement in the old town with eleven tables and no menu. He brings the books. She finds the hole in them before the second course.
chapters.epigraph: “You said I’d see the books.” “I said you would see them. I didn’t say I’d enjoy watching you read them.”
chapters.content:
She chose a basement.

It was in the old town, under a shop that sold funeral paper, down a flight of stone steps so narrow you had to go sideways in heels. It had eleven tables and no menu and a cook called Old Fan who had been there for forty years and decided what you ate by looking at your face. The walls were tiled white, like a hospital. The chairs were plastic. The chilli oil was the best in the province.

She had been coming since she was sixteen. Since the week after the library, when she had walked out of school at lunchtime with her face still burning and got lost in the old town on purpose and found the funeral-paper shop and the steps, and gone down them because they looked like nowhere her mother would ever go.

She had never brought anyone.

She arrived at 7:55, in black trousers and a cream silk shirt and flat shoes, because of the steps, and gold, because she was not going to let him see her without it twice. Old Fan looked up from his wok and saw her and said, “Ah. Princess.” And then saw the man coming down the steps sideways behind her, in a grey suit, with a leather folder under his arm and a coffee cup in his hand, and said nothing at all.

Then he put his ladle down and wiped his hands and bowed. Properly. From the waist.

“Mr. Chen,” said Old Fan.

“Uncle Fan,” said Chen Si, and bowed back.

Aurelia stood at the bottom of the steps and looked from one to the other.

“You know each other,” she said.

“Uncle Fan’s brother was my father’s driver,” said Chen Si. “Twenty years ago.” He looked round the white-tiled room, at the eleven tables and the plastic chairs. Then at her. “You chose this.”

“You said you wanted to see what I chose.”

“I did.” He was quiet for a moment. “I thought it would be the Peninsula. Or the rooftop place at the Harbour Hotel. Somewhere with a view.” He put the folder down on the table nearest the wall. “I didn’t think it would be somewhere I used to come with my mother.”

She went still.

“I didn’t know,” she said.

“I know you didn’t.” He pulled out a plastic chair for her. “That’s why I like it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Old Fan brought food without asking. Cold cucumber with garlic. Pork belly in chilli oil so red it was almost black. A whole fish in a clay pot, bubbling. Rice. Beer for her, in a big green bottle with no glass. Tea for him.

Chen Si looked at the beer bottle.

“You drink from the bottle,” he said.

“Here I do.” She drank from the bottle. “My mother would die.” She put the bottle down. “Open the folder.”

He opened the folder.

It was the books.

Not all of them. He said so at once: “Not all of them. Not yet. You’ll understand why when you see these.” But a great deal. Ledgers for four companies. A shipping firm. A property developer. A chain of pawnshops. An import business that dealt, on paper, in Italian furniture. Bank statements from three countries. Invoices. Long columns of figures in a small precise hand that she recognised from the margin of her counter-offer.

“You keep them yourself,” she said.

“Some of them.” He picked up his tea and didn’t drink it. “I don’t trust accountants. I trust one accountant, a little. He’s seventy and very frightened of me. I check his work.”

She pulled the first ledger toward her across the table, past the fish.

“May I?”

“That’s what they’re for.”

She started to read.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, she would try to explain to Enzo what it was like, and fail.

It was like the first time she had held a loupe to a stone. The world went away. The white tiles, the noise of the wok, the old men at the next table playing cards and arguing, the fish going cold. Even him. There was just the page, and the numbers on it, and the pattern under the numbers, slowly coming up into focus, the way the inside of a sapphire comes up into focus under the glass: the silk, the colour zoning, the tiny crystals of something else trapped inside it a million years ago that tell you where it came from and how much it is worth.

She read for forty minutes without speaking.

He didn’t interrupt her once. When Old Fan came to take the fish and bring the soup, Chen Si shook his head, very slightly, and Old Fan went away again. When she reached out blindly for the beer bottle, Chen Si moved it ten centimetres so that her hand found it. When she reached the end of the third ledger and frowned and turned back two pages and ran her finger down a column, he leaned back in his plastic chair and folded his hands and watched her do it.

He watched her the way he had watched the harbour from her father’s balcony.

As if she were the only thing worth looking at for miles.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Here,” said Aurelia.

She turned the ledger round and pushed it across the table and put her finger on a line.

He looked at it. Then at her.

“The furniture company,” she said. “Milan to here. Walnut dining tables. Twelve of them, in March. Declared at customs at eight thousand euros each. Sold here, two weeks later, to a hotel on the east side, for ninety thousand.” She tapped the page. “That’s how it works, isn’t it? Something cheap that’s said to be expensive. The difference is the money you’re moving.”

“Something like that,” said Chen Si mildly.

“I’m not asking how. I can see how.” She turned two pages. “But here. In June. The same thing. Eighteen tables. Except these were declared at eight thousand euros and sold for ninety thousand and the money came back here—” she turned another page, “—and only sixty went where the rest of it goes. Thirty thousand a table didn’t.” She looked up. “Eighteen tables. That’s more than half a million. It goes somewhere else. To an account with a different bank. And it happens again in August. And September.”

Chen Si didn’t move.

“Someone,” said Aurelia, “is taking a slice of your slice. Quietly. Every time a shipment comes from Milan. Someone who knows the furniture company and the hotel and your accountant’s handwriting well enough that it doesn’t look strange unless you read the whole year at once.” She sat back. “You don’t read the whole year at once. You check the work. Month by month. That’s why you didn’t see it.”

The card players at the next table had stopped arguing.

Old Fan, at the wok, had stopped stirring.

Chen Si looked down at the line under her finger and said nothing for a while.

Then he looked up at her.

“How long have you been reading?” he said.

“Forty-one minutes.”

“My accountant has had those books for two years.”

“Your accountant,” said Aurelia, “is seventy and very frightened of you. Frightened people don’t look for things they don’t want to find.” She picked up the beer bottle. “I’m not frightened of you.”

“No,” said Chen Si slowly. “You aren’t, are you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He did not ask her who she thought it was.

She noticed that. He closed the folder very gently and put his hand flat on top of it and looked at the wall for a while, and she could see him thinking, three or four moves ahead, the way she imagined he played chess. She did not tell him. She didn’t know. She had the shape of it, not the name.

When he looked back at her, his face was perfectly calm.

“Thank you,” he said. “That changes things.”

“I hoped it would.” She put her elbows on the table, which her mother would also have died about. “So let me tell you what else changes.”

He raised his eyebrows.

“You agreed to six points,” said Aurelia. “Seven, with dinner. But you agreed to them because you thought I was a designer with a good eye and a nasty temper who would make a very good front. You didn’t think I’d find half a million euros in forty-one minutes.” She smiled. “So the price has gone up.”

“Has it.”

“Twenty-five per cent.”

He looked at her.

“And,” said Aurelia, “the furniture company. Whoever’s been running it. I want it. Not the person. I don’t care what you do with the person. The company. Milan to here. That’s my city. I speak the language, I know the customs men by their first names, I know which ports my mother’s friends use and which they don’t. You’re running Italian furniture through a man who can’t tell walnut from veneer and steals from you. Give it to me, and I’ll run it through people who can, and nobody will steal from you again, because I’ll be reading every line every month.”

She picked up her chopsticks.

“That’s the counter-offer,” she said. “Twenty-five per cent and the Milan route. Take it or leave it. The fish is getting cold.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si sat back in his plastic chair.

He looked at her for so long that she began, very slightly, at the very back of her mind, to wonder if she had gone too far. If this was the moment when the mild, calm man in the grey suit turned into the thing the newspapers didn’t name.

Then he unfolded his hands.

He reached across the table, past the cold fish, and picked up her beer bottle.

He drank from it. Straight from the bottle. One long swallow. And put it back down in front of her, exactly where it had been.

“Done,” said Chen Si.

She stared at him.

“You don’t drink,” she said. “You hold coffee and never drink it. You’ve been holding that tea for an hour.”

“I don’t drink things other people give me,” said Chen Si. “It’s a habit. A man in my position.” He looked at the bottle. “I drink things I take.”

Something went through her that had nothing to do with negotiations at all.

She looked down at the bottle, where his mouth had been. Then up at him.

He was watching her with that same expression. Interest. Except now there was something else under it, something darker and much warmer, and he was not hiding it, and he was not looking away.

“Twenty-five per cent,” he said quietly. “And Milan. And a seat at the table. And you read every line, every month.” He paused. “And you’ll come to the next meeting. Thursday. With the men who run the routes. They’ll hate you. They’ll try to frighten you. I won’t stop them.”

“Why not?”

“Because,” said Chen Si, “I want to watch you do to them what you just did to me.”

She smiled. Slowly. She couldn’t help it.

“You’ve been negotiated into a corner, Mr. Chen,” she said.

“I know,” said Chen Si. “I walked into it on purpose. I wanted to see what the corner looked like.” He picked up his chopsticks, finally, and took a piece of the cold fish. “It has a very good view.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, he walked her up the narrow stone steps, sideways, him first, so that if she slipped in the dark he would be there.

She didn’t slip.

At the top, in the street, in the smell of incense from the funeral-paper shop and the noise of the old town at night, they stood facing each other under a streetlamp. He had his folder under his arm. She had her hands in the pockets of her trousers.

He knew what he wanted to do next. She could see it. He stepped closer, close enough that she had to tip her head back, and reached out and took one of her hands out of her pocket and held it, not like a handshake, his thumb moving once, slowly, across her knuckles. His hand was warm. He did not let go.

“I don’t want to go yet,” he said, very low. “I’m telling you so you know. I’m going anyway.”

A car was waiting at the corner. Black, long, quiet. A man stood beside it, very large, with his hands at his sides.

“Your driver?” said Aurelia.

“My brother,” said Chen Si. “He insists, on Thursdays.”

She looked at the very large man by the car. He looked back at her. He did not blink.

“He doesn’t look like your brother.”

“We’re not related,” said Chen Si. “It’s a different kind of brother.” He paused. “Zhendong. This is Miss Song.”

The very large man looked at her for four seconds.

“Hm,” he said.

That was all.

“He likes you,” said Chen Si.

“How can you tell?”

“He didn’t check you for a weapon.”

She laughed, the bark again, the one that came out of her before she could stop it, and Chen Si looked at her laughing under the streetlamp in the old town with an expression she would remember for the rest of her life.

“Goodnight, Miss Song,” he said.

“Goodnight, Mr. Chen.”

He let go of her hand last, as if it cost him. He went toward the car. Halfway there, he stopped and turned round.

“Aurelia,” he said.

She went very still. He had not said her name before.

“The thirty thousand a table,” he said. “The account with the different bank. You know whose it is.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “I don’t.”

“You do,” said Chen Si. “You saw the name of the bank. You saw where the branch is.” He was quiet for a moment. “You didn’t say it because you weren’t sure whether I already knew, and you didn’t want to watch my face when I found out. In case it was someone I loved.”

She didn’t say anything.

“It isn’t,” said Chen Si. “I don’t love many people. You can tell me on Thursday.”

He got into the car.

The very large man looked at her once more over the roof of it. Then he got in too.

The car slid away down the narrow street, and she stood under the streetlamp outside the funeral-paper shop, with the taste of chilli oil and beer in her mouth, and his on the bottle, and thought: I am in so much trouble.

And then, in the same breath, the cold clear furious voice that had been doing the numbers on her father’s balcony said:

Good.

chapters.title: Aurelia Song Does Not Do Second Place
chapters.desc: Thursday. Five men who run the routes, one long table, and a woman they have been told to frighten. Then a game of mahjong she has no intention of losing.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule one of a room full of men who want you gone: sit down first.”
chapters.content:
The meeting was on the thirty-ninth floor of a building with no name on it, in a room with a long black table and floor-to-ceiling windows that looked straight across the harbour at her father’s office.

She noticed that the moment she walked in. Song Group Tower, glittering on the other side of the water, forty storeys of gold glass with her father’s name at the top in letters three metres high. You could see it from every chair at the table.

She wondered if Chen Si had chosen the room for that.

She decided he had.

✦ ✦ ✦

There were five of them.

They were already there when she arrived, at two minutes to three, sitting along one side of the long table with their backs to the window, in suits that cost a great deal and did not fit very well. Older men. Fifties, sixties. A man with a shaved head and a gold watch. A thin man with tinted glasses. A heavy man eating sunflower seeds out of his pocket and spitting the shells into a coffee cup. A small neat man in a cardigan who looked like a retired schoolteacher. And, at the end, a tall grey-haired man with a kind, tired, handsome face, who stood up when she came in.

Nobody else did.

“Miss Song,” said the tall man. “I’m Sun Wei. I’ve heard a great deal about you.”

“From whom?”

He smiled. It was a nice smile. Warm. Fatherly. “From Chen Si. He doesn’t usually talk about anyone.”

“Then you’ve heard more than most,” said Aurelia.

Chen Si was not there yet.

She understood that too. He had told her. They’ll hate you. They’ll try to frighten you. I won’t stop them. He wasn’t there yet because he wanted to see what happened when he wasn’t.

There was a chair at the head of the table, empty. His, obviously. There were five chairs along the window side, full. On the other side of the table, the side facing the window, there was nothing at all. No chairs. Somebody had taken them away.

The man with the sunflower seeds spat a shell into his cup and looked at her.

“You can stand,” he said. “It won’t be long.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia looked at the empty side of the table.

Then she looked at the empty chair at the head of it. His chair.

Then she walked down the length of the room, in her heels, in a dark green suit with gold buttons she had designed herself and had made overnight by a tailor who owed her mother a favour, past the five men, and pulled out the chair at the head of the table, and sat down in it.

She crossed her legs. She put her handbag on the table in front of her. She folded her hands on top of it.

The room went very quiet.

“Rule one,” said Aurelia pleasantly, “of a room full of men who want you gone. Sit down first.” She looked along the row of them. “My mother taught me that. She taught me a great many things. Most of them were about walking. That one was about chairs.”

The man with the shaved head laughed. It wasn’t a nice laugh.

“That’s the boss’s chair, little girl.”

“Yes,” said Aurelia. “And he isn’t here. And I am. And someone took away all the other chairs, so I assumed this one was for me.” She smiled at the man with the sunflower seeds. “Unless you’d like to give me yours?”

The man with the sunflower seeds stopped chewing.

Sun Wei, at the end, sat back down slowly. He was looking at her with an expression she couldn’t read. Something like amusement. Something like calculation.

“Miss Song,” he said gently. “Nobody here means you any disrespect. We were simply told that Chen Si was bringing a—consultant. A designer. To advise on the Milan route.” He spread his hands. “You must understand. These gentlemen have been running the routes for twenty years. Some of them since before Chen Si was born. They don’t take kindly to being advised by a young woman with a shop.”

“A shop that lost four million last year,” said the man with the tinted glasses. “We read the papers too.”

“Then you’ll have read,” said Aurelia, “that my mother is closing it in January.”

“We did.”

“She isn’t,” said Aurelia. “I am keeping it open. With my share of the Milan route.” She looked at the man with the tinted glasses. “Which used to be yours, I think. The furniture.”

The man with the tinted glasses went white.

✦ ✦ ✦

The door opened.

Chen Si came in with a coffee cup in his hand and Qian Yu, his assistant, behind him carrying a laptop. He stopped just inside the door and looked at the room.

At the five men along the window. At the empty side of the table. At his own chair at the head of it, with Aurelia Song sitting in it, legs crossed, hands folded on her handbag, smiling.

Nobody breathed.

Chen Si looked at her. His face did not change.

Then he turned to Qian Yu.

“Qian,” he said mildly. “Would you bring me a chair?”

Qian Yu, who had worked for Chen Si for six years and had seen a great many things, put the laptop down very carefully and went out and came back with a chair, an ordinary office chair on wheels, and set it at the corner of the table, at Aurelia’s right hand.

Chen Si sat down in it.

He put his coffee down. He looked along the table at the five men who ran his routes.

“I see you’ve met my partner,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

The meeting lasted two hours.

She would remember almost none of the figures. She would remember everything else.

She would remember the man with the sunflower seeds trying three times to talk over her, and Chen Si not stopping him, and her not stopping either, until the third time, when she simply stopped talking and waited, and looked at him, and kept waiting, in total silence, for forty-five seconds, until he ran out of things to say and his voice trailed off into nothing and the whole table was looking at him, and then she said, “Are you finished?” very kindly, and went on.

She would remember the man with the tinted glasses, who had run the furniture route for eleven years, trying to explain to her why the Milan customs office was impossible to deal with, and her taking out her phone and calling a number and speaking in rapid Italian for two minutes and hanging up and saying, “Dottor Rossi says the November shipment will be cleared on the fourteenth. He sends his regards to my mother.” And the man with the tinted glasses taking off his glasses, and putting them on again, and saying nothing for the rest of the afternoon.

She would remember the small neat man in the cardigan, who ran the pawnshops, not saying anything at all for an hour and a half, and then, at the very end, leaning forward and asking her a single, quiet, very exact question about how she would value a stone that had no papers, and her answering it, properly, at length, with a diagram on the back of an agenda, and the small neat man listening with his head on one side and then sitting back and saying to Chen Si, “She’s right. I’ve been doing it wrong for nine years.”

And she would remember Sun Wei, at the far end of the table, by the window, smiling his warm, tired, fatherly smile, saying very little, watching her the whole time.

And Chen Si, at her right hand, in an office chair, not saying anything at all. Not once interrupting. Not once helping. Sitting back with his coffee he didn’t drink, watching her take his table apart and put it back together again, with an expression on his face that she didn’t dare look at directly, because when she did, her train of thought went straight off a cliff.

✦ ✦ ✦

At five o’clock, he stood up and said, “Thank you, gentlemen,” and the five men stood up and filed out. The man with the sunflower seeds didn’t look at her. The man with the tinted glasses didn’t look at her. The small neat man in the cardigan stopped at her chair on the way out and bowed, very slightly, and said, “Miss Song,” and she understood that she had made a friend.

Sun Wei was last.

He stopped at the door. He looked back at her, in the chair at the head of the table, and at Chen Si beside her.

“Remarkable,” he said warmly. “Truly. I haven’t seen anything like it in twenty years.” He smiled at Chen Si. “You’ve found yourself a treasure, Si.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “I have.”

Sun Wei went out.

The door closed.

Aurelia let out a breath she seemed to have been holding for two hours, and put both her hands flat on the table, because they had started, very slightly, to shake.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Well?” she said, not looking at him.

He didn’t answer.

She turned her head. He was sitting in the office chair, at the corner of the long black table, with Song Group Tower glittering in the window behind him across the harbour. He was looking at her.

“You sat in my chair,” said Chen Si.

“They took the others away.”

“I know. I told them to.”

She stared at him.

“You told them to?”

“I told Qian to tell them to take the chairs away from your side,” said Chen Si. “I wanted to see what you’d do.” He was quiet. “I thought you’d stand. Most people stand. A few people leave. One man, once, sat on the floor.” He looked at her. “Nobody has ever sat in my chair.”

“Are you angry?”

“No,” said Chen Si. “I’m something else. I haven’t worked out what yet.”

He leaned forward and put his hand over hers on the black table, over the shaking, and pressed it flat and held it there until it stopped. He didn’t ask. He didn’t look away from her face while he did it.

“That’s a lie,” he said. “I know exactly what.”

She looked at him.

There was a silence in the room on the thirty-ninth floor. The late sun came across the harbour and lay along the black table in a long gold bar.

“Sun Wei,” said Aurelia.

He didn’t move.

“The account,” she said. “The thirty thousand a table. The bank. It’s his, isn’t it? The branch is in the district where his wife’s family is from. I read his file this morning. Qian gave it to me.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

“You knew.”

“Since Thursday night. Since you didn’t say it.” He picked up his coffee. Didn’t drink it. “I’ve known Sun Wei since I was eighteen. He was the first man in this city who gave me work when I got out. He taught me how the routes ran. He calls me Si. Nobody else does.” He put the cup down. “I’m not going to do anything about it yet.”

“Why not?”

“Because a man who steals half a million is a thief,” said Chen Si. “A man who steals half a million and smiles at you across a table and calls you a treasure is something else. I want to know what.” He looked at her. “I want to know who he’s stealing for.”

She held his gaze.

“You’re playing chess,” she said.

“Always,” said Chen Si. “So are you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, because it was Thursday, and because neither of them seemed to want to leave, he took her to a mahjong parlour.

It was on the ground floor of the same building, behind an unmarked door. Fourteen tables. Old women in cardigans. Smoke. The clatter of tiles like rain on a roof. The woman who ran it, who was eighty and had one gold tooth and called Chen Si little boy, put them at a table in the corner with two of her friends, who were also eighty, and who looked at Aurelia’s green suit and gold buttons and laughed.

“She’s pretty,” said one of them to Chen Si. “Can she play?”

“I don’t know,” said Chen Si. “Can you?”

Aurelia sat down. She took off her rings, one by one, and put them in a row on the edge of the table.

“My grandmother taught me in Milan,” she said. “She was from Ningbo. She said there were only two things a woman needed to be able to do in this world. Read a contract, and count tiles.” She began to shuffle. “I’ve never lost.”

“Never?” said the woman with the gold tooth.

“Never.”

The old women looked at each other.

Chen Si sat back in his chair, with his coffee, and smiled.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t lose.

She played for three hours, against three of the best mahjong players in the old town, two of whom had been playing since before her mother was born, and she did not lose a single round. Not one. She played fast and hard and without mercy, and she counted every tile, and she watched every hand, and when the woman with the gold tooth tried a very old and very clever trick in the second hour, Aurelia looked at her across the table and said, “Nonna, I saw that,” in a voice so sweet it could have stripped paint, and the old woman threw back her head and cackled and slapped the table.

At eleven, the old women gave up.

“She’s a monster,” said the woman with the gold tooth to Chen Si, with enormous approval. “Where did you find her?”

“On a balcony,” said Chen Si.

Aurelia was putting her rings back on, one by one.

“You didn’t play,” she said to him. “You sat there for three hours and watched. Why?”

He looked at her across the mahjong table in the smoke and the clatter and the yellow light.

“Because you play,” he said, “like someone who thinks that if she loses once, she’ll disappear.”

Her hands stopped on the last ring.

“I wanted to see if it was true,” said Chen Si.

She didn’t answer.

She put the ring on. She stood up. She picked up her handbag.

“Goodnight, Mr. Chen,” she said, and her voice wasn’t steady, and she hated it.

“Goodnight, Aurelia.”

She walked out of the mahjong parlour into the night with her chin up and her heels clicking on the tiles and her heart going like a hammer, and didn’t look back.

She didn’t have to. She could feel him watching her the whole way to the door.

chapters.title: The First Ledger She Ever Read
chapters.desc: The Milan route, the first shipment under her name, a customs shed at the docks at four in the morning, and the realisation that she is very, very good at this.
chapters.epigraph: “It isn’t that I like breaking rules. I like knowing exactly which ones I’m breaking, and what they cost.”
chapters.content:
The first crate came in on the fourteenth of November, at four in the morning, exactly as Dottor Rossi had promised.

It was a real crate. That was the point. She had insisted on it, in the second meeting on the thirty-ninth floor, and the man with the tinted glasses had argued for twenty minutes and lost. Inside the crate, packed in straw and tissue and custom-cut foam, there were six walnut dining tables from a workshop in Cantù, north of Milan, that had been making furniture since 1890. Real walnut. Real joints. Real tables, that a real hotel on the east side of the city would put in its real restaurant, and that a real guest might eat a real dinner off.

And tucked into a hollow in the base of each table, under a panel that only a man from Cantù with a very particular screwdriver would ever find, there was a small flat case of grey velvet, and in each case, a necklace.

Her necklaces. Designed at her bench, made by Enzo, stamped with her name. Each one invoiced, on paper, at a price that bore no relation to the amount of gold in it, so that when they were sold, on paper, to a buyer on the east side who would sell them back, on paper, to someone in Singapore, the difference between the numbers would carry a great deal of value from one side of the world to the other.

That was the shape of it, Chen Si would say. She didn’t need the mechanics. She had built them.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the docks to watch it come in.

He told her not to. He said it twice, on the phone, the night before, in his mild voice. You don’t need to be there. Qian will be there. The men will be there. Nobody needs to see your face at a customs shed at four in the morning.

“I need to see it,” said Aurelia.

“Why?”

She thought about it. She was sitting on the floor of her flat at midnight in silk pyjamas with the paperwork spread around her in a circle, every invoice, every manifest, every customs form, and a pot of cold coffee, and a pencil behind her ear.

“Because it’s mine,” she said. “The first one. I designed every piece in it. I want to see it land.”

There was a silence on the line.

“Wear flat shoes,” said Chen Si. “The docks are wet.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She wore flat shoes.

She wore black trousers and a black coat and a black cashmere hat pulled down over her hair and no gold at all, not even her ring, and she stood in the shadow of a stack of containers at the edge of the customs yard at the Iron Docks at 3:50 in the morning, in the cold, in the smell of diesel and salt and rust, and watched a crane lift a forty-foot container off a ship from Genoa and swing it slowly through the dark, under the floodlights, and set it down on the concrete as gently as a hand putting down a cup.

She had never seen anything so beautiful in her life.

“There,” said a voice beside her.

She hadn’t heard him come. She never did. He was in his camel coat, with his hands in his pockets, no coffee for once, standing a little way off in the shadow of the containers, looking at the crane.

“You said you wouldn’t come,” she said.

“I said you didn’t need to.” He didn’t look at her. “I didn’t say anything about me.”

They watched the customs men open the container. They watched the crates come out, one by one, on a forklift, under the floodlights. They watched a man in a peaked cap with a clipboard walk down the line of crates, checking the numbers against a list.

He stopped at the crate from Cantù.

Aurelia stopped breathing.

The man in the peaked cap looked at the label. AURELIA — Song & Associates — Furniture — Cantù. He looked at his clipboard. He looked at the label again. He took a crowbar from his belt and levered up one corner of the lid and looked inside. Straw. Tissue. The curved walnut leg of a table, gleaming under the floodlights.

He put the lid back down.

He made a mark on his clipboard.

He moved on.

She let out her breath. It came out white in the cold air and hung there. Her hands, in her coat pockets, were shaking.

Beside her, Chen Si said, “Well?”

She turned her head and looked at him.

She knew what she was supposed to feel. Relief. Fear. Guilt, maybe. She was twenty-two years old and she had just watched a crate of her own necklaces go through customs inside a dining table, and she knew exactly what that made her, and so did the man standing beside her in the dark.

She didn’t feel any of it.

“I want to do it again,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took her for breakfast afterwards, at five in the morning, at a stall at the edge of the docks where the crane drivers ate. Rice porridge with century egg. Fried dough sticks. Hot soy milk in plastic bowls. They sat on plastic stools in the cold with their coats on and she ate everything, ravenously, because she had been too nervous to eat for two days.

He watched her eat.

“You like it,” he said.

She looked up with a dough stick in her hand.

“Not the porridge,” said Chen Si. “The other thing. The crate.” He was quiet for a moment. “You liked it.”

She thought about lying. She thought about saying something about the money, about saving the shop, about her mother.

She didn’t.

“I liked it,” she said. “I liked every bit of it. I liked the paperwork. I liked Dottor Rossi on the phone. I liked the man with the tinted glasses losing the argument. I liked standing there watching the man with the clipboard and knowing exactly what was in that crate and exactly what would happen if he looked properly, and knowing he wouldn’t, because I’d made sure he wouldn’t.” She put the dough stick down. “Is that terrible?”

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

She laughed.

“I like it too,” he said. “That’s why I’m good at it.” He picked up his bowl of soy milk and held it in both hands and didn’t drink it. “Most people who do what I do, do it because they have to. Because they were born into it, or they owe someone, or they’re greedy. A few of them do it because they like hurting people.” He looked at the soy milk. “I do it because it’s a puzzle. Because the whole city is a machine and almost nobody knows how it really works, and I do. Every piece. Every bribe, every route, every judge. I like knowing.”

“You like knowing which rules you’re breaking,” said Aurelia.

He looked up.

“And what they cost,” she said. “Exactly what they cost.”

Something went across his face. Very fast.

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “That’s it. That’s exactly it.”

They sat on their plastic stools at the edge of the Iron Docks in the dark before dawn and looked at each other, and neither of them said anything, and the crane drivers at the next table watched them with great interest and nudged each other.

✦ ✦ ✦

That week, he gave her the second ledger.

Not the furniture. Something bigger. A shipping company that moved containers between this city and four ports in Southeast Asia, and had done for eleven years, and was, on paper, profitable, and was, in reality, the spine of something she didn’t have a name for yet. It came in four leather volumes and a hard drive.

He gave it to her in her own boutique, after closing, at the counter, under the one light she left on.

“It will take you a month,” he said.

“A week.” She was already opening the first volume. “Why are you giving it to me?”

He stood at the counter and looked at her, in the one light, with the broken necklace in the dark window behind him.

“Because,” said Chen Si, “I’ve been running it for six years, and I have never once had anyone to talk to about it who understood what I was saying.”

She looked up.

He was not smiling. His face was calm and still and very tired, and she understood, with a jolt, that he was telling her something true, and that it had cost him something to say it.

“Zhendong understands,” she said.

“Zhendong understands the parts with guns in them. He doesn’t like the paper.” A very small smile. “He says paper is for people who are afraid of their own hands.”

“And you?”

“I’m not afraid of my own hands,” said Chen Si. “I’m just better at paper.”

She closed the ledger. She put her hand flat on top of it.

“Then sit down,” she said. “And talk to me about it.”

He sat down on the stool on the customer’s side of her counter, the stool where women sat to try on rings, and she sat on her side, and they talked about the shipping company until three in the morning.

It was, she would think later, the most intimate thing that had ever happened to her. More than the boy she had kissed at eighteen in a garden in Milan. More than anything. Two people at a counter in the dark with a ledger between them, talking about money and ports and bribes and the shape of a machine that nobody else could see, finishing each other’s sentences by two o’clock, arguing by half past, laughing by three.

At three, he looked at his watch and stood up.

“I should go,” he said. “You have customers at ten.”

“I do.”

He didn’t go.

He stood on the customer’s side of the counter and looked at her across it, and she sat on her side and looked back at him, with the ledger shut between them and her hand still flat on top of it, and the shop was very quiet, and the one light was very warm, and she could hear her own heart.

“Aurelia,” he said.

“Yes.”

He reached across the counter. Slowly. The way he had held out his coat on the balcony, so that she could take it or not.

He put two fingers under her chin, very lightly, and tilted her face up to the light.

He looked at it. Just looked. At her mouth, and her eyes, and the place where the pencil had left a grey smudge on her cheekbone at midnight that she hadn’t known was there.

He brushed it away with his thumb.

His thumb stayed. It moved, once, along her lower lip, and his eyes went dark, and she felt his hand go very still against her jaw, the way a man goes still when he is holding himself back by force.

“Not tonight,” he said, and his voice was not mild at all. “When I kiss you, I don’t want to stop at three because you have customers at ten.”

Then he took his hand back.

“Goodnight,” he said.

He went out. The bell rang. She heard his car start at the corner and pull away.

She sat at her counter with her hand on the ledger and her face burning where his thumb had been.

She had expected him to kiss her.

She had wanted him to.

And he had looked at her mouth, deliberately, and told her so, in that voice, and then he had not, and walked out, and left her sitting there with it.

“Oh, you bastard,” said Aurelia Song, to nobody, and started to laugh.

chapters.title: He Never Asks Her to Win
chapters.desc: She tests him. She loses a game of chess on purpose. He doesn’t care. Then she finds out what he does care about, and it is not what she expected at all.
chapters.epigraph: “I don’t care if you win. I care that you stop being afraid of what happens if you don’t.”
chapters.content:
She decided to test him in December.

She did not decide it in words. She would not have admitted it, even to herself. But some part of her, the part that had been trained since four years old to know exactly what every person in a room wanted from her and give it to them before they knew they wanted it, had been watching Chen Si for six weeks and could not work him out.

Everybody wanted her to win. That was the rule. Her mother wanted her to win because a daughter who lost was a reflection. Her father wanted her to win because a daughter who won could be shown to ministers. Teachers wanted her to win because it made their numbers good. Boys wanted her to win because they wanted to be seen with the girl who won, and then, when they had been, they wanted to beat her, which was a different kind of wanting, and she had learned to see that one coming from a long way off.

Chen Si watched her win and said nothing. He sat at the corner of his own table while she took his meeting apart. He sat in the smoke of the mahjong parlour for three hours while she destroyed three grandmothers. He sat at her counter until three in the morning while she argued with him about container fees, and when she won the argument, he didn’t look pleased or annoyed. He just looked at her.

She didn’t know what he wanted.

It was driving her mad.

✦ ✦ ✦

He played chess. She had known that since the first week. There was a board in his office on the thirty-ninth floor, a heavy old set with pieces of black and white jade, and he played against himself in the evenings, Qian said, when he was thinking.

On the second Friday of December she walked into his office at seven in the evening without knocking, in a red dress, and sat down on the other side of the board, and said, “Teach me.”

He looked up from his laptop.

“You don’t know how to play chess?”

“I know how the pieces move. My father taught me when I was six. He stopped when I beat him at eight.” She picked up a jade knight and turned it in her fingers. “I want to play you.”

He closed the laptop.

“All right,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lost.

Not at first. At first, she played properly. She was good. Not as good as him; she could see that within ten moves. But good, fast and aggressive and unafraid, and for an hour she made him work, really work, sitting forward with his elbows on his knees and his coffee going cold beside the board. Twice she surprised him. Once she nearly had his queen.

And then, at the end of the hour, in a position where she could see three moves that would keep her in the game and one that would lose it, she took a breath, and chose the one that would lose it.

On purpose.

She moved her rook to a square where he would take it. She sat back. She watched his face.

He looked at the board. He did not take the rook.

Then he looked up at her.

“Why did you do that?” he said.

“Do what?”

“You had the bishop.” He touched it. “Bishop to c4. You’d have pinned my knight. I’d have had to give you the exchange. You saw it. I watched you see it.” He sat back. “Then you put your rook where I could take it.”

“Maybe I didn’t see it.”

“You saw it,” said Chen Si. “You see everything. You found half a million euros in my books in forty-one minutes. You saw a bishop on c4.” His voice was very mild. “You lost on purpose.”

She looked at him across the jade board, in her red dress, with her chin up.

“So?” she said.

“So I want to know why.”

She didn’t answer.

He waited. He was very good at waiting. She was beginning to understand that it was his most dangerous quality.

“I wanted to see what you’d do,” said Aurelia finally. Her voice came out harder than she meant it to. “When I lost. Everybody does something. My mother goes cold. My father changes the subject. Boys at school used to smile, as if they’d been waiting for it.” She lifted her chin higher. “I wanted to see what you’d do. So. Go on. Do it.”

Chen Si looked at her.

Then he reached across the board, and took her rook, and put it to one side.

And then he picked up his own king, and laid it down on its side.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stared at it.

The black jade king lying on its side on the board. The sign, older than either of them, older than the city, that a game was over. That a player resigned.

“What are you doing?” said Aurelia.

“Resigning.”

“You were winning.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “I was.” He sat back in his chair. “But you stopped playing. So I don’t want to play any more. There’s no point in winning against someone who isn’t playing.”

“That’s—” She didn’t know what it was. “That’s not how chess works.”

“It’s how I work,” said Chen Si.

He looked at the fallen king.

“I don’t care if you win, Aurelia,” he said. “I don’t care if you lose. You could lose every game of chess you ever play against me and I’d just want to play another.” He looked up at her. “I care that you’re so afraid of losing.”

She sat very still in her red dress.

“I watched you play mahjong for three hours,” said Chen Si, “against three old women who were laughing and smoking and enjoying themselves. And you didn’t enjoy one minute of it. Not one. You played like someone defusing a bomb.” His voice didn’t change at all. “You walked out of your father’s dining room like someone walking out of a burning building. You sat in my chair at that table because if you’d stood, you thought you’d have lost, and if you’d lost, you thought you’d have stopped existing.” He picked up the fallen king and turned it in his fingers. “That isn’t ambition. That’s fear. Somebody taught it to you, and I would very much like to know who, so that I can find them.”

“It was my mother,” said Aurelia, before she could stop herself. “Obviously. You heard her. Second place is just the first of the losers.”

“I heard her.”

“She says it every time. Every exam. Every competition. Every recital. Every time I came home with a number.” She was talking too fast. She couldn’t stop. “When I was eleven I came second in a piano competition in Vienna. Second, out of a hundred and forty. My mother didn’t speak to me for nine days. Not one word. Not at breakfast, not at dinner, not when I said goodnight. Nine days. And on the tenth day, she came into my room in the morning and opened the curtains and said, Second place is just the first of the losers. I hope you’ve learned that, and went downstairs, and that was it, that was all, it was over.”

She stopped.

She had never told anyone that. Not Serafina. Not anyone.

She had just told it to the most dangerous man in the city, across a chess board, in a red dress, because he had laid down his king.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

He put the king back on the board. Upright. In the middle of the board, on its own, where no king would ever stand in a real game.

“When I was fifteen,” he said, “my father was arrested. He was a deputy governor. He was arrested for corruption, which he hadn’t done, by men who had. He was taken away from our house at six in the morning in his pyjamas. My mother and I stood in the hall and watched. He died in custody four months later, before the trial. They said it was his heart.” His voice was perfectly level. “I don’t talk about it. I’m telling you so that you know that I understand what it is to have somebody take something from you and tell you it was your own fault.”

She couldn’t speak.

“The rest is long,” said Chen Si. “Another night. Tonight is yours.” He looked at her. “I just didn’t want you to think I was saying any of this from somewhere safe.”

He leaned forward across the board.

“You don’t have to win anything for me to see you,” he said. “Not a game. Not a meeting. I saw you on that balcony before you’d done a single thing except stand there shaking. You don’t have to earn it.” He paused. “You can lose a game of chess to me on purpose, Aurelia, and I will still see you. I’ll just be very annoyed that you made me lay my king down when I was three moves from mate.”

She laughed. It came out wet and broken.

“You weren’t three moves from mate.”

“Four,” said Chen Si. “I was being generous.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She cried, then.

Not much. Not for long. She hadn’t cried since she was eleven, and she was out of practice. She sat in the chair on the other side of his jade chess board, on the thirty-ninth floor, in a red dress, and put her face in her hands, and cried silently for about two minutes, with her shoulders shaking.

He didn’t touch her. He didn’t come round the board. He didn’t give her a handkerchief.

He sat on his side, with the king standing alone in the middle of the board between them, and waited, and let her, the way he had let her stand at the balustrade on her father’s balcony.

When she was finished, she wiped her face with the backs of her hands, which ruined her eye make-up entirely, and looked at him.

Then he came round the board.

He crouched in front of her chair and took her face in both his hands and cleaned the black from under her eyes with his thumbs, slowly, one side and then the other, as if it were the only job in the city that mattered. His hands were not quite steady either. He was close enough that she could feel his breath, and he looked at her mouth, and then back at her eyes, and did not move away.

“I look terrible,” she said.

“You look,” said Chen Si, “like a woman who has just lost a game of chess.” His thumbs were still on her cheekbones. “And like the only thing I want to look at. Both.”

She laughed again. Properly.

“Play me again,” she said.

“Properly?”

“Properly. No losing on purpose.” She started setting the pieces back up. Her hands weren’t quite steady. “And if I lose, I’ll lose, and you won’t say anything, and I won’t—I won’t disappear.”

He watched her set up the board.

“And if you win?” he said.

She put the last pawn on its square and looked up at him with her ruined make-up and her chin up.

“Then you’ll owe me something,” she said. “I’ll decide what later.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She lost.

Properly, this time. After two hours. He beat her with a quiet, patient endgame that she didn’t see coming until four moves out, and when she saw it, she sat back and looked at the board and said a word in Italian that would have made her grandmother faint.

He waited.

She looked at the board. She looked at her own king, trapped, with nowhere to go.

She waited to feel it. The thing. The cold, the falling, the nine days of silence.

It didn’t come.

What came instead was something she had not felt since she was very small, before Milan, before runways, before rankings: a kind of fierce, furious, delighted interest. In the endgame. In how he’d done it. In how she would beat it next time.

She reached out, and laid her own king down on its side.

“Again,” said Aurelia.

Chen Si looked at her across the board.

Then he smiled. Not in his eyes, this time. With his whole face. It changed him completely. It made him look his age, which she realised was only twenty-four, and very tired, and very, very glad.
