“Tomorrow,” he said. “It’s two in the morning. You’re going to fall asleep on my rook, and I’m not going to be the one who explains to Qian why there’s a woman in a red dress asleep on my chess board.”

She stood up. She picked up her coat.

At the door of his office, she stopped and looked back at him, sitting behind the jade board in the lamplight, with the city behind him in the window and his cold coffee beside him.

“You never asked me to win,” she said. “Not once. Not in anything.”

“Why not?”

He took his time.

“Because I’d rather you were happy,” he said simply, “than first.”

She went out before he could see her face.

In the lift, alone, going down thirty-nine floors, she leaned her head back against the mirrored wall and closed her eyes and thought: I’m going to marry that man.

And then, because she was Aurelia Song, and had never in her life wanted anything without at once beginning to plan how to get it:

And I am going to write the contract myself.

chapters.title: Dinner on the Forty-Fourth Floor
chapters.desc: He cooks. He tells her what happened to his parents, all of it. Then she gives him an order, and finds out how slowly a man can obey one.
chapters.epigraph: “Kneel.” He looked at her for a long moment. Then he did, without hurrying, as if he had been waiting for someone to ask.
chapters.content:
He lived on the forty-fourth floor of a tower on the harbour, and he cooked.

She had not expected that. She had expected a chef. Staff. A man in a white jacket silently bringing plates. Instead, on the last Saturday of January, he opened the door of the penthouse himself, in a dark blue jumper with the sleeves pushed up and a tea towel over his shoulder, and said, “You’re early. The fish isn’t ready,” and went back to the kitchen.

She stood in the doorway in a black dress and her mother’s red lipstick and a coat she had chosen with great care, and looked at the room.

It was enormous and almost empty. Glass on three sides, the whole harbour spread out below it in the dark, the lights of the city going all the way to the hills. Pale wooden floors. One long sofa. One long table. Books, hundreds of them, in shelves along the one wall that wasn’t glass. The chess set from his office, the jade one, on a low table by the window. No art. No photographs. No sign at all that anyone had ever lived anywhere else.

She took off her coat and went to find the kitchen.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was steaming a fish. A whole grouper, on a plate, in a bamboo steamer over a wok, with ginger and spring onion. He was cutting more spring onion very fine, with a cleaver, very fast, the way she had seen cooks do it in the old town and never seen anyone do it in a penthouse.

She leaned on the doorframe and watched.

“Who taught you?”

“My mother.” He didn’t look up. “She thought a boy should be able to cook for himself. My father thought it was ridiculous. They argued about it for years.” He swept the onion into a bowl. “She won.”

He heated oil in a small pan until it smoked. He poured it over the fish, over the onion and the ginger, and it hissed and spat, and the whole kitchen filled with the smell of it, and she was so hungry she felt dizzy.

“Sit,” he said. “Please.”

She sat.

✦ ✦ ✦

They ate at the end of the long table, by the glass, with the harbour below them. The fish. Greens with garlic. Rice. A soup that had been cooking all afternoon, clear and dark, with dried scallops and pork. A bottle of white wine from Friuli that he had clearly chosen because it was from the north of Italy, and that he opened, and poured, and did not drink.

She noticed.

“You still don’t drink things other people give you.”

“Nobody gave me this. I bought it.” He looked at his glass. “I don’t drink much. I don’t like not knowing exactly what I’m doing.”

“You drank my beer.”

“I took your beer,” said Chen Si. “That’s different.”

He picked up his glass and drank.

She watched him do it, and felt it all the way down her spine, and looked at her fish very hard.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her after dinner. On the long sofa, by the window, with the lights off so they could see the harbour, and the bottle of Friuli on the floor between them.

He had said he would. On the night of the chess game, The rest is long. Another night. She had not asked since. She had waited, for six weeks, which for Aurelia Song was a very long time.

He told her all of it.

His father, Chen Mingyuan, deputy governor of the province. A good man, Chen Si said, not a saint, but good; a man who had refused, very publicly, to approve a land deal on the east side that would have made three other men very rich. One of the three was a man called Fu Jianguo. Fu was a councillor then. He was a vice-minister now.

Six months after the land deal, Chen Mingyuan was arrested for taking bribes he had never taken. The evidence was perfect. Fu had made sure of that.

“They came at six in the morning,” said Chen Si, looking at the harbour. “I told you that. My father went down the stairs in his pyjamas. He looked back at me from the door. He said, Look after your mother. I’ll be home soon.” He was quiet. “He wasn’t. He died in a cell four months later. Before the trial. They said it was his heart. It wasn’t his heart.”

Aurelia didn’t move.

“My mother died the next winter,” said Chen Si. “They said that was her heart too. That one was true. It just broke. She stopped eating. She stopped sleeping. She sat in his chair in the study every night and looked at the door.” His voice didn’t change at all. “I was sixteen. Everything was frozen. The house, the accounts, everything. Fu’s people made sure. So I unfroze some of it. One account. I was very good with computers and very angry. I moved my mother’s money out of a frozen account and into one they couldn’t see, so that she could keep the flat, and the heating, and the doctor who came to the house on Tuesdays.” A very small smile. “It was clever. It was illegal. They caught me in eleven days.” The smile went. “She died in December. I was inside by then. Nobody was with her. They didn’t let me out for the funeral. A guard told me at breakfast, between the rice and the tea, and then asked me to pass the salt.”

“Block C,” said Aurelia.

He turned his head and looked at her.

“Zhendong told you?”

“Zhendong has said four words to me,” said Aurelia. “One of them was hm.” She looked at him. “You told me. Just now. Without saying it. You said they caught me, and your hand went to your arm.”

He looked down. His right hand was on his left forearm, over the sleeve of the dark blue jumper. He hadn’t known it was there.

He took it away.

“Block C,” he said. “Juvenile detention. That’s where I met him. I didn’t stay long. There was a riot, the first winter, and we left. Through the drains.” He stopped there. “That’s the rest of the story. It’s his as much as mine. One day, if you want, I’ll tell you about the drains. Not tonight.”

“Not tonight,” agreed Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat on the sofa in the dark.

She had her shoes off. Her feet were tucked up under her on the long sofa. He was at the other end, with his arm along the back of it, looking at the harbour, and there was a metre and a half of pale grey sofa between them, and she had never been so aware of a metre and a half of anything in her life.

“Fu Jianguo,” she said.

“Yes.”

“He’s a vice-minister now. He was at my father’s party. The night of the balcony. You were there as his guest.” She looked at him. “You were there because of him.”

“Yes.”

“What are you going to do to him?”

Chen Si looked at the harbour.

“I’ve been building something for eight years,” he said. “Since I got out of Block C. Everything. The routes, the companies, the judges, the men on the thirty-ninth floor. All of it. It has one purpose.” He turned his head. “One day, I am going to take everything Fu Jianguo has. His position. His money. His name. His sons’ names. Everything. Legally, if I can. The way he did to my father. I am going to stand in his hall at six in the morning and watch them take him down the stairs.”

She looked at his face in the light from the harbour.

It was perfectly calm. That was the most frightening thing about it.

“And then?” she said.

He was quiet.

“I don’t know,” said Chen Si. “I’ve never thought about then.” He looked at her. “There wasn’t anything after it. There was only it.”

She held his gaze.

“There is now,” said Aurelia Song.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t know who moved first. Later, they would argue about it, for years, at dinner parties, in front of people who were afraid of both of them. She said he did. He said she did. Zhao Zhendong, asked to adjudicate, at a New Year dinner three years later, said, “Hm,” and refused to elaborate.

What she knew was that one moment there was a metre and a half of pale grey sofa between them, and the next there wasn’t, and his hand was in her hair and her hands were in the front of his jumper and he was kissing her.

Not the way she had imagined. She had imagined it a great many times, since a counter at three in the morning and his thumb on her cheekbone and him walking out. She had imagined him the way he played chess: patient, controlled, three moves ahead.

He wasn’t.

He kissed her like a man who had been holding his breath for three months. Hard, and deep, and not at all careful, his hand cradling the back of her head, his mouth opening hers, and she made a sound she had never made in her life and pulled him closer by his jumper and felt him make one too, low in his chest, against her mouth.

She pulled back first. An inch. Breathing hard.

“You walked out,” she said. “At the counter. In November. You looked at my mouth for ten seconds and walked out.”

“Eleven seconds,” said Chen Si, against her mouth. His voice had gone low and rough. “I wanted you to think about it every time you saw me.”

He kissed the corner of her mouth. Then the line of her jaw. Slowly, like a man who knew exactly how well it had worked, and was not sorry at all.

She took his face in both her hands and held it, an inch from hers, and looked at him in the light from the harbour. At his dark eyes, which had gone black. At his mouth.

And something rose up in her, something cold and bright and furious and absolutely delighted, the same thing that had sat down in his chair on the thirty-ninth floor.

“No,” she said.

He went still.

“You made me wait three months,” said Aurelia. “You made me sit at that counter and think about it. You laid down your king. You sat in a mahjong parlour and watched me for three hours.” She let go of his face. She sat back on the sofa, away from him. Just a little. Just enough. “So now you can wait for me.”

He looked at her.

She saw him understand. She saw it go all the way down: something in his face shifting, not offended, not angry. Interested. Very, very interested.

“What do you want?” said Chen Si quietly.

She stood up.

She stood in front of him, barefoot, on his pale wooden floor, in her black dress, with the whole harbour behind her in the glass. He sat on the sofa and looked up at her.

“Kneel,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

The room was very quiet.

She had never said it to anyone. She had never thought she would. It had come out of her the way the counter-offer had, the way she had sat in his chair: from somewhere very deep and very sure, that she had never been allowed to use.

She waited for him to laugh. Or to stand up. Or to look at her the way the boys at school had looked at her when she won, as if they were deciding how to make her pay for it.

He didn’t.

He looked at her, with that black, absorbed, intensely interested expression.

Then he got up off the sofa, and knelt.

He did it slowly. Without hurrying. Without any embarrassment at all, as if it were the most natural thing in the world, as if he had been waiting for a very long time for someone to ask. He knelt on his own floor at her bare feet, the most dangerous man in the city, and looked up at her, and waited.

She stopped breathing.

“Take off your watch,” she said. Her voice wasn’t quite steady. “I don’t want you counting.”

He took off his watch. Slowly. He held it out to her. She took it. It was warm from his wrist, and heavy, and she put it on the window ledge behind her without looking.

“What else?” said Chen Si.

His voice had changed. It was low and rough and very, very calm, and it went straight through her.

“Your jumper,” she said.

He took it off. He did it slowly, too, on purpose, she could see it was on purpose, pulling it over his head and dropping it on the floor beside him, and then kneeling there, bare to the waist, in the light from the harbour, waiting.

She looked at him.

He was lean and pale and his shoulders were broader than the suits made them look, and along the inside of his left forearm, from the wrist almost to the elbow, there was a long, pale, shining burn scar, the skin puckered and tight. Across the palm of the same hand, a single thin white line.

She went down on her knees in front of him.

She didn’t decide to. Her legs did it. She knelt on the floor facing him, so close their knees were touching, and took his left arm, and turned it over, and put her fingertips on the scar at his wrist, and he flinched, very slightly, the first time she had ever seen him flinch at anything.

“Block C,” she said.

“Yes.”

“Does it hurt?”

“Not any more.” His eyes were on her face. “There was a fire, in the riot. The mattresses. There was a grate in the floor and it was too hot to touch, and I didn’t have time to wait for it to cool.” A pause. “The palm is something else. That one I did on purpose. Zhendong has the same one.”

She traced it. All the way up. Slowly. Her fingertips on the puckered, shining skin of it, from his wrist to the inside of his elbow, and then back down, to the thin white line across his palm. Then she lifted his hand and kissed the line. He knelt absolutely still and let her, with his hands on his thighs, and she could see his chest rising and falling, faster and faster, and his jaw tight, and she understood that he was not allowed to move until she said so, and that he knew it, and that it was costing him something enormous not to.

She had never in her life felt anything like it.

He didn’t move his hands. He moved his head, a few centimetres, so that his mouth was against her wrist where she held his arm, and stayed there, on the very edge of what she had allowed him.

“Let me,” he said against her pulse, in that low, mild, dangerous voice. “Please. You can say no.” He lifted his eyes to hers. “But tell me first if you want it too.”

“Chen Si,” she said.

“Yes.”

“You can touch me now.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was slow.

That was the thing she would never be able to explain, afterwards, to anyone, not even Elowen, years later, at three in the morning, drunk on the floor of a flower shop. He had been told he could touch her, and he did, and he was so slow about it that she thought she would die.

He put one hand on her face, very lightly. Then the other. He kissed her gently, which was worse than hard. He found the zip at the back of her black dress and took it down so slowly, centimetre by centimetre, that she could feel every tooth of it come apart, and his knuckles brushing down her spine the whole way, and by the time it reached the bottom she was shaking.

“You’re punishing me,” she said.

“No.” He pushed the dress off her shoulders, and kissed where it had been. “You told me to kneel. You told me to wait. You told me to take off my watch so I wouldn’t count.” His mouth moved along her collarbone. “So I’m not counting. I’m not in any hurry. I have no idea what time it is.” He lifted his head and looked at her, and his eyes were black and amused and absolutely merciless. “You set the terms, Aurelia. I’m just following them. Very carefully.”

She made a sound that was half a laugh and half something she had never heard herself make.

“I hate you,” she said.

“I know,” said Chen Si, and laid her back on his pale wooden floor, in the light from the harbour, and took his time.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took so much time that at some point she forgot that she had been the one giving orders.

He learned her. That was the only word for it. The way he had learned the city, every route, every bribe, every judge: patiently, thoroughly, missing nothing. He found every place on her that made her breath stop and went back to it, and back again, and watched her face the whole time, with that black absorbed attention, as if she were the only puzzle in the city worth solving. When she reached for him, he caught her wrists, very gently, and held them down on the floor above her head with one hand, and looked at her, and said, “Tell me if you want me to let go.”

She didn’t want him to let go.

She found that out lying on his floor with her wrists in his hand and the whole harbour glittering behind him, and it was the most frightening thing she had discovered about herself in twenty-two years: that she, Aurelia Song, who sat in other people’s chairs and never lost, wanted, very badly, for this one man to hold her wrists down and not let go.

“Don’t,” she said. “Don’t let go.”

Something went through his whole body.

“Say it again,” said Chen Si.

“Don’t let go.”

He didn’t.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, much later, on the long grey sofa, under a blanket he had found somewhere, with the harbour gone dark except for the lights of one ship moving very slowly toward the sea, she lay on his chest and listened to his heart.

“I thought,” she said, “I was in charge.”

“You were. And then you told me you didn’t want to be, for a while.” His hand was moving slowly up and down her bare back. “You can tell me to kneel. You can tell me not to let go. Both, in the same night.” His voice went very low. “I like both. Very much.”

She lifted her head and looked at him.

“Nobody,” she said, “has ever let me be both.”

“I know,” said Chen Si. “I could tell.”

He pulled her back up by the nape of her neck and kissed her again, unhurried and thorough, as if the first time had only been an opening offer.

“You’re staying,” he said against her mouth. It was not a question. “I’ll make you breakfast. Then I’ll take you back to bed and you can give me orders again.”

She put her head back down on his chest, smiling. His heart was slow and steady under her ear.

On the window ledge, behind them, his watch lay where she had put it, face down, still ticking. Neither of them knew what time it was.

Neither of them cared.

chapters.title: A Proposal With Terms and Conditions
chapters.desc: Eleven pages, in red ink, on his own cream paper. Clause nine is about the bedroom. Clause ten is a single word. He reads every page, and signs every page, and then asks for an amendment.
chapters.epigraph: “Clause 9. In private, the Wife sets the terms, unless and until she says otherwise. Clause 10. The word is ‘Milan’.”
chapters.content:
She proposed on a Tuesday in March, at eleven in the morning, at the counter of her boutique, exactly where he had first tried to rent it.

She did not tell him in advance. She sent him a letter, on his own thick cream paper, which she had asked Qian for and Qian had given her without a single question, which told her a great deal about Qian. The letter said: A client would like to discuss a commercial arrangement concerning the gentleman on the 44th floor. It was signed with two initials.

He came at 10:59.

He came in alone, with a coffee, and stopped inside the door, and looked at her behind the counter in white—she had chosen white on purpose, and he looked at it, and she saw him understand something—and then at the counter in front of her, where there was a document.

Eleven pages. Stapled. In her handwriting. In red ink.

He put down his coffee.

“Aurelia,” he said.

“Read it,” said Aurelia. “All of it. Then we’ll talk.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He read it standing at the counter.

She had written it over four nights, on the floor of her flat, in silk pyjamas, with a pot of cold coffee and a pencil behind her ear and a feeling, the whole time, of falling from a very great height and not wanting to land. She had written and crossed out and rewritten. She had consulted, in a roundabout way, two lawyers and a priest. She had read eleven marriage contracts from the archives of three old Milanese families, including her mother’s parents’, which had a clause about the ownership of a racehorse.

It began like a contract.

AGREEMENT OF MARRIAGE between AURELIA SONG (“the Wife”) and CHEN SI (“the Husband”).

Whereas the Husband has, on numerous occasions, failed to ask the Wife to win anything; and whereas the Wife has found this intolerable and wishes it to continue indefinitely; the parties agree as follows.

He looked up at her at intolerable.

She looked back at him without expression.

He went on reading.

✦ ✦ ✦

1. The Wife retains her name, her boutique, her designs and every gram of gold she has ever cut. The Husband retains his companies, his routes, his brother and his chess set. What is acquired together is held together.

2. The Wife sits at the table. All tables. Including the ones the Husband would prefer she did not know about.

3. Neither party will lie to the other. About anything. If something cannot be told, it will be said: “I cannot tell you this yet,” and it will be told later.

4. The Husband will not, at any time, attempt to keep the Wife somewhere safe. If he does, the Wife will leave him, and take with her the Milan route, the furniture company, the man in the cardigan who runs the pawnshops, and approximately half of the Husband’s people, who like her better.

He stopped at four.

He read it again.

Then he put his hand flat on the counter, very carefully, and looked down at it, and she saw his shoulders move, once, in what she realised after a moment was a laugh he was trying very hard not to let out.

“Half,” he said.

“I counted.” She folded her arms. “The man with the sunflower seeds hates me. The man with the tinted glasses is afraid of me. Everyone else likes me better. Qian likes me better.”

“Qian,” said Chen Si, “has liked you better since the day you sat in my chair.” He turned the page. “He told me so. He said, Boss, if you don’t marry that woman, I’m going to work for her.”

She did not let her face change.

It was very difficult.

✦ ✦ ✦

5. On the subject of Fu Jianguo, the Wife acknowledges the Husband’s prior claim and will not interfere. But when it is done, she will be standing in the hall beside him at six in the morning. And then they will go and have breakfast.

He read that one twice.

He didn’t say anything about it. He just stood at the counter, very still, looking at the page, and then he lifted his hand and pressed two fingers briefly against his eyes, and went on.

6. The Husband will attend the opening of every collection the Wife makes, in the front row, and will not look at his phone.

7. The Wife will attend the Husband’s brother’s birthday every year and eat whatever he cooks, including fish with heads on.

8. Neither party will ever, under any circumstances, say “second place is just the first of the losers.”

He looked up at her.

She looked back at him.

“Agreed,” he said, before he had even turned the page.

✦ ✦ ✦

Page nine.

9. In private, the Wife sets the terms. She may tell the Husband to kneel, to wait, to take off his watch, to not move, to move, to beg, or anything else she likes, and he will do it, slowly, exactly as he did on the forty-fourth floor. Unless and until she says otherwise. When she says otherwise, he sets the terms, completely, until she says otherwise again. Both parties acknowledge that the Wife will say otherwise frequently and that this is not a contradiction.

He read it.

He read it again.

He did not look up. When he did, his face was perfectly calm, and his eyes were black, and his voice, when it came, was very, very low.

“Frequently,” he said.

“I’ve been considering the evidence,” said Aurelia. Her own voice was not quite as steady as she would have liked. “Six weeks of it. It seemed best to be honest. Clause three.”

“Clause three,” he agreed. He turned the page.

10. The word is “Milan.” If either party says it, at any time, in any room, in any circumstances, everything stops. Immediately. No questions. No sulking. No consequences. Then the parties will lie down together and the one who said it will be held for as long as they want to be held.

The word is “Milan” because it is the city where the Wife learned to be afraid. She would like it to mean something else.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

Outside, on Harbour Road, a tram went past, and the man on the corner was selling chestnuts, and somewhere a car horn sounded, and inside the shop, at the counter, under the one light, the most dangerous man in the city stood and looked at page ten of a marriage contract and did not turn it.

“Aurelia,” he said finally.

“Yes.”

“Have you ever had one before? A word?”

“No.” She lifted her chin. “I’ve never needed one. I’ve never—with anyone else, I was always—” She stopped. She made herself say it, because of clause three. “With anyone else, I was always the one who won. You don’t need a word if you always win.” She looked at him. “With you, I don’t want to. Not always. And that frightens me. So I wanted a word.”

He looked at her across the counter.

“It’s a very good word,” he said.

“I know. I chose it very carefully.”

“I’ll keep it,” said Chen Si. “I’ll keep it safer than anything I own.”

He turned to the last page.

11. This agreement will be renewed after ten years, on the anniversary of its signing, at which point the Wife reserves the right to rewrite every clause.

Signed:

A. Song.

And underneath that, a space.

✦ ✦ ✦

He took a pen out of his inside pocket. A heavy black fountain pen. He uncapped it.

Then he stopped.

“I have one amendment,” he said.

She raised her eyebrows. “One.”

“One.” He turned back to page one. To the top. AGREEMENT OF MARRIAGE between AURELIA SONG (“the Wife”) and CHEN SI (“the Husband”). And he wrote, very small, in the margin, in his precise black hand, and turned it round so she could see.

The Husband would like it noted that he has been in love with the Wife since a balcony in October, when she was shaking in a gold dress and doing sums in her head. He would like it noted that he walked down Harbour Road for six weeks before that to look at a necklace. He would like it noted that he has never in his life been asked to marry anyone, and that he did not know, until this morning, that he had been waiting to be.

She read it twice.

“That isn’t an amendment,” said Aurelia. Her voice had gone very strange. “That isn’t a clause. That doesn’t do anything.”

“No,” agreed Chen Si. “It’s just true.”

He signed every page.

Eleven pages. Every one. In the bottom right-hand corner, in black, beside her red. It took him a long time. He did it slowly, without hurrying, the way he did everything that mattered, and she stood on the other side of the counter and watched him, and somewhere around page six she realised she had stopped breathing, and made herself start again.

When he had signed the last page, he capped the pen, and put it back in his pocket, and slid the contract back across the counter to her.

“Is that a yes?” said Aurelia.

He looked at her.

“Aurelia Song,” he said. “I have read clause nine four times. Of course it’s a yes.”

She laughed. The bark. The one that came out before she could stop it. And then she was laughing properly, helplessly, with her hand over her mouth, at her own counter, in white, and he came round the end of the counter, finally, to her side, the first time he had ever come to her side of it, and took her face in his hands.

“Clause nine,” he said, very low, an inch from her mouth. “Does it start now?”

“It starts,” said Aurelia, “when I close the shop.”

She reached past him and turned the sign on the door to CLOSED.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took him into the workshop.

Enzo was not there. She had given him the day off. She had told him she would need the bench, and he had looked at her over his magnifying glasses with his old brown face perfectly still and said, Cara, I don’t want to know, and gone home.

The workshop was small and bright and smelled of metal and polish and the gas of the torch. There were two benches, Enzo’s and hers, each with its leather skin slung underneath to catch the gold dust. There were tools on every wall. Files and pliers and saws, gravers and burnishers, mandrels for sizing rings, a draw-plate, a rolling mill. A safe. And on her bench, on a square of black velvet, laid out in a long gleaming line, the broken necklace from the window.

He saw it. He stopped.

“You took it out of the window,” he said.

“This morning.” She picked it up. It was heavy. Yellow gold, twisted apart and mended with tiny bright seams of white. “It isn’t for sale any more.”

“Why not?”

She turned and looked at him.

“Take off your coat,” said Aurelia. “And your jacket. And your tie.”

He looked at her, in the bright little workshop, with that black, absorbed attention.

Then he took off his coat. Slowly. And folded it over Enzo’s stool. Then his jacket. Then his tie, which he pulled loose and drew out from under his collar very, very slowly, watching her the whole time, and held out to her.

She took it.

She looked at it. Grey silk. Warm from his neck.

“Sit down,” she said. “On my stool.”

He sat.

She came and stood in front of him. Close. Between his knees. And she put the broken necklace around his neck, over his white shirt, and fastened it at the back, her fingers on the nape of his neck, and he closed his eyes.

“That’s why,” she said. “It isn’t for sale. It’s yours.”

He didn’t open his eyes.

“It’s heavy,” he said.

“I know. It’s nearly four hundred grams.” She ran her finger along the links, along the bright mended seams. “Every time you feel it, I want you to know that I know about breaking. And that I don’t want the break taken out. Not mine. Not yours.”

He opened his eyes.

She held up his grey silk tie, between them.

“Hands,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

He gave her his hands.

He held them out, wrists together, without a word, and she wound his own tie around them, twice, and knotted it, not tight. Not tight at all. Loose enough that he could have pulled free in a second. They both knew it. That was the point.

“If you pull free,” she said, “I stop.”

“I won’t pull free.”

“I know.” She lifted his bound hands and put them behind his head, so that his elbows were up and his chest was open, in his white shirt, with four hundred grams of her gold lying heavy on it. “Keep them there.”

He kept them there.

She undid his shirt. One button at a time. She didn’t hurry either. She had learned that from him, on the forty-fourth floor, and she used it now, with interest, kissing the skin under each button as it came undone, until his breathing had gone rough and loud in the bright quiet workshop and the gold was rising and falling on his bare chest with it.

When she had his shirt open, she took his bound wrists and kissed the burn scar on his left forearm, all the way up from the knot of grey silk to the inside of his elbow, the way she had followed it with her fingers on his floor.

He made a sound she had never heard. His hands, behind his head, tightened in the silk. They didn’t move.

“You’re very good at doing what you’re told,” she said, against his side.

“Only by you,” said Chen Si. His voice had gone to gravel. “Nobody else has ever been worth it.” His bound hands stayed where she had put them. He tipped his head back against them and looked at her. “Counter-offer. You keep every term. I keep my hands exactly here. And in return you let me kiss you once. Just once. Wherever you choose.” A breath. “Do you want that? Say no and I’ll keep still.”

She thought about it for long enough to make him suffer. Then she leaned in and put her mouth on his, briefly, and drew back before he could follow.

“Accepted,” she said. “Once.”

She lifted her head and looked at him: sitting on her stool, in her workshop, with his shirt open and his hands tied with his own tie behind his head and her necklace on his chest, the most dangerous man in the city, looking at her as if she were the only thing in it.

And then, because clause nine allowed for it, and because she wanted to, and because she had never in her life been able to say it to anyone:

“Chen Si,” she said. “Otherwise.”

He went very still.

Then he moved. One pull, and the silk tie came off his wrists as if it had never been knotted at all, and he stood up and caught her by the waist and turned her and set her up on the edge of her own bench, on Enzo’s polishing cloths, among the files and the pliers and the little pots of borax, and stood between her knees, and took her face in his hands.

“Otherwise,” he said, very low, an inch from her mouth. “You’re sure.”

“Clause three. I’m sure.”

He smiled. That black, merciless, absolutely delighted smile from the forty-fourth floor.

“Then hold on to the bench,” said Chen Si, “and don’t let go until I tell you.”

She held on to the bench.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did not let her let go for what felt like hours.

She would remember the bench, hard under her hands, and the cold metal of a file somewhere against her hip, and his voice, low, steady, merciless, telling her exactly what he was going to do before he did it, and then doing it, slowly, until she was shaking. She would remember him saying not yet against her throat, and not yet against her shoulder, and not yet against the inside of her wrist where her pulse was going wild, every time she thought she couldn’t bear it any more, until not yet was the most unbearable thing she had ever heard and she would have done anything at all to hear him say now.

She would remember that she begged. Aurelia Song, who had never begged for anything in her life, sitting on her own workbench among her own tools, with his hands on her and his mouth on her and four hundred grams of her own gold swinging against her skin every time he moved, begged, in Italian and then in Chinese and then in no language at all.

And she would remember that when he finally said it—now, Aurelia, now—in that low rough voice against her ear, she let go of the bench and held on to him instead, and that it was like the moment on the balcony in October when she had looked down at the whole city glittering below her in the dark and thought, for one terrifying second, that she might fall.

She fell.

He caught her.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, they sat on the floor of the workshop with their backs against her bench, among the dropped tools, in his coat, which he had put around both of them.

The necklace was still around his neck. He hadn’t taken it off. He kept touching it, his fingers running along the mended links.

“I’m going to have to explain this to Enzo,” said Aurelia.

“Explain what?”

She looked at her bench. At the scattered files and the knocked-over borax and the polishing cloths on the floor and the faint but unmistakable mark of a man’s hand, on the leather skin underneath, where he had braced himself.

“Everything,” she said.

He laughed. Properly. With his head back against her bench.

She leaned against his shoulder.

The contract was still on the counter in the shop, she thought. Eleven pages. Red ink and black. Signed.

“I didn’t say Milan,” she said.

“I nearly did. Once. At the very end.” She was quiet. “Not because I wanted you to stop. Because I didn’t think I could bear it if you didn’t.”

His hand stopped on the necklace.

He turned his head and looked at her.

“I know,” he said. “I felt it. That’s why I said now.”

She looked at him.

Then she put her face in his neck, in the coat, with the gold between them, and stayed there, and he held her, for as long as she wanted to be held, which was clause ten, though nobody had said the word.

chapters.title: The Song Parents Are Not Told
chapters.desc: A Thursday in May. A palazzo on the Naviglio Grande. Eleven guests, a dress she designed in a week, and a mother in a villa forty minutes away who finds out from a magazine.
chapters.epigraph: “Shouldn’t we tell your parents?” “We will. They read Italian Vogue.”
chapters.content:
She married him in Milan on Thursday the sixteenth of May, at four in the afternoon, and did not tell her parents.

It was not an accident. It was not a whim. She had decided it on the night of the proposal, on the floor of the workshop in his coat, and she had told him so, and he had said, “Are you sure?” and she had said, “Clause three. Yes,” and he had not asked again.

“They didn’t tell me they were closing my shop,” she said. “They told two hundred people. Between the lobster and the cake.” She was lying on his chest, on the long grey sofa, at the time, with the harbour below them. “I want them to find out the way I did. In public. From someone else.”

He had been quiet for a while.

“That’s cruel,” he said finally.

“Yes.”

“I approve,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

She chose Milan because it was where she had learned to be afraid.

She did not say that to anyone except him. To everyone else, she said it was because the light was better, and because the lawyers there were the only ones she trusted to register a marriage between an Italian citizen with a Chinese surname and a man with a very complicated history quickly and quietly, and because the city was full of the best goldsmiths in the world and she wanted one of them at her wedding.

All of that was true.

But the night before, in a hotel suite overlooking the canal, she lay awake in the dark beside him and told him the rest.

“My mother used to take me to the shows,” she said. “From four. I sat in the front row in a little dress she chose, and I wasn’t allowed to move. Not for the whole show. Two hours. If I moved, she knew. She always knew. She would put her hand on the back of my neck, here,” she touched it, “and squeeze. Just a little. Just so I knew.” She was quiet. “I didn’t move at a fashion show from four years old until I was fifteen. And then we came to your city, and I thought, I will never sit still again.”

He didn’t say anything. He put his hand on the back of her neck, where she had touched it, very lightly, and left it there. Warm. Not squeezing. Just there.

She lay in the dark and felt it, and her shoulders came down for the first time in days.

“I want it to be the city where I got married,” she said. “To you. That’s all. I want it to mean that instead.”

“It will,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

The palazzo was on the Naviglio Grande, the long canal in the south of the city, where the old washhouses were and the antique dealers set up their stalls on the last Sunday of the month. It belonged to a family of goldsmiths who had been making jewellery in Milan since 1832 and who had known her grandmother. It had a courtyard full of wisteria, in full purple flower, so heavy it hung down in ropes from the balconies, and a fountain, and a long room on the first floor with windows open onto the canal and the smell of the water and the bells of San Cristoforo across the bridge.

There were eleven guests.

Enzo, who had flown with her, and who wore a suit for the first time in nine years and cried from the moment he saw her.

Qian Yu, who had never left Asia before and had spent the whole flight reading a guide to Milan and taking notes.

The small neat man in the cardigan, who ran the pawnshops, whose name it turned out was Mr. Lu, and who had asked to come, and brought his wife, a tiny smiling woman who spoke no Italian and no English and held Aurelia’s hands in both of hers and said nothing at all.

The old goldsmith who owned the palazzo, who was ninety-one, and his son, and his grandson.

Dottor Rossi from the customs office, who had brought flowers, and who winked at her.

A registrar from the commune, in a sash.

Zhao Zhendong.

And at the very back of the long room, by the window, in a leather jacket and black jeans and boots with oil on them, arriving at 3:58 with her hair still wet from the rain and a motorcycle helmet under her arm, Serafina Song.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia saw her sister in the doorway and stopped walking.

She had sent the invitation by post, to a garage in the industrial district of the city where she knew Serafina sometimes slept. She had not known if it would arrive. She had not known if Serafina would open it. They had not spoken properly in two years, since the night Serafina had walked out of her own engagement dinner and Aurelia had stood at the top of the stairs and watched her go and said nothing, because their mother was standing at the bottom.

Serafina was twenty-one. She was taller than Aurelia, and thinner, and had cut her own hair short with what looked like kitchen scissors. She had a burn scar on the back of one hand. She stood in the doorway of the long room in Milan with rainwater dripping off her leather jacket onto the old goldsmith’s marble floor and looked at her sister.

At the dress.

Aurelia had designed it in a week. Ivory silk, very plain, cut close to the body, with long sleeves and a high neck and no lace and no beads and nothing at all to look at, until she turned round. The back was open from the nape of her neck to the base of her spine. And down the centre of it, from shoulder blade to shoulder blade, fastened at the nape and falling in a long gleaming line to the small of her back, there was a single chain of yellow gold. Twisted apart in the middle, and mended, with a seam of white.

Serafina looked at it.

“You look,” she said finally, in Italian, in a voice that was not entirely steady, “like a gilded bird.”

It was what she had always called her. Since they were small. Gilded bird. It had never been a compliment.

Aurelia lifted her chin.

“Yes,” she said. “But I let myself out of the cage. Look.” She turned, so that Serafina could see the back. The broken chain. “I did it myself.”

Serafina looked.

Then she put her helmet down on the old goldsmith’s marble floor, and crossed the room in three long strides in her oily boots, and put her arms round her sister, and held on.

Over Serafina’s shoulder, Aurelia saw Chen Si at the far end of the room, by the registrar, in a dark grey suit, watching. He didn’t move. He didn’t come over. He just watched, with that still, absorbed attention, as if he were committing it to memory.

Beside him, Zhao Zhendong, who was best man, and who had flown eleven hours and had not said one word to anyone since landing except, to Dottor Rossi at the door, “No,” looked at the two sisters holding on to each other in the middle of the room, and then looked away out of the window, at the canal.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were married at four.

The registrar read the articles of the civil code aloud, in Italian, and then in English for the benefit of Qian, who was nodding along very seriously and taking notes. Article 143: With marriage, husband and wife acquire the same rights and assume the same duties. Chen Si listened to it with great attention. At the same rights, he glanced sideways at her, very briefly, and she knew he was thinking about clause nine, and she had to look at the floor.

Then the registrar asked if they wished to say anything.

She had not planned to. She had written eleven pages. She thought that was enough.

But Chen Si said, “Yes,” in his mild voice, and turned to her, in the long room full of wisteria light, with the bells of San Cristoforo starting across the canal, and said, in careful, slightly accented Italian that she had not known he spoke:

“Ti ho vista per la prima volta su un balcone. Tremavi, e facevi i conti. Da allora non ho più voluto guardare nient’altro.”

I saw you for the first time on a balcony. You were shaking, and doing sums. Since then I haven’t wanted to look at anything else.

The old goldsmith, who was ninety-one, said “Ah,” under his breath, and put his hand on his heart.

Enzo sobbed out loud.

Aurelia stood in her ivory dress with the broken chain down her spine and looked at him. At the man who had walked down Harbour Road for six weeks to look at a necklace. Who had laid down his king. Who had knelt on his own floor because she told him to.

“When did you learn Italian?” she said, in Chinese, under her breath.

“Since March,” said Chen Si, also in Chinese. “Every night. On the phone, with Enzo. He’s a very harsh teacher.”

She laughed. She was crying, she realised. She didn’t care.

She turned to the registrar.

“Sì,” she said. “Lo voglio. Yes. I do. Write it down.”

Chen Si did not wait for the registrar to tell him he could. He took her face in both hands, in front of eleven guests and a man in a sash, and kissed her, not the polite kiss of a wedding photograph but a long one, deep and unhurried, as if the room were empty and he had all afternoon. When he let her go, her lipstick was on his mouth and Enzo was sobbing again and the registrar had forgotten what came next.

“Mine,” said Chen Si, very low, in Chinese, for her alone. “Now write that down.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Six days later, in a villa on the shore of Lake Como, forty minutes north of the city, Vittoria Song sat on her terrace at breakfast with a pot of coffee and the June issue of Italian Vogue.

She turned the pages slowly. She always did. She read the society section last, the way some people saved the best part of a meal.

On page two hundred and eleven, under the heading MATRIMONI, there was a photograph.

A long room with windows open onto a canal. Wisteria. A woman in ivory silk, seen from behind, walking away from the camera, with her back bare and a single broken chain of gold running down her spine. Beside her, holding her hand, a slight dark man in grey, looking not at the camera, not at the room, but at her.

The designer Aurelia Song, 22, daughter of the property magnate Song Weiren and the former model Vittoria Conti, married the businessman Chen Si in a private ceremony at the Palazzo Ferraris on the Naviglio Grande on 16 May. The bride wore her own design. The couple will live in Asia, where Ms. Song’s label, AURELIA, will open a second boutique in the autumn. The bride’s parents were not present.

Vittoria Song looked at the photograph for a full minute.

Then she closed the magazine, very gently, and put it face down on the table, and poured herself another cup of coffee, and drank it, and her hand, holding the cup, did not shake at all.

It was only afterwards, when the maid came to clear the breakfast things, that anyone noticed the coffee cup.

There was a crack in it. Right down the side, from the rim to the base. A thin, perfect line.

Nobody knew how it had happened.

chapters.title: Blood Brothers at the Reception
chapters.desc: Zhao Zhendong gives a speech of nine words. Serafina gives a warning. And on the wedding night, in a suite above the canal, the bride finds a use for her veil.
chapters.epigraph: “He is my brother. You are his. So you are mine.” — the complete best man’s speech of Zhao Zhendong
chapters.content:
The reception was in the courtyard, under the wisteria, at a long table with a white cloth and candles in glass, and there were eleven guests and food for forty, because the old goldsmith’s son had married a woman from Puglia who believed that if there was not too much food, there was not enough.

Aurelia sat at the head of the table in her ivory dress, with the broken chain cold down her spine and her husband beside her.

Her husband.

She kept thinking it. She kept turning her head to look at him, as if he might have changed in the last hour. He hadn’t. He was sitting beside her in his dark grey suit, with a glass of Franciacorta in front of him that he had poured himself and was actually drinking, listening to the old goldsmith tell a very long story about her grandmother in 1961, and every so often, under the table, without looking at her, he put his hand on her knee and left it there for a moment, and took it away again.

Every time, she lost the thread of the story completely.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao Zhendong gave the best man’s speech.

Nobody had asked him to. Chen Si had told her, the week before, that his brother would not speak, that his brother did not make speeches, that his brother had once been asked to say a few words at the opening of a warehouse and had stood in front of two hundred people for forty seconds in total silence and then said, “Open,” and walked off.

So when Zhao stood up at the end of the meal, very large, in a black suit, and picked up his glass, the whole table went quiet. Qian put down his fork. Enzo stopped crying. Mr. Lu’s tiny wife looked up at him in terror.

Zhao looked down the table at Chen Si.

Then he looked at Aurelia.

He looked at her for four seconds. She had counted, the night in the old town. It was always four.

“He is my brother,” said Zhao Zhendong. “You’re his. So you’re mine.”

He drank.

He sat down.

There was a silence in the courtyard under the wisteria.

Then the old goldsmith, who was ninety-one, began to clap, slowly, with great dignity, and then everyone was clapping, and Enzo was crying again, and Aurelia turned to look at Chen Si and found that his face had gone very still and his hand, on the white tablecloth, had closed into a fist.

“That’s nine words,” she said, under her breath.

“I know,” said Chen Si. His voice was not steady. “That’s the most I’ve ever heard him say at once. In nine years.”

She looked down the table at Zhao. He was eating a piece of cake with his fork, very carefully, looking at nobody.

She picked up her glass and raised it to him.

He looked at it. He looked at her.

Then, very slightly, he raised his own.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina found her by the fountain, at nine, when the candles had burned down and the old goldsmith’s grandson had put music on and Qian was dancing, very badly and very happily, with Mr. Lu’s tiny wife.

She had a bottle of beer. She had taken off her leather jacket. Under it she was in a black vest, and her arms were thin and strong and scarred in small places, burns and cuts, the arms of someone who worked with engines.

“So,” she said. “Chen Si. You know what he is.”

“Better than anyone.”

Serafina drank from her bottle. She looked across the courtyard at the slight man in grey, who was standing by the wall with his brother, not dancing, watching Aurelia over the rim of a glass.

“There are men in the industrial district,” said Serafina, “who build cars for people who need to get away from things. Very fast. Very quietly. Some of those people are running away from him.” She looked at her sister. “I’ve heard things. About what he does to people who cross him. He doesn’t shout. He doesn’t hit. He just—takes everything. Slowly. Until there’s nothing left.” She was quiet. “I want you to know I know. And I want you to know that if you ever need to get away from him—”

“I won’t.”

“If you ever do,” said Serafina, very low and fierce, in the voice she had used at ten, when she had found Aurelia crying in the bathroom after Vienna, “you call me. Day or night. Any city. I will have a car outside in an hour and nobody, not him, not his giant, not God, will ever find you. Do you understand?”

Aurelia looked at her sister by the fountain in the wisteria light.

“I understand,” she said. “Thank you.” She took the bottle out of Serafina’s hand and drank from it, the way she drank from the bottle in the old town. “And Sera. He’s never once asked me to win.”

Serafina stared at her.

“What?”

“Not once. Not at anything. He laid down his king.” Aurelia gave her back the bottle. “He knows what our mother is. He saw her at the party. He’s the only person who has ever looked at me and not wanted me to be first.” She smiled. “If you ever need to get away from her, Sera. You call him. He’ll have a car outside in ten minutes.”

Serafina picked at the label on her bottle with her thumbnail and didn’t say anything for a while.

“You’re in love with him,” she said finally. “You. Aurelia.”

“Yes.”

Serafina looked across the courtyard again. At Chen Si by the wall. He had seen them looking. He inclined his head, very slightly, toward Serafina. A greeting. A promise. Something.

Serafina looked back at her sister.

“God help him,” she said.

He was already crossing the courtyard. He had waited exactly as long as he was willing to. He nodded to Serafina, politely, and held out his hand to his wife.

“Dance with me,” he said. “I’ve shared you all day.”

He did not wait for an answer. He took her hand and drew her out under the wisteria, among the candles and Qian’s bad dancing, and pulled her in close, his palm flat and warm on her bare back over the broken chain, and danced with her as if there were nobody else in Milan. Over his shoulder she saw her sister watching them with her beer, and saw Serafina’s face change, slowly, from suspicion to something that looked almost like relief.

✦ ✦ ✦

The suite was at the top of the palazzo, under the roof, with a balcony over the canal.

The old goldsmith had insisted. It had been his own wedding suite, in 1952. It had a ceiling painted with clouds and a very old bed with posts of carved walnut and curtains of faded green silk, and long windows open onto the balcony, and below it the canal, black and silver, with the lights of the bars along the towpath reflected in it and the sound of people laughing somewhere and a guitar.

She stood on the balcony in her ivory dress and looked at it.

He came out behind her. She heard him. She always heard him now.

He put his arms round her from behind and pulled her back against him, hard, and bent his head and put his mouth to the side of her neck, just above the clasp of the chain, and stayed there, breathing her in, as if he had been waiting since four o’clock to do exactly this and could not wait one minute more.

“A balcony,” he said. “You’re not shaking.”

“No.” She looked at the water. “I was. All day. I didn’t show it.”

“I know,” said Chen Si. “I could tell. Your left hand. You kept touching the ring.”

She looked down. Her right hand was at her left, turning the wedding ring. Yellow gold, very plain, very heavy, made by Enzo the night before from a bar of gold she had melted down from her grandmother’s earrings. She hadn’t known she was doing it.

She turned round.

“Clause nine,” she said.

His face didn’t change. But something in him went still, the way it did, all through, like a man hearing a sound in the dark.

“Yes,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went inside. He followed her.

She stopped by the old walnut bed. She reached up and took the veil out of her hair. It was very simple: a long, fine length of ivory silk tulle, no lace, no embroidery, that she had worn pinned at the back of her head and falling over the broken chain to the floor. She held it in her hands.

“Turn round,” she said.

He turned round.

She stood behind him and lifted the veil and folded it, once, twice, three times, into a long soft band, and put it over his eyes, and knotted it at the back of his head. Not tight. Loose enough that he could have pulled it off in a second. They both knew it.

He stood very still.

“Can you see?” she said.

“No.”

“Good.” She put her hands on his shoulders. She felt him breathe. “All day, everyone looked at me. A hundred photographs. The man from Vogue. The old goldsmith’s grandson with his phone. Enzo, crying. You.” She ran her hands down his arms, slowly. “Especially you. You haven’t stopped looking at me since four o’clock.”

“No,” said Chen Si. “I haven’t.”

“So now you don’t get to.” She put her mouth close to his ear. “Now you have to find me without looking.”

She felt it go through him. All the way through, from his shoulders down.

She stepped back.

She took off her shoes. She took off her earrings, one, two, and dropped them into a dish on the dressing table, where they rang like small bells. He turned his head, very slightly, toward the sound.

Then she reached behind her for the clasp at the nape of her neck. The broken chain. It held the dress. She had designed it that way. When the chain came undone, everything came undone.

She undid it.

The ivory silk slid off her shoulders and down and lay on the old goldsmith’s floor in a pale pool, and she stood in the suite with the painted clouds in nothing at all but the long gold chain, which she held in one hand, and looked at her blindfolded husband, standing by the bed, listening.

“Where am I?” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found her.

He did it slowly. He didn’t reach out blindly, the way she had expected. He stood still and listened, with his head tilted, the way she had seen him listen to a room full of men before he spoke. Then he took one step toward her voice. Then another. She moved, quietly, barefoot, on the old wooden floor. He stopped, and listened again, and turned, exactly toward her, as if he could hear her heart.

“You’re cheating,” she whispered.

“You’re breathing,” said Chen Si. “I’ve been listening to you breathe for seven months. I’d know it anywhere.”

His hand found her. Her shoulder. Very lightly. Just his fingertips.

He went still.

His fingertips moved. Down her arm. Slowly. To her elbow. Her wrist. Back up. Across her collarbone. And she watched his face, under the folded veil, change completely as he understood that there was nothing at all between his hand and her skin.

“Aurelia,” he said. His voice had gone to almost nothing. “You took off the dress.”

“I took off everything,” said Aurelia. “Except this.” She lifted the broken chain and laid it in his palm, still warm from her spine. “I wanted you to find out by touch.”

He closed his hand around the gold.

He didn’t say anything. He stood blindfolded in the suite with the painted clouds and the long windows open onto the canal, holding her chain in one hand, with the other hand resting very lightly on her bare shoulder, and she could see him shaking.

“Clause nine,” he said finally, very low. “What are your terms?”

She took his hand, the one with the chain in it, and lifted it, and wound the chain once round his wrist, and then once round her own, so that they were joined by it, gold between them, a long loose loop.

“You don’t take off the blindfold,” she said. “You don’t let go of the chain. You learn me with your hands and your mouth, all of me, every single centimetre, and you don’t look, not once, not until I say.” She stepped closer, until she was against him, his suit against her bare skin. “And you don’t hurry.”

“I never hurry.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “That’s why I married you.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t hurry.

He learned her by touch, in the dark behind the veil, on the old walnut bed with the green silk curtains, with the gold chain looped between their wrists, and the canal outside, and the guitar somewhere on the towpath playing something slow.

He learned her the way he had learned her ledgers, the way he had learned his city. Patiently. Thoroughly. Every centimetre, exactly as instructed, and not one centimetre faster than he wanted. His hands first, and then his mouth, following his hands. The inside of her wrist, where the chain was. The crook of her elbow. Her shoulder. The long line of her spine where the broken chain had lain all day, every vertebra, one at a time, as if he were counting them, which, she realised, with a laugh that turned into something else, he was.

“You said you wouldn’t count,” she gasped.

“I said I wouldn’t count time,” said Chen Si, against the small of her back. “You never said anything about bones.”

She would have laughed if she could have breathed.

Somewhere after the bones, he stopped, with his forehead against her shoulder and his fingers on the knot of the veil, not pulling it. Just resting there.

“Let me see you,” he said. “One look. Please. You can say no.”

“No,” she said, and felt him laugh against her skin, and take his hand away from the knot, and go back to work. He kept to it, exactly, and she loved him for it.

He couldn’t see her. That was the thing that undid her, in the end. He couldn’t see her face, or her body, or anything, and so he listened, the way he had listened for her breathing in the dark of the room. Every sound she made, every catch of her breath, every time she said his name, he heard, and he followed it, and went back to it, and stayed there, until the sounds she was making were not ones she had ever made in her life, and the chain was pulling tight between their wrists because her hand had closed into a fist in the green silk.

“Look at me,” she said, finally. Her voice was wrecked. “Chen Si. Take it off. Look at me.”

He reached up with his free hand and pulled the veil away.

And looked at her.

She saw his face when he did. In the candlelight, in the suite under the painted clouds. She saw it all, everything, every single thing he had ever felt about her since a balcony in October, all of it at once, naked and enormous and absolutely unguarded.

Nobody had ever looked at her like that.

Not her mother. Not the photographers. Not the boys at school, or the man from Vogue, or two hundred people at her father’s party.

He looked at her as if he had found her in the dark.

“There you are,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

Later, she lay across his chest with the chain still looped loosely round both their wrists, and the veil somewhere on the floor, and the canal outside gone quiet, and listened to the bells of San Cristoforo strike two.

“Signora Chen,” he said, into her hair.

“Don’t.”

“Signora Chen,” said Chen Si. “Aurelia Chen. Wife.” He was smiling. She could feel it. “My queen.”

She lifted her head.

“That’s the first time you’ve said that.”

“I’ve been thinking it since the thirty-ninth floor,” said Chen Si. “When you sat in my chair.” He looked at her in the dark. “I was saving it for when it was true.”

She put her head back down on his chest.

Somewhere in a villa on Lake Como, forty minutes north, her mother was asleep, and did not know. In six days she would open a magazine.

Aurelia lay in the dark in the old goldsmith’s wedding bed with her husband’s heart under her ear and a broken gold chain round her wrist, in the city where she had learned to be afraid, and was not afraid of anything at all.

chapters.title: A Necklace on the Hit List
chapters.desc: He has been staring at a list of names for an hour. She drapes a sapphire collar worth more than all of them across his shoulders. He makes her count the stones.
chapters.epigraph: “My King, everyone on that list is worth less than this necklace. Look at me instead.”
chapters.content:
The list had nineteen names on it.

She knew because she had read it upside down from across his desk, on the forty-fourth floor, on a Tuesday night in August, while he sat behind it in his shirtsleeves with a pen in his hand and his coffee going cold, and did not look up.

Nineteen names. Some of them she knew. A judge. Two men from the planning department. A banker. The owner of a security company. A journalist who had written, last spring, a very careful article about the land on the east side. Beside each name, in his small precise hand, there were notes. Dates. Amounts. Lines connecting one name to another, and all of the lines, eventually, if you followed them, going back up to one name at the top of the page that was not written down at all, because it didn’t have to be.

Fu.

He had been looking at it for an hour.

He did that. Every few weeks. Took out the list and sat with it and moved the lines around in his head like pieces on a board. She had learned not to interrupt. She had learned that when he looked at the list, his face went somewhere very cold and very far away, somewhere she suspected was a hall at six in the morning and a man going down the stairs in his pyjamas, and that he came back from it slowly.

But it had been an hour.

And she had something to show him.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had finished it that afternoon.

It had taken Enzo and her four months, and it had taken the Song Group’s bank, which did not know it, eight hundred thousand dollars in sapphires from a dealer in Colombo who had known her grandmother. A collar. High, close, rigid, the way the old Maharaja pieces were, the kind of thing that sat at the base of a woman’s throat like a hand. Forty-one sapphires, all from the same mine in Ratnapura, all the same impossible cornflower blue, graded and matched over three months so that not one of them was a fraction of a shade off from the others. Set in platinum. Each one held by four tiny claws so fine that they disappeared, so that the stones looked as if they were floating against the skin.

It was called Numero Uno. She had named it in a fury, at two in the morning, after a phone call with her mother.

It was the most beautiful thing she had ever made.

She took it out of its case, in the bedroom, and held it in the mirror against her own throat. Then she took it off again, and took off everything else, and put on his shirt from that morning, the white one, which came to the middle of her thighs, and walked barefoot down the long pale corridor to his study with forty-one sapphires and eight hundred thousand dollars in her hands.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t look up when she came in.

“Five minutes,” he said.

“You said that an hour ago.”

“I meant it an hour ago, too.”

She walked round the desk. She stood behind his chair. She looked down at the list over his shoulder, at the nineteen names and the lines, at the empty space at the top.

Then she lifted the collar, and laid it across his shoulders, over his white shirt, like a stole. Cold platinum and cold stone against the back of his neck.

He went still.

“My King,” said Aurelia, in her most poisonously sweet voice, into his ear, “you’ve been staring at that list for an hour. Everyone on it, put together, is worth less than this necklace.” She leaned down until her cheek was against his. “Look at me instead.”

He didn’t move for a moment.

Then he put the pen down.

He reached up, slowly, and touched one of the sapphires on his shoulder. He ran his thumb over it. Then the next one. And the next. As if reading them.

“Ratnapura,” he said.

She stared at him.

“How do you know that?”

“The colour. The silk inside. You told me in March, in the old town, how to tell a Sri Lankan stone from a Kashmir one. You drew it on a napkin.” He touched another one. “You’ve matched them all. Every one. That must have taken months.”

“Three,” said Aurelia.

“Forty-one stones,” said Chen Si. Of course he had counted. He turned his chair round. Slowly. On its base. Until he was facing her, and she was standing between his knees in his shirt, barefoot, with her hair down, and her collar of sapphires across his shoulders like something a king would wear in an old painting. He looked up at her.

His face was not cold any more. It wasn’t far away.

It was very, very close, and it was looking at her with an expression that made the floor tilt.

“What’s it called?” he said.

She lifted her chin.

“Numero Uno,” she said.

He looked at her. He knew. She could see him know. The phone call. Her mother. Two o’clock in the morning.

“Put it on,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t let her do it herself.

He stood up and took the collar off his own shoulders and turned her round, gently, by the hips, so that she was facing the long dark window of his study, where the harbour glittered forty-four floors below, and the glass held their reflection: a slight dark man in a white shirt behind a woman in a white shirt, with a collar of blue light in his hands.

He lifted her hair aside. He put the collar round her throat. Cold. Heavy. It settled into the hollow at the base of her neck like a hand. He fastened it at the back. His fingers lingered on the clasp.

Then he undid the top button of the shirt she was wearing. His shirt.

And the next.

And the next, very slowly, watching her in the glass the whole time, until it was open all the way down, and he slid it off her shoulders, and let it fall.

She stood in his study in nothing but forty-one sapphires, in front of the window, with the whole city looking up.

“Chen Si,” she said. Her voice had gone very small. “The window.”

“Forty-fourth floor,” said Chen Si, behind her. “Nobody can see in.” He put his mouth against her shoulder. “Only me.”

She looked at herself in the glass. At the blue light at her throat. At his hands, coming round her from behind, resting very lightly on her waist.

“Clause nine,” she said.

“Yes?”

She closed her eyes.

“Otherwise,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

She felt him smile against her shoulder.

“Hands on the desk,” said Chen Si.

She put her hands on the desk. Flat. On either side of the list with the nineteen names. She was facing the window, bent very slightly forward, and in the glass she could see the collar, and her own face, and him behind her.

“Don’t move them,” he said. “Not until I say.”

“And if I do?”

“Then I stop,” said Chen Si, “and we start again from the beginning.” His hands moved, very slowly, from her waist, up her ribs. “And you count.”

“Count what?”

He touched the collar. The first stone, at the left of her throat.

“The sapphires,” he said. “Out loud. One at a time. Every time I touch one.” His voice was very low and very calm and absolutely without mercy. “If you lose count, I start again. From one.”

She opened her eyes and looked at him in the glass.

“That’s evil,” she said.

“You’re the one who matched them all,” said Chen Si. “I want to hear how proud you are.” He touched the first stone again. “One.”

“One,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lost count at nine.

He started again.

He touched the first stone, at the left of her throat, with one fingertip, and she said one, and then he kissed her shoulder, slowly, his mouth open against her skin, and touched the second, and she said two, and his other hand moved down her side, over her ribs, and the third, three, and she could see him in the glass watching her face, and the fourth, four, and by the seventh her voice had stopped being a voice, and at the ninth his hand moved and she lost it completely, and said something that was not a number in any language, and he stopped.

He took his hands away. Completely.

“One,” said Chen Si.

She made a sound of pure fury.

He laughed against the back of her neck.

“You can stop me,” he said. “You know the word.”

“I’m not saying it.”

“I know you’re not.” He touched the first stone. “One.”

“One,” said Aurelia, through her teeth.

She got to fourteen the second time.

She got to twenty-two the third.

The fourth time, she got to thirty-five, with her hands flat on his desk and her whole body shaking and his mouth against her spine and her own reflection in front of her in the dark glass, wild-eyed and flushed, with forty-one stones of blue light at her throat, and her voice saying the numbers in a way she would never be able to hear in a meeting again without going red. Thirty-three. Thirty-four. His hand. Thirty-five. His mouth. And at thirty-six he did something she didn’t see coming and her hands came off the desk and grabbed for him.

He stopped.

“Hands,” said Chen Si.

She put them back. She was laughing and nearly crying at the same time.

“I hate you.”

“I know,” he said, and kissed the side of her neck, just above the collar. “One.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fifth time, she got to forty-one.

She didn’t know how. She would never know how. She stood at his desk with her palms pressed so flat on the wood that they left marks, and said every number, clearly, out loud, while he did everything he had been doing and more, slowly, deliberately, the whole time watching her face in the glass. She said thirty-eight with her eyes closed. She said thirty-nine in a whisper. She said forty like someone falling.

He touched the last stone. At the right of her throat.

She opened her eyes and looked at him in the window.

“Forty-one,” said Aurelia Song.

He went very still behind her.

“Number one,” he said, in a voice she had never heard from him. “You did it. All of them.” His arms came round her. “Now you can let go.”

She let go of the desk.

He turned her round and lifted her onto it, onto his list, onto the nineteen names and the lines and the empty space at the top where Fu was, and she wrapped herself around him with forty-one sapphires at her throat and the whole city glittering behind them, and stopped counting anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, a long time afterwards, she lay on the rug on the floor of his study with her head on his chest and the collar still on, because she had refused to take it off, and looked at the ceiling.

The list was somewhere under the desk. It had slid off at some point. Neither of them had noticed.

“I’m going to sell it,” she said. “At auction. In Geneva. In November.” She touched one of the stones. “It will make three times what the stones cost. Maybe four. It will pay for the second boutique and the third. And everyone who sees it will know it’s mine.” She was quiet. “And I will send the catalogue to my mother.”

“With the name.”

She smiled at the ceiling. “Numero Uno. Aurelia Chen. Estimate on request.”

He laughed. She felt it in his chest.

“You’ve ruined it,” she said. “For me. I’ll never be able to look at it again without thinking about this.”

“Good,” said Chen Si.

He reached up and touched the first stone, at the left of her throat.

She went still.

“One,” he said.

“No,” said Aurelia, and started to laugh, helplessly, and rolled over on top of him, collar and all, on the floor of his study, and put her hand over his mouth, and he laughed into her palm, the most dangerous man in the city, flat on his back on his own rug with his list under his desk and his wife’s eight-hundred-thousand-dollar necklace swinging an inch above his face.

“Two,” he said, muffled.

She kissed him to make him stop.

He didn’t stop.

chapters.title: Chen Si Lost an Argument (Once)
chapters.desc: It is about bodyguards. It is the only argument he has ever lost. It ends with Zhao Zhendong teaching his brother’s wife to shoot, and then fixing the dishwasher.
chapters.epigraph: “Clause four, darling. Half your people. I counted.”
chapters.content:
It was about bodyguards.

It began on a Wednesday in September, after the second boutique opened, in the new mall on the east side, with a party that two hundred people came to and that three newspapers wrote about, and one of those newspapers printed a photograph of Aurelia Chen on the front of its business section, in gold, laughing, under the headline THE QUEEN OF HARBOUR ROAD.

On Thursday morning, a car followed her from the flat to the boutique.

She noticed it at the second set of lights. A grey saloon, three cars back. It was still there at the fourth set. It was there when she turned onto Harbour Road. It pulled into the kerb on the opposite side of the street when she parked, and sat there, with its engine running, for forty minutes, and then pulled out and drove away.

She told him that night, at dinner, because of clause three.

He put down his chopsticks.

He did not say anything. Across the table, his face had gone very calm.

“Who was it?” said Aurelia.

“I don’t know yet,” said Chen Si. “I will by tomorrow.” He picked up his chopsticks again, and put them down again. “From tomorrow, you’ll have two of Zhendong’s men. In a car behind you. Everywhere.”

“No,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

It went on for eleven days.

It was, everybody agreed afterwards, the worst eleven days in the history of the Syndicate. Qian, who had worked for Chen Si for seven years and had never once seen him in a bad mood, kept a drawer of antacids in his desk and got through two boxes. The man with the sunflower seeds, at the Thursday meeting, made a joke about married life and Chen Si looked at him for nine seconds without blinking, and the man with the sunflower seeds did not make another joke for the rest of the year.

Because Chen Si did not shout. He did not slam doors. He did not threaten. He did not, as far as anyone could tell, even raise his voice.

He just argued.

Quietly. Logically. Relentlessly. Every night, at dinner, on the long grey sofa, in bed, in the car. He laid it out like a case. The grey saloon. The photograph in the newspaper. The fact that half the city now knew her face and her name and which boutique she was in on which day. The fact that she was married to him, which meant that anyone who wanted to hurt him had, since May, a much easier way to do it than trying to hurt him. The fact—he said this one only once, on the fourth night, staring at the ceiling in the dark—that his mother had been alone in the house when she died, and that he had been in Block C, and that nobody had been there.

“Two men,” he said. “In a car. You won’t see them. You won’t know they’re there.”

“I’ll know,” said Aurelia.

“Then pretend you don’t.”

“I won’t be followed,” said Aurelia. “I won’t be watched. I won’t be kept somewhere safe.” She turned her head on the pillow and looked at him. “Clause four, darling.”

He closed his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not argue the way he did.

She was Aurelia Song. She had been trained by Vittoria Conti, who had once made a buyer from Bergdorf Goodman cry in a showroom in Milan without raising her voice above a murmur. She did not lay things out like a case.

She just won.

On the fifth day, she cancelled the Milan shipment. She did not tell him she was going to. She simply rang Dottor Rossi in the morning and explained, in rapid and charming Italian, that there would be a small delay, and then rang the hotel on the east side and explained, in rapid and charming Cantonese, that their walnut tables would be a month late, and then sat in her boutique and waited.

At four o’clock, the man with the tinted glasses rang Chen Si in a panic.

At six o’clock, Chen Si came home.

He stood in the doorway of the kitchen, where she was making pasta, in an apron that said KISS THE COOK that Qian had bought her as a joke, and looked at her.

“You cancelled the shipment,” he said.

“Postponed,” said Aurelia. “Until such time as I am able to travel to the Iron Docks at four in the morning to supervise it without a grey saloon full of Zhendong’s men behind me.” She stirred the sauce. “It’s my route. You agreed. Clause two. I sit at the table. Clause four. You don’t keep me somewhere safe.” She tasted the sauce. “Would you like some? It’s my grandmother’s.”

“That’s blackmail.”

“That’s negotiation.” She put the spoon down. “You taught me. On the thirty-ninth floor. Find what the other person can’t afford to lose.”

He looked at her.

“I can’t afford to lose you,” said Chen Si.

She stopped stirring.

“I know,” she said. “That’s why you’re going to lose this argument.”

His eyes went down, very deliberately, to the apron.

KISS THE COOK.

He crossed the kitchen and took the wooden spoon out of her hand and put it down, and kissed the cook. Slowly. Thoroughly. With the sauce bubbling behind her and her back against the counter, until she had forgotten which of them was supposed to be winning.

When he lifted his head, she had both fists in his shirt.

“That doesn’t change anything,” she said.

“I know,” said Chen Si. “I’m still going to argue with you. I just wanted to taste the sauce first.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth day, she went to see Zhao Zhendong.

She did not tell Chen Si. She found out where Zhao’s office was, at the Iron Docks, in the old warehouse with the iron stairs and the sign that said only ZHAO — IMPORT/EXPORT, and she drove there herself, in her own car, with nobody behind her, and walked up the iron stairs in heels, and knocked on the door.

He opened it himself.

He was in a black T-shirt. He had a gun in pieces on the desk behind him, on a cloth, and an oily rag in his hand. He looked at her on his doorstep for four seconds.

“Hm,” he said.

“I need you to teach me to shoot,” said Aurelia.

Zhao looked at her.

“Why.”

“Because your brother wants two of your men to follow me everywhere I go,” said Aurelia, “and I won’t have it. And he won’t sleep. He hasn’t slept properly for eight days.
