He lies awake and stares at the ceiling and thinks about his mother.” She lifted her chin. “So I need to be able to look after myself. Properly. So that when I tell him I don’t need two men, it’s true.” She paused. “And you’re the best. Everybody says so. Even people who are frightened of you.”

“Especially people who are frightened of me,” said Zhao.

He looked at her.

Then he stood aside and let her in.

✦ ✦ ✦

He taught her for three days.

At a range in the hills that she had not known existed, behind a quarry, owned by a man who owed Zhao something and asked no questions. Zhao did not talk much. He showed her how to hold it. How to stand. How to breathe out before you squeezed, not pulled. How to take it apart and put it back together, which she learned faster than anyone he had ever taught, he said, which was the longest sentence he said to her in three days.

She was good.

Not as good as him. Nobody was as good as him. But good. Steady hands, from eight years of setting stones under a loupe. A good eye. No flinching. On the second day she put six rounds through a paper target at fifteen metres in a group he could cover with his palm, and he looked at it, and looked at her, and said, “Hm,” in a different tone.

On the third day, she asked him.

“Is it true,” she said, putting the gun down on the bench and taking off the ear defenders, “about the drains? In Block C?”

He went still.

He looked at her, in the cold sunlight behind the quarry. Longer than four seconds.

“He told you,” he said.

“He told me there was a story about drains. He said it was his and yours. He said he’d tell me one day.” She looked at him. “He hasn’t yet.”

Zhao looked at the hills.

“He carried me,” he said finally. “Half the way. Through the water. In the dark. I was bleeding. He was sixteen and he weighed fifty kilos.” He was quiet. “Before that, in the riot, three of them came for him. I got in the way. One of them had a piece of bed frame.” He touched his own left side, under his arm, down toward his hip, briefly, the way you touch something to check it is still there. “He held it shut with his shirt for an hour. His arm was burned to the elbow from the grate and he didn’t notice until the next day.” A pause. “Then he planned the way out. He’d been studying the drains for months. He knew every pipe. He got us out.” He looked at her. “I would be dead.”

She didn’t say anything.

“He wants two men behind you,” said Zhao, “because the last time someone he loved was alone, he was in a cell and couldn’t do anything. And she died.” He picked up the gun and began to take it apart, very slowly, on the bench. “He will never say that. He will argue about cars and photographs. He will never say that.”

“He said it,” said Aurelia. “On the fourth night. In the dark.”

Zhao’s hands stopped.

He looked at her.

“Then he loves you,” said Zhao Zhendong, “more than I knew.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She came home on the eleventh night with a small black handgun in her gold clutch and a certificate from a range in the hills that didn’t exist, and put both on the kitchen counter in front of him.

He looked at them.

He looked at her.

“Zhendong,” he said.

“Three days. He says I’m the fastest he’s ever taught to strip one.” She leaned on the counter. “I won’t have two men behind me. I won’t be watched. But I will carry this, everywhere, and I will tell you where I’m going, every day, by text, and if I ever see a grey saloon again I will call you before I do anything else.” She paused. “And I’ll learn to drive properly. Serafina will teach me. Evasive driving. In the industrial district. At night.”

“Serafina,” said Chen Si faintly.

“My sister,” said Aurelia. “Who builds getaway cars. You’ve met her.”

He looked at the gun on the counter.

“That’s not two men,” he said.

“No. It’s one woman.” She came round the counter. She stood in front of him. “Who loves you. And knows about your mother. And won’t ever be alone in a house with nobody there, because she won’t let you keep her in one.” She took his face in her hands. “I know you can’t afford to lose me, Si. You won’t. But not like that. Not by putting me in a box.”

He closed his eyes.

He didn’t say anything.

“I lose,” said Chen Si.

She went very still.

“I lose,” he said again. He opened his eyes. They were wet. “No men. No car. The gun. The texts. Serafina.” A breath. “And the Milan shipment goes on Thursday.”

“Thursday,” agreed Aurelia.

“I’ve never lost an argument,” said Chen Si. “Not since I was fifteen. Not one.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “Qian told me. He’s going to have it engraved on something.”

He didn’t laugh. He pulled her into him by the waist, hard, so that the counter and the gun and the certificate were behind her and there was nothing between them at all, and put his face in her hair and held on.

“The man in the grey saloon,” he said against her temple, in his mildest voice. “I found him on the second day. He won’t be driving behind anyone again.” His arms tightened. “If anyone ever touches you, Aurelia, I will take this city apart to get to them. I’m telling you so you know. It isn’t part of the argument.”

She didn’t answer. She held on too.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao came to dinner on the Saturday.

He came every few weeks. He ate a whole steamed fish with his hands, in silence, for two hours. Aurelia had stopped finding it alarming in about June and now found it restful. She told him so, and he looked at her for four seconds and said, “Hm.”

After dinner, the dishwasher broke.

It made a sound like a dying animal and stopped, with water in it, and an error light flashing. Chen Si looked at it with the polite incomprehension of a man who had built a criminal empire on paper and had never once in his life touched an appliance. Aurelia, who had grown up with eleven servants in a villa on Lake Como, looked at it with exactly the same expression.

Zhao put down his chopsticks.

He got up. He went to the dishwasher. He opened it. He looked inside. He knelt down on their kitchen floor in his black suit and took the front panel off with a knife from the block on the counter, and put his arm into the machine up to the elbow, and pulled out, after a moment, a small piece of glass from a broken wine glass, and a clump of something unspeakable, and a single sapphire.

He held up the sapphire.

They all looked at it.

“That’s from Numero Uno,” said Aurelia slowly. “The spare. I had a spare cut, in case. I lost it in June.” She looked at Chen Si. “How did it get in the dishwasher?”

Chen Si looked at the ceiling.

Zhao put the panel back on. He pressed a button. The dishwasher started again, humming, perfectly happily.

He stood up. He handed the sapphire to Aurelia. He washed his hands at the sink.

Then he looked at his brother, and at his brother’s wife, and at the gun in her gold clutch on the counter, and at the cancelled shipment that wasn’t cancelled any more, and he did something neither of them had ever seen him do.

He laughed.

Short. Low. Once. Like a door opening somewhere far away.

“He lost,” said Zhao Zhendong, to nobody in particular. “Good.”

And sat back down, and finished his fish.

chapters.title: The Song Family Is Coming to Dinner
chapters.desc: Four months after the magazine, a letter arrives in her mother’s handwriting. They would like to be proud of her. Aurelia knows exactly what that will cost.
chapters.epigraph: “Your father and I would like to come to dinner. We would like to be proud of you.” — Vittoria Song, letter, 2 October
chapters.content:
The letter came on the second of October, four months and ten days after page two hundred and eleven of Italian Vogue.

It came to the boutique on Harbour Road, by hand, in a cream envelope with her mother’s initials embossed on the flap in dark blue, V.C.S., and it was written in her mother’s handwriting, which Aurelia had not seen in four years, and which still made the back of her neck go cold.

Aurelia,

Your father and I have been in Shanghai and then in Milan for the summer. We have now returned. We would like to come to dinner, with your husband, at your home, on Saturday the twelfth. We would like to meet him properly. We would like to be proud of you.

Your mother.

She read it standing at the counter. Then she read it again. Then she went into the workshop and gave it to Enzo, who read it over the top of his magnifying glasses and handed it back without a word.

“Well?” said Aurelia.

“We would like to be proud of you,” said Enzo, in Italian, very slowly, as if tasting it. He picked up his tweezers. “In forty years, cara, I have never heard of that woman wanting anything for free.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She showed it to Chen Si that night, on the long grey sofa.

He read it twice. He held it up to the light from the lamp, the way she held a stone, and turned it, and looked at the watermark, and the way the ink had sat on the paper, and the place where her mother had pressed hardest with the pen, which was on the word proud.

“She wants something,” he said.

“Obviously.”

“Something big. She’s waited four months. She’s been in Shanghai and Milan. That’s where your father’s banks are.” He put the letter down on the low table, by the jade chess board. “She’s been finding out about me.”

Aurelia went still.

“How much can she find out?”

“A great deal, if she’s good.” He looked at her. “Is she good?”

Aurelia thought about her mother. About Vittoria Conti at twenty-six, walking into her father’s office in Milan, a model with a degree in economics that nobody had known about, and walking out three hours later with a contract that had made the Contis the second-richest family in Lombardy. About a buyer from Bergdorf Goodman, crying in a showroom. About a crack in a coffee cup, which she had heard about from the maid, who had told Serafina, who had told her.

“She’s the best I’ve ever met,” said Aurelia. “Except you.”

“Second,” said Chen Si. “I’ll take it.”

She laughed, despite everything, and put her bare feet in his lap, and he held them, absently, warm in both hands, while he read the letter a third time.

“Then let her come,” said Chen Si. “Let’s see what she wants.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She spent ten days getting ready for it.

She did not admit that was what she was doing. She told Enzo she was finishing the Geneva pieces. She told Qian she was redesigning the second boutique’s window. She told Chen Si nothing, because of clause three, and when he asked she said, “I’m preparing,” and he looked at her and didn’t ask again.

She chose the menu. She changed it four times. She chose the wine, and then changed it, because the first one was Italian and that would look as if she was trying, and the second one was French and that would look as if she was trying not to. In the end she chose a white from the north of China, from a vineyard in Ningxia, because it was very good and her mother would never have heard of it, and would therefore have nothing to say.

She chose the flowers. She had them done by the florist in the hotel downstairs, who did them very badly, and she sent them back, and had them done again, and they were still bad, and she sat on the floor of the flat at midnight on the Thursday with a bucket of white roses and tried to do them herself, and cut her hand on a thorn, and cried for three minutes for no reason she could explain.

He found her there.

He knelt down on the floor beside the bucket of roses and took her hand and looked at the cut, which was small, and took a handkerchief out of his pocket, and wrapped it round her finger.

“Your mother won’t look at the flowers,” he said.

“She’ll look at everything,” said Aurelia. “She’ll look at the flowers and the wine and the plates and the way I hold my fork and the colour of my nails and whether I’ve put on weight, and whether you have, and whether the flat is too big or too small or too empty, and she will find the one thing that’s wrong, and she will say it, very kindly, at exactly the moment when it will hurt the most.” She looked at the roses. “She always finds it.”

He was quiet.

“Then let’s give her something to find,” said Chen Si.

She looked up at him.

“What?”

“You’ve been trying for ten days to make it perfect,” he said. “So that there’s nothing for her to find. She’ll know you’ve tried. She always knows. That’s the thing she’ll find.” He picked up one of the white roses from the bucket and turned it in his fingers. “So don’t try. Leave something wrong. On purpose. Choose it. Then when she finds it, it won’t be hers. It’ll be yours.”

She stared at him.

“Leave something wrong,” she said.

“One thing. Your choice.”

She looked at the roses.

Then she started to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

She chose the dishwasher.

It was still making a faint whine, since Zhao had fixed it. Not loud. Just a high thin sound, like a mosquito, all the way through every cycle. She had been going to have it replaced on the Friday.

She didn’t.

She ran it on the Saturday at seven forty-five, fifteen minutes before her parents were due, and left the kitchen door open.

✦ ✦ ✦

They arrived at eight exactly.

Her father first. Song Weiren, fifty-eight since Friday, at a birthday dinner his elder daughter had not been invited to, silver-haired and soft-spoken and very well dressed, in a navy suit with a pocket square that her mother had certainly chosen. He looked older than at the party. He looked tired. He shook Chen Si’s hand at the door and held it for a moment longer than he needed to and looked at him with an expression that Aurelia, after a moment, recognised as fear.

Then her mother.

Vittoria Song, née Conti, in black. Of course in black. Black silk, very simple, cut by the same house in Milan that had cut her wedding dress thirty years ago. Diamonds at her ears, small. Her grandmother’s ring. Her hair in a perfect low knot. She was fifty-three and she looked forty and she walked into the flat on the forty-fourth floor as if it had been built for her to walk into.

She looked at the room. The glass. The harbour. The long grey sofa. The books. The jade chess board. The white roses, which Aurelia had arranged herself, badly, and left.

Then she looked at her daughter.

Aurelia had decided, at six o’clock, standing in front of the mirror, not to wear gold. For the first time in her life. She was in a dark green dress, plain, with long sleeves, and no jewellery at all except her wedding ring, which was gold, very plain, very heavy, made from her grandmother’s earrings.

Her mother looked at the ring.

“Ciao, Mamma,” said Aurelia.

“Ciao, tesoro,” said Vittoria Song, and kissed her, once, on each cheek, without touching her at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

Dinner was perfect.

That was the strange thing. She would remember it afterwards as one of the most frightening evenings of her life, and nothing went wrong at all. Her father talked to Chen Si about shipping, carefully, in the way of a man feeling for the edge of a cliff in the dark. Her mother talked to Aurelia about Milan, about the new collection at the house that had cut her wedding dress, about a cousin who had married a count, about the weather on Lake Como in August. She praised the fish. She praised the wine; she asked where it was from, and when Aurelia said Ningxia, she paused for half a second, and then said, “How interesting,” and drank it.

She did not mention the boutique.

She did not mention the wedding.

She did not mention the magazine.

She sat at her daughter’s table on the forty-fourth floor and ate her daughter’s food and was charming, for two hours, and the whole time, at the edge of everything, in the kitchen, the dishwasher whined.

At ten o’clock, over the coffee, Vittoria Song put down her cup.

“That sound,” she said.

Everybody stopped.

“In the kitchen,” said Vittoria pleasantly. “It’s been going all evening. A little whistle. Is it the dishwasher?” She smiled at Chen Si. “You must have someone look at it. In a flat like this, it’s such a shame. One little thing, and it’s all you can hear.”

The table was very quiet.

Aurelia looked at her mother across the coffee cups.

And she smiled.

“My brother-in-law fixed it,” she said. “Zhao Zhendong. You may have heard of him. He took the front off with a kitchen knife in his good suit and put his arm in up to the elbow and pulled out a sapphire.” She picked up her own cup. “It whistles now. I like it. I decided to keep it.”

Her mother looked at her.

For a moment, just a moment, something moved behind the perfect face. Something Aurelia had never seen there before.

Uncertainty.

Then it was gone.

“How charming,” said Vittoria Song.

Under the table, very lightly, Chen Si’s knee touched Aurelia’s, and stayed there.

✦ ✦ ✦

It came at the door.

She had known it would. Her mother always saved it for the door. The coat on, the bag in hand, the car downstairs, no time for a reply. The way she had said, at the door of Aurelia’s bedroom in Milan, when Aurelia was eleven, second place is just the first of the losers, and then gone downstairs.

Her father had already gone down to the car. He had shaken Chen Si’s hand again, in the doorway, and held it again, and said, very quietly, “Thank you for having us,” in the voice of a man who had been told to say it.

Her mother stood in the doorway of the flat in her black coat.

“Thank you for dinner, tesoro,” she said. “It was lovely. You’ve done very well.” She looked past Aurelia at the room. At the glass. At the harbour. At Chen Si, standing by the sofa with his hands in his pockets. “Both of you.”

“Thank you, Mamma.”

“Your father,” said Vittoria, “would like to have lunch with your husband. Next week. Just the two of them. About the bridge.”

Aurelia went cold.

“The bridge,” she said.

“Harbour Bridge Two.” Her mother smiled. It was the smile from the cover of Vogue. “It’s the most important thing your father has ever done. You know that. It’s been his dream for ten years. And there’s a little difficulty with the ministry. A signature that won’t come. Your husband knows the right people. Everyone says so.” She pulled on her gloves. “We would be so proud, tesoro. If you could help your father. Just this once. Family helps family.”

She kissed Aurelia once on each cheek, without touching her.

“The minister’s name,” she said, at the door, as if remembering something unimportant, “is Fu. Fu Jianguo. Your husband will know him.”

And she was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia closed the door.

She stood with her back against it, in her green dress, with no gold on.

Chen Si had not moved from beside the sofa.

“She knew,” said Aurelia. Her voice came out very flat. “She found out. In Shanghai, or Milan, or wherever. She found out about Fu. About your father. She knows what he did to your family.” She looked at him across the long room. “And she came here and ate your food and praised your wine, and at the door, she asked you to go to Fu Jianguo, the man who killed your father, and ask him for a favour. For her. For a bridge.”

Chen Si didn’t say anything.

“We would like to be proud of you,” said Aurelia. “That was the price. That was always the price.”

In the kitchen, the dishwasher finished its cycle, and stopped whining, and the flat went completely silent.

Chen Si took his hands out of his pockets.

He crossed the room. He came and stood in front of her, where she was standing against the door, and put one hand flat on the wood beside her head and the other at her waist, and pulled her in off the door and against him, as if her mother might still be on the other side of it and he wanted her to hear.

“Aurelia,” he said. “She found the thing.”

“What thing?”

“The one thing that’s wrong. You left the dishwasher for her. She didn’t want the dishwasher.” He looked at her face. “She found me. Fu. My father. She found the only thing in this flat she knew you couldn’t fix.” He was quiet for a moment. “She’s very, very good.”

Aurelia looked at him.

Then she reached up, and took his face in both her hands, and held it, hard.

“She’s not better than you,” she said fiercely. “She’s not better than me. She doesn’t get to walk in here and put that man’s name in your mouth. Not in our house. Not ever.”

“What are you going to do?”

Aurelia let go of his face.

She went to the hall table. She picked up her phone and turned it over in her hand.

“My father,” she said, “will have lunch with my husband next week. About the bridge.” She looked up. “And I am going to be at that lunch. And I am going to choose the restaurant.”

Chen Si looked at her.

“Which restaurant?” he said.

Aurelia smiled. It was not her mother’s smile.

It was much, much worse.

“Italian,” she said.

chapters.title: What Her Father Wants
chapters.desc: Lunch at the best Italian restaurant in the city. Her father lays it out: a bridge, a signature, a minister, and his son-in-law’s name on a letter. Chen Si listens to all of it. Aurelia orders the risotto.
chapters.epigraph: “It’s only a letter. A few lines. Your name at the bottom. It would mean so much.” — Song Weiren
chapters.content:
The restaurant was called Da Gianni, and it was on the sixty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel, and it was the most expensive Italian restaurant in Asia.

It had a chef from Bologna and a sommelier from Piedmont and a maître d’ from Naples called Carmine who had been there since it opened and knew every important person in the city by name and by order. It had white tablecloths and silver and a view of the whole harbour, and it had, which was the point, eleven waiters, every one of them Italian.

Aurelia had eaten there once a week, at sixteen, with her mother, at the table by the window, every Saturday, after piano.

She booked that table.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father was already there when they arrived. He stood up. He shook Chen Si’s hand. He kissed Aurelia, carefully, on the forehead, the way he used to when she was small, before Vienna, before the rankings, before everything.

“Papà,” she said.

“Tesoro,” said Song Weiren. He looked at her. “You look well. Married life.” He smiled, a little uncertainly. “I didn’t think you’d come. Your mother said it would just be the two of us.”

“Mamma says a lot of things,” said Aurelia, and sat down.

Carmine came. He kissed her hand. He said, in Neapolitan, that it had been three years and she was more beautiful than ever and that he had heard she had married, and was this the lucky man, and he looked at Chen Si and his smile faltered very slightly, the way everyone’s did, and then came back.

“Signora Chen,” he said, “the usual?”

“The usual, Carmine. And for my father, the veal. And for my husband—” she looked at Chen Si.

“Whatever she recommends,” said Chen Si.

“The risotto,” said Aurelia. “All three of us. And a bottle of the Barolo. The 2010.”

Carmine bowed and went away.

Her father looked at her.

“You always had the risotto,” he said. “Every Saturday.”

“I know, Papà.”

He looked at her, and something went across his tired, soft-spoken face that she didn’t understand at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told them about the bridge over the antipasti.

He was good at it. He had always been good at it. Her mother was the cold one, the clever one, the one who found the crack in everything; her father was the warm one, the one who made you want to help him. He talked about the harbour. About the old ferry crossing that took forty minutes, and the bridge that would take four. About the hospital on the far side, and the ambulances that couldn’t get there in time. About the jobs. Twenty thousand jobs, for six years. About his own father, who had come to this city with nothing in 1962 and sold watches from a suitcase on Harbour Road, three doors down from where Aurelia’s boutique was now, and had stood on the waterfront and looked across at the far shore and said, one day someone will build a bridge.

“It’s been my dream,” said Song Weiren, “for ten years. Since your grandfather died. I promised him. At the hospital.” He turned his glass on the tablecloth. “I’ve done everything. The money is there. The engineers are there. The designs are approved. The land is bought. Everything.” He looked up. “Except one signature.”

“From the ministry,” said Chen Si.

“From the vice-minister for infrastructure.” Her father’s voice dropped. “He’s had the file for eleven months. He won’t sign. He won’t say why. He won’t meet me. My people can’t get near him.” He looked at Chen Si across the table. “Your people can. Everyone says so. Everyone says that if you want something from the ministry, there is one man in this city who can make it happen.” He spread his hands. “I’m not asking you to do anything—improper. I would never ask that. Just a letter. A few lines, to the minister, saying that you know me, that you know the project, that you support it. Your name at the bottom.” He tried to smile. “It’s only a letter. It would mean so much. To me. To your mother.” He looked at his daughter. “To the family.”

The table was very quiet.

Out of the corner of her eye, Aurelia saw Carmine, by the bar, polishing a glass very slowly.

“The vice-minister for infrastructure,” said Chen Si, “is Fu Jianguo.”

“Yes,” said her father.

“You know who he is.”

“I know he’s difficult.”

“You know,” said Chen Si, very mildly, “what he did to my father.”

Song Weiren went white.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was strange, Aurelia thought, from somewhere far away, watching her father’s face. It was the first time she had ever seen him understand that he had walked into a room he did not know the size of.

“I—” said her father. “Vittoria said—she said it was old history. She said it was a misunderstanding, years ago, between families. She said you would understand that business is business.” He looked at Aurelia. “Tesoro, I didn’t know. I didn’t know it was—I thought it was—”

“You didn’t ask,” said Aurelia.

“I didn’t think—”

“You never do, Papà.” She said it very gently. “Mamma tells you what to think, and you think it. You always have. She told you to close my shop in January. She told you to stand up at your own birthday and drink while she called me a loser. She told you to come here today and ask my husband to write a letter to the man who had his father arrested in his pyjamas and left him to die in a cell.” She picked up her glass of Barolo. “And you did. Because it was easier than asking her why.”

Her father stared at her.

“Aurelia,” he said. “That’s not fair.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “It isn’t. Nothing in our family ever was.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The risotto came.

Saffron. Milanese. Bright gold, with a single piece of bone marrow on top, the way her grandmother had made it, the way she had eaten it every Saturday at sixteen at this table by this window, with her mother across from her counting every grain she ate.

Nobody touched it.

Chen Si had not said anything since what he did to my father. He was sitting back in his chair, with his glass of Barolo in his hand, and he hadn’t drunk it, and he was looking at her father with an expression she knew, now. The one from the list with nineteen names on it.

Very cold. Very far away. A hall at six in the morning.

Under the table, she put her hand on his knee.

He didn’t move. But after a moment, his hand came down and covered hers.

“Mr. Song,” said Chen Si.

Her father flinched.

“I want to understand,” said Chen Si, in his mild voice. “Not the bridge. The bridge is a good bridge. I’ve seen the designs. The hospital is real. The ambulances are real. Your father on the waterfront is real.” He put his glass down. “What I want to understand is why Fu Jianguo won’t sign.”

“I told you, I don’t—”

“You do,” said Chen Si. “A man doesn’t sit on a file for eleven months for no reason. Fu doesn’t do anything for no reason. I’ve been watching him for nine years. He never says no. He says not yet. And then he waits until you’re desperate enough to give him what he actually wants.” He tilted his head. “What does he want from you, Mr. Song?”

Her father looked at his risotto and didn’t answer. Carmine, at the bar, put down the glass he was polishing.

“A share,” he said finally. “Of the contract. For his son. Fu Kang. Fifteen per cent. Through a company in Macau that has his son’s name nowhere on it.” He closed his eyes. “I said no. In March. I said no, because I’m not—I won’t—” He stopped. “And he stopped returning my calls.”

Aurelia sat very still.

“You said no?” she said.

Her father opened his eyes. “I’ve done many things, tesoro. I’m not proud of all of them. But my father sold watches from a suitcase. He never paid a bribe in his life. I promised him a bridge. I didn’t promise him a bridge with Fu Jianguo’s son’s name hidden inside it.” His voice cracked. “So I said no. And then your mother said—your mother said that your husband—that there was another way. That if your husband wrote a letter, Fu would have to sign. Because Fu is afraid of your husband.” He looked at Chen Si. “Is he? Is Fu afraid of you?”

Chen Si looked at him.

“Not yet,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, Aurelia would think about that lunch more than almost anything else in her life.

Not because of the bridge. Not because of Fu. Because of her father’s face when he said I said no.

She had never seen it before. In twenty-two years. Her soft, warm, tired father, who did what her mother told him and changed the subject at dinner and had stood up at his own birthday and drunk to her humiliation. She had thought, for most of her life, that he had no spine at all.

And he had said no to Fu Jianguo. In March. For his father, who sold watches from a suitcase.

She picked up her fork.

She ate the risotto. All of it. Every grain. Slowly. And her father watched her do it, across the table by the window where she had sat every Saturday at sixteen, and his eyes filled, and he looked away, out at the harbour, at the far shore where there was no bridge.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si paid.

He did it before her father could reach for his wallet, a small movement to Carmine across the room that nobody else saw, and Carmine came and murmured that it was taken care of, and Song Weiren looked at his son-in-law with the expression of a man who did not know whether he had been given a gift or a warning.

At the lift, her father stopped.

“I’m sorry,” he said to Chen Si. “For asking. I didn’t know. I should have known. I should have asked.” He looked at his daughter. “I should have asked about a great many things.”

Aurelia didn’t say anything.

“The letter,” said Chen Si.

Her father shook his head. “Forget the letter. I won’t ask again. Not for that. Not to that man.”

“I’m not going to write a letter,” said Chen Si.

“I know. I understand.”

“I’m going to think about it,” said Chen Si. “The bridge. Fu’s son. The company in Macau.” He pressed the button for the lift. “I’m going to think about it very carefully. And then I’m going to tell your daughter what I think. And then she will decide.” He looked at Aurelia. “Not me. Her.”

Her father looked at him.

Then at Aurelia.

The lift came. The doors opened.

Her father got in. He turned round. He looked at his elder daughter, standing in the lobby of the sixty-first floor in a dark green dress with no gold on, beside the most dangerous man in the city, who had just told him that she would decide.

“You were always the clever one,” said Song Weiren. “Your mother always said. The clever one, and the beautiful one, and the one who would be first.” He tried to smile. “She never once said you’d be the brave one.”

The doors closed.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, going home, she didn’t say anything.

Chen Si didn’t either. He sat beside her in the back, with his hand over hers on the seat between them, and looked out of the window at the harbour going by, at the far shore, where there was no bridge.

“He said no to Fu,” she said finally. “My father.”

“Yes.”

“And my mother found another way.” She looked out of her own window. “She always finds another way. She found you. She found Fu. She found your father. She sat at our table and praised the wine and at the door she put that man’s name in your mouth, so that my father wouldn’t have to.” Her voice was very flat. “She wants you to make Fu sign. She doesn’t care how. She doesn’t care what it costs you. She just wants the bridge, so that she can stand on it at the opening in black silk and be proud.”

Chen Si was quiet.

He lifted her hand off the seat, turned it over, and kissed the inside of her wrist, once, where the pulse was, still looking out of the window, as if it were something he did to think. Then he put it back under his.

He turned his head and looked at her. “What do you want?”

She turned and looked at him.

“Me?”

“You,” said Chen Si. “Not your mother. Not your father. Not me. You.” He looked at her. “I meant what I said at the lift. You decide. Whatever you decide, I’ll do. If you want me to write the letter, I’ll write it.”

She stared at him.

“To Fu? The man who—”

“Yes.” His voice didn’t change at all. “If you want your father’s bridge, and that is the price, I’ll pay it. For you.” He looked at her. “But I don’t think that’s what you want.”

She looked at him, in the back of the car, with the harbour going past.

“No,” she said slowly. “It isn’t.”

“What is?”

She thought about it. About her father in the lift. I said no. About the risotto. About a man who sold watches from a suitcase on Harbour Road three doors down from her shop and had never paid a bribe in his life.

About Fu Jianguo’s son, Fu Kang, and a company in Macau.

She turned her hand over under his, on the seat, and laced her fingers through his.

“I want my father’s bridge,” said Aurelia. “Built. Properly. No bribe. No letter. No fifteen per cent for Fu Kang hidden in Macau.” She looked at him. “And I want Fu Jianguo to sign it anyway. Because he has to. Because he’s afraid not to.” She lifted her chin. “Not of you. Of me.”

Chen Si looked at her.

Slowly, very slowly, he began to smile.

“Clause five,” he said. “You won’t interfere with my prior claim.”

“I won’t,” said Aurelia. “I’m not going to touch Fu Jianguo. I’m going to touch his son.”

He pulled her across the seat by their laced hands and kissed her, there in the back of the car with the harbour going past, hard and deep and not at all mild, his other hand spread at the back of her head, until the driver put the partition up without being asked.

“Do you know,” said Chen Si against her mouth, a little breathless, “what it does to me when you say things like that?”

“Yes,” said Aurelia, and kissed him back.

chapters.title: Aurelia Says No to Her Mother
chapters.desc: The house on the Peak, the morning room, three Italian maids pretending to polish silver. She says it in Italian, so that everyone understands. Then she goes shopping for Fu Kang.
chapters.epigraph: “No, Mamma. Not for the bridge. Not for you. Not ever.” — in Italian, so the maids understood too
chapters.content:
She went to the house on the Peak on a Monday morning, at nine, without telling anyone she was coming.

Not even Chen Si. She texted him from the car, as she had promised: Going to see my mother. Peak house. Gun in my bag. Back by twelve. And he texted back, eleven seconds later, one word.

Win.

She looked at it until the screen went dark.

Then she put the phone in her bag, next to the gun, and got out of the car.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother was in the morning room.

She always was, at nine. The morning room faced east, over the garden and the long drop of the Peak to the harbour, and it was full of light and white flowers and Venetian glass, and her mother sat at the little table by the window every morning from nine until ten with a pot of coffee and the Italian newspapers and the day’s list, and nobody was allowed to disturb her. Not her husband. Not her daughters. Not the deputy minister, once, who had arrived unexpectedly at nine-fifteen and been made to wait in the hall.

There were three maids in the room. There always were. Two Filipino, one Italian from Bergamo, Signora Pina, who had been with the family since Milan, since before Aurelia was born, and who had held her as a baby. They were polishing silver at the long sideboard. They were always polishing silver at nine. Aurelia had understood, at about the age of twelve, that this was so that there would always be witnesses.

Vittoria Song looked up from Corriere della Sera.

“Tesoro,” she said. “What a surprise. You should have called.”

“I didn’t want to,” said Aurelia.

She did not sit down. She stood in the middle of the morning room in the light from the east windows, in a white suit, in gold—she had put on gold that morning, every piece she owned, the earrings from the balcony and the cuffs from the Geneva collection and the collar she had made in September from the leftovers of Numero Uno and her wedding ring—and looked at her mother across the room.

“You sent Papà to ask my husband to write to Fu Jianguo,” she said.

Her mother turned a page of the newspaper.

“Your father has a bridge to build.”

“You knew who Fu was. You found out. In Shanghai, or Milan, or wherever. You found out what Fu did to his father.” Aurelia’s voice was perfectly level. “And you sent Papà to ask anyway. And you didn’t tell him why. You let him walk into that restaurant and put that man’s name on the table without knowing what it meant.”

“Your father,” said Vittoria, “doesn’t need to know what things mean. He needs to know what to say.” She folded the newspaper. “I gave him the right thing to say. He said it badly. He always does.”

“He said no to Fu.”

Her mother went very slightly still.

“In March,” said Aurelia. “Fu wanted fifteen per cent for his son. Papà said no. Because Nonno sold watches from a suitcase and never paid a bribe in his life.” She took a step forward. “Did you know that? Did he tell you he said no?”

Vittoria Song looked at her daughter.

“Of course he told me,” she said. “I told him he was a fool.”

At the sideboard, Signora Pina stopped polishing.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You told him he was a fool,” said Aurelia slowly.

“Fifteen per cent of a bridge is nothing. It’s the cost of doing business. Every bridge in the world has fifteen per cent of something hidden in it.” Her mother poured herself more coffee. “Your father has sentimental ideas about his father. His father sold watches from a suitcase because he wasn’t clever enough to sell anything else. I married your father because he was not his father. I was wrong about that, apparently.” She sipped her coffee. “So I found another way. Your husband. Fu is afraid of him, everyone says. One letter from Chen Si and the file signs itself. No fifteen per cent. Your father keeps his precious principles. Everyone wins.” She put the cup down. “I thought you’d be grateful. I was helping.”

“You were using him.”

“I was using what I had,” said Vittoria. “That’s all anyone does. That’s all you do, tesoro. You married a man everyone is frightened of. Don’t pretend it wasn’t because you wanted everyone to be frightened of you, too.”

The morning room was very quiet.

Aurelia stood in the light from the east windows and looked at her mother.

She had imagined this conversation for twelve years. Since Vienna. Since nine days of silence and a curtain opened in the morning. In every version she had imagined, she was shaking, or crying, or shouting, and her mother was cold and still and perfect and won.

She was not shaking.

She found that out, standing there. She looked down at her own hands, covered in gold, and they were perfectly steady. Steady as they were under a loupe at two in the morning, setting a stone. Steady as they had been at fifteen metres behind a quarry with Zhao’s gun.

She looked up.

And she said it in Italian. Clearly. Slowly. In the Milanese Italian her mother had spoken to her since she was born, so that Signora Pina at the sideboard would understand every word, and the two other maids would understand enough.

“No, Mamma.”

Her mother looked at her.

“No,” said Aurelia again. “Non per il ponte. Non per te. Mai.” Not for the bridge. Not for you. Not ever. “My husband will not write to Fu Jianguo. Not for Papà, not for you, not for anyone. You will not ask him again. You will not send Papà to ask him again. You will not put that man’s name in my house again, at my table, in my husband’s hearing, as long as you live.”

The silver on the sideboard had stopped moving altogether.

“And you will not,” said Aurelia, “ever again stand up at a dinner and tell two hundred people what I’m worth.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria Song put down her coffee cup.

She did it very carefully. In the saucer. Without a sound. She looked at her elder daughter standing in the morning room covered in gold, and her perfect face did not move at all.

“And if I do?” she said pleasantly.

“Then I’ll stop coming,” said Aurelia. “To anything. Ever. You’ll find out about my life from magazines. You’ll find out about my collections from the auction catalogues. You’ll stand at galas and people will ask you about your daughter, the designer, the one married to Chen Si, and you’ll have to say you haven’t spoken to her in years, and they’ll look at you the way people looked at me at Papà’s birthday.” She picked up her bag. “And Papà will get his bridge anyway. Without you. Without the letter. Without fifteen per cent.”

For the first time, something moved in her mother’s face.

“How?”

“That,” said Aurelia, “is my business.”

She went to the door of the morning room.

At the door, she stopped, and looked back. Not at her mother. At the sideboard. At Signora Pina, who had held her as a baby, standing very still with a silver coffee pot in one hand and a cloth in the other, looking at her with tears running down her old face.

“Grazie, Pina,” said Aurelia gently. “For the silver.”

She went out.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, she sat without telling the driver to move.

Then she took out her phone and looked at his one word.

Win.

She typed back.

I didn’t win. I just said no.

His reply came four seconds later.

That’s the only kind that counts.

She put her head back against the seat and closed her eyes and laughed, silently, until her ribs hurt.

Then she opened her eyes and said to the driver: “Harbour Road. And then I need you to find me a list of every jeweller in Macau.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Fu Kang was thirty-one, handsome, idle, and very, very fond of watches.

She knew all of it by Thursday. Qian had a file on him. Chen Si had a better one. Mr. Lu, the small neat man in the cardigan who ran the pawnshops, had the best one of all, because Fu Kang had pawned three watches in the last two years when his allowance ran out, at three different shops, under three different names, and every one of those shops belonged to Mr. Lu.

“He likes Swiss,” said Mr. Lu, sitting across from her in the workshop at the back of the boutique, with his cardigan buttoned up to his chin and his tea untouched. “Independent makers. Small. Very rare. The kind you have to wait four years for. He buys them through a dealer in Macau, Mrs. Chen. Always the same dealer. Always cash.” He paused. “The dealer is odd. He was a bookkeeper, until three years ago. Now he sells watches worth half a million each, and he has a shop with no customers but one.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“And the shop belongs to a company,” she said.

“Which belongs to a company,” agreed Mr. Lu. “Which belongs to a company. Which is registered in Macau.” He smiled very slightly. “I haven’t followed it all the way. I’m only a pawnbroker.”

“You’re not only anything, Mr. Lu.”

He bowed his head, pleased.

“If someone were to follow it,” said Aurelia slowly, “all the way. And if at the end of it there were fifteen per cent of a great many things. Not just a bridge. Every bridge. Every contract Fu Jianguo has ever sat on for eleven months. And if all of it were going through a watch shop with no customers in Macau, into a company with Fu Kang’s name hidden in it somewhere—”

“Then someone would have a very interesting file,” said Mr. Lu.

“And if Fu Kang were the kind of young man who couldn’t resist a very rare watch—”

Mr. Lu looked at her over his tea.

“Mrs. Chen,” he said. “You don’t make watches.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “But I know a man in Geneva who does. He’s seventy-four. He makes four a year. There’s a waiting list of nine years.” She smiled. “He knew my grandmother.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She told Chen Si that night, in bed, in the dark, with her head on his chest.

All of it. Mr. Lu. The watch shop. The company in Macau. The old man in Geneva. Fu Kang, who couldn’t resist.

He listened without interrupting. When she had finished, he was quiet.

“Not Fu Jianguo,” he said finally. “His son.”

“Clause five. The father’s yours.”

“I’m going to sell his son a watch,” said Aurelia. “The rarest watch in the world. One of four. Through his own dealer in Macau. And I’m going to make him pay for it the way he pays for everything. Through the company.” She traced a line on his chest with one finger. “And when he does, I’ll be the seller. I’ll be at the other end of the money. I’ll see every company it goes through on the way to me. Every single one. All the way back to the account with his name in it.”

“And then?”

“And then I’ll have a file,” said Aurelia. “And I’ll go and have lunch with Fu Kang. At Da Gianni. And I’ll show it to him. And I’ll tell him that if his father’s signature is on my father’s bridge by Christmas, the file stays in my safe. And if it isn’t, it goes to the anti-corruption commission, and the newspapers, and his father’s enemies, of whom there are many.” She was quiet. “And then Fu Kang will go home and tell his father. And his father will sign. Because he’s afraid. Not of you. Of what his son has been doing in his name.”

Chen Si didn’t say anything. His hand had stopped moving on her back.

“That,” he said finally, “is the most beautiful thing anyone has ever said to me in bed.”

She laughed.

“I’m serious,” said Chen Si. “I’ve been watching Fu for nine years. I’ve never once thought of going through his son.” He turned his head on the pillow. “His son is an idiot. I thought he was irrelevant.”

“Idiots are never irrelevant,” said Aurelia. “My mother taught me that. They’re just doors nobody bothers to lock.”

He was quiet.

“Clause five,” he said. “When it’s done. When it’s Fu. I’ll be standing in his hall at six in the morning.”

“And I’ll be standing beside you,” said Aurelia.

“And then breakfast.”

He turned over in the dark. He found her face with his hand.

“Aurelia,” he said. “Clause nine.”

She went very still.

“I’ve been thinking,” said Chen Si, very low, “about you standing in your mother’s morning room. Covered in gold. Saying no.” His thumb moved on her cheekbone. “I’ve been thinking about it all day. Since your text. I couldn’t think about anything else. Qian asked me three times if I was ill.”

“Were you?”

“Very.” His mouth found her jaw. “Tell me what you want.”

She lay in the dark and thought about it.

Then she reached over to the bedside table, where she had taken off every piece of gold she owned, and put it in a pile, and found the cuffs from the Geneva collection, two heavy bands of yellow gold, hinged, that locked with a tiny bolt, and held them out to him in the dark.

“Put these on me,” she said. “And then don’t let me take them off.”

He took the cuffs.

He took her wrists, one at a time, and locked the gold around them, and she heard the tiny bolts click home in the dark, one, two. He lifted her hands above her head and laid them on the pillow, side by side, and held them there with one hand, not hard, just enough.

“Is that what you wanted?” he said.

“Yes,” said Aurelia. Her voice had gone very small. “All day, I was the one saying no. I want to be the one who can’t.”

He put his mouth against her ear.

“You can,” he said. “You know the word.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “I won’t.”

And for the rest of the night, she didn’t.

He made her wait for everything. He kissed the inside of each wrist, just above the gold, where the cuffs had already warmed to her pulse, and then went nowhere near her mouth for so long that she said his name twice, the second time not nicely. When she tried to bring her hands down he caught the cuffs in one hand, and the tiny bolts clicked against each other, and he said, very low, “You told me not to let you,” and didn’t. He told her what he was going to do in Italian, which he had learned from Enzo and had clearly been saving, and got one verb wrong on purpose so that she would laugh, and then, while she was laughing, did it.

Near dawn she said “Sì,” and meant yes, and meant him, and he understood both.

chapters.title: Her Mother’s Last Card
chapters.desc: Vittoria Song does not lose. She has one card left, and it has Serafina’s name on it: an illegal street race, a jilted fiancé’s family, and a photograph in a police file.
chapters.epigraph: “You have something I want, tesoro. And I have your sister.”
chapters.content:
The card came in an envelope, the way everything from her mother came.

It was delivered to the boutique on Wednesday the thirtieth of October, by a courier who did not wait for a signature. Inside there was no letter. Just a photograph, eight by ten, glossy, taken at night with a long lens.

A road in the industrial district. Wet. Floodlights from a factory. Two cars side by side at a line painted on the tarmac, a crowd of people in the dark on either side, and between the cars, with her hand raised and a white scarf in it, about to drop it, a tall thin girl in a leather jacket with her hair cut short with kitchen scissors.

On the back, in her mother’s handwriting:

The police have one of these. So does Li Zhenhua. Call me.

✦ ✦ ✦

Li Zhenhua was the man Serafina had been supposed to marry.

Not the man himself. His father. Li Zhenhua owned the third-largest construction company in the province and had wanted, for reasons of his own, to join it to the Song Group by marrying his son to the younger Song girl. The engagement dinner had been at the Harbour Hotel, two years ago, two hundred guests. Serafina had stood up between the soup and the fish and said, in front of all of them, that she would rather marry a carburettor, and walked out.

Li Zhenhua had never forgiven it. Everyone knew. He had told three people at three different parties that one day the Song girl would pay for it. He had a nephew in the city police. He had another nephew in the road-traffic division, which was very interested in illegal street racing in the industrial district, and which had, so far, not been able to catch anyone, because the people who raced in the industrial district were very fast and very careful and had very good friends.

Until now.

Aurelia sat at the counter with the photograph in her hands while two trams went past outside.

Then she called her mother.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Tesoro,” said Vittoria Song. “I knew you’d call.”

“What do you want?”

“You know what I want.” Her mother’s voice was warm. Pleasant. The voice she used for buyers. “I want the letter. One letter, from your husband to Fu. Before Christmas. That’s all.” A pause. “And I want you to come to the Christmas party at the Peak. With your husband. In gold. And smile.”

“And if I don’t?”

“Then on the second of January, the photograph goes to Li Zhenhua’s nephew in the traffic division, with a name, and an address, and the dates of every race your sister has driven in for two years. I have them all. I’ve had someone watching her since she left.” Vittoria’s voice didn’t change at all. “Illegal racing on public roads carries three years now. They changed the law in the spring. Li Zhenhua will make sure it’s three. He’ll make sure it’s somewhere unpleasant. And when she comes out, she won’t be allowed to drive anything again. Ever.” A pause. “She’d hate that, wouldn’t she? More than prison.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

“She’s your daughter,” she said.

“She was,” said Vittoria. “She left. She chose a carburettor.” Her voice softened, very slightly, the way it did when she was about to say the worst thing. “You didn’t leave, tesoro. You stayed and fought me. I respect that. That’s why I’m giving you a choice. One letter. One party. One smile.” She paused. “Or your sister in a cell for three years. You decide.”

The line went dead.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t tell Chen Si.

That was the first time. She would think about that afterwards, with shame. Clause three. Neither party will lie to the other. About anything. She didn’t lie. But she didn’t tell him either. She put the photograph in the safe in the workshop, under the Geneva pieces, and went home and made pasta and sat on the long grey sofa with him after dinner and talked about the Milan shipment and the watchmaker in Geneva and Fu Kang, and didn’t say anything about her sister, or her mother, or a road in the industrial district.

He knew.

Of course he knew. He watched her all evening with that still, absorbed attention. At eleven, in bed, in the dark, he said, “Aurelia. Is there something you can’t tell me yet?”

It was the form of words. I cannot tell you this yet. It was in clause three.

She lay in the dark and didn’t answer.

“Yes,” she said finally.

“All right,” said Chen Si.

He found her hand under the sheet and laced his fingers through hers. “I’m very good at waiting,” he said into her hair. “You’ve complained about it. In red ink.” A pause. “But if it’s something that can hurt you, you tell me before it does. That isn’t clause three. That’s me.”

He didn’t ask anything else. He put his arm around her and held her, and didn’t ask, and she lay awake until four with her eyes open, thinking about her sister’s hand in a photograph, raised, with a white scarf in it, about to drop.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the industrial district on the Saturday night.

Alone. She texted him, as she had promised. Going to see Serafina. Industrial district. Gun in bag. Back late. He texted back: Be careful. Not win, this time. Be careful. She read it twice before she put the phone away.

The garage was at the end of a street of shuttered workshops, under a railway bridge, where the trains went over every eleven minutes and shook the whole building. It had no sign. It had a steel shutter, half up, and light coming out from under it, and music, very loud, and the smell of petrol and hot metal and something frying.

She ducked under the shutter in a black coat and flat shoes.

There were six cars inside. Four of them were in pieces. One was up on a lift with its wheels off. And one was in the middle of the concrete floor under a single hanging lamp, low and long and matte black, with its bonnet up, and her sister’s legs sticking out from underneath it on a creeper board.

“Sera,” said Aurelia.

The legs went still.

Then the creeper rolled out, and Serafina Song lay on her back on the board on the concrete floor, in overalls tied round her waist and a vest covered in oil, with a spanner in one hand and a smear of black across her forehead, and looked up at her sister upside down.

“The gilded bird,” she said. “In my garage. What happened? Did someone die?”

“Not yet,” said Aurelia.

She took the photograph out of her coat, and held it out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina looked at it, lying on the creeper.

Then she sat up. She took it. She turned it over and read the back. The police have one of these. So does Li Zhenhua. Call me.

She didn’t say anything.

She got up. She went to a workbench against the wall, where there was a kettle and two mugs and a frying pan on a camping stove, and turned off the music. In the sudden quiet, a train went over the railway bridge, and the whole garage shook.

“When?” said Serafina.

“The thirtieth. Wednesday.”

“And you’ve been carrying it around since Wednesday.” Serafina turned round. “Not telling me.”

“I was deciding.”

“Deciding what?”

Aurelia didn’t answer.

Serafina looked at her. Then her face changed. Went cold and flat and furious, exactly like their mother’s, which neither of them would ever have admitted.

“She wants something from you,” said Serafina slowly. “And I’m the price. If you don’t give it to her, she sends me to Li Zhenhua.” She laughed, short and hard. “Of course. Of course she does. And you were deciding.” She threw the photograph down on the workbench. “What does she want? What’s it worth? What am I worth, Aurelia? What’s the going rate for your little sister these days?”

“A letter,” said Aurelia. “From Chen Si. To the man who killed his father. Asking him for a favour.”

Serafina went still.

“And a party,” said Aurelia. “At Christmas. At the Peak. In gold. And a smile.”

The garage was very quiet. Somewhere far off, another train was coming.

“You haven’t told him,” said Serafina.

“No.”

“Why not?”

Aurelia looked at her sister across the concrete floor.

“Because he’d write it,” she said. “He’d write the letter. He told me so. If it was what I wanted, he’d write to Fu Jianguo and ask him for a favour and put his name at the bottom, for me. He’d do it tomorrow.” Her voice cracked. “And he would never, ever forgive himself. And I would never forgive myself. And she knows that. That’s why she chose it. She knows he’d do it for me. She knows it would kill him. She wants me to be the one who asks.”

Serafina stared at her.

“And so you came here,” she said slowly. “To ask me. If I’d rather go to prison.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “I came here to tell you what she’d done. Because you have a right to know. Because I was wrong not to tell you on Wednesday.” She lifted her chin. “And to tell you that I am not going to ask him. And I am not going to let her send you anywhere.”

“How?”

“I don’t know yet,” said Aurelia. “I’ll find out.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The train went over. The garage shook. A spanner fell off a shelf somewhere and clanged on the concrete.

Serafina looked at her sister and wiped her hands on a rag, slowly, finger by finger.

Then she went to the workbench and picked up the kettle.

“Tea,” she said, roughly. “You look like death. And I have something to show you.”

She made tea in two mugs, one of which said WORLD’S OKAYEST MECHANIC, which Aurelia did not comment on. She gave Aurelia the other one. Then she went to a filing cabinet in the corner, a battered grey one with a broken drawer, and pulled the broken drawer out with a jerk, and took out a folder, and dropped it on the workbench.

“Open it,” she said.

Aurelia opened it.

It was receipts.

Bank transfers. Invoices. Statements from a sponsorship account at a bank in Luxembourg. Every month, for two years. For parts. Tyres. Engines. The rent on the garage under the railway bridge. The entry fees for the legal races, the real ones, at the circuit in the north of the province, that Serafina had been entering under a false name since the spring. A new gearbox from Germany. A transporter. Fuel.

Thousands. Tens of thousands. Hundreds of thousands, over two years.

All of it from the same account.

AS Holdings. Luxembourg.

Aurelia looked at the folder.

She did not look up.

“I found them in August,” said Serafina. “I went to the bank. In person. I wanted to know who my anonymous sponsor was. They wouldn’t tell me. So I paid a man in the industrial district who used to work for a bank in Luxembourg to find out.” She folded her arms. “AS, Aurelia. Aurelia Song. You’ve been paying for everything. For two years. Since the night I walked out of that dinner and you stood at the top of the stairs and didn’t say anything.”

Aurelia closed the folder.

“I didn’t want you to know,” she said.

“Why not?”

“Because you’d have stopped taking it.”

“Damn right I would.” Serafina’s voice was shaking. “I don’t need your money. I don’t need anyone’s money. I left so I wouldn’t need anyone’s money.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “That’s why I didn’t tell you.” She looked up. “You left. I didn’t. I stood at the top of the stairs and watched you go and I didn’t say anything, because Mamma was at the bottom, and I was afraid. And afterwards I thought, I can’t go with her, I can’t be brave like that, but I can do this. I can make sure she never has to come back. I can make sure the only thing she ever has to need is a gearbox.” Her voice broke. “It was the only brave thing I knew how to do.”

Serafina stared at her.

Then she put her mug down on the workbench, very hard, so that the tea slopped over, and crossed the garage in three long strides, and put her arms round her sister, oil and all, and held on.

“You idiot,” she said into Aurelia’s hair. “You gilded idiot.”

“I know.”

“I named the car after you,” said Serafina, muffled. “The black one. In the middle. I didn’t know it was you, I just—I called it Gilded. Because it’s fast and beautiful and impossible to live with.” She laughed, wetly. “I was going to tell you one day. As an insult.”

Aurelia laughed too. It came out of her like the bark, the one from the balcony, and then it turned into something else, and the two of them stood in the middle of a garage under a railway bridge in the industrial district at midnight and held on to each other while a train went over and shook the whole world.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning, with the tea gone cold and the folder between them on the workbench, Serafina said:

“The legal races. At the circuit in the north.”

Aurelia looked up.

“I’ve been entering under a false name since March,” said Serafina. “Because if I raced under my own, Mamma would find out, and someone would get hurt. But I’m good. I’m really good. I came second in the provincial championship in September.” She made a face. “Second. I know. Don’t say it.”

Aurelia didn’t say it.

“There’s a final race of the season. December. The twenty-first. If I win it, I get a licence. A real one. National. I can race anywhere. Legally.” She looked at her sister. “If I’m a licensed national driver with a team and a sponsor and my name in the papers, it’s a lot harder to send me to prison for three years for something I did on a road in the industrial district two years ago. Li Zhenhua would look like what he is. A man with a grudge.” She paused. “But I’d need to race under my own name. And I’d need a real sponsor. Not an account in Luxembourg. A name. On the car.”

Aurelia looked at her sister and did the sum, and found, for once, that she liked the answer.

“AURELIA,” she said slowly.

“On the bonnet,” said Serafina. “In gold. Where Mamma will see it.”

Aurelia began, very slowly, to smile.

“The twenty-first of December,” she said. “That’s four days before the Christmas party.”

“I know,” said Serafina. “I checked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went home at four in the morning, with oil on her coat.

He was awake. Of course he was. He was sitting on the long grey sofa in the dark, with the harbour behind him, with a cup of coffee he hadn’t drunk, waiting.

She sat down beside him. She took his hand.

“I can tell you now,” she said.

And she did. All of it. The photograph. Her mother. Li Zhenhua. The letter, and the party, and the smile. The folder of receipts. AS Holdings. A black car called Gilded.

He listened without interrupting. When she had finished, he was quiet.

“You didn’t tell me,” he said finally, “because you knew I’d write the letter.”

“Yes.”

He looked at the harbour.

“You’re right,” said Chen Si. “I would have.” He was quiet. “I would have written it on Wednesday night, and sent it on Thursday, and never told you it hurt.”

“I know.”

He turned his head and looked at her.

“Thank you,” he said, “for not letting me.”

She put her head on his shoulder, in her oily coat.

He lifted it again with two fingers under her chin, the way he had once at her counter, and looked at her face in the light from the harbour. There was a black smear of engine oil along her cheekbone. He wiped it away with his thumb, slowly, and then looked at his thumb.

“Last time it was pencil,” he said.

“Last time you didn’t kiss me afterwards.”

“I was being strategic,” said Chen Si, and kissed her, oil and all, and then put her head back on his shoulder himself, as if it belonged there and he had only borrowed it.

“The twenty-first,” she said. “The circuit in the north. Will you come?”

“Will you?” said Chen Si. “You hate cars. You told me. You get sick in the back of them.”

“I’ll be in the stands,” said Aurelia. “Front row. In gold.” She closed her eyes. “Where she can see me.”

chapters.title: The Racing Team She Pretends Not to Fund
chapters.desc: Six weeks to make Team AURELIA real. A gold logo on a black bonnet. A watch from Geneva in a box on Fu Kang’s table. And a mechanic who thinks the designer is a joke, until she rebuilds the sponsorship deck in a night.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t pretend to fund it any more.” “No. Now I pretend I’m not terrified.”
chapters.content:
It took six weeks.

She would remember them afterwards as the six busiest weeks of her life, and among the happiest, which surprised her. She had three things to do and she did all three at once, the way she had once read four ledgers at a basement table and found half a million euros: by not stopping.

The first thing was the watch.

The old man in Geneva was called Monsieur Aubert. He was seventy-four. He had made four watches a year for fifty-one years, entirely by hand, in a workshop above a bakery in the old town, and he had known her grandmother in 1968, when she had come to Geneva with her first husband to buy a watch and had argued with Monsieur Aubert’s father for two hours about the finishing on a balance cock, and won.

Aurelia rang him on the fourth of November.

“Mademoiselle Song,” he said, in French, when she had explained who she was. “Your grandmother was the only customer my father was ever afraid of.” A pause. “What do you need?”

She told him.

Not all of it. Enough. A young man in Macau who bought rare watches through a dealer with no other customers. A watch, the rarest in the world, offered to that dealer, quietly, as if by accident. A sale. Paid for in the young man’s usual way.

Monsieur Aubert did not answer at once.

“You want me to sell a watch,” he said finally, “to a crook.”

“I want you to sell a watch to a crook,” said Aurelia, “so that I can find out where the crook keeps his money. And then I want you to never see the money. It will go into an account in my name, and stay there, and I will send you back the full price from my own account the same day. You’ll be paid twice. Once by me, and once, on paper, by him.” She paused. “And at the end of it, his father will sign a bridge that will save ambulances eighteen minutes on the way to a hospital.”

Another long silence.

“Your grandmother,” said Monsieur Aubert, “would have done exactly the same thing.” He sighed. “I have one watch. Finished in September. A minute repeater with a tourbillon and a moon phase, in white gold. The client who ordered it died in August. I have not offered it to anyone else.” A pause. “It is the best thing I have ever made. I will want it back, Mademoiselle. When you are finished with your crook.”

“You’ll have it back,” said Aurelia. “I promise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The second thing was the sponsorship.

She thought it would be easy. She had built a jewellery label from nothing at twenty. She had a second boutique and a waiting list and an auction in Geneva in two weeks with Numero Uno in it. She thought a racing team would be simpler than a boutique.

It was not.

Serafina’s team was four people. Serafina. A mechanic called Big Wu, who was forty and enormous and had been in prison twice for things he would not discuss. A girl called Mouse, who was nineteen and did the electronics and the data and had a ring in her nose and did not speak to anyone except Serafina. And a man called Mr. Kwok, who was sixty-eight and had driven taxis for forty years and now drove the transporter and made everyone’s lunch.

They looked at Aurelia, the first day she came to the garage under the railway bridge in a cream suit and heels, the way the men on the thirty-ninth floor had looked at her.

“So this is the gilded bird,” said Big Wu.

“This is my sister,” said Serafina. “She’s paid your wages for two years.”

Big Wu looked at Aurelia’s heels.

“Can she change a tyre?”

“No,” said Aurelia. “Can you read a sponsorship contract?”

Big Wu stared at her.

“Neither can Serafina,” said Aurelia. “I’ve seen the one she signed with the tyre company in June. They’re paying her in tyres. Only tyres. For three years. In exchange for exclusive rights to her image, worldwide, in perpetuity.” She put her bag down on the workbench, next to the kettle. “Which means if she becomes famous, they own her face. Forever. For tyres.”

The garage went quiet.

Serafina went white.

“What?”

“Page eleven,” said Aurelia. “Clause fourteen. In very small print. I found it last night.” She took off her jacket and hung it on a hook next to Big Wu’s overalls. “I’m going to fix it. And then I’m going to rebuild the whole deck. Every sponsor, every logo, every clause. And then we’re going to make Team AURELIA real. With a name, and a budget, and a licence application, and a press release.” She looked at Big Wu. “And you’re going to teach me how to change a tyre. Because if my name is going on that car, I’m going to know what’s inside it.”

Big Wu looked at her.

Then he picked up a wheel brace and held it out.

✦ ✦ ✦

She learned to change a tyre in fourteen minutes.

By the end of the week, she could do it in four. By the end of the second week, Mouse had started speaking to her, in single words, about telemetry. By the end of the third week, Mr. Kwok was making her lunch with everyone else’s, and putting extra chilli in it, because he had noticed she liked it.

She rebuilt the sponsorship deck in a night.

She sat on the floor of the garage at two in the morning, under the hanging lamp, in Big Wu’s spare overalls with the sleeves rolled up and a pencil behind her ear, with her laptop on a tyre and Serafina asleep on the back seat of Gilded, and she went through every contract Serafina had ever signed and every sponsor she had ever talked to and every team in the national championship and what they were paid and by whom, and at some point after four, without her hearing a thing, someone laid a camel coat over her shoulders and set a paper cup of hot soy milk on the tyre beside her laptop. Under the cup, on a torn corner of cream paper, in a small precise hand: Drink this. I didn’t. — C.S. She drank it. She pulled the coat closed. She did not look up from clause fourteen of a tyre contract, because if she had, she would have gone after him; and at six o’clock in the morning she woke her sister up and showed her.

Forty pages. Logos. Numbers. A budget for a full national season. A list of eleven companies, every one of them a luxury brand, every one of them one that Aurelia knew someone at, who would want their name on a car driven by a twenty-one-year-old woman who had walked out of her own engagement and now raced under her own name, sponsored by her sister, in gold.

“It’s a story,” said Aurelia. “That’s what they’re buying. Not a car. A story. Two sisters from Milan. The one who left and the one who stayed. The gilded bird and the mechanic.” She tapped the screen. “They’ll pay for that. All of them. They’ll pay for it because it’s true.”

Serafina sat in the back seat of Gilded and looked at forty pages on a laptop.

“You did this tonight,” she said. “Why?”

Aurelia looked at her sister, rumpled and oily and half-asleep in the back of a car with her name on it.

“Because I’m good at this,” she said. “Because I can read a contract and count tiles. Nonna said those were the only two things a woman needed.” She smiled. “And because I don’t want to pretend I’m not funding you any more. I want everyone to know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The third thing was Fu Kang.

The watch went to the dealer in Macau on the twentieth of November. Through a broker in Hong Kong who had worked with Monsieur Aubert for thirty years and asked no questions. The dealer rang Fu Kang the same afternoon. Mr. Lu, who had a nephew who worked in the café opposite the watch shop, reported that Fu Kang arrived in Macau the next morning, by helicopter, and spent forty minutes in the shop, and came out without the watch, but with an expression, the nephew said, of a man in love.

The money moved on the twenty-sixth.

Aurelia watched it move.

She sat at her bench in the workshop at the back of the boutique at eleven at night, with Chen Si on the stool where women sat to try on rings, and Qian with a laptop, and Mr. Lu in his cardigan with a cup of tea he didn’t drink, and they watched the money go. From the watch shop. To a company in Macau. To a company in the British Virgin Islands. To a company in Hong Kong. To a trust in Liechtenstein. To an account in Singapore. And from there, at last, to the account Aurelia had set up for Monsieur Aubert, in Geneva, under her own name.

She followed it all the way back.

It took four hours.

At three in the morning, Qian sat back from his laptop and took off his glasses and rubbed his eyes and said, “There.”

On the screen, at the top of a chain of seven companies, there was a name. A trust in Liechtenstein. The settlor of the trust was a company in Hong Kong. The sole director of the company in Hong Kong was a lawyer who had once, eleven years ago, been at university with a young man called Fu Kang. And the beneficiary of the trust, the person whose money it really was, in the one document Qian had found that no one had thought anyone would ever look for, was named.

Fu Kang.

And underneath that, the second beneficiary.

Fu Jianguo.

Nobody in the workshop said anything.

Then Mr. Lu put his tea down on Enzo’s bench, very carefully, and said, “Mrs. Chen. I have been a pawnbroker for thirty-one years. I have never seen anything so beautiful.”

Chen Si didn’t say anything at all.

He was looking at the screen. At the second name. Fu Jianguo.

His face had gone very still and very far away.

Aurelia put her hand on his knee.

He didn’t move. Then his hand came down and covered hers, and held it, so hard it hurt.

“That,” he said, very low, “is not his son’s money. That’s his.”

“Yes.”

“He’s the beneficiary. Him. In his own name. On a document.” His voice didn’t change at all. “Nine years. I’ve never once found his name on anything.” He looked at her. “You found it in six weeks. With a watch.”

“Mr. Lu found it,” said Aurelia. “And Qian. And Monsieur Aubert. And a nephew in a café.” She turned her hand over under his. “I just sold a watch.”

“You have never just done anything,” said Chen Si, so low that only she heard it. Under the bench, where Qian and Mr. Lu could not see, his foot found her ankle and stayed there.

“Clause five,” he said. “His name on a document. That’s my prior claim. I won’t use it yet.”

“I know.”

“You use it,” said Chen Si. “For the bridge. For your father. Have lunch with Fu Kang. Show him the son’s name. Don’t show him the father’s.” His thumb moved on her wrist. “Keep the father’s name for me. In your safe. Under the Geneva pieces.”

“For the hall,” said Aurelia. “At six in the morning.”

He nodded once, and did not let go of her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had lunch with Fu Kang at Da Gianni on the third of December.

She booked the table by the window. She wore gold. She ordered the risotto.

Fu Kang was handsome and idle and wore the white gold minute repeater on his wrist, and he flirted with her for twenty minutes, because he did not know who she was married to, which told her a great deal about how much his father told him. At the end of twenty minutes she slid a folder across the white tablecloth and watched him open it.

She watched him read.

She watched him find his own name, at the top of a chain of seven companies, beside a watch shop in Macau with one customer, beside fifteen per cent of eleven contracts, beside a bridge.

She watched him go white.

“The vice-minister’s signature,” said Aurelia pleasantly, “on the Harbour Bridge Two file. By the twentieth of December. No fifteen per cent. No company in Macau. No conditions.” She picked up her fork. “If it’s there, this folder stays in my safe forever, and nobody ever sees it. If it isn’t, on the twenty-first it goes to the anti-corruption commission, and to three newspapers, and to a man called Li Zhenhua, who I believe your father owes money.”

Fu Kang stared at her.

“Who are you?” he whispered.

Aurelia smiled at him across the risotto.

“I’m the designer,” she said. “I make jewellery.” She looked at his wrist. “That’s a very beautiful watch, by the way. Monsieur Aubert will want it back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The signature came on the nineteenth.

It came by fax, at four in the afternoon, to the Song Group offices, where her father was sitting at his desk. He rang her at 4:07. He couldn’t speak for the first minute. When he could, he said only, “Tesoro. It’s signed. Fu signed it. No conditions. Nothing.” And then, “Was it you?”

“It was the bridge, Papà,” said Aurelia. “It was always a good bridge.”

She heard him breathe out, a long way off, at his desk.

“Your grandfather,” he said finally, “would have been very proud.”

She put the phone down.

She sat at her bench in the workshop.

Then she took the white gold minute repeater out of the box on the bench in front of her, where it had arrived that morning by courier from Macau in a plain brown envelope with no note, and wound it, and pressed the slide.

It chimed the time. Four low notes for the hours. One double note for the quarter. Then the minutes, high and quick. Twelve. Clear and soft and perfect, like water falling on glass.

She packed it in tissue and sent it back to Geneva, to a workshop above a bakery, with a note.

Thank you. It did exactly what it was made to do. — A.

Two days later, she put on every piece of gold she owned and sat in the front row of the grandstand at the circuit in the north of the province, in the cold, beside her husband, and watched her sister race.

chapters.title: Sisters at a Racetrack
chapters.desc: The final race of the season. A black car with a gold name on the bonnet. A grandstand in the cold. Aurelia, who gets sick in the back of taxis, watches her sister drive at two hundred kilometres an hour, and does not look away once.
chapters.epigraph: “Don’t watch the car. Watch the gap. The car goes where the gap is.” — Serafina Song
chapters.content:
She had never been to a motor race in her life.

She had been to fashion shows and auctions and the opera and the races at Happy Valley, where the horses were. She had been to a polo match in Argentina, once, with her father, and fallen asleep. She had never stood in a grandstand on a cold December morning in the north of the province and listened to twenty-four engines start at once.

It went through her like a hand through water.

She grabbed the rail in front of her. Beside her, Chen Si did not move at all, but his hand came down over hers on the rail and stayed there.

“That,” said Aurelia, over the noise, “is obscene.”

“Your sister’s is the loudest,” said Chen Si.

She looked down the pit lane. Twenty-four cars, in rows, on the grid, under a white sky. Red ones, blue ones, silver ones, covered in logos. And in the fourth row, low and long and matte black, with the number 7 on its side in white and, across its bonnet, in gold, in the same serif letters that were painted over the door of 18 Harbour Road, a single word.

AURELIA.

She had seen it in the garage. She had seen it on the transporter. She had seen the proofs of it on her laptop at two in the morning. She had not seen it here, on the grid, under a white sky, with eleven thousand people in the grandstand and cameras everywhere and her sister in the cockpit with her helmet on.

Her eyes stung. She told herself it was the cold.

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina had come to the grandstand before the race, at nine, in her fireproof suit with the top half tied round her waist and her helmet under her arm. She had looked at her sister in the front row in gold, every piece she owned, in a white coat with fur at the collar, with her husband beside her in camel, and she had laughed out loud.

“You look,” she said, “like you came to buy the circuit.”
