“I might,” said Aurelia. “Later.”

Serafina looked at Chen Si.

He looked back at her. They had met twice, at the wedding and once at the garage, and they had said perhaps forty words to each other in total, and none of them had been warm.

“Mr. Chen,” said Serafina.

“Miss Song.”

“If she throws up,” said Serafina, “hold her hair.”

“I will.”

“And don’t let her look away at the start. She’ll want to. Everybody does the first time.” She looked at her sister. “Don’t watch the car, Lia. Watch the gap. The car goes where the gap is.”

She hadn’t called her Lia since they were children.

Aurelia couldn’t answer. She nodded.

Serafina went back down to the pit lane, and put on her helmet, and got into a black car with her sister’s name on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twenty laps.

The lights went out, and the noise was the noise of the end of the world, and twenty-four cars went down the long straight toward the first corner like something poured, and Aurelia did not look away.

She wanted to. Serafina had been right. Every part of her body wanted to close its eyes. The cars were too close together. The corner was too tight. They were going too fast. Somewhere in the middle of that river of red and blue and silver was a black car with her name on it and her sister inside it, and if anything went wrong, if anyone touched anyone, if a tyre went, if—

Don’t watch the car. Watch the gap.

She watched the gap.

She saw it open, at the first corner, on the inside, between a red car and the kerb. Less than a car’s width. She saw it a second before anyone else in the grandstand, because she was looking for it, and her whole body went cold, and she thought no, Sera, no, it’s too small—

The black car went through it.

Like a needle. Like a thread through a loupe. Through a gap that wasn’t a gap, on the inside, two wheels on the kerb, and out the other side, and she was fourth, and then third, and the grandstand made a sound like an animal, and Aurelia realised she had stopped breathing and that she was gripping Chen Si’s hand on the rail so hard that her rings were cutting into his fingers. He did not take his hand away. That night she would find four small red crescents across his knuckles, and he would refuse to let her put anything on them, and she would catch him, twice, looking at them.

He hadn’t said anything.

She looked at him.

He was watching the track with an expression she had seen only once before: on the night of the counter-offer, when she had made him tell her his own number in four minutes.

“She’s very good,” said Chen Si.

“She’s insane.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “That’s what very good means.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She was third for eleven laps.

Second for six.

On lap eighteen, coming out of the long right-hander at the far end of the circuit, the car in first place, a silver one with a Japanese logo, went wide by a metre, and the black car with the gold name on its bonnet was already there, in the space it had left, as if it had known before the silver car did.

First.

Aurelia didn’t hear the grandstand. She didn’t hear anything. She stood at the rail in the front row in the cold with every piece of gold she owned on and watched her sister drive the last two laps of the season in first place, alone, nothing in front of her but grey tarmac and white sky, and she didn’t look away once.

The black car crossed the line.

The flag came down.

And Aurelia Chen, who did not cry in public, who had walked out of her father’s dining room with her chin up and sat in the head chair of a criminal empire and told her mother no in front of three maids and a silver coffee pot, stood in the front row of the grandstand at the circuit in the north and sobbed out loud, with both hands over her mouth, while eleven thousand people shouted her sister’s name.

Chen Si turned her into his chest and held her there while she cried, one hand spread in her hair, in front of eleven thousand people and every camera at the circuit, as if none of them existed.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t need to.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, on the podium, in the cold, Serafina stood on the top step with a trophy in one hand and a magnum of champagne in the other and her short hair standing up in sweaty spikes, and looked out over the crowd.

Then she found her sister in the front row, and pointed the champagne at her, and shouted something that nobody could hear over the noise, and sprayed it.

Most of it went over the photographers.

Some of it went over Aurelia’s white coat with the fur at the collar.

She didn’t care.

She stood in the front row with champagne in her hair, laughing, and looked up at her sister on the podium, and that was the photograph that went on the front of the sports pages the next morning, and the business pages, and, three weeks later, in Milan, on page one hundred and four of Italian Vogue.

SORELLE, said the headline. Sisters.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother was there.

Aurelia saw her as they came out of the grandstand. In the VIP lounge above the pit lane, behind glass, in black. Standing at the window, alone, with a glass of something in her hand, looking down at the podium. At the black car parked below it with the gold name on its bonnet.

Beside her, not quite next to her, stood a heavy grey-haired man in a dark suit with the face of someone who had been made a fool of and was trying to work out by whom.

“Li Zhenhua,” said Chen Si.

“She brought him,” said Aurelia. “She brought him to watch. So that he’d see Sera, and know her face, and know her car.” She looked up at the glass. “So that on the second of January, when the photograph arrives, he’d know exactly who it was.”

Chen Si looked up at the VIP lounge.

“Wait here,” he said.

“Chen Si—”

“I’m not going to do anything,” said Chen Si mildly. “I’m going to say hello.”

He went.

✦ ✦ ✦

She watched through the glass.

She couldn’t hear. She saw her husband walk into the VIP lounge, in his camel coat, with his hands in his pockets, and stop beside Li Zhenhua, and say something. She saw Li Zhenhua turn and look at him, and the colour go out of his face, all at once, the way it went out of everyone’s face. She saw her mother turn round at the window.

She saw Chen Si say something else. Briefly. Pleasantly. A few words.

She saw Li Zhenhua put his glass down on the windowsill, very carefully, and nod, twice, quickly, the way a man nods when he wants a conversation to be over.

She saw Chen Si turn to her mother.

She saw her mother look at him. Black silk. Diamonds. Perfect face. She saw her mother lift her chin, the way Aurelia lifted hers.

She saw Chen Si say one sentence.

And then he turned round and walked out of the VIP lounge and came back down the stairs to her, and took her arm, and walked her toward the car park, as if nothing had happened at all.

“What did you say?” said Aurelia.

“To Li Zhenhua? I said congratulations. His nephew in the traffic division has been promoted. To a post in the far west of the province. It’s a very good post. Lots of fresh air. It starts on the first of January.” He opened the car door for her. “He was very grateful.”

She stared at him.

“And to my mother?”

Chen Si was quiet for a moment.

“I said,” he said, “that I had read clause eight of my marriage contract on the way here, to make sure I remembered it correctly. And that I would not say what it was, because she would recognise it.” He looked at her. “And that if she ever sent a photograph of either of her daughters to anyone, ever again, I would stop being polite.”

Aurelia sat down in the car rather hard.

“Either,” she said.

“Serafina,” said Chen Si, “and you.” He got in beside her. “Your mother has two daughters. I married into both of them.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Serafina came to the car before they left.

She was still in her fireproof suit, with the top tied round her waist, and champagne in her hair, and the trophy, which she hadn’t put down. She leaned in at Aurelia’s window.

“Did you watch the gap?” she said.

“I saw it before you went for it,” said Aurelia. “At the first corner. I thought you were going to die.”

“I thought so too,” said Serafina cheerfully. “Big Wu says I’m not allowed to do that again until I have a contract with a life insurance clause.” She looked past her sister, at Chen Si, sitting in the back of the car in his camel coat. “Mr. Chen. You went to see my mother. What did you say?”

Chen Si looked at her for a moment.

“Something she didn’t want to hear,” he said.

Serafina looked at him. Then she held out her hand. Not to shake. Palm up. Covered in oil and champagne and rubber.

He looked at it.

Then he took his hand out of his pocket and laid it flat on hers. His left hand. With the thin white line across the palm.

She looked down at the line. She looked up at him.

“Zhao Zhendong has one of those,” she said. “My sister told me what it means.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

Serafina was quiet for a moment.

“Then I don’t need to cut mine,” she said roughly, and closed her hand round his, once, hard, and let go, and went back to her car.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the back of the car, on the long drive south, in the dark, with the motorway lights going over them one after another, Aurelia put her head on his shoulder.

“I didn’t throw up,” she said. “I nearly did. At the first corner.”

“I know. I had my hand ready for your hair.” He turned his head and kissed her hair, which smelled of champagne. “You didn’t close your eyes once. I watched.”

She was quiet for a few miles.

“Si. The Christmas party. At the Peak. On the twenty-fifth.” She lifted her head. “My mother said I had to come. In gold. With you. And smile.” She looked at him in the passing lights. “That was the price. For not sending the photograph.”

“The photograph’s gone. You don’t have to go.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. She lifted her chin. “I want to go.”

He looked at her.

“In gold,” said Aurelia. “With you. And I want to smile.” She settled back against his shoulder. “Because I’ll be the only person in that house who knows that she lost. And I want to watch her know it too.”

He laughed in the dark.

“My queen,” he said.

“Don’t,” said Aurelia. “Not yet. Save it.”

“For what?”

“For the party,” said Aurelia. “I want you to say it there. Out loud. In front of everyone.”

chapters.title: My Queen Is Not a Title
chapters.desc: Christmas at the Peak. Two hundred guests, her mother in black, the vice-minister by the fire. Chen Si says two words out loud in front of the people who matter. Then, upstairs, in the room she grew up in, he makes her watch.
chapters.epigraph: “My queen.” It wasn’t a title. It was a warning, addressed to everyone in the room at once.
chapters.content:
The house on the Peak at Christmas was always the same.

A tree in the hall, eight metres tall, flown in from Austria, decorated entirely in white and silver by a designer from Milan who came every year for a week and was never allowed to change anything. Candles in every window. A string quartet in the music room. Two hundred guests. Champagne from her mother’s cousin’s vineyard in Franciacorta. The same caterers, the same lobster, the same cake, the same faces.

The only thing that was different this year was that Aurelia Chen came through the front door at eight o’clock on her husband’s arm, in gold, and every person in the hall stopped talking.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had made the dress herself.

Not designed it. Made it. With her own hands, at the bench, every night for five weeks after the garage closed, with Enzo standing behind her saying things in Italian that she ignored. It was not silk. It was gold. Thousands of tiny links of yellow gold, each one smaller than a grain of rice, woven together by hand into a fabric so fine and so flexible that it moved like water, like liquid, like the gold silk she had worn on the night of the balcony, except that it weighed four kilos and caught every light in the room and threw it back, so that when she walked, she shone.

It had taken five weeks of nights and nine hundred hours of work, most of it Enzo’s and two bench hands he had summoned from Valenza, and every franc the Geneva auction had paid her in November, including the price of Numero Uno.

It was, the man from Vogue would write in February, having seen a single photograph, the most beautiful dress made in Asia in this century.

She walked through the hall of her mother’s house in it.

She did not look for her mother. She did not need to. She could feel her, somewhere, the way you feel a draught.

✦ ✦ ✦

They found each other in the music room, by the fire.

Vittoria Song was in black. She was always in black. She was standing with the wife of an ambassador and the man who had designed the opera house, who was sober this year, and she turned when the room changed around her, the way it always did when Aurelia came in, and she looked at her daughter.

At the dress.

She looked at it and did not speak.

Aurelia watched her mother’s face. She had watched it for twenty-three years. She knew every movement it could make.

She had never seen it do this.

It didn’t go cold. It didn’t go still. It didn’t smile its Vogue smile. For one second, in front of the fire in her own music room, Vittoria Conti, who had walked runways in Paris and Milan and had made a buyer from Bergdorf Goodman cry, looked at the dress her daughter had made with her own hands from the gold of everything she had ever sold, and her face showed exactly what she felt.

Aurelia had expected anger.

It was grief.

Then it was gone.

“Tesoro,” said her mother. “You came.”

“You asked me to,” said Aurelia. “In gold. And smile.” She smiled. “Here I am.”

Her mother looked at her for a moment longer. Then at Chen Si beside her.

“Mr. Chen,” she said.

“Mrs. Song,” said Chen Si.

The ambassador’s wife, who knew nothing, said brightly, “What a beautiful dress. Who made it?”

“I did,” said Aurelia.

The ambassador’s wife laughed, as if she had made a joke.

Vittoria Song did not laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Fu Jianguo was by the fire in the drawing room.

She had known he would be. He came every year. He was a vice-minister and her father was the Song Group and every year at Christmas he stood by the fire in the drawing room with a glass of her mother’s cousin’s champagne and people came to him, one by one, the way people came to a bishop.

He was sixty-one. Grey. Thin. Very ordinary. A soft face and rimless glasses and a cardigan under his suit jacket, like a retired teacher. Like Mr. Lu. If you passed him on the street you would not look twice.

She saw Chen Si see him.

She felt it go through her husband, standing beside her in the doorway of the drawing room. Nothing visible. Nothing anyone else would have noticed. His face did not change. His hand on her arm did not tighten. He simply went still, all through, the way he went still over the list with nineteen names on it, and for a moment he did not breathe.

“You don’t have to,” said Aurelia.

“I know,” said Chen Si.

He walked into the room.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did not go to Fu.

That was the thing she would remember. He walked into the drawing room with her on his arm in four kilos of gold, and the room parted, the way rooms did, and he walked straight past the fire. Past Fu Jianguo. Close enough that Fu had to step back half a pace to let them by. And he did not look at him.

He went to the window at the far end of the room, where her father was standing with three men from the bank and the head of the port authority and the man who owned the biggest television channel in the province, and her father turned, and saw them, and his face lit up.

“Tesoro,” said Song Weiren. “Chen Si.” He took his son-in-law’s hand in both of his. “I wanted to thank you. Both of you. The bridge—”

“Don’t thank me,” said Chen Si. “I didn’t do anything.”

“But—”

“I didn’t write a letter,” said Chen Si. His voice was mild and pleasant and pitched, very precisely, to carry. To the men from the bank. To the head of the port authority. To the owner of the television channel. To the fire, at the other end of the room, where a grey man in rimless glasses was standing very still with a glass in his hand. “I didn’t make a call. I didn’t speak to anyone at the ministry.” He turned and looked at Aurelia, beside him, in her gold. “My wife did that. All of it. By herself.”

The men from the bank looked at Aurelia.

The head of the port authority looked at Aurelia.

“In my house,” said Chen Si, “and in my business, and in this city, when my wife speaks, she speaks for me. She doesn’t need my name. She has her own.” He lifted her hand, the one with the heavy gold ring made from her grandmother’s earrings, and kissed it, once, in front of all of them. “She is my queen.”

He said it clearly. Not to her. To the room.

It was not a title. Everybody in the room understood that at once. It was not a compliment, or an endearment, or a joke. It was a statement of fact, and a line drawn on the floor, and a warning, addressed to every single person within earshot, and most particularly to one grey man by the fire.

This woman is mine. And I am hers. Touch her, and you touch me.

Nobody said anything.

Then her father, who had said no to Fu Jianguo in March for a man who sold watches from a suitcase, put his hand on his son-in-law’s shoulder and squeezed it, once, hard, and said, “Thank you.”

And at the other end of the room, by the fire, Fu Jianguo put his glass down on the mantelpiece, and walked out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother found her at ten, on the landing, at the top of the stairs.

The same landing. The same stairs. Where she had stood three years ago, at twenty, and watched Serafina walk out of the front door and said nothing, because their mother was at the bottom.

Vittoria Song stood at the bottom.

She looked up at her elder daughter in her dress of gold.

“You made it,” she said. “The dress. Yourself. With your hands.”

“Yes.”

“From the auction. From the necklace.” Her mother’s voice was very quiet. “Numero Uno.”

“Yes.”

Vittoria looked up at her.

“I sat in the front row of the show where your grandmother wore her last gown,” she said. “In Milan. In 1966. I was six weeks old, on my nurse’s knee. My mother used to tell me about it. The gown was by Valentino. It was the most beautiful thing anyone had ever seen.” She was quiet. “It was not as beautiful as that.”

Aurelia stood very still on the landing.

“I wanted to be a designer,” said Vittoria Song. “When I was your age. My father said it was for shopgirls. He said a Conti did not make things. A Conti was seen in things.” She looked at her daughter’s dress. “So I was seen. For twenty years. On every runway in Europe.” Her voice didn’t change at all. “I never once made anything.”

She turned and walked away down the hall, in black, toward the music room, where the quartet was playing, and did not look back.

Aurelia stood on the landing in four kilos of gold and held on to the banister, because her legs had stopped working.

She didn’t know how long she stood there.

When she looked up, Chen Si was at the top of the stairs behind her. He had heard. Of course he had. The doors in that house were glass.

He held out his hand.

“Show me your room,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her room was at the end of the east corridor.

It had not been changed since she was eighteen. A white room. White furniture from Milan. White curtains. A white piano that she had not touched since Vienna. Shelves of trophies and medals and certificates and framed rankings, every one of them first. Every single one. 1st. 1st. Winner. 1st Place. In gold frames, in rows, from floor to ceiling, from the age of five to the age of seventeen. The only thing missing from those shelves was a certificate from her final year at school, that said 2nd.

Her mother had not framed it.

And on the wall opposite the bed, floor to ceiling, a mirror. A long mirror in a gilt frame, from her grandmother’s house in Milan, that Aurelia had stood in front of every morning from fifteen to eighteen, to check that she was perfect before she went downstairs.

Chen Si closed the door behind them.

He looked at the trophies. All of them. Slowly. The way he had looked at her ledgers.

Then he looked at her, standing in the middle of the white room in her dress of gold, in front of the mirror.

“You checked yourself in that every morning,” he said. “Before you went down.”

“Yes.”

“To make sure there was nothing for her to find.”

“Yes.”

He came and stood behind her.

In the mirror, she watched him. Slight and dark and still, in his grey suit, behind her. His hands came up and rested, very lightly, on her shoulders, on the gold.

“Clause nine,” he said.

She looked at him in the glass.

“Otherwise,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Don’t look away,” said Chen Si.

He found the clasp at the back of her neck. The dress fastened there, the way the wedding dress had. When the clasp came undone, everything came undone.

He didn’t undo it.

He put his mouth against the side of her neck, just above it, and kept his eyes on hers in the mirror.

“You looked in this every morning to see if you were good enough,” he said, against her skin. “Tonight you’re going to look in it and watch what you do to me.”

She stopped breathing.

“Don’t close your eyes,” he said. “Not once. If you close them, I stop.” His hand moved, slowly, from her shoulder down her arm, over the gold. “I want you to see it. Every second of it. I want you to see your face when I—”

He told her.

He told her exactly, in a low voice against her ear, what he was going to do, while she watched him in the mirror. And then he did it. Slowly. Without hurrying. With his eyes on hers in the glass the whole time.

She did not close her eyes.

She stood in the white room where she had been perfect every morning for three years, in front of her grandmother’s mirror, in a dress made from everything she had ever sold, with her husband behind her, and she watched. She watched his hands on the gold. She watched his mouth on her neck. She watched her own face change, in the glass, in ways it had never changed in that mirror before: lose its perfection, lose its composure, lose its chin-up and its smile and everything her mother had ever taught it, until the woman in the mirror was flushed and wild-eyed and open-mouthed and not perfect at all, and she had never in her life looked more like herself.

When he finally undid the clasp, four kilos of gold slid off her shoulders and down her body and lay at her feet on her mother’s white carpet in a pool of light, with a sound like rain.

“Look,” said Chen Si, against her ear.

She looked.

“That,” he said, “is what I see. Every day. That is the woman I married. Not the one who was perfect every morning.” His arms came round her from behind. “This one.”

She looked at the woman in the mirror.

She didn’t look away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, on the narrow white bed she had slept in at seventeen, under the shelves of trophies, with the party going on below them, very faintly, the quartet and the voices, she lay on his chest and looked up at all the gold frames.

1st. 1st. Winner. 1st Place.

“She never framed the second,” she said.

“I noticed.”

“I always thought it was because she was ashamed.” She was quiet. “Tonight I thought, maybe she couldn’t bear to look at it. Because it was the only one that was mine. Not hers.” She closed her eyes. “She wanted to be a designer, Si. She never told me. In twenty-three years.”

He didn’t say anything. His hand moved slowly up and down her back.

“I don’t forgive her,” said Aurelia.

“You don’t have to.”

“I don’t. Not for Vienna. Not for the nine days. Not for the party. Not for Sera.” She opened her eyes. “But I understand her now. A little. And I hate that.”

“I know,” said Chen Si.

She lifted her head and looked at him.

“You said it,” she said. “Downstairs. In front of everyone. In front of him.”

“It isn’t a title,” said Chen Si. “I wanted him to know that. I wanted them all to know.” He touched her face. “A title is something you’re given. You can lose it. It can be taken away. They can come at six in the morning and take it down the stairs.” His voice went very low. “Nobody gave you this. You took it. You sat in my chair.”

She looked at him.

Then she put her head back down on his chest.

On the floor by the long mirror, the dress lay in its pool of gold. On the shelves above them, the trophies shone in their frames. Below them, very faintly, her mother’s quartet played something by Puccini, and two hundred people drank her mother’s cousin’s champagne, and talked about the Song girl’s dress, and her husband, and the vice-minister who had walked out.

Aurelia lay in the white room where she had been perfect and fell asleep, for the first time in that house in her whole life, without checking the mirror first.

chapters.title: A Snake in the Syndicate
chapters.desc: A car on the coast road at two in the morning, and a lorry that shouldn’t be there. Someone inside is selling his schedule. Aurelia knows who. Chen Si knows too, and invites him to dinner.
chapters.epigraph: “Keep your friends close.” “I keep my snakes closer. Then I know which way they’re facing.”
chapters.content:
The lorry was on the coast road at 2:14 in the morning on the twenty-eighth of December, and it should not have been there.

Chen Si was in the back of the car, coming home from a meeting in the east that had gone on too long. Zhao was driving. Zhao always drove, on the coast road, at night. It was the only road from the east into the city that did not go through a tunnel, and Zhao did not like tunnels. He said they had only two ends.

The coast road had a cliff on one side and the sea on the other and a long blind bend above the old fishing harbour at Lantern Bay, and at 2:14 in the morning, as they came round the bend at eighty kilometres an hour, there was a lorry parked across both lanes, sideways, with its lights off.

Zhao saw it at forty metres.

Chen Si would remember, afterwards, that Zhao didn’t brake. Anyone else would have braked. Braking was what the lorry was there for. A car braking hard on a blind bend at eighty would stop, or spin, and either way it would be sitting still in the road, in the dark, in front of a lorry, and whoever was behind the lorry would have all the time in the world.

Zhao didn’t brake.

He dropped two gears and put his foot down and turned the wheel hard to the left, toward the cliff, toward a gap between the front of the lorry and the rock face that was perhaps a car’s width and a half, and went through it with the passenger side scraping along the cliff in a long scream of metal and sparks, and out the other side, and kept going, and did not slow down for four kilometres.

Behind them, in the mirror, Chen Si saw muzzle flashes. Three. Four. Very small. Very far away, very quickly.

Nothing hit.

At the fourth kilometre, Zhao said, “Hm.”

It was the only thing either of them said until they were home.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia was awake.

She was always awake, on the nights he came back late on the coast road. She sat on the long grey sofa with a book she didn’t read and a cup of tea she didn’t drink, and she listened for the lift.

She heard it at 2:51.

She heard his key. She heard his footsteps in the hall, the way she always heard them now. She heard them stop.

Then she heard a second set of footsteps, heavier, and Zhao’s voice, very low, saying something, and the front door closing again.

She put down her book.

Chen Si came into the room.

He was in his camel coat. He was perfectly calm. His tie was straight. His hair was tidy. There was not a mark on him.

His hands were shaking.

She had never once, in fourteen months, seen his hands shake.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her standing in the middle of the room, because he couldn’t sit down. The lorry. The bend. The cliff. The muzzle flashes in the mirror.

She listened without moving.

When he had finished, she got up from the sofa, and went to him, and took both his shaking hands in hers, and held them, hard, until they stopped.

“Who knew you would be on that road,” she said. “Tonight. At two in the morning.” Her voice was very level. “The meeting was arranged on Thursday. You didn’t tell me where it was until this morning. Zhendong always takes the coast road because he hates tunnels. Who knew all three of those things?”

He looked at her.

“Qian,” he said. “Zhendong. You.” A pause. “And whoever was at the meeting on Thursday when it was arranged.”

“Who was at the meeting on Thursday?”

He didn’t answer.

She didn’t need him to. She had been at the meeting on Thursday. On the thirty-ninth floor. At the head of the table, in his chair, which was hers now, at every meeting, while he sat in an office chair at the corner. Five men along the window. The man with the shaved head. The man with the tinted glasses. The man with the sunflower seeds. Mr. Lu, in his cardigan.

And at the end, by the window, with his warm, tired, fatherly smile, Sun Wei.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You knew,” said Aurelia.

They were on the sofa now. He had sat down eventually. She had made him. He was holding a glass of whisky that she had poured for him and put into his hand, and he had drunk half of it, which she had never seen him do.

“Since the furniture,” he said. “Since the basement, in the old town. Since you found the thirty thousand a table.”

“That was fourteen months ago.”

“Yes.”

“You’ve known for fourteen months that Sun Wei was stealing from you. And you let him sit at the table. Every Thursday.” Her voice was very quiet. “You let him call you Si.”

“I wanted to know who he was stealing for,” said Chen Si. “I told you. On the thirty-ninth floor. A man who steals half a million is a thief. A man who steals half a million and smiles at you and calls you a treasure is something else.” He looked at the whisky. “I found out in October. I didn’t tell you.”

“Clause three.”

“I was going to tell you. After Christmas. After the race and the party and your mother. I didn’t want to put it on you as well.” He closed his eyes. “That was wrong. I’m sorry.”

“Who?” said Aurelia.

He opened his eyes.

“Fu Kang,” he said.

She went cold.

“The money from the furniture went to an account in his wife’s family’s district,” said Chen Si. “From there, to a company. From there, to a company in Macau.” A very small, very tired smile. “The same seven companies. You followed them yourself, in your workshop, with a watch. Sun Wei has been paying Fu Kang. For two years. Not for nothing. For information about me.” He drank the rest of the whisky. “And since the third of December, since you had lunch with Fu Kang at Da Gianni and slid a folder across the table, Fu Kang has had a very good reason to want me dead.”

“Me,” said Aurelia. “He wants me dead. I’m the one who had lunch with him.”

“He doesn’t know that.” Chen Si put the empty glass down on the floor. “He thinks you work for me. Everybody does. Except the people in this room, and Zhendong, and your father, and the men on the thirty-ninth floor.” He turned his head and looked at her. “I said it at the Christmas party. She speaks for me. He heard it as I sent her.” He was quiet. “So he sent a lorry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything.

She sat on the sofa in her silk pyjamas and looked at the harbour, and thought about it, the way she thought about everything. A machine. A puzzle. Seven companies, a lorry on a bend, a fatherly smile at the end of a long black table.

“You’re not going to do anything,” she said finally. “Are you.”

“Not yet.”

“Why not?”

“Because if I do anything to Sun Wei now,” said Chen Si, “Fu Kang will know that I know. And he will run to his father. And his father will protect him. And I will have spent nine years building something, and lose it all for a lorry.” He looked at her. “And because Sun Wei is not the only one. A man who sells my schedule for two years has friends. On the thirty-ninth floor. In the routes. I don’t know who they all are. I need to know who they all are.”

“So you’ll wait.”

“So I’ll invite him to dinner,” said Chen Si.

She turned and looked at him.

“There’s a dinner,” he said. “Every year. On New Year’s Eve. On a boat, in the harbour. Everyone who matters in the Syndicate. The men from the thirty-ninth floor. The men who run the docks for Zhendong. The judges who are ours. Sun Wei has organised it for eleven years. He chooses the boat. He chooses the menu. He chooses the wine.” Chen Si was very quiet. “This year, I’m going to let him choose everything. And I’m going to watch who he talks to. And who he doesn’t. And at the end of the night, I’ll know.”

“And if he tries again?”

“He won’t try again on a boat full of the people he needs to keep believing in him,” said Chen Si. “He’s not stupid. He’s a snake.” He was silent for a moment. “Snakes are very predictable, once you know which way they’re facing.”

Aurelia looked at him.

At his calm face. At his hands, which had stopped shaking. At the empty whisky glass on the floor.

“You were nearly killed tonight,” she said.

“Zhendong doesn’t brake.”

“You were nearly killed, Chen Si.”

He looked at her.

“Yes,” he said. “I was.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry.

She wanted to, very badly. She wanted to scream. She wanted to go to the thirty-ninth floor and find Sun Wei’s office and set fire to it. She wanted to take the gun out of her gold clutch and drive to Fu Kang’s apartment in the Mid-Levels and put the barrel against his idle, handsome, watch-loving forehead.

She didn’t do any of it.

She took his face in her hands, the way she had on the night of the dishwasher, and held it, very hard, and looked at him.

“Clause four,” she said. “You don’t keep me somewhere safe. So I’m coming to the dinner.”

“I know.”

“And I’m sitting beside you.” Her voice was shaking. She made it stop. “And I’m going to watch Sun Wei too. All night. Every word. Every glass. And if he so much as looks at you the wrong way, I will—”

“I know,” said Chen Si. He put his hands over hers, on his face. “I know you will.” He was quiet. “That’s why I married you.”

She kissed him. He was already reaching for her, both hands, hauling her in, as if he had held himself together since the bend at Lantern Bay only so that he could do this.

Hard. Not gently. Not slowly. Not the way she ever kissed him, the way he had taught her to on the forty-fourth floor and on the thirty-ninth and on her own workbench. Hard, and frightened, and furious, with both hands in his hair and her knees on either side of him on the long grey sofa, and he made a sound against her mouth that was not like any sound she had heard him make, and pulled her down.

No clauses.

No words.

No orders, and no obeying, and no counting, and no mirrors, and no one leading. For the first time since a balcony in October, neither of them was setting the terms. She pulled his coat off and his jacket and tore two buttons off his shirt and didn’t care, and he dragged her silk pyjamas off over her head and threw them somewhere into the dark, and they didn’t make it off the sofa, and they didn’t try, and it was fast and rough and clumsy and desperate, the two of them holding on to each other on the long grey sofa in the dark with the harbour glittering below and a lorry on a bend somewhere behind them and muzzle flashes in a mirror, and she bit his shoulder hard enough to leave a mark and he said her name into her throat like something tearing.

It was not like anything they had done before.

It was not a game.

It was two people who had nearly lost each other at 2:14 in the morning, holding on.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, she lay on top of him on the sofa under his coat and listened to his heart, which was still going much too fast.

“You were scared,” she said.

He was quiet.

“Yes,” he said.

“Of the lorry?”

“No.” His hand moved slowly on her back. “Zhendong doesn’t brake. I wasn’t scared of the lorry.” He was quiet again. “I was scared on the four kilometres after. When I knew we were safe. And I sat in the back of the car and thought, if he had braked, I would never have come home. And you would have sat on this sofa with a cup of tea you didn’t drink and listened for the lift. And it wouldn’t have come.” His voice went very low. “And nobody would have been here with you. Like my mother. In the study. Looking at the door.”

She lifted her head and looked at him.

“I won’t be alone,” she said. “Ever. Not like that.” She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart. “If anything ever happens to you, I won’t sit and look at the door. I’ll go and find whoever did it, and I’ll take everything they have, and then I’ll come back and sit in your chair.” She lifted her chin. “And everyone will know whose chair it is.”

He looked at her.

“I believe you,” he said. A very small smile. “It isn’t a comfort. It’s the most frightening thing anyone has ever said to me.”

She put her head back down on his chest.

On the floor beside the sofa, his phone buzzed. Once. A text.

He reached down and picked it up and looked at it.

Then he showed it to her.

It was from Sun Wei.

Si! Heard about the coast road. Terrible. Thank God you’re safe. Don’t worry about a thing — I’ve booked the Pearl for New Year’s Eve, same as always. Best menu yet. You and your queen at the top table. Looking forward to it. — W.

She read it twice.

“Your queen,” she said.

“He heard it at the party,” said Chen Si. “Everyone did.”

She looked at the text.

Then she handed the phone back to him.

“Reply,” she said. “Tell him we’re looking forward to it.”

He looked at her.

“Tell him,” said Aurelia Chen, “that I’ll choose the wine.”

chapters.title: The Glass of Wine at the Harbour Dinner
chapters.desc: New Year’s Eve on a boat called the Pearl. She chooses the wine. She opens every bottle herself. At midnight he takes her glass, because he only drinks what he takes. Twenty minutes later, his hand starts to shake.
chapters.epigraph: “I only drink what I take.” He took her glass. It was the only rule he had ever had that could be used against him.
chapters.content:
The Pearl was a three-deck cruiser with teak floors and brass rails and a dining room on the middle deck with windows all the way round, and every year on New Year’s Eve it went out into the harbour at nine o’clock with forty people on board and came back at two in the morning with forty people who had all, at midnight, watched the fireworks over the city together and drunk to the same man.

Sun Wei had organised it for eleven years.

This year, Aurelia chose the wine.

She did it properly. She did everything properly. She went to the cellar of a merchant on the Peak whom she had known since she was sixteen and chose forty bottles herself: champagne for midnight, a white from Friuli for the fish, a red from Montalcino for the beef. She had them delivered to the boatyard on the thirty-first at noon in sealed cases and she was at the boatyard at noon to watch them come off the van, and she checked every seal, and she had the cases locked in the galley store, and she kept the key.

At nine o’clock, when the forty guests came up the gangway in their dinner jackets and evening dresses, she was standing at the top of it in gold, beside her husband, and every person who came on board saw her there.

Sun Wei came up the gangway last, in a beautiful dinner jacket, with his warm, tired, fatherly smile, and kissed her hand.

“Mrs. Chen,” he said. “I hear you chose the wine.”

“Every bottle,” said Aurelia.

“Then I’m sure it will be perfect,” said Sun Wei, and went to find his seat.

✦ ✦ ✦

She watched him all night.

She had told Chen Si she would. On the sofa, on the twenty-eighth, with his shirt torn open and his hands shaking. Every word. Every glass. And she did. She sat at the top table, at her husband’s right hand, in gold, with the city going past outside the windows, and she ate the fish and the beef and talked to the judge on her left about his granddaughter’s piano lessons, and she watched Sun Wei.

She watched who he talked to. The man with the shaved head, three times, briefly, at the bar. The man with the sunflower seeds, once, on the stairs to the upper deck. Two judges. A man from the port authority. The captain of the Pearl.

She watched who he didn’t. Mr. Lu, in his cardigan, who sat at the end of the second table and ate very little and watched Sun Wei too. The man with the tinted glasses. Qian.

She watched him not drink. All night. He held a glass of the Friuli and then a glass of the Montalcino, and he raised them, and he put them down, and the level in them did not change.

She watched him not look at Chen Si.

That was the thing. She noticed it at about ten-thirty. He looked at everyone. He laughed with everyone. He went from table to table with his warm hand on people’s shoulders, the way he had every year for eleven years. And he did not once look at the top table, where Chen Si sat with his wife in gold.

Not once.

As if there were something there he could not bear to see.

✦ ✦ ✦

“He’s not drinking,” she said, under her breath, at eleven, while the waiters cleared the beef.

Chen Si nodded, very slightly, at the judge’s story.

“And he hasn’t looked at you all night.”

“I know.” He turned his water glass on the tablecloth. He had not drunk any wine either. He had held a glass of the Montalcino, as he always held things, and not touched it. “I’ve been counting. He’s looked at you eleven times.”

She went cold.

“At me?”

“At your hands. Every time you’ve picked up a glass.” His voice was perfectly mild. He was smiling slightly, at the judge across the table, who was telling a story. “He wants to know what you’re drinking.”

She looked down at her own glass. Water. She had drunk nothing else all night. She had told herself it was so that she would be sharp, and it was. It was also because she had not, in the end, quite trusted herself to be careful enough.

“The wine is clean,” she said. “I checked every seal. I kept the key. I opened every bottle myself, in front of the sommelier.”

“I know you did,” said Chen Si.

“Then what is he—”

The lights on the middle deck dimmed. The captain’s voice came over the speakers. Ladies and gentlemen, five minutes to midnight. If you’d like to make your way to the upper deck—

And all around them, chairs scraped back, and forty people stood up and began to move toward the stairs, and the waiters came round with trays of champagne flutes, already poured, gold and fizzing, from the bottles she had chosen and opened herself.

✦ ✦ ✦

The upper deck was open to the sky.

It was cold. December cold, with the wind off the water. The city was all around them, every tower lit, and the harbour was full of boats, hundreds of them, sitting on the black water with their lights on, waiting. Forty people in evening clothes stood at the rails with glasses of champagne in their hands and their breath going white.

Sun Wei stood at the bow.

He had a microphone. He always gave the toast. Eleven years. He held a glass of champagne in one hand and the microphone in the other and he smiled his warm, fatherly smile at the forty people on the upper deck, and began to talk.

Aurelia didn’t listen.

She was standing beside Chen Si at the rail on the starboard side, with a flute of champagne in her hand that a waiter had given her on the stairs. She had not drunk from it. She was watching Sun Wei. And as she watched him, for the first time all night, he looked at the top table. At where the top table would have been. At her. At the glass in her hand.

And then away.

“Ten,” said Sun Wei into the microphone, and forty people said it with him. “Nine.”

Chen Si, beside her, was holding nothing.

She noticed it then. Everyone on the upper deck had a glass. The waiters had made sure. Everyone except him. Because he did not drink things other people gave him. Because when the waiter on the stairs had held out the tray, he had shaken his head, very slightly, the way he always did.

I don’t drink things other people give me. A man in my position. I drink things I take.

“Six,” said forty people. “Five.”

He turned his head and looked at her. In the light from the city, with the wind in his hair.

“Four,” said forty people.

And he reached out, smiling, the way he had once reached across a plastic table in a basement in the old town and taken her beer bottle, and took the champagne flute out of her hand.

“Three.”

“Si,” said Aurelia. Something cold had closed round her heart like a fist. “Si, don’t—”

“Two.”

“I only drink what I take,” said Chen Si, and lifted the glass to her.

“One.”

The sky over the harbour broke open into gold. Every boat sounded its horn. Forty people cheered and drank.

He drank.

✦ ✦ ✦

Nothing happened.

That was the worst part, she would think later. Nothing happened at all. The fireworks went on. Gold and red and white, over the towers, over the water, so bright you could see every face on the upper deck. He finished the champagne and put the empty flute on the rail and put his arm round her waist and kissed her, at midnight, under the fireworks, in front of the whole Syndicate, the way he had never kissed her in front of them before, long and slow and possessive, one hand spread at the small of her back, so that every man on that deck would remember whose she was, and around them people laughed and cheered and somebody whistled.

“Clause nine,” he murmured against her mouth, “starts the second we’re off this boat.”

“You don’t get to decide when clause nine starts.”

“No,” he agreed, and his thumb moved once along the gold at her hip. “I’m hoping.”

Sun Wei, at the bow, was looking at the sky.

Aurelia stood in the circle of her husband’s arm with the fireworks going off over the harbour and told herself she was being stupid.

The wine was clean. She had checked every seal. She had kept the key.

The wine was clean.

She looked at the empty flute on the rail.

The wine.

Not the glass.

She hadn’t checked the glasses.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 12:19, his hand started to shake.

She saw it first. They were back in the dining room on the middle deck, where the waiters were bringing coffee and little plates of sweets, and he was standing by the window talking to the judge, and he lifted his coffee cup, and the cup rattled very faintly in the saucer.

He looked down at it.

He put it down. Carefully. On the windowsill.

He looked at his hand.

Then he looked across the room, straight at her, and his face did not change at all, and she knew.

She was beside him before she knew she had moved.

“Si.”

“I’m all right.”

“Your hand.”

“I know.” His voice was very calm. Very quiet. Pitched so that the judge, who was still talking, did not hear. “My heart is doing something strange. Very fast and then very slow. I can feel it missing.” He looked at her. “The glass.”

Her own voice came out perfectly steady. She had no idea how. “Not the wine. The glass. Something on the glass. All the flutes on the upper deck. They knew you wouldn’t take one. They knew you’d take mine.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

He swayed.

Very slightly. Nobody else would have seen it. She saw it, and put her arm round his waist, as if she were leaning on him, laughing, a wife at a party, and took his weight.

He was very cold.

“Don’t let them see,” he said, into her hair. “If they see, it starts. Tonight. Everything I’ve built. Don’t let Sun Wei see.”

She looked over his shoulder.

At the far end of the dining room, by the bar, with a cup of coffee he was not drinking, Sun Wei was looking at them.

He was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did three things in the next four minutes, and she would never afterwards be able to remember deciding to do any of them.

She laughed. Loudly. A wife at a party, with her arm round her husband, laughing at something he had said into her hair. She tipped her head back and laughed, and the judge turned and smiled, and three people at the next table looked over and smiled too.

She said, in a clear, carrying, slightly tipsy voice that she had heard her mother use at a hundred parties, “Oh, darling, you’re freezing, you stood out there without your coat, come on,” and she steered him, smiling, laughing, with her arm round his waist and all his weight on her, across the dining room, past the tables, past Mr. Lu, who looked up from his coffee and went very still, past the bar, past Sun Wei, close enough to touch.

And at the door to the stairs, where Zhao Zhendong was standing in a black suit with his hands at his sides, watching the room the way he always watched rooms, she looked up at him, and said, in a voice that no one else could hear:

“Poison. Now. Hospital. Nobody can know.”

Zhao looked at his brother’s face.

He did not say hm.

He picked Chen Si up.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, she would remember the run down the gangway. Zhao carrying him, like a child, like nothing, down the narrow steps to the lower deck and out onto the stern, where the Pearl’s tender was tied, a small fast launch with a pilot who worked for Zhao and asked no questions. She would remember the cold. The fireworks still going off over the city, red and gold, lighting up the black water. Chen Si’s face in the light of them, grey, with his eyes open, looking at her.

“Aurelia,” he said.

“Don’t talk.”

“Sun Wei. Don’t let him—”

“I know,” said Aurelia. She was kneeling in the bottom of the launch in her gold dress, holding his head in her lap, with her hand flat on his chest. His heart was going under it like something trapped. Very fast. Then nothing. Then very fast. “I know, Si. I know. I won’t let him have anything. Not one thing. Not one chair.” Her voice cracked. She made it stop. “I’ll sit in yours.”

He looked up at her.

In the light of the fireworks, he smiled.

“My queen,” he said.

Then his eyes closed.

“No,” said Aurelia. “No. Si. Open them. Look at me. Look at me.”

They didn’t open.

Under her hand his heart went fast, fast, fast, and then stopped, and she stopped with it. The launch hit a wave and threw spray over both of them, cold as the balcony, and she counted, because counting was the only thing she had ever been able to do when everything else went. Uno. Due. Tre. On quattro it came back: one heavy thud against her palm, and then the flutter again, like a bird against glass.

She bent over him in the bottom of the launch with her forehead against his and her hand flat on his chest and counted every beat out loud, in Italian, all the way across the harbour, so that if it stopped again she would know the exact second, and so that, wherever he was, he would hear her voice doing sums.

Zhao, at the bow, did not look round. But she saw his shoulders move every time she lost count, and every time she started again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The launch hit the hospital pier at Harbour General at 12:41.

Zhao had called ahead. There were people waiting on the pier, in scrubs, with a trolley. A doctor, a woman of about fifty with short grey hair and very calm eyes, who took one look at Chen Si and said, “Cardiac. Something he ingested. How long ago?”

“Forty-one minutes since he drank,” said Aurelia. “Twenty-two since his hand started shaking. From a champagne glass. At midnight.”

The doctor looked at her. At the gold dress. At the gun, which had fallen out of her clutch onto the bottom of the launch and which Aurelia had not noticed and Zhao picked up without a word and put in his own pocket.

“I’m Dr. Ma,” said the doctor. “I’m the toxicologist here. I’m very good. Do you know what it was?”

“No.”

“Do you know who did it?”

Aurelia looked at her.

“Yes,” she said.

Dr. Ma looked at her for a moment longer.

“Then you go and do what you have to do,” she said. “And I’ll do what I have to do. And we’ll meet in the middle.” She turned to the trolley. “Go.”

They went.

Aurelia stood on the hospital pier in the cold in her gold dress, with her hands covered in nothing at all, no blood, nothing to show, and watched them take him up the ramp and through the doors and away.

Zhao stood beside her.

He didn’t say anything.

After a while, she turned and looked up at him.

“If he dies,” she said.

“He won’t die,” said Zhao.

“If he dies—”

“He won’t die,” said Zhao Zhendong again, in a voice she had never heard from him, low and certain and absolutely flat. “He carried me through a drain in the snow with a hole in me. He is not going to die from a glass.” He looked at the hospital doors. “And if he does, I’ll be beside you. When you do what you’re going to do.”

She looked at him.

Then she turned round, in her gold dress, and walked back down the pier to the launch.

“Where are you going?” said Zhao.

“Back to the Pearl,” said Aurelia. “It’s New Year’s Eve. I’m the host’s wife. I left in the middle of the party.” She stepped down into the launch. “I need to go back and tell forty people that my husband has had too much champagne and gone home to bed. And I need to finish my coffee. And I need to smile at Sun Wei.”

Zhao looked at her from the pier. Four seconds. Then longer.

Then he got into the launch beside her.

“I’ll stand at the door,” he said.

chapters.title: The Week He Couldn’t Get Out of Bed
chapters.desc: A private room on the ninth floor with no name on the door. A heart that won’t keep time. A rumour, by the second of January, that the Don is dying. And a woman in yesterday’s gold, running everything in his name.
chapters.epigraph: “Food poisoning. Oysters. He’s furious. He’s working from bed.” She said it forty times in three days. She said it so well that she nearly believed it herself.
chapters.content:
She went back to the Pearl.

She stood at the top of the stairs to the middle deck at 1:20 in the morning, in gold, with her hair a little wind-blown and her cheeks a little pink from the cold, and laughed, and said to the judge, “He’s mortified. Three glasses and he’s anyone’s. Zhendong’s taken him home to bed,” and the judge laughed, and the story went round the room in four minutes.

She finished her coffee.

She ate a sweet, a little square of nougat with pistachio, that tasted of nothing at all.

She went and found Sun Wei at the bar, and put her hand on his arm, and said warmly, “Uncle Wei, thank you. It was the best year yet. He said to tell you,” and watched his face.

It did nothing. Warm, tired, fatherly. He patted her hand.

“I’m so glad,” he said. “Tell him to drink some water.”

“I will,” said Aurelia.

His eyes, behind the warmth, were watching her hands.

She was not holding a glass.

✦ ✦ ✦

The Pearl came back to the boatyard at two. She was the last off. She stood at the top of the gangway beside the empty space where her husband should have been and said goodnight to forty people, one by one, and every one of them looked past her, for him, and she laughed and said oysters and champagne and mortified and bed.

Zhao stood at the bottom of the gangway the whole time, in the dark, with his hands at his sides. People walked very fast past him.

At 2:31, the last car pulled away.

She walked down the gangway. She walked to the end of the pier, where the launch was waiting. She stepped down into it.

And then her legs went.

Zhao caught her. He didn’t say anything. He sat her down on the bench in the stern of the launch and took off his jacket and put it round her and sat down beside her, a large dark silent shape in the cold, and the pilot started the engine, and they went back across the harbour toward the lights of Harbour General, and she sat with her face in her hands, in gold, and shook.

She did not cry.

She was not going to cry until she knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was alive.

Dr. Ma met her at the door of the ICU at 2:58. She had changed into scrubs. She looked very tired and very calm.

“He’s alive,” she said, before Aurelia could open her mouth.

Aurelia put her hand on the wall.

“It was a cardiac glycoside,” said Dr. Ma. “A plant poison. Something like oleander, or a refined extract. It does terrible things to the rhythm of the heart. It’s very old. Poisoners have used it for two thousand years.” She looked at Aurelia. “It’s also one of the few poisons that has an antidote. An antibody, made for people who overdose on heart medication. We had it in the pharmacy. We gave it to him at 1:06. His heart is still not right. It will take days. Possibly a week. He will be very weak for a long time after that.” She paused. “If he had been anywhere but a pier at this hospital within twenty-five minutes, he would be dead.”

Aurelia didn’t say anything.

“Twenty-two minutes,” said Dr. Ma. “You said twenty-two minutes, on the pier. You knew. To the minute.” She looked at her. “Most people don’t know what time it is when something like this happens. They’re screaming.”

“I wasn’t screaming,” said Aurelia.

“No,” said Dr. Ma. “I noticed.” She held the door of the ICU open. “Go and see him. Ten minutes. Then you need to sleep.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in a room at the end, behind glass, with wires coming out of him and a screen above the bed with a green line on it that jumped and stuttered and jumped. He was very grey. His eyes were closed. Somebody had taken off his dinner jacket and his shirt and his watch and put him in a hospital gown, and he looked, lying there, younger than she had ever seen him, and much smaller.

She sat down on the chair beside the bed in her gold dress and took his hand.

It was cold. It was the left hand. The one with the thin white line across the palm.

She held it in both of hers and watched the green line on the screen jump and stutter and jump, and listened to the machine beep, and did not cry.

After a while, his fingers moved in hers.

She looked up. His eyes were open. Just a little. Just enough.

“Aurelia,” he said. It was almost nothing. A breath.

“I’m here.”

“Sun Wei.”

“I went back to the boat,” said Aurelia. “I told forty people you’d had too much champagne. I said oysters. I ate a piece of nougat. I thanked him for the party.” She held his hand harder. “He thinks it didn’t work. He thinks you’re at home, drunk, in bed. He watched my hands all night.”

Something moved in his grey face. It might have been a smile.

“Clever,” he said.

“I learned from you.”

His eyes went, very slowly, down to the gold dress, wet at the hem with harbour water, and to the black jacket hanging off her shoulders like a tent.

“That’s Zhendong’s jacket,” he said. “Give it back to him.” It was barely a breath. “I lend you coats. Not him.”

“You’re wearing a hospital gown, Si.”

Something moved in the grey face again. More this time. Almost the balcony.

“Then take the blanket,” said Chen Si. “You can be angry in a blanket.”

She laughed. It came out of her like the bark and cracked in the middle. She took the thin blanket off the foot of the bed and put it round her own shoulders, over Zhao’s jacket, because he was watching, and he did not close his eyes until she had.

He closed his eyes again. His hand in hers tightened, very slightly.

“Don’t let them know,” he said. “How bad. If they know—Sun Wei will move. Tomorrow. The day after. He’ll call a meeting. He’ll say I’m—”

“I know, Si.”

“The routes. The judges. Qian has the—”

“Si.” She bent down until her face was close to his. “I know. All of it. I read the books. Every line. I’ve read them every month for fourteen months. I know where everything is.” She lifted his cold hand and put it against her cheek. “Clause two. I sit at the table. All the tables.” Her voice shook. “Go to sleep. I’ve got it.”

He opened his eyes and looked at her.

“My queen,” he said, very faintly.

And slept.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not sleep.

She went home at five in the morning, in Zhao’s car, still in the gold dress, and took it off, and stood in the shower with the water as hot as it would go. She did not cry. She put her forehead against the tiles and her palm flat on her own chest and counted, because the flat was very quiet and hers was the only heart in it, and it was keeping perfect time, and she hated it for that. At sixty she made herself turn off the water, and put on a black suit and every piece of gold she owned and her wedding ring, and at seven o’clock she was in his office on the thirty-ninth floor, at his desk, in his chair, with Qian across from her and four phones on the desk in front of her and a pot of coffee that she actually drank.

“Food poisoning,” she said. “Oysters. On the boat. He’s furious. He’s been sick all night. Dr. Ma has told him to stay in bed for a week, and he’s working from bed, and he’s in a filthy temper, and anyone who calls him directly will regret it. Everything comes through me.”

Qian looked at her. He had been with Chen Si for seven years. He kept a drawer of antacids in his desk. He was forty-four, and very tired, and his eyes were red.

“Is he going to—” he said.

“Dr. Ma says a week. Maybe more. Then weak, for a long time.”

Qian closed his eyes briefly.

“Then for a week,” said Aurelia, “he has food poisoning, and he is working from bed, and I am his voice. Every call. Every meeting. Every signature. Nobody sees him. Nobody speaks to him. Not the men on the thirty-ninth floor. Not the judges. Not Sun Wei.” She looked at Qian. “Especially not Sun Wei.”

“And if Sun Wei asks to see him?”

“He’s vomiting,” said Aurelia. “He doesn’t want anyone to see him vomiting. He’s very vain. You know how vain he is.”

Qian looked at her.

He had never in seven years heard anyone call Chen Si vain.

“Yes, Mrs. Chen,” he said, and something in his tired face eased very slightly. “Very vain. Terribly. I’ll tell everyone.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The rumour started on the second of January.

She heard it first from Mr. Lu, at eleven in the morning, who came up to the thirty-ninth floor in his cardigan with a cup of tea he didn’t drink and closed the door behind him and said, “Mrs. Chen. They are saying in the pawnshops that the Don is dying.”

She didn’t look up from the ledger she was reading.

“Who is saying it?”

“Everyone. Which means someone started it.” Mr. Lu sat down. “The story is that he was not drunk on New Year’s Eve. That he collapsed. That the giant carried him off the boat. That he is in a hospital somewhere with no name on the door.” He paused. “It is a very detailed story, Mrs. Chen. For a rumour.”

She turned a page.

“Somebody on the boat,” she said. “Somebody who saw him carried. Somebody who knew where the launch went.”

“Somebody,” agreed Mr. Lu, “who knew what would happen to him at midnight, and was watching to see if it did.”

She looked up.

Mr. Lu’s small neat face was perfectly still behind his round glasses.

“I watched him too, Mrs. Chen,” he said. “On the boat. All night. He did not drink. He did not look at the top table. And at twenty past twelve, when you laughed and took your husband across the room, he was the only person at the bar who did not turn to watch you go.” He put his cup down. “Because he already knew where you were going.”

She was silent.

“Mr. Lu,” she said finally. “Why are you telling me this?”

He looked at her.

“Because my wife,” he said, “held your hands in Milan and said nothing at all. She doesn’t do that with many people.” A very small smile. “And because I have run the pawnshops for thirty-one years, and Sun Wei has never once asked me a question about how to value a stone. You asked me nothing, and you knew. He has asked me nothing, and he doesn’t.” He stood up. “I would rather work for someone who knows.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third of January, Sun Wei called a meeting.

Not on the thirty-ninth floor. In a private room at a restaurant in the old town, at lunch, on the fifth. The message came to Qian, not to her. A meeting of the senior men, to discuss continuity arrangements, given Chen Si’s illness.

Qian brought it to her in his hand, as if it might bite.

Continuity arrangements.

She read it twice.

Then she went to the hospital.

He was awake. He had been awake, on and off, for two days. The green line on the screen still jumped and stuttered, but less. He was still grey. He could not lift his head off the pillow without his heart doing something that made the machine beep and a nurse come running, and so he lay very still, and looked at the ceiling, and hated it.

She showed him the message.

He read it lying flat, holding the phone above his face with a hand that shook.

“Continuity,” he said.

“He’s going to tell them you’re dying,” said Aurelia. “He’s going to say someone needs to hold things together. Temporarily. Until you’re well. And he’s going to offer.” She sat down. “And the man with the shaved head will agree, because he’s been talking to Sun Wei at the bar. And the man with the sunflower seeds will agree, because he hates me. And two judges, and the man from the port authority. And by the end of lunch on the fifth, Sun Wei will be holding everything. Temporarily.” Her voice was very flat. “And you’ll never get it back.”

He put the phone down on his chest.

He looked at the ceiling.

“I can’t get up,” he said. His voice cracked on it. The first time she had ever heard it crack. “Aurelia. I can’t get up. I tried this morning, to go to the bathroom, and my heart went—and the nurse—” He stopped. “I can’t get up.”

She took his hand.

“I know,” she said.

“If I could walk into that room—just walk in. Just sit down. That’s all it would take. They’d see me and it would be over.” His hand in hers was shaking. “And I can’t lift my head off this pillow.”

She looked at him. At the grey face. At the wires. At the green line jumping.

At the most dangerous man in the city, lying flat in a hospital gown, with tears running sideways out of the corners of his eyes into his hair, because he could not get up.

“Then I’ll walk in,” said Aurelia Chen.

He turned his head on the pillow, very slowly, and looked at her.

“I’ll walk in,” she said. “I’ll sit down. In your chair. And they’ll see me.” She held his hand harder. “And it will be over.”

“They won’t—Aurelia, they won’t accept—”

“They accepted me on the thirty-ninth floor.”

“With me in the room.”

“With you in an office chair at the corner, saying nothing.” She lifted her chin. “You didn’t say anything for two hours, Si. Not once. You let me do it. I did it.” She bent down and kissed his forehead, which was cold and damp. “I can do it again.”

He caught her wrist before she could straighten up. There was almost no strength in his hand, and he used all of it, and pulled her back down until her mouth was on his, and kissed her, badly, weakly, with the machine above the bed beeping its disapproval, as if he would rather his heart did something stupid than let her leave without it.

“Come back tonight,” he said against her lips. “Every night. I don’t care what Dr. Ma says.”

He didn’t argue about the meeting any more.

“You’ll need my signature,” he said finally. “On things. The routes. The judges. If Sun Wei tries to move money—and I can’t hold a pen.”

“I know.” She smiled. It was not a nice smile. It was the one from the school library, and from the morning room, and from a white tablecloth at Da Gianni. “I’ve been practising your signature since March. Since the marriage contract. Eleven pages. You signed every one.” She stood up. “It’s very distinctive. I’ve got it almost perfect.”

He stared at her.

Then, lying flat in a hospital bed on the ninth floor with wires coming out of him and his heart stuttering on a screen, Chen Si began to laugh.

Very weakly. It made the machine beep. A nurse came running. He couldn’t stop.

“Get out,” said the nurse to Aurelia, furiously. “You’re making it worse.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “I’m going.”

At the door, she looked back. He was lying very still now, with the nurse checking the wires, and his eyes were closed, and he was still smiling.

“Almost perfect,” he said, to the ceiling. “Almost.”

“Perfect by the fifth,” said Aurelia, and went to sign his name.

chapters.title: Aurelia Signs His Name
chapters.desc: Forty documents in three days. One forged signature, perfect. A transfer Sun Wei tries to slip through at midnight. And Enzo, at three in the morning, teaching her the last stroke.
chapters.epigraph: “Your si is too round. He doesn’t round anything. Look—he cuts it. Like a stone.” — Maestro Enzo Bellini, 3 a.m., 4 January
chapters.content:
There were forty documents.

Qian brought them to the thirty-ninth floor on the morning of the third in two boxes, and stood them on the desk, and stood beside them, looking at her with his tired red eyes.

“These are the ones that can’t wait,” he said. “Payments. Contracts. Two leases. A transfer to the judges’ fund, which is due on the seventh. The renewal of the shipping licence. A letter to the port authority. Nineteen invoices for the furniture route, which you would normally sign anyway.” He paused. “Twenty-one of them need his signature. Not yours. His. The banks won’t accept anything else. The judges won’t. The port won’t.”

Aurelia looked at the two boxes.

“And if they don’t get it?”

“Then by the end of the week,” said Qian, “every one of them will know that something is wrong. And they’ll go to Sun Wei. Because Sun Wei is the one who has always been there when the boss wasn’t.”

She took the lid off the first box.

“Then they’ll get it,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had not lied to him in the hospital. She had been practising since March.

Not on purpose, at first. It had begun with the marriage contract. Eleven pages, his black ink beside her red, his signature in the bottom right-hand corner of every one. She had looked at it so many times in the first weeks, on the floor of her flat, lying on her stomach with the contract in front of her, that she had started tracing it with her finger without meaning to. Then with a pencil, on a napkin. Then, one night in April, at her bench, with a fine-nibbed pen, on a sheet of the cream paper Qian had given her, over and over, until the sheet was black with it.

She had told herself it was because she was a designer. Because she noticed lines. Because his signature was beautiful: a sharp, plain, angular hand with no flourishes, the characters cut rather than written, like something engraved.

It had been because she was in love with him, and she had wanted to know what his hand felt like from the inside.

She sat at his desk on the thirty-ninth floor with forty documents in two boxes and a fountain pen of his that she had taken from the drawer, heavy and black, and a sheet of blank cream paper, and wrote his name.

Once. Twice. Eleven times.

It was very good.

It was not perfect.

✦ ✦ ✦

“The si,” said Enzo.

It was three in the morning on the fourth. She had gone to the boutique at midnight, because she could not sit in the flat on the forty-fourth floor any more with the long grey sofa and the jade chess board and nobody on either, and because she needed a bench and a loupe and good light. Enzo had found her there at one. He had not asked how. He had simply come in through the workshop door in his coat and pyjama trousers, and looked at her, and at the papers spread across her bench, black with his name, and taken off his coat and sat down beside her.

Now he was holding a sheet under the magnifier, the one they used for checking engravings, and frowning.

“What’s wrong with the si?”

“You round it. Here. At the turn.” Enzo pointed with the tip of his tweezers. “Look at his. On the contract.” He put the contract under the magnifier beside her sheet. “He doesn’t round anything. He cuts it. Like a stone. Like a bench jeweller cutting a seat for a claw. He lifts the pen, a tiny lift, and comes back down. You can see it in the ink. There’s a place where it’s thinner.” He looked at her over his glasses. “You’re writing it. He engraves it.”

She looked. He was right. In his signature, at every corner, there was a tiny break. Not a break. A lift. A hairline where the nib had come up off the paper for a fraction of a second and come down again a little further on, so that every turn was a cut and not a curve.

She had been tracing his signature for nine months and had never seen it.

“How did you see that?” she said.

Enzo shrugged.

“Forty years of reading other men’s hallmarks, cara,” he said. “I know a man by the way he cuts a line.” He pushed a fresh sheet toward her. “Again. Lift at the turn. Don’t think. Cut.”

She lifted at the turn.

She did it forty times.

At five in the morning, with the sky going grey outside the boutique window and the broken necklace’s empty place on the velvet in the dark window, Enzo put the forty-first sheet under the magnifier beside the contract and looked at both, side by side, without a word.

Then he took off his glasses.

“Basta,” he said. “If I didn’t know, I wouldn’t know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She signed twenty-one documents between seven and nine on the morning of the fourth.

At his desk. In his chair. With his pen. Qian stood beside her and turned the pages and took each one away as she signed it, and neither of them said anything, and the only sound in the office on the thirty-ninth floor was the scratch of the nib, and the tiny lift at every turn.

When she had finished, Qian gathered them up and squared the edges and stood holding them.

“Mrs. Chen,” he said. “I have worked for him for seven years. I have seen his signature eleven thousand times.” He looked down at the papers in his hands. “I couldn’t tell.”

“Enzo could have,” said Aurelia. “Before three o’clock this morning.”

“Then I won’t show them to Enzo,” said Qian, and went to send them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The transfer came at midnight.

She was still on the thirty-ninth floor. She had gone to the hospital at six, and sat with him for an hour while he slept, and held his hand, and watched the green line, which was steadier, a little, though not enough. She had come back at eight because there was nowhere else to go, and read the ledgers again, every line, because reading was the only thing that stopped her thinking.

At 11:52 her laptop chimed.

It was the bank. One of the banks. The one in Singapore, at the end of the chain of seven companies, where the money from the shipping route went before it went anywhere else. An automatic notice: a transfer had been requested from one of the Syndicate’s holding accounts to an external account. Requested by an authorised signatory. Awaiting confirmation by a second.

Eleven million dollars.

To a company in Macau.

She looked at the screen.

The requesting signatory was Sun Wei. Of course it was. He had been a signatory on the Singapore account for nine years, because he had been there before Chen Si, because he had taught Chen Si how the routes ran. The second signatory, the one whose confirmation was needed, was Chen Si.

Sun Wei had sent it at midnight.

Because at midnight, a sick man in bed, with food poisoning, with a filthy temper, being sick, would not be looking at his bank notifications. And the transfer would sit there, awaiting confirmation, until the morning. And at nine in the morning, if it had not been rejected, the bank’s rules said it would go through on the authority of one signatory alone, as a matter of urgency, because Sun Wei had invoked an emergency mandate on the account, a clause he had written himself nine years ago, when he was the only adult signatory, and that nobody had read since.

Eleven million dollars, gone to Macau by nine in the morning.

And on the fifth, at lunch, in a private room in the old town, Sun Wei would tell the senior men that he had needed to move money urgently to protect the routes while the Don was ill, and that he had tried to reach the Don, and the Don had not answered, which proved how ill the Don was.

She sat at his desk and looked at the notification.

Then she picked up his pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not reject it.

That would have been the obvious thing. A single click. Rejected by second signatory. And Sun Wei would know, at once, that someone was reading the notifications at midnight. And he would know it was not a man with food poisoning.

She did something else.

She wrote a letter. On his cream paper, in his hand, with his pen, lifting at every turn. To the bank in Singapore. To the director of private clients, a man called Mr. Tan, whom Chen Si had met twice and who was, according to the file Qian kept, very old-fashioned and very careful and liked letters.

Dear Mr. Tan,

I am writing to inform you that I have been unwell over the New Year, and that during my illness, certain instructions may have been given in my name, or with my apparent consent, which I did not authorise.

Effective immediately, and until further written notice from me, no transfer from any account of which I am a signatory may be made without the confirmation of my wife, Mrs. Aurelia Chen, whose signature is attached, and who has my full authority to act for me in all matters.

Please also hold, but do not reject, the transfer request received at 23:52 today. I would like it to remain pending. I would like the requesting signatory not to be informed of this instruction.

With thanks for your discretion,

Chen Si.

And beneath it, her own signature. A. Chen. In red ink. Round and confident and entirely hers.

She scanned it. She sent it to Mr. Tan’s private address, the one in Qian’s file, at 12:31 in the morning.

At 12:44, a reply came.

Dear Mr. Chen. Received and understood. The transfer will remain pending indefinitely. The requesting party will receive no notification. Please give my regards to Mrs. Chen. I look forward to meeting her. — Tan.

She read it three times.

Then she put her head down on his desk, on her folded arms, in the dark office on the thirty-ninth floor, with the harbour glittering outside and her father’s name lit up in gold on the tower across the water.

The desk smelled of him. Cedar and rain and cold coffee. At her elbow there was a cup he had put down on the thirty-first, before the boat, full, untouched, with a skin on it now. Nobody had dared to move it, and she had not let them. She lay with her cheek on his blotter and looked at it.

I held it, Si. Eleven million. I held it.

She didn’t say it out loud. There was nobody in the big room to say it to. Nobody told her she had done well. Nobody laid down a king.

She stayed there until the cleaner came at five and found her asleep, with his pen still in her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the hospital at six in the morning and told him.

All of it. The forty documents. Enzo at three o’clock. He engraves it. The transfer at 11:52. The letter to Mr. Tan. The reply.

He listened lying flat, with his eyes on her face.

When she had finished, he didn’t say anything.

“You held it,” he said finally. “You didn’t reject it.”

“If I’d rejected it, he’d have known.” She was sitting on the edge of his bed, which the nurses had told her four times not to do. “This way, he thinks it’s sitting there waiting for nine o’clock. He thinks it will go through. He’ll walk into that lunch at one o’clock today thinking he has eleven million dollars in Macau and nobody stopped him.” She looked at him. “And then I’ll walk in.”

He looked at her.

“Show me my signature,” he said.

She took a folded sheet out of her bag. A copy of the letter to Mr. Tan. She held it above his face, where he could see it without lifting his head.

He looked at it. At every character. At the tiny lift at every turn.

His hand came up off the blanket, shaking, and touched it. The bottom of the page. His own name. In his own hand. That he had not written.

“That’s mine,” he said.

“I know,” said Aurelia. “That’s the point.”

“No.” His fingers stayed on the paper. “I mean—I look at it, and I don’t—I can’t tell. Aurelia. I can’t tell.” He looked up at her. His eyes were wet. “I don’t know which of us wrote it.”

She looked down at him.

At his hand, shaking, on the paper. At the signature that was his and hers at the same time. At his face.

“Both of us,” she said.

She put the letter down on his chest, under his hand, and leaned down and kissed him, very gently, because his heart couldn’t take anything else, on his cold dry mouth.

He kissed her back. Very slightly. It was all he could do.

The machine above the bed beeped, once, sharply.
