A nurse appeared in the doorway.

“Mrs. Chen,” she said. “Get off the bed.”

“I’m going,” said Aurelia.

She got off the bed. She picked up her bag. At the door, she looked back at him, lying flat with the letter on his chest and his hand on it, looking at the ceiling, and smiling.

“The lunch is at one,” she said. “I’ll come and tell you afterwards.”

“Aurelia. Sit in my chair,” said Chen Si.

“I always do,” said Aurelia.

chapters.title: The Board Meeting Without a Don
chapters.desc: A private room in the old town, twelve men, one empty chair at the head of the table. Sun Wei has prepared a speech about continuity. Aurelia walks in alone, in black, and sits down before he can give it.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule one of a room full of men who want you gone.” She didn’t say it out loud this time. She didn’t have to.
chapters.content:
The restaurant was called the Jade Hall, and it was on the second floor of an old building on Temple Street, and it had a private room at the back with a round table for twelve and a lazy Susan in the middle and red silk on the walls, and it had belonged to the Syndicate for thirty years.

Sun Wei had chosen it because it was neutral. Not the thirty-ninth floor, which was Chen Si’s. Not the boat, which was his. A room in the old town where the senior men had eaten together for thirty years, since before Chen Si was born, where decisions had been made by men who were dead now, and where it would feel, to the men sitting round the table, like history.

He had chosen it very carefully.

She had known he would.

✦ ✦ ✦

They were all there by five to one.

Twelve chairs. Eleven men. The man with the shaved head and the gold watch. The man with the tinted glasses. The man with the sunflower seeds, already eating them. Mr. Lu, in his cardigan, at the far side. Two judges. The man from the port authority, who was not, strictly speaking, a member of anything, and who had come because Sun Wei had asked him personally. Two men from Zhao’s side, who ran the warehouses at the Iron Docks, large and silent, who had come because they had been told that something was happening and wanted to see what. A man from the shipping company whom Aurelia had met twice. And Qian, standing by the door, because Qian always stood by the door, with a laptop under his arm and an expression of total blankness.

Sun Wei stood at the head of the table.

He did not sit. There were twelve chairs and eleven men and he did not sit in the twelfth, the one at the head, with its back to the window. He stood beside it with his hand on the back of it, in a dark suit, with his warm, tired, fatherly face, and when the clock on the wall said one, he cleared his throat.

“Gentlemen,” he said. “Thank you for coming. I know it’s a difficult time. I know you’ve all heard the rumours.” He looked round the table. “I wish I could tell you they weren’t true.”

The room went very quiet.

“I’ve spoken to the doctors,” said Sun Wei gently. “Not directly. Through people. Si is very ill. Much worse than food poisoning. His heart.” He shook his head. “They don’t know if he’ll recover. If he does, it will be months. Many months. He won’t be able to—” He stopped. He looked down at his hand on the back of the empty chair. “Eight years ago, I gave a boy of eighteen his first job in this city. I taught him how the routes ran. I watched him build all of this. I love him like a son.” His voice cracked. It was very convincing. “And I won’t watch it fall apart because he can’t get out of bed.”

He lifted his head.

“So I’m proposing,” said Sun Wei, “a continuity arrangement. Temporary. Until he’s well. Someone to hold things together. Make the decisions that can’t wait. Keep the routes running, the judges paid, the banks happy.” He paused. “I’ve done it before. When he was young. I know how it works. I would be honoured—”

The door opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia came in alone.

She was in black. A black suit, very plain, with long sleeves and no jewellery at all except her wedding ring and, at her throat, a single heavy chain of yellow gold, twisted apart in the middle and mended with white.

Not hers. His. The broken necklace. The one she had given him on the night of the proposal, that he wore under his shirt every day, that the nurses had taken off him on New Year’s Eve and put in a plastic bag with his watch. She had taken it out of the bag that morning, at the hospital, and fastened it round her own neck, and he had watched her do it from the bed and said nothing at all.

She did not look at Sun Wei.

She walked round the table. Past the man with the shaved head, who stopped talking. Past the judges. Past Mr. Lu, who did not look up, but whose hands, folded on the tablecloth, went very still. Past the man with the sunflower seeds, who stopped chewing.

To the head of the table.

Sun Wei was standing beside the twelfth chair with his hand on the back of it.

She stopped in front of him.

“Uncle Wei,” she said pleasantly. “You’re standing in my way.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Nobody breathed.

Sun Wei looked down at her. His face was still warm. Still fatherly. But behind it, for the first time, she saw something move, very fast, like a fish under dark water.

“Mrs. Chen,” he said. “I didn’t know you were coming. I’m so sorry. I should have—this must be terribly difficult for you. Please. Sit. Anywhere.” He gestured round the table. “We were just discussing—”

“I heard,” said Aurelia. “Continuity arrangements.” She looked at his hand on the back of the chair. “Would you move your hand, please? I’d like to sit down.”

His hand didn’t move.

“Mrs. Chen,” said Sun Wei gently. “I understand. You love him. We all do. But this is—you must understand—this is not a jewellery shop. These men have been running these routes for thirty years. Some of them since before Si was born. They need someone who understands—”

“Which routes?” said Aurelia.

He stopped.

“I’m sorry?”

“Which routes,” said Aurelia, “do these men need someone to understand? Let me see.” She didn’t look at a single paper. She didn’t take out a phone. She stood at the head of the table in black, with his necklace at her throat, and looked round at the eleven men, one by one, and spoke, very calmly, in the voice she had used to read a ledger in a basement in the old town.

“Mr. Hu,” she said to the man with the shaved head. “The east coast. Three ports. Fishing boats out of Lantern Bay on the second and fourth Tuesday of every month. Your margin went down four per cent in the autumn because of the new coastguard station at Shek O, and you haven’t told anyone, because you’ve been making it up by skimming the fuel budget. Two per cent. I don’t mind. Everybody skims fuel. But I noticed.”

The man with the shaved head went white.

“Mr. Kwan.” The man with the tinted glasses. “You used to run the furniture route. You don’t any more. I do. You run the pawnshop supply instead, under Mr. Lu, and you’re very good at it, and you hate me, and you’re wrong to, because I doubled your share in November and you didn’t notice because you never read your own statements.” She tilted her head. “Read them.”

The man with the tinted glasses opened his mouth, and closed it.

“Mr. Pei.” The man with the sunflower seeds. “The airport. Cargo. Eleven years. You’ve never once been short. Not one dollar. You’re the most honest man at this table, and you think I’m a spoilt rich girl who sat in the boss’s chair because she could, and you’re half right.” She looked at him. “I sat in it because nobody else had the nerve.”

The man with the sunflower seeds stared at her.

Then, very slowly, he put a sunflower seed in his mouth, and cracked it, and said nothing.

She went round the table. All of them. The judges, by the cases they had sat on and how much they had been paid. The man from the port authority, by the number of containers he had waved through last quarter and the name of his mistress, which she did not say out loud but let him see she knew. The men from Zhao’s side, by the warehouses they ran and the night shifts they worked and the fact that one of them had a daughter at university in Melbourne, studying medicine, which she said with a smile, as a compliment, and which the man accepted with a stunned nod. The man from the shipping company, by the four ports in Southeast Asia and the eleven ships and the spine of the whole thing, the thing she had sat up reading at her counter until three in the morning with Chen Si across from her, finishing his sentences.

It took eleven minutes.

She did not look at a single note.

When she had finished, she turned back to Sun Wei.

“You wanted someone who understands the routes,” she said. “I do. All of them. Every line. Every month. For fourteen months.” She looked at his hand, still on the back of the chair. “I asked you to move your hand, Uncle Wei.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He moved it.

He did it slowly, smiling, as if it were his own idea. He took his hand off the back of the twelfth chair and stepped back half a pace and spread both hands, palms out, the gesture of a reasonable man giving way to an unreasonable woman for the sake of peace.

“Of course,” he said warmly. “Of course, Mrs. Chen. Forgive me. Please.”

She sat down.

In the twelfth chair. At the head of the round table in the Jade Hall, with its back to the window and the red silk on the walls and the lazy Susan in front of her, where men who were dead now had made decisions for thirty years. She crossed her legs. She put her hands flat on the tablecloth.

Sun Wei did not sit. There was no chair for him now. He stood beside her, half a pace back, with his hands spread.

“Very impressive,” he said, to the table. Pleasantly. Kindly. “Truly. Mrs. Chen has an extraordinary memory. We all saw that on the thirty-ninth floor.” He looked down at her. “But a memory isn’t authority, my dear. Knowing the routes isn’t the same as having the right to run them. Si never gave you that. He never signed anything. Did he?” His voice was soft. “And Si is in a hospital bed, and can’t speak for himself. And until he can—”

“He has,” said Aurelia.

Sun Wei stopped.

She held out her hand, without looking. Qian, at the door, crossed the room and put a single sheet of cream paper into it.

She laid it on the tablecloth in front of her. Then she turned the lazy Susan, slowly, so that the paper went round the table in front of every man, one by one, and they could all read it.

To all whom it may concern.

During my illness, my wife, Aurelia Chen, has my full and complete authority to act for me in every matter, without exception. Her word is my word. Her signature is my signature. Anyone who does not accept this does not accept me.

Chen Si.

And the signature. Sharp, plain, angular. Cut, not written. With a tiny lift at every turn.

✦ ✦ ✦

The paper went round the table.

The man with the shaved head looked at it and looked away. The judges looked at it and looked at each other. Mr. Lu read it twice, and then looked at her, and his small neat face did not change at all, except that something very bright came into his eyes behind his round glasses.

It reached Sun Wei.

He picked it up.

She watched him read it. She watched him look at the signature. She watched him look at it, the way Enzo had looked at it under the magnifier at five in the morning. He had known Chen Si since he was eighteen. He had seen that signature ten thousand times.

She watched him not be able to tell.

“When was this signed?” said Sun Wei. His voice was still warm. It had lost something. “He’s too ill to hold a pen. Everyone says so.”

“Everyone says a lot of things,” said Aurelia. “Everyone said he was dying.” She looked at him. “Who started that, I wonder? It was very detailed. For a rumour.”

The room was very quiet.

“Yesterday,” said Aurelia. “At the hospital. He signed it yesterday, propped up on three pillows, while Dr. Ma took his blood pressure and told him not to. It took him four minutes. His hand was shaking.” She looked at the paper in Sun Wei’s hand. “You can see it. At the end of the si. There’s a place where the ink is thicker. That’s where he had to stop.”

Sun Wei looked down at the paper.

At the end of the si. At the place where the ink was thicker.

Where she had stopped, at five in the morning, because Enzo had said basta.

“He also wrote to the bank,” said Aurelia pleasantly. “In Singapore. Mr. Tan. On the fourth. A letter just like this one. So that, while he was ill, nobody could move any money without me.” She tilted her head. “Very wise, I thought. You never know, when someone’s ill, who might try to take advantage.”

She watched it land.

She watched him understand, all at once, standing beside her in the Jade Hall with a sheet of cream paper in his hand: the transfer at 11:52. Pending. Eleven million dollars, not in Macau. Sitting in Singapore, frozen, with her name on it.

His face didn’t change.

His hand, holding the paper, did.

Very slightly. Just once. A small tremor.

The way Chen Si’s hand had trembled on the coffee cup at 12:19 on New Year’s Eve.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Well,” said Sun Wei.

He put the paper down on the lazy Susan. He smiled at the table. Warm. Fatherly. Tired.

“That settles it, then,” he said. “Of course. If Si has said so. His word is law, as always.” He bowed slightly to Aurelia. “Mrs. Chen. Forgive an old man. I was only trying to help.”

“I know you were, Uncle Wei,” said Aurelia. “I know exactly what you were trying to do.”

He looked at her for a moment.

Then he turned and walked out of the private room at the Jade Hall, and the door closed behind him.

Nobody said anything.

Then the man with the sunflower seeds, Mr. Pei, who had run cargo at the airport for eleven years and never been one dollar short, cracked a seed between his teeth, and spat the shell into his teacup, and said, to nobody in particular:

“Well. That was something.”

And Mr. Lu, at the far side of the table, in his cardigan, began, slowly, to clap.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the hospital at four.

He was awake. He was propped up on one pillow, which Dr. Ma had allowed that morning, and the green line on the screen was steadier than she had seen it, and his face was a little less grey.

He looked at her in the doorway, in black, with his necklace at her throat.

“Well?” he said.

She came and sat on the edge of his bed. The nurses had given up.

“I sat in your chair,” she said.

“And?”

“And I went round the table and told every one of them exactly what they did and how much they skimmed and who they were sleeping with, and I didn’t look at a single note. It took eleven minutes.” She took his hand. “And then Qian gave me your letter, and I turned the lazy Susan, and it went round in front of all of them. And Sun Wei read it. And he couldn’t tell.”

He was quiet.

“And then I told him about Mr. Tan,” she said. “And his hand shook.”

Chen Si closed his eyes.

“And then he said, forgive an old man,” said Aurelia, “and walked out. And Mr. Pei said that was something. And Mr. Lu clapped.” Her voice wobbled, very slightly, for the first time all day. “Mr. Lu, Si. He clapped.”

He opened his eyes and looked at her.

“You did it,” he said. “Without me.”

“Not without you. With your signature. That I forged. With your necklace. That I stole out of a plastic bag.” She touched it at her throat. “I wore it so they’d know. So they’d look at me and see you.”

He looked at the necklace.

“They didn’t see me,” he said. “They saw you.” His hand tightened on hers, very slightly. It was all the strength he had. “They’ll always see you now.” He was quiet for a moment. “Sun Wei will try again. He knows it was you who stopped the transfer. He knows you read the notifications. He knows you’re not a jewellery shop.” His eyes were very dark in his grey face. “He’ll come for you next. Not me. You.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. She lifted his hand and kissed the white line across his palm. “Let him.”

His fingers closed, very weakly, round hers. His eyes went to the necklace at her throat and stayed there.

“Keep it on,” he said. “Until I can take it off you myself.”

“That sounds like an order.” She leaned down until her mouth was almost on his. “You’re in no position to give orders, Mr. Chen. You’re allowed one pillow.”

“Then I’m saving them,” said Chen Si. “All of them. Clause nine has been very patient.” His mouth moved against hers, barely. “So have I.”

The machine above the bed beeped, once, sharply, and they both looked at it, and she laughed into his shoulder, and did not get off the bed.

chapters.title: The Traitor at the Table
chapters.desc: She invites the senior men to dinner on the forty-fourth floor. Eleven guests, a soup that takes eight hours, and a list of three names in her head before anyone picks up a spoon.
chapters.epigraph: “The glasses came from a caterer. The caterer has a brother-in-law. The brother-in-law has a brother-in-law.” She liked chains. She had built a career on them.
chapters.content:
She knew before the soup was served.

That was the thing they would all say about it afterwards, in pawnshops and warehouses and the back rooms of restaurants in the old town, for years. She knew before the soup. It became a saying. When someone in the Syndicate saw something coming a long way off, they said it: she knew before the soup. Qian heard it once, two years later, from a dock worker who had never met her, and went home and told his wife, and his wife laughed for ten minutes.

But that was later.

On the night of the eighth of January, at seven o’clock, she stood in the kitchen on the forty-fourth floor in a dark red dress with Chen Si’s necklace at her throat and stirred a pot of soup that had been on the stove since eleven that morning, and thought about glasses.

✦ ✦ ✦

The glasses had come from a caterer.

She had found that out on the second of January, in the morning, an hour before Mr. Lu came up to the thirty-ninth floor with his tea and his rumour. She had rung the boatyard. She had rung the captain of the Pearl, who was frightened and helpful and told her that the boat had been catered, as it was every year, by a company called Silver Service, which supplied everything: the food, the waiters, the linen, the cutlery, the glasses. Sun Wei had used them for eleven years.

Silver Service belonged, on paper, to a woman called Hu Lan.

Hu Lan was married to a man called Tang Qiang.

Tang Qiang’s sister was married to a man with a shaved head and a gold watch who ran three ports on the east coast and skimmed two per cent off the fuel budget, and whose name was Hu Jun, and whom everyone on the thirty-ninth floor called Mr. Hu.

She had sat at Chen Si’s desk on the second of January with that chain written out on a sheet of paper in front of her and checked every link of it twice.

Then she had folded it and put it in her bag and not shown it to anyone.

Not yet.

✦ ✦ ✦

The poison had come from somewhere else.

Dr. Ma told her that, on the sixth, in a corridor outside the ICU, in a low voice. A refined extract. Not a plant someone had picked in a garden. Something made in a laboratory, by someone who knew what they were doing, and then dissolved in something clear and painted inside the rim of a glass with a brush, so that a man drinking champagne would get the whole dose in the first swallow.

“It’s very specialised,” said Dr. Ma. “You can’t buy it. You’d have to know a chemist. Or a pharmacologist. Or someone who works with heart medication.”

Aurelia had gone back to the thirty-ninth floor and read the ledgers again.

On the fifth line of the March accounts for one of the shipping company’s subsidiaries, a company that imported pharmaceuticals from India, perfectly legally, mostly, there was a payment, every quarter, to a consultant. A pharmacologist. A retired professor at the university. For advice on regulatory compliance. The payments were authorised by the port authority’s liaison officer, who sat on the subsidiary’s board as a favour to Chen Si, and who had been on the Pearl on New Year’s Eve, and had talked to Sun Wei twice, once at the bar and once on the stairs.

His name was Lam.

She added it to the sheet of paper in her bag.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third name she found on the seventh.

It was not in the ledgers. It was in a hospital.

At three in the morning on the seventh of January, a man in hospital scrubs had walked onto the ninth floor of Harbour General with a clipboard and a syringe in his pocket, and had got as far as the corridor outside Chen Si’s room before he found the corridor occupied.

By Zhao Zhendong. Sitting on a plastic chair. Where he had been sitting, every night, from midnight until six, since New Year’s Eve.

Aurelia did not know exactly what had happened in that corridor. Zhao had told her only: “A man came. He left.” And the man had left, by all accounts, very quickly, and without his syringe, and with one arm hanging at an angle arms did not usually hang at. And nobody on the ninth floor had heard a thing.

The man was found the next morning at the bottom of a flight of stairs in a car park in the old town, alive, and very willing to talk to anyone who would listen about who had paid him.

Zhao had listened.

The man had been paid by a judge.

Not any judge. One of theirs. One of the two who had sat at the round table in the Jade Hall on the fifth, and looked at her letter going round on the lazy Susan, and looked at each other. A small, round, cheerful man called Judge Yip, who had sat on eleven of the Syndicate’s cases in nine years and been paid for every one, and who liked to tell people at dinner about his granddaughter’s piano lessons.

He had been sitting next to her at the top table on the Pearl.

She had talked to him about the piano lessons for twenty minutes, while she watched Sun Wei not drink.

She added the third name to the sheet.

✦ ✦ ✦

At seven-thirty, they began to arrive.

She had invited eleven of them. The same eleven who had sat round the table at the Jade Hall. She had sent the invitations herself, by hand, on the cream paper, in her own handwriting and her own name. Mrs. Chen requests the pleasure of your company at dinner on the forty-fourth floor, on the eighth of January, at half past seven. Mr. Chen sends his apologies. He is still unwell, and still vain.

Every one of them came.

Mr. Hu, with the shaved head and the gold watch, smiling too much. Mr. Kwan, with the tinted glasses, not smiling at all. Mr. Pei, who ran the airport cargo, with a pocket full of sunflower seeds that he did not, for once, eat. Mr. Lu, in a cardigan, with his tiny smiling wife, who held Aurelia’s hands at the door and said nothing, as she had in Milan. Lam, from the port authority, who shook her hand with a damp palm. The two men from Zhao’s side, enormous and silent, who stood in the hall and looked at the harbour through the glass as if they had never seen it from this high. The man from the shipping company. Judge Wong, who was tall and thin and grey and said very little.

And Judge Yip, small and round and cheerful, who kissed her on both cheeks and said, “Mrs. Chen! The piano lessons! My granddaughter passed her grade five,” and Aurelia said, “Congratulations, Judge. You must be very proud,” and took his coat.

Sun Wei was not invited.

Nobody mentioned him.

Zhao was there.

Not at the table. In the doorway to the kitchen, in a black suit, with his hands at his sides, where he could see everyone. Every one of the eleven guests saw him when they came in. Every one of them looked away.

✦ ✦ ✦

They sat down at eight.

The long table by the glass, with the harbour below. Eleven guests. Aurelia at the head of it, in Chen Si’s chair, in red. Qian at the foot, because she had asked him to sit, for once, and he had looked at her in astonishment and sat.

She served the soup herself.

It was Chen Si’s mother’s soup. He had told her about it, on the night of the fish, the first night on the forty-fourth floor: clear and dark, with dried scallops and pork and a whole old hen and ginger and red dates, simmered for eight hours until it was so clear you could read through it. His mother had made it every New Year. He had made it for her that first night, without telling her whose it was, and told her only when she asked for a second bowl. She had asked him to write down how, and he had, on a sheet of cream paper, in his sharp angular hand.

She had made it from that sheet, starting at eleven that morning.

She went round the table with the tureen, in her red dress, with his necklace at her throat, and ladled soup into eleven bowls, and every man at the table watched her do it.

When she reached Judge Yip, she served him last. She filled his bowl to the brim. She smiled at him.

Then she went back to her chair at the head of the table, and sat down, and folded her hands.

Nobody picked up a spoon.

They were waiting for her. The way men at a table always waited for the host. She could feel them waiting.

She didn’t pick up her spoon either.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Before we eat,” said Aurelia.

The room went still.

“I want to tell you a story,” she said. “About New Year’s Eve. It won’t take long. The soup will stay hot. It’s been on the stove for eight hours. It can wait another five minutes.”

She looked down the table.

“The wine on the Pearl was clean,” she said. “I chose it myself. I kept the key. I opened every bottle. Some of you watched me.” She looked at Mr. Pei, who nodded slowly. “But the glasses weren’t mine. The glasses came from the caterer. The same caterer Sun Wei has used for eleven years. Silver Service.”

She looked at Mr. Hu.

He was smiling. His smile had gone stiff at the edges.

“Silver Service belongs to a woman called Hu Lan,” said Aurelia. “Who is married to a man called Tang Qiang. Whose sister,” she said gently, “is your wife, Mr. Hu.”

Mr. Hu stopped smiling.

“Someone painted the inside of a champagne flute,” said Aurelia. “One. Not forty. With something very special, that you can’t buy, that someone had to make in a laboratory. Because they knew my husband wouldn’t take a glass from a tray. Because they knew he would take mine.” She looked down the table. “So they didn’t need forty poisoned glasses. They needed one. In my hand.”

Nobody moved.

“Thirty-nine people drank champagne on that deck at midnight,” said Aurelia. “Every one of you who was up there. Nobody else so much as felt dizzy. Did they?” She looked at her own empty hand on the tablecloth. “Because the glasses on the trays on the stairs were clean. Only the one in my hand wasn’t.” She lifted her eyes. “Because the waiter on the stairs who gave me mine was told which one to give me. And he was told by the man who hired him. Who was told by his employer. Who was told by her husband’s brother-in-law.” She paused. “Mr. Hu.”

Mr. Hu’s face had gone a strange mottled colour.

“That’s a lie,” he said.

“It’s a chain,” said Aurelia. “I like chains. I’ve built a career on them.” She turned. “And the thing on the brush. That came from a laboratory. From a pharmacologist. A retired professor at the university, who has been paid every quarter for three years for regulatory advice by a company whose payments are authorised by the port authority’s liaison officer.” She looked at Lam. “You.”

Lam went white.

“And on the seventh,” said Aurelia, “at three in the morning, a man walked onto the ninth floor of Harbour General with a syringe in his pocket. He didn’t get very far.” She did not look at Zhao in the doorway. Nobody at the table needed her to. “But he was very happy to explain, afterwards, who had paid him.” She turned her head, slowly, to the small round cheerful man at the middle of the table, with his bowl of soup filled to the brim in front of him. “Your granddaughter passed her grade five, Judge Yip. Congratulations. I hope she keeps playing.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The silence on the forty-fourth floor was absolute.

Outside, below, the harbour glittered. A ferry crossed it, very slowly, all its lights on.

Nobody had picked up a spoon.

“Three names,” said Aurelia. She had not raised her voice once. She had not taken a single paper out. “Mr. Hu. Mr. Lam. Judge Yip.” She looked at the other eight. “The rest of you, I believe, didn’t know. I believe Sun Wei came to some of you, in the autumn, and talked about continuity, and the future, and how young Si was, and how a man needs friends who were there before. And some of you listened, and some of you didn’t. And none of you knew about the glass.” She paused. “I could be wrong. If I’m wrong, I would like you to tell me now. Before the soup gets cold.”

Nobody said anything.

Mr. Pei, at the far side of the table, took a sunflower seed out of his pocket, and looked at it, and put it back.

“Mrs. Chen,” said Judge Wong. The tall thin grey one, who said very little. “What do you want?”

Aurelia looked at him.

“I want you to eat your soup,” she said. “It was his mother’s recipe. He wrote it down for me in March. It took eight hours.” She picked up her spoon. “I want you to eat it, and know that you’re eating at his table, and that he’s alive, and that I am sitting in his chair, and that I knew before the soup.”

She looked at the three men.

At Mr. Hu’s mottled face. At Lam’s white one. At Judge Yip, small and round, staring down into a bowl of clear dark soup filled to the brim.

“The three of you,” said Aurelia Chen, “will not be eating.”

She nodded, once, very slightly, to the doorway.

Zhao Zhendong unfolded his arms.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t touch them. Not at the table. He didn’t need to. He came into the dining room, very large, very quiet, and stood behind Mr. Hu’s chair, and Mr. Hu got up. He stood behind Lam’s, and Lam got up. He stood behind Judge Yip’s, and the small round cheerful man looked up at him, and then at Aurelia, and opened his mouth.

“Mrs. Chen,” he said. “Please. I have a family. My granddaughter—”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “So did he.”

Judge Yip closed his mouth.

The two men from Zhao’s side, at the end of the table, stood up without being asked and went to the door and opened it.

The three of them went out. Zhao went last. At the door, he looked back at her, at the head of the table, in red, with her spoon in her hand.

He looked at her for four seconds.

Then he inclined his head. Just slightly. The way you bow to someone at a table where men who are dead now made decisions.

The door closed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The eight who were left sat in silence.

Then Mr. Lu picked up his spoon.

He did it very carefully. He lifted it, and dipped it into his bowl, and brought up a spoonful of clear dark soup, and tasted it. And his small neat face, behind his round glasses, did something that none of them had ever seen it do.

It crumpled.

“His mother,” said Mr. Lu. “Chen Lan. I knew her. When he was a boy. She used to make this at New Year and bring it to the shop, in a flask, for my father.” He put the spoon down. His hands were shaking. “I haven’t tasted it in ten years.”

His tiny wife put her hand on his arm.

Mr. Pei picked up his spoon.

Then Mr. Kwan, with his tinted glasses. Then Judge Wong. Then the man from the shipping company. Then the two men from Zhao’s side, coming back in from the hall, sitting down, picking up their spoons in their enormous hands.

Then Qian, at the foot of the table, with his red eyes, who had never in seven years sat down at Chen Si’s table, picked up his spoon, and ate, and put his hand over his face.

Aurelia sat at the head of the table and watched them eat.

She didn’t eat. She couldn’t. She sat in his chair in her red dress with his necklace at her throat and her spoon in her hand and watched eight men eat his mother’s soup in silence on the forty-fourth floor, and the ferry crossed the harbour below with all its lights on, and somewhere across the water on the ninth floor of Harbour General a man was lying very still under a screen with a green line on it that jumped, and steadied, and jumped, and steadied.

She would tell him, in the morning.

She would tell him she knew before the soup.

She would tell him that Mr. Lu had cried.

She would not tell him, not yet, that after the eight of them had gone, at eleven, she had sat alone at the long table in front of eleven empty bowls and one full one, Judge Yip’s, still filled to the brim, and that she had eaten it, cold, every spoonful, because it was his mother’s, and it had taken eight hours, and she was not going to waste a single drop on a man who had tried to kill him.

chapters.title: What She Does to the Traitor
chapters.desc: Not a gun. Not a knife. Not Zhao. Contracts, deeds, a frozen account, a forty-page file, and one suitcase. Quietly. Thoroughly. Completely. By breakfast, Sun Wei owns nothing but the clothes he is standing in.
chapters.epigraph: “When someone hurts her, he doesn’t get loud. He gets quiet.” It turned out she did too.
chapters.content:
She did not ask Zhao to do anything to Sun Wei.

He offered. On the ninth of January, at six in the morning, in the corridor outside Chen Si’s room on the ninth floor, where he had been sitting on a plastic chair all night, he looked up at her as she came out of the lift with two cups of coffee, and said, without any preamble at all, “Sun Wei.”

“No,” said Aurelia.

He looked at her.

“Not you,” she said. She gave him a coffee. “Not that. Not for him.”

“He tried to kill my brother.”

“I know.”

“With a glass. With a syringe. In a hospital bed.” Zhao’s voice didn’t change at all. “He sent a man to put a needle in him while he slept.”

“I know, Zhendong.” She sat down on the plastic chair beside him. “And if you do what you want to do, he’ll be dead, and that will be the end of it. And everyone in the old town will say Zhao Zhendong did it, and they’ll be right, and they’ll be afraid of you, which they already are.” She held her coffee in both hands. “And nobody will ever understand what he actually did. What he took. What he was.”

Zhao looked at her.

“I want them to understand,” said Aurelia. “All of them. Every man on the thirty-ninth floor. Every judge. Every dock worker who ever took a wage from Sun Wei and called him Uncle. I want them to watch it happen, slowly, in daylight, and understand exactly what happens to someone who touches him.” She drank. “Si would never shout. He’d never hit anyone. He’d just take everything, one piece at a time, until there was nothing left.” She looked at the door of the room, where her husband was asleep. “He can’t get out of bed. So I’m going to do it for him.”

Zhao turned the coffee cup round in his hands and didn’t drink it.

“Hm,” he said finally.

It was a different hm. She had learned them all now. There were at least seven.

This one meant: I understand. And I’m sorry for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her four days.

She did it from the thirty-ninth floor, from Chen Si’s desk, in Chen Si’s chair, with Qian and Mr. Lu and a lawyer called Ms. Fong, whom she had found on the second of January in Qian’s files and hired on the third, and who was forty-six and wore enormous glasses and had once, according to the file, made a High Court judge apologise in open court for mispronouncing her client’s name.

She did it on paper.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first thing was the money.

Eleven million dollars in Singapore, pending, frozen, with her name on it. That was the easy part. On the ninth, at ten in the morning, she wrote to Mr. Tan, in her own hand this time, in red, and asked him to cancel the transfer and to remove Sun Wei as a signatory from every account of which Chen Si was also a signatory, effective immediately, on the grounds of attempted fraud, evidence attached.

Mr. Tan replied at 10:41.

Done. All eleven accounts. I have taken the liberty of reviewing Mr. Sun’s other activity over the past two years. I attach a summary. I think you will find page four of particular interest. — Tan.

Page four was a list of every transfer Sun Wei had made from Syndicate accounts to accounts of his own, or his wife’s family’s, or companies in Macau, over the past twenty-six months.

It came to thirty-one million dollars.

She sat at the desk and looked at it.

Then she gave it to Ms. Fong.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second thing was the companies.

Sun Wei sat on the boards of nine of the Syndicate’s legal fronts. He had shares in six. He had been given them, over the years, by Chen Si, out of gratitude, out of affection, out of the memory of a boy of eighteen being given his first job. Every share had been given with a contract. Every contract had been drawn up by the Syndicate’s lawyers. And every contract, Ms. Fong discovered on the afternoon of the ninth, had a clause in it, on page seven or eight or nine, in small print, that Chen Si had insisted on, years ago, for everyone, without exception, because he trusted nobody completely.

In the event that the shareholder is found to have acted against the interests of the company or its principal, all shares shall revert to the principal at nominal value.

Nominal value was one dollar.

“He put that in every contract,” said Ms. Fong, holding one up to the light from the window on the thirty-ninth floor, through her enormous glasses. “Every one. Even the ones he gave his own assistant.” She looked at Qian, who went slightly pink. “Your husband doesn’t trust anybody, Mrs. Chen.”

“He was betrayed when he was fifteen,” said Aurelia. “By people his father trusted.”

Ms. Fong put the contract down.

“Then he learned well,” she said. “Shall I draft the notices?”

“All six,” said Aurelia. “One dollar each. I’ll pay him in coins.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The third thing was the house.

Sun Wei lived in a beautiful house in the Mid-Levels with a garden and a view of the harbour and a koi pond, which he had bought four years ago with a mortgage from a small private bank called Harbour Trust, which nobody had ever heard of, which had eleven clients, and which belonged, through four companies, to the Syndicate.

To Chen Si.

The mortgage had been very generous. Very low interest. Very long term. Very kind. The kind of mortgage a young man of twenty-two who had just taken over an empire gives to the man who gave him his first job.

It also had a clause in it. On page fourteen.

Ms. Fong found it on the morning of the tenth and read it out loud, slowly, in her clear cold courtroom voice, while Mr. Lu sat with his hands folded on his cardigan and listened with great attention.

The lender may call in the full outstanding balance of the loan, with thirty days’ notice, in the event of fraud by the borrower against the lender or any party connected with the lender.

“Thirty days,” said Ms. Fong. “He owes four million. He doesn’t have four million. He has thirty-one million in Macau that he can’t touch, because the anti-corruption commission will be watching every account in Macau with his name near it from the morning of the twelfth.” She looked up. “He’ll have to sell the house. In thirty days. To the only buyer who can close that fast.” She paused. “Which, I suspect, will also be you.”

“At what price?”

“Whatever you offer,” said Ms. Fong. “He won’t have a choice.”

Aurelia looked out of the window, at the harbour, at her father’s tower across the water.

“The outstanding balance,” she said. “Exactly. Not one dollar more.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The fourth thing was the file.

Forty pages. Everything. The furniture route and the thirty thousand a table. The seven companies in Macau. The payments to Fu Kang, every one, for two years, for Chen Si’s schedule. The caterer, and Mr. Hu’s wife’s brother. The pharmacologist, and Lam. The man with the syringe, and Judge Yip. The transfer at 11:52. Mr. Tan’s page four. Thirty-one million dollars.

She wrote it herself. Over two nights, on the floor of the flat on the forty-fourth floor, in silk pyjamas, with a pot of coffee and a pencil behind her ear, the way she had written her marriage contract. Ms. Fong checked every line.

It was the most precise thing she had ever made. More precise than Numero Uno. Every fact matched to every other fact, every chain closed, every link soldered, so that you could pick it up anywhere and follow it all the way round and end up where you started, at a man with a warm, tired, fatherly smile.

She did not send it to the anti-corruption commission.

She did not send it to the newspapers.

She had eleven copies made, bound in plain grey card, and on the morning of the eleventh, she sent one, by hand, to each of the eleven men who had sat round the table at the Jade Hall. Including the three who were no longer in a position to read it.

And she sent a twelfth copy, by hand, to the beautiful house in the Mid-Levels with the koi pond.

With a note. On cream paper. In red.

Uncle Wei. Breakfast. Tomorrow. The Jade Hall. Seven o’clock. Come alone. — A.C.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came.

He came alone, at seven, up the stairs at the Jade Hall to the private room at the back with the red silk walls and the round table for twelve.

She was sitting at the head of it.

There was nobody else in the room. No Zhao. No Qian. No Ms. Fong. Just Aurelia, in a white suit, with Chen Si’s necklace at her throat, and a pot of tea, and two cups, and in front of the empty chair opposite her, a small brown paper envelope and a single sheet of paper.

Sun Wei stood in the doorway.

He looked older. Much older. In four days. His warm, tired, fatherly face had gone grey and loose, and his beautiful suit hung on him as if he had lost weight overnight, and his eyes, which had watched her hands all night on New Year’s Eve, were red-rimmed and very tired.

He had read the file. She could see it on him.

“Sit down, Uncle Wei,” she said.

He sat.

She poured him a cup of tea. She pushed it across the table. He looked at it.

“I’m not going to poison you,” said Aurelia. “That’s your trick, not mine.”

He didn’t touch it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“The envelope,” she said, “contains six dollars. In coins. That’s the nominal value of your shares in the six companies. Under clause seven, or eight, or nine, depending on which one. He put it in all of them. Even Qian’s.” She folded her hands. “As of nine o’clock yesterday, you own nothing in any company connected with my husband. You sit on no boards. You are a signatory on no accounts. Mr. Tan sends his regards.”

Sun Wei looked at the envelope.

“The sheet of paper,” said Aurelia, “is a notice from Harbour Trust. Calling in your mortgage. Four million and eleven thousand dollars, within thirty days. Clause fourteen.” She paused. “You can’t pay it. Your money in Macau is being watched as of this morning. So you’ll have to sell the house. There’s an offer on the back. For the exact balance. From a company called AS Holdings, in Luxembourg.” She smiled very slightly. “I believe you’re familiar with the name. You found it once, when you were looking into my sister.”

He turned the sheet over. He read the offer.

His hand, on the paper, did the thing again. The small tremor.

“And the file,” said Aurelia. “You’ve read it. Eleven men have read it. The three who were with you have read it in places where they have a great deal of time to read. Nobody else has read it yet.” She looked at him. “Not the commission. Not the newspapers. Not Fu Jianguo. Who would be very interested, I think, in the parts about his son.”

Sun Wei looked up at her.

“What do you want?” he said. His voice had gone hoarse.

“I want you to leave,” said Aurelia. “Today. With one suitcase. Not the house. Not the koi. Not anything in Macau. One suitcase, and the clothes you’re wearing, and six dollars.” She tapped the envelope. “There’s a car downstairs. Zhendong’s driving. He’ll take you to the border. He won’t touch you. I’ve asked him not to, and he does what I ask now.” She paused. “On the other side of the border, you can go wherever you like. You can never come back. If you come back, the file goes to the commission and the newspapers and Fu Jianguo on the same morning. If you contact Fu Kang, or anyone who works for him, ever, the same. If anything happens to my husband, or to me, or to my sister, or to anyone I love, for the rest of your life, by anyone, for any reason, even if you had nothing to do with it, the same.”

She leaned back in her chair.

“That’s all,” she said. “That’s the offer. You can take it or leave it. The tea is getting cold.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Sun Wei didn’t say anything.

He looked at the envelope with six dollars in it. At the notice from Harbour Trust. At the cup of tea he had not touched.

“He would have killed me,” he said finally. “Si. If he could get out of bed. He would have had Zhao Zhendong put me in the harbour.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “He wouldn’t. He’d have done exactly what I’ve done. Slowly. On paper. In daylight. And he’d have sat across this table from you and watched you understand it.” She looked at him. “I learned it from him. You taught him. Isn’t that funny?”

Sun Wei looked at her.

“I gave him his first job,” he said. His voice broke. “I taught him the routes. I called him Si. Eight years. I loved him like a—”

“You loved him like a bank,” said Aurelia. “You took thirty-one million dollars out of him over twenty-six months and sold his schedule to the son of the man who killed his father. You put poison in my glass because you knew he’d take it from me. You sent a man with a needle to his hospital bed.” Her voice did not rise at all. “Don’t say son to me, Uncle Wei. Not at this table. Not in this room. His father was taken down the stairs in his pyjamas by men like you. He doesn’t have a father. He has a brother, and he has me.”

The room was very quiet.

Sun Wei looked at her for a long time.

Then he picked up the envelope with six dollars in it, and put it in his inside pocket, and stood up.

At the door of the private room, he stopped, and looked back at her, sitting at the head of the round table at the Jade Hall in white, with the necklace at her throat.

“He doesn’t know what he married,” he said.

“He knows exactly what he married,” said Aurelia Chen. “He read clause four.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao drove him to the border.

He told her afterwards that Sun Wei did not speak once in two hours. That he sat in the back of the car with one suitcase on his knees and looked out of the window at the city going by, and then the suburbs, and then the hills, and that at the checkpoint he got out of the car without a word and walked across with his suitcase, an old man in a beautiful suit that didn’t fit him any more, and did not look back.

“Did you say anything to him?” said Aurelia.

They were in the corridor on the ninth floor of Harbour General. It was eleven at night. Chen Si was asleep. Zhao was on his plastic chair.

“One thing,” said Zhao, and looked at the door of his brother’s room for a while before he said what.

“I told him,” he said, “that she asked me not to touch him.” He was quiet. “And that she was the only person in the world who could ever ask me that.”

She sat down on the plastic chair beside him.

They sat there, in the corridor, not talking.

Then, after a while, very carefully, as if it were something heavy he had been carrying for a long way, Zhao Zhendong put his hand on top of hers on the arm of the chair, for one second, and took it away again.

At midnight she went in.

The room was dark except for the green line on the monitor. She thought he was asleep until she sat down on the edge of the bed in her white suit, and his eyes opened, all at once, the way they always did.

“You’ve been at the Jade Hall,” he said. His voice was a thread. “I can smell the tea. Tell me.”

So she bent until her mouth was at his ear and told him in a whisper, as if it were something indecent. Six dollars, in coins. One suitcase. The border. The koi pond, at the exact outstanding balance, not one dollar more.

On the monitor, the green line went up. Not much. Enough.

“My queen,” said Chen Si, “I would like it noted that I find you terrifying.” His fingers found hers on the blanket and held on. “And that if I could get out of this bed, I would not let you out of mine for a week.”

“Noted.” She kissed the inside of his wrist, just above the tape. “Your heart’s racing, Mr. Chen. Dr. Ma will think I’ve been up to something.”

“You have,” he said, and fell asleep holding her hand, and she did not take it back until the nurses changed at six.

chapters.title: Zhao Guards the Door
chapters.desc: Fourteen nights on a plastic chair outside a room on the ninth floor. A man with a syringe. A woman who falls asleep on his shoulder at four in the morning. Zhao Zhendong has never had a sister. He finds out what it is like.
chapters.epigraph: “He is my brother. You are his. So you are mine.” He had said it at a wedding in Milan. He had not known, then, that he meant it.
chapters.content:
He sat outside the door for fourteen nights.

From midnight until six. Every night. On a grey plastic chair that a nurse had brought him on the first night, at three in the morning, when she found him standing in the corridor in a black suit with his hands at his sides, and had looked at him, and gone away, and come back with the chair, and put it down beside him without a word.

He did not ask anyone’s permission. Nobody asked him to leave. On the second night, a security guard came up from the ground floor, a young man with a radio, and saw him, and stopped at the end of the corridor, and stood there for a while, and then went back down. On the third night, Dr. Ma came out of the room at two in the morning, and saw him, and said, “Do you need anything?” and he said, “No,” and she said, “Coffee’s at the end of the corridor,” and went away.

He didn’t drink the coffee.

He sat on the chair with his back to the wall and his hands on his knees, facing the lift, and watched it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was good at sitting outside doors.

He had done it since he was nine. At the steel yard, outside the office, where the man who had adopted him counted money and drank, and sometimes came out, and sometimes it was better if Zhao was already there when he did. At the detention centre, outside the shower block, at night, when Chen Si was in there alone, because the other boys didn’t like him, because he talked like a rich boy and held his chopsticks properly and read books.

He would do it again, in three years, outside a different door, in a house on a hill, every night, for a florist who left it open a hand’s width. He didn’t know that yet.

He only knew that his brother was on the other side of this one, and that somebody had tried to kill him with a glass, and would try again, and that the only thing in the world Zhao knew how to do about it was sit here, between the lift and the door, and wait.

✦ ✦ ✦

The man with the syringe came on the seventh night.

At 3:04. Zhao heard the lift before it arrived. Lifts made a sound in their shafts, a kind of hum that changed as they came up, and at three in the morning on the ninth floor of a hospital there was nothing else to hear. He heard it come up from the ground floor without stopping. He heard it slow. He watched the doors.

A man came out in pale green scrubs, with a clipboard, and a lanyard, and a mask pulled down under his chin. Thirty. Thin. Walking quickly, like someone who belonged there.

He saw Zhao and didn’t stop. That was the mistake. A real nurse would have stopped. A real nurse would have looked at the very large man in a black suit sitting on a plastic chair outside a patient’s door at three in the morning and said Can I help you? or Visiting hours are over or at least Excuse me.

This one walked straight past him toward the door.

Zhao stood up.

He did not say anything. He didn’t need to. He put out his arm, the way you would put out an arm to stop someone stepping into a road, and the man walked into it, and stopped, and looked up.

Zhao looked down at him.

The man’s right hand was in the pocket of his scrubs. Holding something.

“I need to check his line,” said the man. “Doctor’s orders.”

“Which doctor,” said Zhao.

The man opened his mouth.

Zhao took his wrist. The one in the pocket. He took it gently, the way you would take something from a child, and drew it out of the pocket, and looked at what was in the hand. A syringe. Full. Capped.

He looked at it for a while.

Then he looked at the man again.

“Not in there,” said Zhao.

He did not hurt him in the corridor. He did not want Chen Si to hear anything through the door. He walked the man down the corridor to the fire stairs, with one hand on his wrist and one on the back of his neck, quite slowly, the way you would walk a drunk friend home, and opened the fire door, and went through it, and closed it behind them.

What happened on the fire stairs was quiet.

When he came back, six minutes later, he had the syringe in his pocket and the man’s lanyard in his hand, and he sat back down on the plastic chair and put his hands on his knees and watched the lift.

At 3:40, Chen Si’s door opened, and Dr. Ma came out, and looked at him, and looked at the lanyard in his hand, and looked at the fire door at the end of the corridor.

“Did something happen?” she said.

“A man came,” said Zhao. “He left.”

Dr. Ma looked at him, and then at the fire door again.

“I’ll have them check the stairs,” she said. “For anyone who might have fallen.”

“Yes,” said Zhao. “Someone might have.”

Aurelia came at ten past four, with the coffees. He told her the way he told everything. A man came. With a syringe. For him. He left.

She did not sit down.

She set both coffees on the floor, very precisely, side by side, and went into the room. He heard nothing through the door. When he looked in, she was standing at the bed with one hand on the rail, not touching her husband, counting the drops falling in the drip chamber with her lips moving, the way she counted anything when there was nothing else she could do. Her other hand was pressed flat over her mouth.

She stood like that until six. When she came out, her face was perfectly composed and there was blood on her lower lip where she had bitten it, and she picked up the two cold coffees from the floor and gave him one.

“Thank you,” she said. It was all she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia came every night.

Not at midnight. Later. At two, or three, or four, after she had finished whatever she was doing on the thirty-ninth floor or at the boutique or on the floor of the flat on the forty-fourth. She came up in the lift in whatever she was wearing, the black suit, or the red dress, or once, on the sixth night, in silk pyjamas with a coat over them, and she always brought two coffees, and she always gave him one, and she always sat down on the plastic chair beside his, which the nurse had brought on the second night without being asked, and they always sat there for a while, not talking, before she went in.

He had not known her, before.

He had seen her. In the old town, under a streetlamp, in flat shoes. At dinner, eating his fish. In Milan, in ivory, with a broken chain down her back. He had said nine words to her at her wedding, which was the most he had said to anyone at once in years, and he had meant all nine. He is my brother. You’re his. So you’re mine.

He had not known, then, what it would mean.

He found out in the corridor on the ninth floor.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the sixth night, she fell asleep on his shoulder.

At 4:20. She had come in her pyjamas and coat, at three, with the coffees, and sat down, and told him about the forty documents, and Enzo, and the tiny lift at every turn. She had told him about Mr. Tan. She had told him about the Jade Hall, and the lazy Susan, and Mr. Lu clapping, and she had laughed, telling it, a short, wild, exhausted laugh, and then she had stopped talking.

And her head had come down on his shoulder.

He didn’t move.

He sat on the plastic chair in the corridor at 4:20 in the morning with his brother’s wife asleep against his arm, in silk pyjamas and a coat, with a cold coffee in her lap that he took out of her hand very carefully before she dropped it, and he did not move for an hour and forty minutes.

He had never had a sister.

He had had a man at a steel yard who counted money and drank. He had had the detention centre. He had had a brother, for ten years, who had carried him through a drain in the snow. He had had men who worked for him and men who were afraid of him and men who wanted to kill him and women, sometimes, briefly, who wanted something from him and went away when they found out what he was.

He had never had anyone fall asleep on his shoulder because they trusted him.

He sat very still and watched the lift and listened to her breathe.

At six, when the day nurse came on and the corridor lights went up, she woke with a jerk and sat up and looked at him and at his shoulder and went red.

“I fell asleep on you,” she said. “How long?”

He looked at the lift.

“A while,” he said.

She looked at him for a moment, as if she were deciding whether to be embarrassed, and decided not to be.

“Thank you,” she said.

He didn’t answer. He didn’t have an answer. He picked up the cold coffee he had taken out of her hand at 4:20 and held it out to her, and she took it, and drank it, cold, and made a face, and laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the eighth night, she asked him about the drains.

She had asked before. In the hills, behind the quarry, with the gun. He had told her a little. The blade. The hour. Si’s burned arm. I would be dead.

She asked again in the corridor. Properly. With the coffees. At three.

“Tell me all of it,” she said. “He won’t. He says it’s yours. So you tell me.”

He looked at the lift.

Then he told her.

All of it. The press shop, where they folded the uniforms, and the thin rich boy who noticed that he folded them before he put them in. The canteen, and the boy sitting down at the end of his table with a book, every day, for a week, when nobody sat at Zhao’s table. The book, which Zhao couldn’t read, and which the boy turned round so he could see, and then, when he saw Zhao’s face, said nothing about, and the next day brought a different book, a simpler one, with pictures, and read it to him. Out loud. In the canteen. In front of everyone.

“Nobody had ever read me anything,” said Zhao. “I was fifteen. I couldn’t read. Nobody knew. He knew in one look.”

She didn’t say anything.

He told her about the riot. The smoke. Gao, who was seventeen and had killed a man, coming down the aisle between the bunks with a piece of bed frame. Chen Si closing his book and putting it down very carefully on the blanket. Zhao coming down off the top bunk without deciding to.

The cold line, under his arm, down toward his hip.

The hour on the floor in the smoke, with Chen Si kneeling in front of him pressing his own shirt into the wound with both hands, red to the wrist. Zhendong. I know where the river goes.

The grate in the floor of the shower block, and Chen Si getting it up somehow, with a piece of the bed frame, while Zhao lay in the smoke and could not lift his head. By the time they reached the clinic, Si’s arm was burned from the wrist to the elbow. Si said it was the road, in the ditch. Zhao had believed him for ten years.

The drain. The water. The dark. Chen Si carrying him, the last half kilometre, fifty kilos carrying eighty, through water up to their chests, in the dark, talking to him the whole way, so he wouldn’t fall asleep. Telling him the story from the book. The simple one, with pictures. All of it, from memory, the whole way.

The snow.

“When we came out,” said Zhao, “it was snowing. I lay in the ditch by the road and looked up. I couldn’t feel anything. I told him not to take me to a hospital. Hospitals have records. I told him to let me go.” He looked at the lift. “He said no.”

Aurelia was crying. Silently. He could hear it.

“He paid the doctor with the book,” said Zhao. “The first one. The one I couldn’t read. It was his father’s. A first edition. The only thing he had left.” He was quiet. “I asked him once, years later, what it was. The book. He said it didn’t matter. He said he’d paid for something better with it.”

“What was it?” said Aurelia, through her tears.

Zhao didn’t answer straight away.

“Journey to the West,” he said. “The monkey king. A first edition. From 1592.” He looked at the floor. “I found out later what it was worth. More than the clinic. More than the town. He gave it to a back-room doctor for three days of stitches and a drip.”

She put her face in her hands.

He sat beside her and didn’t touch her and waited, the way his brother would have waited, the way his brother had waited for her on a balcony and across a chess board. He didn’t know how to do anything else.

After a while, she wiped her face with the backs of her hands, and looked at him.

“I’m going to find that book,” she said. Her voice was wet and fierce. “Books like that don’t just disappear. Somebody sold it, somebody bought it, it’s gone to auction or a collector. I know every auction house in Europe and Asia. I’m going to find his father’s book and buy it back.”

Zhao looked at her.

He looked at her for a lot longer than four seconds.

“It might take years,” he said.

“Then it’ll take years.”

“It might cost—”

“I don’t care what it costs,” said Aurelia Chen. “I set the price.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the fourteenth night, Chen Si was moved out of intensive care, to a room on the sixth floor with a window and no wires, and Dr. Ma said that he could go home on the fifteenth, if he promised to do nothing at all for six weeks, and he promised, and nobody in the room believed him.

Zhao sat outside the door on the sixth floor that night anyway.

At two in the morning, the door opened. Not a nurse. Chen Si. In a hospital gown, holding on to the doorframe, grey and thin and swaying slightly, with a drip stand beside him that he was holding on to with his other hand.

He looked down at his brother on the plastic chair.

“Go home,” he said.

“No.”

“Zhendong. It’s been two weeks. Go home. Sleep in a bed.”

“No.”

Chen Si looked at him. Then, very slowly, holding on to the doorframe and the drip stand, he lowered himself down onto the second plastic chair, the one Aurelia always sat in, beside his brother, in the corridor, at two in the morning.

They sat there.

“She told me,” said Chen Si, after a while. “About the man with the syringe. About the fire stairs.”

“Hm.”

“She told me she fell asleep on you.”

Zhao looked at the lift.

“She told me,” said Chen Si, “that you told her about the drains. All of it. The book. The monkey king.” He was quiet. “You’ve never told anyone.”

“She asked.”

“Lots of people have asked.”

Zhao didn’t say anything.

“She’s mine,” he said finally. “I said it in Milan. I meant it. I didn’t know what it meant.” He looked at his hands on his knees. “I know now.”

Chen Si turned his head and looked at his brother.

Then he reached over, slowly, with his left hand, the one with the white line across the palm, and laid it flat on Zhao’s left hand, on his knee, palm to palm. The way they had in a back room behind a clinic in the next town, ten years ago, with a knife and a drip and a book gone.

They sat like that, in the corridor on the sixth floor, at two in the morning, not saying anything.

At three, the lift hummed.

They both looked up.

The doors opened, and Aurelia came out, in a black coat over silk pyjamas, with three coffees in a cardboard tray, and stopped dead, and looked at the two of them on the plastic chairs: her husband in a hospital gown with a drip stand, and his brother in a black suit, holding hands.

“Oh, for God’s sake,” she said. “Both of you. Bed. Now.”

They looked at each other.

Neither of them moved.

She put the coffees down on the floor and sat down on the floor of the corridor in front of them, in her pyjamas, with her back against the opposite wall, and picked up a coffee, and drank it.

“Fine,” said Aurelia. “Then I’ll stay too.”

Chen Si looked down at her, on the floor in her pyjamas with two cups, because she had picked up his as well as her own.

“One of those is mine,” he said.

“You’re not allowed coffee. You’re not allowed anything.” She drank from his cup, looking at him over the rim. “You’re a man in a hospital gown holding hands with his brother at three in the morning. You don’t get coffee. You get to look at me.”

He looked at her. It was, Zhao thought, the first time in fourteen nights that his brother had looked like himself.

“That,” said Chen Si, “is a much better offer.”

“Hm,” said Zhao, and moved his chair two inches further away from both of them.

chapters.title: A Laptop, a Gun, and a Very Tired Co-Ruler
chapters.desc: His first night home. He wakes at three in the morning and she is in the chair beside the bed, asleep sitting up, with a laptop on her knees and a gun on the table and his necklace at her throat. He finally understands what he married.
chapters.epigraph: He had thought he married a wife. He had married a co-ruler, who slept sitting up with a gun on the bedside table, so that he wouldn’t have to.
chapters.content:
He came home on the fifteenth of January, in a wheelchair, which he hated.

He hated it so much that at the door of the hospital he tried to stand up out of it, and his heart did something, and Dr. Ma, who was walking beside him, put one hand flat on his chest and pushed him back down into it without looking, the way you push a door shut, and said, “Six weeks, Mr. Chen. You promised.”

“I didn’t think you’d hold me to it.”

“I hold everyone to everything,” said Dr. Ma. “It’s why I’m very good.” She looked at Aurelia. “He’s not to climb stairs. He’s not to lift anything heavier than a cup. He’s not to work. He’s not to be angry. He’s not to have sex.”

Aurelia raised her eyebrows.

“For how long?”

“Until I say,” said Dr. Ma. “I’ll know. I always know.”

Chen Si closed his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

The flat on the forty-fourth floor had changed.

He noticed it as soon as Zhao wheeled him in. He noticed everything; it was the only thing about him that had not got weaker. The long grey sofa had been moved, so that it faced the window straight on, and there was a blanket on it, and a pile of books he had been meaning to read, and a table at the end of it with a jug of water and a glass. The jade chess board had been moved from the low table by the window to the table beside the sofa, within reach of someone lying down. There was a rail along the wall of the corridor to the bedroom, brass, new, at hand height, that had not been there a month ago.

And in the bedroom, beside his side of the bed, there was an armchair.

A deep, square, ugly leather armchair, the colour of old saddles, that he had never seen before. It did not match anything. It sat beside the bed like a dog.

“Where did that come from?” he said.

“Enzo,” said Aurelia. “It was in his flat. He’s had it for thirty years. He brought it from Milan in a crate.” She looked at it. “He says it’s the only chair in Asia a person can sleep in properly sitting up.”

He looked at the chair.

He looked at her.

“Why would anyone need to sleep sitting up?” he said.

She didn’t answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

He found out at three in the morning.

He woke because his heart missed. It did that, still. Dr. Ma said it would for weeks: a skip, a stumble, a beat that came late, as if his heart had forgotten for a moment what it was doing and then remembered. It woke him, most nights, once or twice. He lay in the dark and waited for the next beat, and it always came, and he always lay awake afterwards for a long time.

He woke at three, and waited, and the beat came, and he turned his head on the pillow.

The lamp beside the bed was on, very low.

She was in the chair.

Enzo’s ugly leather armchair, the colour of old saddles. She was sitting in it, sideways, with her legs tucked up under her, in silk pyjamas and his old grey jumper, which came down over her hands. She was asleep. Sitting up. Her head had fallen sideways against the wing of the chair. Her hair was coming down.

On her knees, open, glowing, there was a laptop.

He could see the screen from the bed. It was a ledger. The shipping company. The column of figures for December. Her cursor was blinking halfway down it, where she had stopped, at some point, and fallen asleep in the middle of a line.

On the bedside table, between his glass of water and his pills, beside the lamp, there was a gun.

Her gun. The small black one, from the range behind the quarry, from the gold clutch. Not in the clutch. Out. On the table. Within reach of the chair. With the safety on, he noticed, because he noticed everything, and the magazine in, and the grip turned toward her hand.

And at her throat, on top of his old grey jumper, gleaming in the low light from the lamp, his necklace. The broken one. That she had taken out of a plastic bag at the hospital on New Year’s Day and fastened round her own neck and not taken off since.

He lay very still and looked at her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He understood, lying there, that she had done this every night.

Not just tonight. Every night. At the hospital, she had come at two or three or four with the coffees and sat in the corridor with Zhao and gone in and sat beside his bed until six. And then gone to the thirty-ninth floor and run everything. And then gone to the boutique. And then come back. He had known that. He had thought, lying in the hospital, that she must be sleeping somewhere, at some point, in the day, between.

She hadn’t been.

She had been sleeping in chairs.

He looked at the laptop on her knees. At the ledger. December. She had been reading his books, at three in the morning, beside his bed, so that if anything moved in them, anything at all, she would see it before anyone else did.

He looked at the gun on the table. Grip toward her hand. So that if anyone came through the door of the flat on the forty-fourth floor at three in the morning, as someone had come through a door on the ninth floor of Harbour General at three in the morning, she would not have to reach for her bag.

He looked at the necklace at her throat.

I wore it so they’d know, she had said, at the hospital, on the fifth. So they’d look at me and see you.

✦ ✦ ✦

He had thought he was marrying a wife.

He had known she was clever. He had known on the balcony, watching her do sums in her head while she shook. He had known she was ruthless; he had known it in the basement in the old town, when she found half a million euros in forty-one minutes and raised her price. He had known she was brave. He had known she was frightened, under it, all the time, of disappearing. He had known she would sit in his chair.

He had written my queen in his head on the thirty-ninth floor, and said it out loud in Milan, and in front of two hundred people at the Peak, and meant it every time.

He had not understood, until three in the morning on the fifteenth of January, lying in his own bed unable to lift anything heavier than a cup, what it meant.

It meant this.

A woman asleep sitting up in an ugly chair, with his empire on her knees and a gun by her hand and his necklace at her throat, keeping watch.

So that he wouldn’t have to.

He had been keeping watch his whole life. Since a hall at six in the morning. Since Block C. Since a drain in the snow. He had never once, in eleven years, slept through a night without some part of him listening for a door.

He had slept through four nights in a row in the hospital, after the first week. He had not known why. He had thought it was the drugs.

It was her. In the chair. With the gun. Listening for him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He reached out.

It took a long time. His arm was weak. His heart did a small stumble as he moved, and he stopped and waited for it to settle, and then went on. He reached across the gap between the bed and the ugly leather armchair, and found her hand, where it lay on the keyboard of the laptop, under the sleeve of his old grey jumper, and put his own over it.

She woke the moment he touched her.

Not slowly. Not the way people wake. All at once, her eyes open, her other hand already moving toward the bedside table, toward the gun, before she knew she was awake.

Then she saw him.

Her hand stopped.

“Si,” she said. “Is it your heart? Is something—should I call—”

“No,” said Chen Si. “No. It’s fine. It skipped. It came back.”

She looked at him. In the low light. Her face was creased on one side from the wing of the chair. Her eyes were red. She looked more tired than he had ever seen anyone look.

“Then why are you awake?” she said.

“Aurelia,” he said. “How long have you been sleeping in chairs?”

She didn’t answer.

“Since New Year’s Eve,” he said. “Since the boat. Every night.”

She looked at the laptop.

“Fifteen nights,” she said finally. “Sixteen. I lost count around the ninth.”

“You never lose count.”

“I lost count,” said Aurelia. Her voice cracked. “I lost count, Si. I don’t know what day it is. I signed forty documents in your name and I sat at the Jade Hall and I made eleven men eat your mother’s soup and I sent Sun Wei across the border with six dollars and I haven’t slept lying down since the boat and I don’t know what day it is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He pulled.

Not hard. He couldn’t pull hard. He held her hand and pulled, very slightly, toward the bed.

“Come here,” he said.

“Dr. Ma said—”

“Dr. Ma said not to have sex,” said Chen Si. “She didn’t say anything about sleeping.” He pulled again. “Come here. Lie down. Next to me. Lying down.”

“I need to finish December—”

“December can wait.”

“Someone might—”

“Zhendong is downstairs,” said Chen Si. “In the lobby. He’s been there since we came home. He thinks I don’t know. He’s sitting on the sofa by the lifts with a newspaper upside down.” He held her hand. “Nobody is coming through that door tonight. Not past him. You know that.”

She looked at the door.

She looked at the gun on the bedside table, grip toward her hand.

She looked at him.

Very slowly, she closed the laptop. She put it on the floor beside the chair. She stood up, in his old grey jumper and her silk pyjamas and his necklace, and her legs nearly went, because she had been sitting folded up in a chair for five hours, and she held on to the bedside table.

Then she climbed into the bed beside him, carefully, on his left side, away from his heart, and lay down.

Lying down.

He felt her whole body go slack at once, all of it, as if someone had cut a string. She made a sound, very small, against his shoulder. Not a word. Just a sound. The sound of something very heavy being put down after being carried a very long way.

He put his arm round her. It was all he could do. His weak arm, round her shoulders, holding her against his side.

“There,” he said.

She was already asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

He lay awake.

He lay in the dark, with the lamp still on low, and his wife asleep against his side for the first time in sixteen nights, lying down, and he looked at the things on the bedside table. His water. His pills. Her gun, grip turned toward the empty chair.

He looked at the ugly leather armchair, the colour of old saddles, sitting beside the bed like a dog.

He looked at the laptop on the floor, closed, with December inside it, unfinished.

He thought about clause four. The Husband will not, at any time, attempt to keep the Wife somewhere safe.

There was no clause about the other way round.

She hadn’t needed one. She had just done it. She had kept him safe. For sixteen nights. In a corridor, and a chair, and the Jade Hall, and the thirty-ninth floor, and the forty-fourth. With his signature and his necklace and his mother’s soup and a gun and a laptop and no sleep.

He had built an empire so that nobody could ever take anything from him again.

And when somebody had tried, he had been lying flat on his back in a hospital gown, unable to lift his head, and she had walked into a room full of men who wanted her gone and sat down in his chair and made them eat.

He had not married a wife.

He turned his head and looked down at her, asleep against his shoulder, with her mouth slightly open and her hair everywhere and a crease on her cheek from Enzo’s chair and his necklace rising and falling at her throat with her breathing.

He had married a co-ruler.

And she was, he thought, without any question at all, better at it than he was.

✦ ✦ ✦

She slept for eleven hours.

He didn’t move for most of them. His arm went dead at around six. He didn’t move it. At nine, Zhao came up, and opened the bedroom door very quietly, and looked in, and saw them, and stood in the doorway for a while, and then went away again, and Chen Si heard him in the kitchen making congee.

At two in the afternoon, she woke.

She woke slowly, this time. The way people wake. She lay against his side for a while with her eyes closed, and he felt her come up out of it, a little at a time, and then her eyes opened, and she lifted her head, and looked at him.

“What time is it?” she said.

“Two in the afternoon.”

She stared at him.

“I have a meeting at the thirty-ninth floor at—”

“Qian moved it,” said Chen Si. “I texted him at seven. With my left hand. It took four minutes.” He smiled. “I told him my co-ruler was asleep and nobody was to wake her or I would be very angry. And then I remembered I’m not allowed to be angry. So I told him Dr. Ma would be very angry. He believed that.”

“Your co-ruler,” she said. “That isn’t in the contract.”

“No,” said Chen Si. “It should be. I want to add it. When we renew.” He looked at her. “Clause twelve. The Wife is not the Husband’s queen. She is his equal. He would like it noted that he found this out at three in the morning, from a chair.”

She looked at him.

Then she put her face back down against his shoulder and started to laugh, helplessly, into his hospital-smelling T-shirt, and then she was crying, and then she was doing both, and he held her with his one good arm and let her, for as long as she wanted, which was clause ten, though nobody had said the word.

In the kitchen, Zhao Zhendong turned off the stove, and put the lid on the congee, and stood at the window looking out at the harbour, listening to his brother’s wife cry and laugh in the next room, and did not go in.

chapters.title: He Is Weak for Six Weeks
chapters.desc: No stairs. No work. No anger. No sex. He hates every minute. She makes him eat. And on the forty-second day, when Dr. Ma finally says yes, the Wife reads clause nine very carefully, and finds a way to make sure he doesn’t lift a finger.
chapters.epigraph: “Nothing strenuous,” said Dr. Ma. “Then you won’t move,” said Aurelia. “At all. I’ll do it.”
chapters.content:
He was a terrible patient.

Everyone had known he would be. Dr. Ma had known; she said so, on the second day, when she came to the flat to check his heart and found him on the sofa with his laptop, and took the laptop away, and put it in her bag, and took it with her, and did not give it back for three weeks. Qian had known; he had bought a second drawer’s worth of antacids. Zhao had known; he had moved into the spare room without asking anyone and appeared in the kitchen every morning at seven to make congee, which Chen Si would not otherwise have eaten.

Aurelia had known best of all.

She had married a man who could not sit still while a list with nineteen names on it existed in the world. Who had built an empire from the age of eighteen so that nobody could ever take anything from him again. Who did not drink things other people gave him, and did not sleep through the night, and had never once in fourteen years not known exactly what was happening in every corner of his city.

And now he could not climb stairs.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first week, he was angry.

Not loudly. He couldn’t be loud; Dr. Ma had forbidden it, and in any case he didn’t know how. He was angry the way he did everything: quietly, precisely, relentlessly.
