He lay on the long grey sofa with the blanket over his knees and the jade chess board beside him and looked at the harbour with an expression that made Qian, who came every afternoon with a summary of the day, stand in the doorway for a full minute before he dared to come in.

He didn’t eat.

He said he wasn’t hungry. He said the congee was too thin, or too thick. He said the fish had too many bones. He said the soup—his mother’s soup, which Aurelia made again on the fourth day, from the sheet of cream paper in his handwriting, starting at eleven in the morning—was very good, and then didn’t finish it.

On the fifth day, she sat down on the end of the sofa with a bowl of rice porridge and a spoon and said, “Open.”

He looked at her.

“I’m not a child.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “A child would eat. Open.”

“Aurelia—”

“Dr. Ma says you’ve lost six kilos. You were thin before. You look like a coat hanger.” She held up the spoon. “I didn’t sit in your chair at the Jade Hall so you could starve yourself on a sofa out of spite. Open.”

He looked at the spoon.

Then he opened.

✦ ✦ ✦

She fed him for four days.

She did not let anyone else do it. Not Zhao, who offered, silently, by appearing at the end of the sofa with a bowl. Not the nurse Dr. Ma sent every morning. She sat on the end of the long grey sofa three times a day with a bowl and a spoon and fed the most dangerous man in the city like a child, one spoonful at a time, and he let her, with an expression of total, furious humiliation, and ate.

On the third day, he started to laugh.

Halfway through a bowl of congee. He was looking at her, sitting cross-legged on the sofa in his old grey jumper with the spoon held up, and the corner of his mouth went, and then the rest of it, and then he was laughing, weakly, with his head back against the cushions, which made his heart skip, which made her put the bowl down and press two fingers to the side of his neck with an expression of terror, which made him laugh harder.

“What?” she said. “What?”

“Mr. Pei. Mr. Kwan. Judge Wong,” said Chen Si, when he could breathe. He wiped his eyes. “If they could see me now. Being fed congee with a spoon.”

“They’ll never know.”

“Zhendong knows.”

From the kitchen, very quietly, there came a sound that might have been hm.

She picked up the bowl again.

“Open,” she said, and he did, still laughing.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second week, he was frightened.

She knew because he stopped being angry. He stopped saying the congee was too thin. He ate everything she gave him. He lay on the sofa and read the books she had put there, or pretended to, and looked at the harbour, and was very polite to everyone, and very quiet.

And at night, he didn’t sleep.

She knew because she didn’t either. She had moved back into the bed. She did not sleep in Enzo’s chair any more; he had made her promise. But she lay beside him in the dark and listened, and his breathing never went slow, and every hour or so she felt him go very still, all through, the way he went still over the list, and then let out a breath.

On the ninth night, she said, into the dark, “Is it your heart?”

He didn’t answer.

“It skips,” he said. “Every night. Ten times. Twenty. I count.” His voice was very quiet. “And every time, I wait. For the next one. And I think, what if it doesn’t come?”

She turned over and put her hand flat on his chest.

She felt it. His heart, under her palm. Steady. Steady. Then a stumble, a missed beat, a gap. Then, late, a hard thump, as if it had remembered.

He went rigid under her hand.

“There,” he said. “That one.”

“It came back.”

“This time.”

She kept her hand where it was. She felt the next beat, and the next, and the next.

“I’ll count for you,” she said.

He turned his head on the pillow.

“You don’t have to listen,” said Aurelia. “I’ll do it. I’ll keep my hand here. All night. I’ll count. And if one doesn’t come back, I’ll know before you do, and I’ll do something about it.” She pressed her palm flatter. “You go to sleep. I’m very good at counting. Ask the forty-one sapphires.”

He was silent.

Then, very slowly, she felt it: all the stiffness going out of him, the way it had gone out of her in the bed on the first night home, as if a string had been cut. His breathing changed. Went long. Went slow.

He slept.

She lay awake with her hand on his heart and counted, all night, every beat, until the sky went grey over the harbour. Eleven skips. Every one came back.

She did it for eleven nights.

On the twelfth night, he put his hand over hers on his chest, and said, “You can stop now. I think I can listen to it myself.”

She didn’t stop. But she let him think she had.

✦ ✦ ✦

The third and fourth weeks, he got better.

Slowly. Then less slowly. He walked to the window and back without holding the rail. He walked to the kitchen. He made tea, once, standing up, and Zhao watched him do it from the doorway with an expression of such total, silent alarm that Chen Si laughed and spilled half of it. He played chess against himself. He played chess against Zhao, who did not know how to play chess, and who sat across the jade board for two hours while Chen Si explained the rules, and then beat him, on the third game, by doing something that was not in any of the rules, which Chen Si spent forty minutes trying to work out was legal, and which turned out to be.

On the twenty-third day, Dr. Ma gave him back his laptop.

On the twenty-fourth, Qian brought him the summaries, and he read them, every line, and then put them down, and looked at Aurelia, who was sitting at the long table by the window with her own laptop, running his empire.

“You moved the east coast route,” he said.

“Mr. Hu isn’t running it any more. Obviously.” She didn’t look up. “I gave it to Mr. Pei. He’s honest. He’s never been one dollar short. He was furious. He said he only knew about planes. I told him a port is just an airport for boats.” She typed something. “He’s doing very well.”

He went back to the summaries. The judges’ fund, cut by thirty per cent; there was one fewer judge. And one more line that made him look up again.

“You doubled Mr. Lu’s share.”

She looked up.

“He clapped,” she said. “At the Jade Hall. Nobody asked him to.”

Chen Si looked at her across the room.

“It’s better,” he said finally. “All of it. Every change. It’s better than I had it.”

“I know,” said Aurelia, and went back to her screen.

He got up. Slowly, without the rail. He crossed the room to the long table and turned her chair round by its back, laptop and all, and bent and kissed her, one hand under her jaw, long and slow and with every bit of the hunger he had not been allowed to use for twenty-four days, until her hands had left the keyboard and were holding on to his jumper.

“Eighteen more days,” he said against her mouth. His heart was going hard; she could feel it through the wool. He did not care. “I’m counting too.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the forty-second day after the boat, his twenty-eighth at home, Dr. Ma came for the last time.

She listened to his heart, with her stethoscope, in silence, on the long grey sofa, while Aurelia stood by the window with her arms folded and did not breathe. She took his blood pressure. She looked at a printout from the machine he had worn on his chest for twenty-four hours the week before, a long strip of paper with a line on it, and ran her finger down it, slowly, the whole length.

Then she took off her stethoscope.

“Well,” she said. “You’re very lucky.”

Aurelia let out her breath.

“Your heart is not what it was,” said Dr. Ma. “It may never quite be. It will skip, sometimes, when you’re tired or frightened or angry. You’ll take one tablet a day for the rest of your life. You’ll see me every three months.” She put the printout in her bag. “But you can climb stairs. You can work, a little, if you stop when you’re tired, which you won’t. You can be angry, a little, if you must, which you will.”

She stood up.

At the door, she stopped, and looked back at the two of them: him on the sofa, her by the window.

“And the other thing,” she said. “You can do that too.” She looked at Chen Si. “Nothing strenuous. Not yet. Your heart is still healing. If it races, you stop.” She looked at Aurelia. “I mean it. Nothing strenuous.”

She went out.

The door closed.

There was a long silence on the forty-fourth floor.

Chen Si looked at his wife across the room.

Aurelia looked back at him.

“Nothing strenuous,” she said.

Chen Si smiled, very slowly, and didn’t say anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the dressing room.

He heard her in there for a while. Drawers. A cupboard door. When she came out, she was in nothing but his old grey jumper, which came to the middle of her thighs, and she was holding something in her hands, long and pale and soft, trailing on the floor.

A silk scarf. Hermès. Pale gold, with a pattern of carriages. Her grandmother’s. She had worn it in her hair on the night of the counter-offer, he remembered, under the black dress, though nobody else would have noticed.

She came and stood in front of the sofa.

“Clause nine,” she said.

He looked up at her.

“Dr. Ma said nothing strenuous,” said Aurelia. “She said if your heart races, you stop.” She ran the silk through her fingers. “So I’ve been thinking. About how to make absolutely sure you don’t do anything strenuous. At all.”

His face didn’t change. But his eyes went very dark.

“And?” he said.

“And you won’t move,” said Aurelia. “Not a finger. Not once. You’ll lie there, and I’ll do everything. All of it. Very slowly.” She held up the scarf between them. “And this is so that you don’t forget.”

He looked at the scarf.

He looked at her.

“Bedroom,” said Chen Si. “I’m not allowed to do anything strenuous on a sofa.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She tied his wrists to the headboard.

Not tight. Not tight at all. The silk was soft and old and she wound it once round each wrist and once round the carved wooden bar of the headboard, and knotted it so loosely that he could have slipped his hands out in a second. They both knew it. That was the point. It was not to stop him. It was to remind him.

“If your heart races,” she said, kneeling over him on the bed, “you tell me. You say it out loud, and I stop.”

“I know.”

“If you don’t tell me, and I feel it, I stop anyway. And I don’t start again for a week.”

He looked up at her from the pillow, with his wrists in her grandmother’s silk above his head.

“That,” he said, “is a very cruel threat.”

“I learned from you.” She put her hand flat on his chest, over his heart, the way she had for eleven nights. “I’m keeping my hand here the whole time. I’m going to count every beat, like you made me count the sapphires.” She bent down until her mouth was an inch from his. “If it goes over a hundred, I stop.”

He laughed. He couldn’t help it. It made his heart jump under her palm, and she felt it, and raised her eyebrows, and he stopped laughing.

“Eighty-four,” said Aurelia, and she was smiling.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was very slow.

She was slower than she had ever been. Slower than he had been on the night of the forty-fourth floor, when she had told him to kneel and he had taken off his watch. She had learned it from him, and she used it now, every bit of it, with her hand flat on his chest the whole time, counting.

She kissed him. His mouth. His jaw. The corner of his mouth, the other corner. She kissed the burn scar on the inside of his left forearm, all the way up from the silk at his wrist to his elbow, and felt his heart quicken under her palm, and stopped, and waited, and said, “Ninety-one,” and he closed his eyes and laughed under his breath, and waited too, until she said, “Eighty-six,” and went on.

She took his shirt off. She couldn’t take it all the way off, because of his wrists, so she unbuttoned it and pushed it open and left it, and he lay there in her grandmother’s silk with his shirt open and his ribs showing, because he had lost six kilos and was still a coat hanger, and she looked at him, and her face did something he couldn’t read.

“What?” he said.

“You’re so thin,” she said, and her voice cracked.

“I’m getting better.”

“I know.” She put her mouth against his ribs. One at a time. Very gently. As if counting those too. “I fed you every one of these.”

His heart did something under her hand that was not racing at all. It was something else.

She felt it.

She lifted her head and looked at him.

“Seventy-nine,” she said. “It slowed down.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si. He was looking at her with an expression she had seen only once before, on a blindfolded man finding her in the dark in Milan. “It does that. When you do that.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not let him move.

Not once. Not a finger. She did everything, the way she had said she would, slowly, with her hand on his heart, counting. Every time it climbed, she stopped, and waited, and kissed him somewhere soft and unimportant, his eyebrow, his shoulder, the inside of his wrist where the silk was, until it came down again. And every time she stopped, he made a sound, very low, that was not quite a protest and not quite a laugh, and pulled, very slightly, against the silk, and didn’t pull free.

Once, near the end of an hour, he said her name, very quietly.

“One hand,” he said. “Let me have one. Please. I won’t do anything strenuous with it. I just want to touch your face.” His eyes were black. “You can say no. Do you want it?”

She looked at him for a long moment, with her palm on his heart. Then she reached up and undid the knot on his left wrist, and he lifted that hand, slowly, and laid it against her cheek, and kept it there, and did not ask for anything more.

“Ninety-two,” she said, and turned her face into his palm.

It took a very long time.

She didn’t mind. She had nowhere to be. Nobody was going to come through the door; Zhao had gone home to his own flat for the first time in six weeks that afternoon, after Dr. Ma left, without a word, with a look at the two of them that said everything. The empire could wait. December was finished. January was finished. February could wait.

She had waited forty-two days.

She could wait a little longer.

When it finally happened, it was the gentlest thing that had ever happened between them. Not a game, though it had started as one. Not a contract, though there were clauses all through it. Her above him, slow, careful, with her hand on his heart and his wrists in her grandmother’s silk, and his eyes on her face the whole time, open, and her counting, out loud, like a lullaby, eighty-eight, eighty-nine, ninety, and him saying her name between the numbers, and at the end, when everything in both of them went bright and quiet at once, she felt his heart under her palm go fast, very fast, and she didn’t stop, because she knew, she knew from the forty-one sapphires and the eleven nights and the whole of her body, that this time, it was allowed.

And then it slowed.

And slowed.

And came back, steady, steady, under her hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, she untied the silk.

She did it very carefully, one wrist and then the other, and kissed each one, where the silk had been, though it had left no mark at all. Then she lay down beside him, on his left side, away from his heart, and put her hand back on his chest.

“Sixty-eight,” she said.

He laughed in the dark.

“You counted the whole time.”

“Every beat.”

“Even at the end?”

She was quiet for a moment.

“No,” she said. “Not at the end. I lost count at the end.” She pressed her palm flatter. “It went over a hundred. I felt it. And I didn’t stop.”

“I know,” said Chen Si.

“Dr. Ma said if it races—”

“It didn’t race,” said Chen Si. “It ran. There’s a difference.” He turned his head and looked at her. “It ran toward something. Not away.”

She looked at him in the dark.

Then she put her face against his shoulder, and kept her hand on his heart, and counted, silently, until she fell asleep.

Lying down.

chapters.title: The Word Is Milan
chapters.desc: The danger is over. He is safe. She is fine. She is fine for nine days. On the tenth, in the middle of the boutique, holding a champagne flute for a client, her hands stop working. She says the word for the first time, and it isn’t in bed.
chapters.epigraph: “If either party says it, at any time, in any room, in any circumstances, everything stops.” — Clause 10. She had always thought it would be in the dark.
chapters.content:
She was fine.

She told everyone so. She told Enzo, who looked at her over his magnifying glasses on the first morning she came back to the boutique, in the second week of February, and said nothing at all. She told Serafina, who rang every day from the garage and asked, in a voice that pretended not to care, how is he, and then, how are you, and Aurelia said, fine, both times. She told Qian, who brought her the summaries on the thirty-ninth floor every afternoon now, to her desk, which had been his desk, which was theirs, and who looked at her face every afternoon a moment longer than he needed to.

She told Chen Si.

“I’m fine,” she said, on the long grey sofa, on the evening of the first day she went back to work, when he asked. “Really. It’s over. You’re better. Sun Wei is gone. Mr. Hu and Lam and Judge Yip are where they are. The routes are running. The banks are happy. Dr. Ma says you’ll live to ninety if you take your tablet and stop working at midnight, which you won’t.” She put her head on his shoulder. “It’s over, Si. We won. I’m fine. Also, Dr. Ma says you’re allowed stairs now. So tonight you can carry me to bed, and I’ll time you.”

“That sounds strenuous.”

“It’s eleven metres. I measured.” She tipped her face up to his, bright and perfect and absolutely sure. “I’ll count out loud. You like it when I count.”

He looked down at her, at the smile she had put on for him the way she put on gold, and smiled back, because she wanted him to.

He didn’t say anything.

He put his arm round her and looked at the harbour.

Then he stood up, with no warning, and picked her up off the sofa, and carried her the eleven metres to bed, and she was laughing too hard to count. He laid her down and followed her down and kissed her as if he had been waiting six weeks to do it standing up, and afterwards he did not let go of her. He held her until she slept, and lay awake watching her face, because he had seen the smile she put on for him, and he knew exactly what it was made of.

She was fine for nine days.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the tenth day, a client came to the boutique to celebrate.

A woman called Mrs. Leung, whose husband owned a chain of hotels, and whose daughter was getting married in April, and who had commissioned a parure from AURELIA in the autumn: a necklace, earrings, a bracelet and a tiara, in yellow diamonds and gold, for the wedding. It had taken Enzo four months. It was the most important commission the boutique had ever had.

It was finished.

Mrs. Leung came at four on a Thursday, with her daughter and two friends, to see it, and Aurelia closed the shop to everyone else and laid it out on black velvet on the long glass counter, under the lights, and the daughter put her hands over her mouth and cried, and Mrs. Leung said, “Oh, Mrs. Chen,” and the two friends took photographs, and it was, Aurelia would think later, one of the best moments of her working life.

And because it was a celebration, Lily, her assistant, who was twenty-six and very efficient and had been with her since the second boutique opened, brought out a bottle of champagne on a tray.

With five flutes, already poured, gold and fizzing under the lights.

✦ ✦ ✦

Lily held the tray out to her first.

Aurelia reached for a flute.

Her hand stopped.

It stopped in the air, a few centimetres from the stem of the glass. She looked at it. She told it to move. It did not move. It hung there, her own hand, with her wedding ring on it and gold at the wrist, in the air above a tray of champagne, and would not go any further.

“Mrs. Chen?” said Lily.

Aurelia looked at the glasses.

Five flutes, fizzing under the lights.

She saw the inside of the rims. She couldn’t see anything on them; there was nothing on them; Lily had poured them in the back, from a bottle Aurelia had bought herself at the merchant on the Peak, into glasses Aurelia had bought herself in Milan, and washed herself, last week, because she had started washing all the glasses in the boutique herself and had not told anyone why.

She could see a brush.

A fine brush, painting the inside of the rim. Forty glasses on the upper deck of the Pearl. One in her hand. Four. Three. Two. His hand reaching out, smiling. I only drink what I take.

Her hand began to shake.

Not a little. Not the tremor she had seen in Sun Wei’s hand at the Jade Hall, or Chen Si’s on the coffee cup. All of it. All at once. Her hand, and then her arm, and then the rest of her, standing at her own counter in front of Mrs. Leung and her daughter and two friends with their phones out, shaking so hard that her rings clicked against each other.

“Mrs. Chen?” said Lily again, in a different voice.

Aurelia couldn’t breathe.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t remember, afterwards, how she got to the workshop.

She remembered Enzo’s hand on her elbow. She remembered his voice, in Italian, very calm, saying something to Mrs. Leung about a small emergency, about Mrs. Chen being called away, about Lily showing them the tiara. She remembered the workshop door closing. She remembered sitting on the floor of the workshop with her back against her own bench, where she had once sat in a camel coat after the proposal with her husband beside her, among the dropped tools, and not being able to get any air into her chest at all.

Her heart was going like something trapped, fast and then faster.

She thought, very clearly: This is what it felt like. For him. On the boat. This is what it was.

She thought: I’m dying.

She knew she wasn’t. Some cold clear part of her, the part that had been doing the numbers on her father’s balcony, knew exactly what this was. She had read about it at three in the morning in Enzo’s chair, on her laptop, between ledgers, without admitting to herself why she was reading it. It had a name. It happened to people after things. It was not dangerous. It would pass.

It didn’t feel like it would pass.

It felt like the bottom of the harbour.

Enzo was kneeling in front of her. He was saying something. She couldn’t hear it. She could see his old brown face, very close, very frightened, his magnifying glasses pushed up onto his forehead.

“Call him,” she managed. It came out as almost nothing. “Enzo. Call—”

“I called him,” said Enzo. “Cara. I called him four minutes ago. He’s coming.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He came in nine minutes.

She found out later that he had been on the thirty-ninth floor, in a meeting, with Mr. Pei and Mr. Kwan and the man from the shipping company, and that his phone had rung, and he had looked at it and seen Enzo, and answered it, and listened for six seconds, and stood up in the middle of Mr. Kwan’s sentence and walked out of the room without a word. That he had not waited for the lift. That he had taken the stairs. Thirty-nine floors. With his heart.

That Zhao, who had been in the lobby, had seen him come out of the stairwell at a run, grey, with his hand pressed to his chest, and had not asked a single question, and had driven from the thirty-ninth floor to Harbour Road in four minutes, through every red light on the way.

She didn’t know any of that.

She only knew that the workshop door opened, and he was there, in his shirtsleeves, breathing much too hard, with his tie gone and his face grey and his hand on the doorframe, and that he saw her on the floor against the bench, and that his face did something she had never seen it do.

He crossed the workshop. He went down on his knees in front of her. He didn’t touch her. He put his hands out, palms up, in front of her, and held them there.

“Aurelia,” he said. “I’m here. Look at me.”

She looked at him.

“Breathe with me,” said Chen Si. “In. Slowly. Four.”

She couldn’t.

“Three,” he said. “Two. One. Out. Slowly. Four. Three. Two. One.” His hands didn’t move. “Again. In.”

She tried. It came in ragged. It went out ragged.

“Again,” said Chen Si. “You’re very good at counting. Count with me.”

She counted with him.

It took a long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

When she could talk, she said it.

She didn’t decide to. She was sitting on the floor of the workshop with her back against the bench and his hands held out in front of her, palms up, and her breathing had come down from wherever it had been and was almost a breath again, almost, and she looked at him, at his grey face and his hand still pressed, every so often, against his own chest, and she knew he had run, and she knew he shouldn’t have, and she knew what it had cost.

And the word came up out of her.

“Milan,” said Aurelia.

He went completely still.

She saw it land. All the way down. Clause ten. If either party says it, at any time, in any room, in any circumstances, everything stops.

She had written it. Eleven pages. Red ink. She had always, always thought it would be in the dark. In bed. With his tie round her wrists or her grandmother’s silk round his. In the middle of a game she had started. A word for when the game went too far.

She had never once imagined saying it on the floor of her own workshop, at four in the afternoon on a Thursday, in front of Enzo, with Mrs. Leung’s yellow diamonds on the counter in the next room.

“Milan,” she said again. Her voice broke. “Si. Milan. Milan. Milan—”

He didn’t say anything.

He didn’t need to. He knew what came next. It was in the clause. She had written it.

Then the parties will lie down together and the one who said it will be held for as long as they want to be held.

He gathered her up.

There, on the floor of the workshop. He sat down properly, with his back against her bench, among the tools, in his shirtsleeves, and pulled her into his lap and put both arms round her and held her. Not gently. Hard. As hard as his weak arms could. With her face in his neck and his face in her hair, and his heart going much too fast against her back, and hers going much too fast against his chest.

And she fell apart.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had cried in front of him before.

Across a jade chess board, at twenty-two, in a red dress, for two minutes, about Vienna and nine days of silence. In the bed after Milan, a little. On the morning he woke her at two in the afternoon and told Qian his co-ruler was asleep.

She had never fallen apart.

She did now.

All of it. Everything she had not let herself feel for forty-two days and nine more. The boat. The glass in her hand. Four, three, two. His hand reaching for it. Twenty-two minutes. The launch, and the fireworks, and his eyes closing. My queen. Dr. Ma on the pier. The ICU. The green line jumping and stuttering. Sitting in a gold dress on a plastic chair in a corridor at three in the morning, not crying, because she would not cry until she knew. The forty documents. The tiny lift at every turn. The Jade Hall. Sun Wei’s hand on the back of his chair. The soup. Judge Yip’s bowl, filled to the brim. Eating it, cold, alone, at eleven at night. Six dollars in an envelope. Sixteen nights in a chair with a gun. Counting his heart for eleven nights. Feeding him with a spoon. His ribs.

All of it came up out of her at once, on the floor of the workshop, in his lap, in his arms, and she sobbed. Not silently. Not with her shoulders shaking and her face in her hands. Out loud. Like a child. Like something tearing. For a long, long time.

He held her.

He didn’t say anything. He didn’t say it’s over. He didn’t say you’re safe. He didn’t say I’m here. He held her, as hard as he could, on the floor among the tools, and rocked, very slightly, without seeming to know he was doing it, the way you rock someone very small. And let her.

Enzo stood in the doorway of the workshop for a moment. Then he went out, very quietly, and closed the door, and she heard him, through it, faintly, telling Mrs. Leung in his gentlest Italian that the champagne was on the house, and that Mrs. Chen sent her apologies, and that the tiara would look magnificent.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t know how long it lasted.

When it was over, she was lying against his chest, on the floor, with her face wet against his shirt and her breath coming in long ragged shudders, and his arms still round her, and his hand moving slowly up and down her back.

His heart had slowed down. She could feel it. Steady. Steady.

“You ran,” she said. Her voice was wrecked. “Up the stairs. From the thirty-ninth floor. With your heart.”

“Down the stairs,” said Chen Si. “I ran down. It’s easier.”

“Dr. Ma said—”

“Dr. Ma said nothing strenuous.” He put his face in her hair. “Dr. Ma has never had Enzo ring her and say she can’t breathe.”

She started crying again. Less, this time. Quieter.

“I said it,” she said. “The word.”

“I know.”

“I never thought—I thought it would be in bed. In the dark. I thought it would be about—” She stopped. “I didn’t think it would be about this.”

“I did,” said Chen Si.

She lifted her head and looked at him.

He was looking down at her. His face was grey and tired and his eyes were wet. He looked more frightened than he had looked on the launch, with the fireworks going off and his heart stopping.

“You wrote it in March,” he said. “The word is Milan because it is the city where the Wife learned to be afraid.” He touched her wet face. “You never said it in bed. Not once. In ten months. Not with the tie, not with the cuffs, not with the sapphires. You never needed to. You weren’t afraid of anything I did.” His thumb moved on her cheekbone. “I always knew, when you said it, it would be about something else. Something that wasn’t a game.”

She looked at him.

“How did you know?”

“Because I know you,” said Chen Si. “You’ve spent six weeks being the strongest person in this city so that I didn’t have to be. Nobody can do that forever. And you would never, ever ask for help.” He held her face. “So you wrote a word, in March, before any of it. So that when the day came, you wouldn’t have to ask. You’d only have to say it.”

She stared at him.

She had not known that. She had written it, eleven pages, red ink, four nights on the floor of her flat. She had not known that was what she was doing.

He had.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stayed on the floor of the workshop until it was dark.

Enzo went home at six. He knocked on the door first, very softly, and when nobody answered, he opened it a crack and looked in, and saw them on the floor against the bench, her asleep against Chen Si’s chest and Chen Si awake, holding her, looking at the wall.

Chen Si looked up at him.

Enzo didn’t say anything. He put a blanket on the end of the bench, the old wool one he kept for the nights he slept at the workshop, and went out, and locked the front door of the boutique behind him, and left the key under the mat, where she would know to look for it.

At eight, she woke.

She lay against his chest without moving.

“Si,” she said. “I’m not fine. I haven’t been since the boat. I told everyone I was.”

“I know,” said Chen Si. “Nobody believed you.”

She was quiet.

“Dr. Ma,” she said finally. “She said she knows someone. For people who—after things. A woman. She gave me a card in January. I put it in my bag.” She swallowed. “I never called.”

He didn’t say anything for a while.

“I’m coming with you,” he said. “When you call. And when you go.”

She lifted her head and looked at him.

“You’d do that?”

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “Every time.” He looked at her. “After Block C, after the back room with Zhendong bleeding, I spent eight years building a wall and I never talked to anyone about any of it. Not until you, on a sofa, in January. That wasn’t clever. I was lucky.” He touched her face. “I’d like you to be clever instead.”

She put her head back down on his chest.

“Tomorrow,” she said. “I’ll call tomorrow.” And then, after a moment: “And Si. If you ever run down thirty-nine flights of stairs again, with your heart, I will divorce you and take half your people.”

He laughed in the dark of the workshop, among the dropped tools, with his arms round her.

“I know you will,” he said. “That’s why I married you.”

chapters.title: The Collection Called “Balcony”
chapters.desc: A year after the boat. Therapy on Tuesdays. A florist from the Walled City married to her brother-in-law. And a collection about the worst night of her life, which she models for exactly one person, piece by piece.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re making jewellery about the night your mother humiliated you.” “No. I’m making jewellery about the man who didn’t try to fix it.”
chapters.content:
She went to see the woman on Tuesdays.

Her name was Dr. Ho. She was sixty, and small, and had an office on the twelfth floor of a building in Central with a window that looked at another building and a box of tissues on every surface, and she did not say very much. In the first session, Aurelia talked for fifty minutes without stopping, about the boat and the glass and the brush and the launch and the green line, very fast, very precisely, the way she read a ledger, and at the end Dr. Ho said, “You’ve told me everything that happened. You haven’t told me one thing you felt,” and Aurelia sat in the chair and could not think of a single word to say.

She went back the next Tuesday.

And the next.

Chen Si drove her. Every Tuesday, at nine, in the black car, himself, because Zhao was busy that year with something at the Docks that neither of them asked about. He drove her to the building in Central and parked in the car park underneath and sat in the car for fifty minutes with a coffee he didn’t drink and a book, and when she came out, he didn’t ask what she had said. He just drove her home, the long way, along the harbour, and held her hand on the gear stick.

Once, in the third week, she came out with her face blotched and furious and got into the car and said, “Don’t.”

He didn’t. He drove the long way, and at the red light by the ferry pier he lifted her hand off the gear stick and kissed her knuckles, one at a time, without looking at her, and put it back.

“That wasn’t don’t,” she said.

“No,” he agreed. “That was a red light.”

She laughed for the first time that day, and at the next light she put his hand on her knee herself, and left it there.

She never asked him what he did for those fifty minutes.

She found out in March, from Qian, who found out from the parking attendant: he didn’t read the book. He sat in the car with it open on his knee and looked at the concrete wall in front of him, and every Tuesday, at about the forty-minute mark, he put the book down and put his hand over his eyes and stayed like that until she came.

✦ ✦ ✦

That was the year Zhao got married.

She heard it in April. From Chen Si, at breakfast, who had come home very late the night before from a registry office, where he had been a witness, and who put down his coffee and said, “Zhendong married someone yesterday.”

Aurelia put down her croissant.

“Married.”

“At the registry office. Yesterday afternoon. I was the witness.” He looked at his coffee. “She asked him. With a contract. Three pages. Handwritten.” A very small pause. “He signed it without arguing.”

“Who is she?”

Chen Si looked at her across the table with an expression of enormous, delighted, barely concealed malice.

“A florist,” he said. “From the Walled City. Her father moves cargo for him.” He picked up his coffee. “I believe you were at school together. Lin Elowen.”

Aurelia sat very still.

Then she put her croissant down very carefully on her plate, and stood up, and went to get her coat and her enormous sunglasses.

“Where are you going?” said Chen Si, with great innocence.

“To a flower shop,” said Aurelia. “In the Walled City. I need to watch her face while I tell her I know.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went. She watched Elowen’s face. It was, she told Chen Si that night, worth the drive.

It was more than that. She did not tell him the rest. She did not tell him about the moment, halfway through, when she had looked at Elowen Lin behind her counter in a green apron with her hands full of eucalyptus and seen, under the composure and the old cool rivalry, something that she recognised from the inside. A woman who had married a dangerous man to protect her father. Who did not yet know what she had married.

She had said, at the door, the only serious thing she said all afternoon. When one of them bleeds, the other one does something terrible. And when we bleed, darling, they both do. Make sure you’re ready for that. I wasn’t.

She had been thinking of a launch in the dark, with fireworks over the harbour.

Elowen hadn’t known that. Elowen had looked at her strangely, and nodded, and Aurelia had put on her sunglasses and left.

She went to Dr. Ho the next Tuesday and talked for fifty minutes about Elowen Lin, and the number two beside her name at seventeen, and a library, and a boy with a physics notebook, and at the end Dr. Ho said, “You’ve spent your whole life competing with her. Have you ever once told her that you’re frightened?” and Aurelia laughed out loud in the chair and said, “God, no,” and then sat very still, and then reached for the tissues.

✦ ✦ ✦

She started the collection in May.

She did not plan to. She was supposed to be working on the autumn pieces for the third boutique, the one opening in Singapore, near Mr. Tan, who had become a friend. She sat down at her bench at two in the morning with a pencil and a sheet of paper, the way she had on the night of the balcony, and meant to draw a ring for Singapore, and drew a coat instead.

A long coat. Over a woman’s shoulders. Too big for her. Falling to her knees.

She sat and looked at it.

Then she drew it again, smaller. As a pendant. A tiny coat of gold, hanging from a chain, over a tiny figure.

Then as a brooch. Then as earrings. Then as a cuff, wrapping round a wrist the way a coat wraps round a body, the gold textured like cashmere, brushed and soft-looking, so that you wanted to touch it.

By five in the morning, the bench was covered.

✦ ✦ ✦

She called it Balcony.

Eleven pieces. All in a gold she developed with Enzo over three months, an alloy with a little copper and a little silver, brushed by hand until it had the soft warm colour of camel cashmere in lamplight. No stones. Not one. Everything in it was about texture and weight and the way it lay on skin.

A collar that sat on the shoulders like the collar of a coat turned up against the wind. A long chain that fell down the back and ended at the base of the spine in a tiny gold coat button. Earrings like two drops of rain, the moment before they fell. A ring shaped like a hand, very small, open, palm up, the way a hand is held out when it is offering something and not insisting. A bracelet engraved, on the inside, so that only the wearer would ever see it, with a line of tiny characters in a sharp angular hand, cut not written.

I’m more interested in what you do in the dark.

And a necklace. The last piece. The centre of the collection. A heavy collar of brushed camel gold, twisted apart in the middle, and mended, with a seam of bright white.

The broken necklace. Again. Bigger. Softer. Coat-coloured.

“You’re making jewellery,” said Enzo, at the bench in July, holding the collar up to the light, “about the night your mother humiliated you in front of two hundred people.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “I’m making jewellery about the man who didn’t try to fix it.”

Enzo looked at her over his magnifying glasses.

“Does he know?”

“Not yet,” said Aurelia. “I’m going to show him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She showed him in September.

On the forty-fourth floor, on a Sunday night, with the lights off and the harbour glittering below and the eleven pieces laid out on black velvet on the long table by the window, under a single lamp.

He came home at nine. He stopped in the doorway.

He looked at the table.

He looked at it, from the doorway, without coming in. She watched him read it. The coat collar. The rain earrings. The open hand. The broken necklace, coat-coloured.

“That’s the balcony,” he said. “That’s my coat.”

“Yes.”

He came into the room. Slowly. He stood at the table and looked down at the pieces under the lamp. He didn’t touch them. He picked up the bracelet, finally, the plain wide band of brushed gold, and turned it over, and saw the engraving on the inside, and read it, and put it down very carefully.

For a while he didn’t say anything.

“It’s called Balcony,” said Aurelia. “It launches in Paris. In March. At the shows.” She was standing by the window in his old grey jumper. “I wanted you to see it first. Before anyone. Before Enzo photographs it. Before the press.” She paused. “Before my mother.”

He looked up at her.

“Why?”

“Because it’s yours,” she said. “All of it. I made it out of the worst night of my life, and it isn’t the worst night any more. It’s the night I met you.” She lifted her chin. “I wanted you to know that before I told the whole world.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

He picked up the collar. The coat collar, the one that sat on the shoulders like a turned-up lapel. He held it in both hands, under the lamp.

“Put it on,” he said.

She went still.

“Not like that,” said Chen Si. His voice had gone very low. “Not over the jumper.” He looked at her across the long table. “I want to see it the way it was meant to be seen. I want to put every piece on you myself. One at a time.”

She looked at him.

“Clause nine,” she said. “Otherwise?”

“Otherwise,” said Chen Si.

She took off the grey jumper.

She stood by the window on the forty-fourth floor in nothing at all, with the whole harbour behind her, and he came round the table with the coat collar in his hands and stood in front of her and laid it on her shoulders. Cold, and then warm. Heavy. Settling into the hollows of her collarbones like the collar of a coat turned up against the wind.

He stepped back and looked at her.

“One,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He put them on her one at a time.

Slowly. Without hurrying. Looking at each one on her before he went back to the table for the next. The long chain down her spine, ending in its tiny gold button at the base of her back, which he fastened with his fingers on the nape of her neck and then ran his hand all the way down after it, following the gold, over every vertebra, until his palm rested where the button lay, and stayed there, and she stopped breathing.

“Two,” he said, against her shoulder.

The rain earrings. He put them in himself, one and then the other, his fingers on her earlobes, and then put his mouth just below each one, where the gold drops touched her neck, so that she felt the cold metal and his warm mouth at the same time, and her knees went.

“Three. Four.”

The open hand ring. He slid it onto her finger and then lifted her hand and kissed the palm, where the little gold hand lay open against her skin, offering.

The cuffs. The brooch, which had nowhere to go, because she was wearing nothing to pin it to, and which he held for a moment, and then laid in the hollow at the base of her throat, cold, and told her to keep still so that it wouldn’t fall, and then made it very, very difficult to keep still.

“Seven,” he said. “Don’t let it fall.”

“Si—”

“Don’t let it fall,” said Chen Si, and put his mouth against her ribs.

She didn’t let it fall.

She didn’t know how. She stood by the window with her hands pressed flat against the cold glass behind her and his mouth moving over her slowly and the brooch balanced in the hollow of her throat, rising and falling with her breathing, and she held absolutely still, and it was the hardest thing she had ever done in her life, harder than counting forty-one sapphires, harder than the Jade Hall, and when she finally, finally made a sound she couldn’t stop, the brooch slid sideways off her collarbone and he caught it, without looking, in his hand, before it hit the floor.

“Seven and a half,” he said.

She laughed, wildly, against the glass.

✦ ✦ ✦

The broken necklace was last.

He brought it from the table. Heavy. Coat-coloured. Twisted apart in the middle and mended with white.

He stood in front of her, with everything else on her already, ten pieces of brushed camel gold catching the lamplight on her bare skin, and held it up between them.

“This is the one you gave me in the workshop,” he said. “Bigger. I still wear the first one.” His other hand went to his own throat, under his shirt, where it was. “Every day. Since the proposal. I took it off for the hospital. You wore it. Then you gave it back.”

“I know.”

“This one is yours,” said Chen Si.

He fastened it round her neck.

It settled over the coat collar, heavy, the break lying exactly at the hollow of her throat, the bright white seam against her skin.

He looked at her.

At eleven pieces of gold made out of the worst night of her life, on her body, by the window, with the harbour behind her.

“I didn’t try to fix it,” he said. “On the balcony. You put that in the collection.”

“Yes.”

“It wasn’t that I didn’t want to.” He put his hand flat over the broken necklace, over the break, over her heart. “I wanted to go back into that dining room and take your mother apart in front of everyone.” His voice was very low. “I didn’t, because I could see you were already doing it yourself. In your head. Doing the sums. I wasn’t going to take that away from you.” He looked at her. “I’ve never wanted to fix you. You were never broken.”

She looked at him.

Then she took his face in both hands, with the little open gold hand on her finger against his cheek.

“Eleven,” she said. “That’s all of them. You can stop counting now.”

He didn’t. He lifted her off her feet and took her down onto the rug by the window, in front of the harbour, with eleven pieces of gold on her, and none on him, and they didn’t stop counting for a very long time.

✦ ✦ ✦

Balcony launched in Paris in March.

The man from Vogue wrote that it was the most intimate collection shown in Paris in a decade: jewellery that looks as if it was made to be taken off by one person only.

He was more right than he knew.

The bracelet with the engraving on the inside was not in the collection. There was only ever one. She wore it every day, on her left wrist, under her sleeve.

He never asked her for it back.

chapters.title: The Paris Show
chapters.desc: Six days before the presentation, a rival house shows a coat-collar necklace that is hers, line for line. Someone sold her sketches. Her atelier is in pieces. She has three nights. He is in the front row, and does not look at his phone.
chapters.epigraph: “They stole the drawings. They can’t steal the hands.” — Maestro Enzo Bellini, Paris, 3 a.m.
chapters.content:
The presentation was on the fourth of March, at the Palais de Tokyo, at eight in the evening, in a room with a concrete floor and white walls and three hundred chairs, and every important person in jewellery in the world was coming.

On the twenty-sixth of February, six days before, a house called Delorme showed its spring collection at the Grand Palais.

Aurelia watched it on her laptop, in a hotel room on the Rue de Rivoli, at eleven at night, with Chen Si asleep beside her and Enzo in the next room and the whole atelier, eleven people, in the rooms down the corridor.

She watched it because you watched everything, in Paris, in March. Because Delorme was old and grand and important and had been making jewellery for queens since 1871, and because a new collection from Delorme mattered.

The fourth piece down the runway was a collar.

Brushed gold. Warm. The soft camel colour of cashmere in lamplight. Sitting on the model’s shoulders like the collar of a coat turned up against the wind.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t move.

She watched the fifth piece. Earrings. Two drops of gold like rain, the moment before they fell.

The sixth. A ring. A tiny open hand, palm up.

The seventh. A long chain down the back, ending at the base of the spine in a tiny gold button.

She closed the laptop.

She sat on the edge of the bed in the dark in the hotel on the Rue de Rivoli with the laptop closed on her knees, and her hands, she noticed, from a long way away, were perfectly still.

Dr. Ho would have been proud of them.

Then she got up and went next door and knocked on Enzo’s door until he opened it, in his pyjamas, with his glasses on his forehead, and she held out the laptop, and opened it, and played it for him from the fourth piece.

Enzo watched it.

He watched all of it, standing in the doorway of a hotel room in Paris in his pyjamas. His old brown face did not change at all. When it was finished, he took the laptop out of her hands and closed it and handed it back.

“Someone sold the drawings,” he said, in Italian. “Someone in the atelier.”

“Yes.”

“Not me,” said Enzo.

She looked at him.

“I know it’s not you,” she said. “Enzo. Dio. I know.”

“I wanted to say it out loud,” said Enzo. “So that later, when you are going through everyone, you don’t have to wonder.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went through everyone.

Not that night. That night she went back to her room and lay down beside her husband, who had woken when she left, and was sitting up in the dark, waiting, and she told him, and he listened, and when she had finished he said only, “What do you need?” and she said, “I don’t know yet,” and he said, “All right,” and lay back down, and put his arm round her, and neither of them slept.

In the morning, she went through everyone.

Eleven people. The atelier. She had chosen every one of them herself. Enzo. Lily, her assistant, twenty-seven now, efficient, loyal, who had been with her since the second boutique. Two bench jewellers from Valenza whom Enzo had trained. A setter from Jaipur. A polisher from Hong Kong. Two pattern-cutters, who made the wax models and the paper templates from her drawings so that the bench jewellers could cut the metal. A photographer. A girl who did the books. A boy who did the boxes.

She sat in the hotel’s small meeting room with the door closed and Ms. Fong on a video call from home, in enormous glasses, and Qian on another, and went through everyone. Every phone. Every bank account she could see. Every email. Every flight. Every hotel bill.

It took nine hours.

At seven in the evening, Qian, on the screen, said, “Mrs. Chen. The pattern-cutter. Paul. The younger one.”

She looked at the screen.

“He flew to Paris on the third of January,” said Qian. “Alone. For two days. He told you it was his grandmother’s funeral, in Lyon. His grandmother died in 2015.” A pause. “He stayed at a hotel on the Rue Saint-Honoré. Two hundred metres from the Delorme atelier. And on the sixth of January, a company in Andorra paid forty thousand euros into his sister’s account.”

Aurelia closed her eyes.

Paul. Twenty-four. Quiet. Talented. Very, very good with wax. He had cried at the wedding of one of the polishers last year. He had made her a birthday card, in December, by hand, with a drawing of the broken necklace on it in gold ink.

He had made the paper templates for every piece in Balcony.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t call him into the meeting room.

She went to find him. In the workroom the atelier had set up in the hotel’s second-floor ballroom, among the crates and the cases and the long tables covered with black velvet where Balcony lay, eleven pieces, waiting.

He was at a table in the corner, alone, cleaning a wax model with a soft brush. He looked up when she came in. He saw her face. He put the brush down.

She stood in front of his table.

She didn’t say anything. She looked at him, the way she had looked at Sun Wei across the round table at the Jade Hall, the way she had looked at the man with the sunflower seeds when he talked over her, the way she had learned to look at people from the most dangerous man in the city.

Paul started to cry.

“My sister,” he said. “Madame. My sister. She’s sick. In Lyon. The treatment isn’t—our insurance doesn’t—they said forty thousand, and they came to me, the men from Delorme, in December, they knew about her, I don’t know how they knew, and they said forty thousand, just the templates, just paper, you’d never know, it would be months before—” He was sobbing. “I’m sorry. I’m sorry. I’m so sorry.”

She looked at him.

At his face. At the wax model on the table in front of him. At the birthday card he had made her in December, which was in her bag, she realised, because she carried it everywhere.

She thought about Sun Wei. Six dollars in an envelope. One suitcase. The border.

She thought about Chen Si’s mother in the study, looking at the door.

She thought about a woman in Lyon, sick, whose brother had sold the drawings for forty thousand euros because the insurance wouldn’t pay.

“What’s her name?” she said.

Paul looked up.

“Your sister,” said Aurelia. “What’s her name?”

“Claire,” he whispered.

“What does she have?”

He told her.

Aurelia stood in front of his table.

“You’re fired,” she said finally. “You’ll leave tonight. You won’t work in jewellery again; I’ll make sure of that, and so will Delorme, because they won’t want you anywhere near them once this is over.” She took out her phone. “And tomorrow morning a company in Luxembourg called AS Holdings is going to pay your sister’s hospital in Lyon for the rest of her treatment. All of it. Whatever it costs.” She looked at him. “Not because of you. Because of her. Because her brother was frightened and stupid and loved her, and I know what that’s like.”

Paul stared at her.

“Get out, Paul,” said Aurelia gently. “Before I change my mind.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Then she went upstairs and fell apart in the bathroom for eleven minutes.

She locked the door and sat on the edge of the bath in her black dress, and what she could not stop seeing was not Paul’s face. It was the collar on the Delorme runway, on a stranger’s shoulders, under a stranger’s lights: the balcony, the coat, the only night of her life that had been given to her without a price, worn by someone who had paid forty thousand euros for it. Her teeth began to chatter. She put both palms flat on the cold enamel and pressed until her wrists ached, and said his name once, under her breath, as if it were the word.

Not the way she had on the floor of the workshop. Not that. She had learned, on Tuesdays, in an office in Central with tissues on every surface, the difference. She sat on the edge of the bath in the hotel on the Rue de Rivoli and shook, and breathed, four in, four out, the way he had taught her on the workshop floor, and let it happen, and let it pass.

When she came out, he was sitting on the bed.

“Qian told me about Paul,” he said. “What did you do?”

She told him.

He listened. When she got to AS Holdings is going to pay your sister’s hospital, something moved in his face.

“Sun Wei got six dollars,” he said.

“Sun Wei put poison in my glass,” said Aurelia. “Paul sold paper to save his sister.” She sat down beside him. “Dr. Ho says I don’t have to be you every time. She says I’m allowed to be me.”

He looked at her.

“What do you need?” he said again. He took her hand off the bedspread and held it in both of his, tight enough to hurt a little, and his voice stayed perfectly mild. “If the answer is that you’d like Delorme to stop existing, say so. I can have it done by the fourth.”

She almost laughed. She looked at her hands, held in his.

“Three nights,” she said. “And Enzo. And every bench jeweller I have. And four hundred grams of gold I don’t have yet. And something Delorme can’t steal, because it isn’t on paper.”

“What isn’t on paper?”

Aurelia looked up.

“The engraving,” she said. “On the inside of the bracelet. The one only I wear.” She touched her wrist, under her sleeve. “Delorme stole the shapes. They didn’t steal the hand.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They worked for three nights.

In the second-floor ballroom of the hotel on the Rue de Rivoli, with the doors locked and the curtains drawn, at eleven long tables under work lamps. Every bench jeweller. Enzo. Lily. The setter from Jaipur. The polisher from Hong Kong. The girl who did the books, who turned out to be very good with a burnisher. The boy who did the boxes, who made tea.

They didn’t throw Balcony away.

That was what she had decided, on the edge of the bath. Delorme had shown the shapes. They would be on every magazine in Paris by the end of the week. If AURELIA showed a coat collar on the fourth of March, everyone would say she had copied Delorme.

So she didn’t change the shapes.

She changed what was inside them.

Every piece. All eleven. Every one of them, on its inside surface, where it would lie against the skin, where only the wearer would ever see it, got an engraving. Cut by hand. Not written. Lifted at every turn. In a sharp angular hand that she had learned at three in the morning in her workshop from a man who read other men’s hallmarks for forty years.

A line, inside each piece, in his hand.

Not from the bracelet. New lines. She had written them out on cream paper on the first night, at midnight, at a table in the ballroom, eleven of them, one for each piece, and given the paper to him, and he had read it twice, and then picked up his fountain pen and written them all out again in his own hand, slowly, lifting at every turn, so that Enzo could transfer them.

Inside the coat collar: You can be angry in a coat.

Inside the rain earrings: You’re shaking. And on the other: I’m angry.

Inside the open hand: Keep it as long as you like.

Inside the long chain, all the way down, one character on each link: I thought whoever made it must know something about breaking.

And inside the broken necklace, the coat-coloured one, along the seam where the white gold mended the break:

Don’t let them talk you into taking out the break.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the evening of the fourth of March, at eight o’clock, at the Palais de Tokyo, three hundred people sat on white chairs in a concrete room, and every one of them had seen the Delorme collection six days before.

The lights went down.

There were no models.

That was the other thing she had decided. No runway. No faces. Eleven plinths of white concrete in the middle of the room, under eleven narrow beams of light, and on each plinth, one piece of Balcony, lying on black velvet.

Turned over.

Inside out. Engraving up. So that the first thing anyone saw, walking up to each plinth, was not the shape. Not the coat collar or the rain or the open hand, which Delorme had stolen, and which everyone had seen.

It was the line inside. In a stranger’s hand. Cut, not written.

You can be angry in a coat.

And on the wall behind the plinths, projected very large, in white on black, the only text in the whole room:

BALCONY. AURELIA CHEN. Shapes can be copied. This can’t. Every piece engraved by hand with a line said to the designer on the worst night of her life, by the man who didn’t try to fix it. Turn them over. Wear them inside out. The words are for you alone.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was in the front row.

Clause six. The Husband will attend the opening of every collection the Wife makes, in the front row, and will not look at his phone.

He sat in the front row of three hundred white chairs in a dark grey suit, beside Enzo, who was crying already, and Lily, and Serafina, who had flown in from a race in Bahrain that morning and come straight from the airport in her team jacket with AURELIA on the back and had refused to change. He did not look at his phone. His phone, Qian told her afterwards, buzzed forty-one times during the presentation, because a shipment in Rotterdam had gone wrong, and Mr. Pei was trying to reach him.

He didn’t look at it once.

He sat in the front row and watched three hundred people get up from their chairs and walk slowly round eleven white plinths, bending, reading, in silence. He watched the man from Vogue stop at the coat collar and read You can be angry in a coat and put his hand over his mouth. He watched the creative director of Delorme, who had come, of course, to watch the copy, stop at the broken necklace and read the line along the seam, and straighten up, and look around the room, and find Aurelia standing at the back by the wall in black with no jewellery on except one plain wide bracelet on her left wrist, and look at her.

Then the creative director of Delorme, who had made jewellery for queens since 1871, inclined her head. Very slightly.

The way you bow to someone who has won.

✦ ✦ ✦

Afterwards, at two in the morning, in the hotel on the Rue de Rivoli, she lay on the bed in her black dress with her shoes off and the bracelet still on and stared at the ceiling.

He was lying beside her. Still in his suit. Neither of them had the energy to undress.

“They’re calling it the best presentation of the season,” she said. “Vogue wants an interview. Le Monde wants an interview. The New York Times wants an interview. Delorme wants to buy the collection. Delorme.” She laughed weakly. “The woman from Delorme came up to me at the end and said, Madame Chen, we owe you an apology, and I would like to offer it in the form of a very large cheque. I said no.”

He turned his head to look at her.

“I don’t want their money. I said I wanted them to tell the press who sold them the drawings, and that they had bought them, and that they were sorry.” She closed her eyes. “She said she’d think about it.”

“She’ll do it,” said Chen Si.

“How do you know?”

“Because she bowed,” said Chen Si. “I saw her. People who bow, pay.”

She turned her head on the pillow and looked at him.

“Forty-one times,” she said. “Your phone, during the show. Qian told me. Rotterdam.”

“Mr. Pei sorted it out. You were right about him.” He turned his head. “Clause six. I didn’t look.”

She looked at him.

“You wrote out all eleven lines for me at midnight, in your own hand,” she said. Her voice wobbled. “I didn’t think you’d remember them. Not exactly. Not from the balcony, three years ago.”

“Aurelia,” he said. “I remember every word I’ve ever said to you. And every word you’ve said to me.”

She turned over and put her face in his shoulder, in his suit, in the hotel in Paris at two in the morning, and stayed there.

After a while he found her left wrist in the dark and turned it over. “Three hundred people tonight would have paid anything to read the inside of it,” he said. He put his mouth on the inside of the band, so that she felt the line through the gold. “Only one person reads this one. I’d like that in a clause.”

“There isn’t a clause about that.”

“There will be,” said Chen Si, against her pulse. “I’ll draft it in the morning. Go to sleep, Madame Chen. You beat Delorme in three nights. You’re allowed.”

She did not go to sleep for some time.

In the morning, Le Monde ran a photograph on its front page.

Not of the collection. Of a single plinth, under a single beam of light, with a broken necklace on it, turned inside out, and the line along the seam.

Don’t let them talk you into taking out the break.

Under it, the caption said: The designer’s husband declined to be photographed. Asked about the engravings, he said only: “They’re hers. I just said them first.”

chapters.title: The Song Parents Ask for Tickets
chapters.desc: After Paris, everyone wants to see the collection in Asia. A letter arrives in her mother’s handwriting asking for two seats. Aurelia sends them. In the back row. Then her father comes to the front anyway.
chapters.epigraph: “We would be very grateful for two tickets.” It was the first time in twenty-five years her mother had written the word grateful.
chapters.content:
The Asian presentation of Balcony was in June, at the museum on the harbour front, in the long glass hall on the ground floor that looked out at the water, and it was the hottest ticket in the city.

Everyone wanted one. The deputy minister. The woman who owned the biggest television channel in the province. Three ambassadors. The man who designed the opera house. Mrs. Leung, whose daughter had been married in April in yellow diamonds and had cried all the way through the ceremony. Elowen, who rang and said, “I suppose I have to come,” in a voice of enormous suffering, and then arrived a week early at the boutique with a bucket of white peonies for the display and refused to discuss it.

Lily kept the list. It had four hundred names on it and two hundred seats.

On the eleventh of May, a letter came.

Cream envelope. Dark blue initials on the flap. V.C.S.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia,

Your father and I have read about the collection in Paris. We have seen the photographs in Vogue and Le Monde. We understand that it will be shown at the museum in June.

We would be very grateful for two tickets.

Your mother.

She read it standing at the counter, the way she had read the first one, two years ago, the one that said we would like to be proud of you.

Then she read it again.

Grateful.

Twenty-five years. She had never once seen her mother write that word. Not on a birthday card. Not on a thank-you note to a hostess. Vittoria Conti did not write grateful. She wrote thank you, which was a transaction, and how kind, which was a dismissal, and nothing else.

She took the letter into the workshop and showed it to Enzo.

He read it. He read it twice. He handed it back.

“Grata,” he said, in Italian, very slowly. “In forty years, cara, I have never heard that woman say it.”

“Neither have I.”

“What are you going to do?”

Aurelia looked at the letter.

✦ ✦ ✦

She asked Dr. Ho.

On the Tuesday. In the office on the twelfth floor in Central, with the window that looked at another building and the tissues on every surface. She took the letter out of her bag and gave it to Dr. Ho, and Dr. Ho read it, slowly, and gave it back.

“What do you want to do?” said Dr. Ho.

“I want to send them two tickets in the back row,” said Aurelia. “Behind the press. Behind the buyers. Behind Mrs. Leung’s daughter’s bridesmaids. In the last two seats by the door, where they can’t see anything except the backs of people’s heads.” She folded the letter. “I want my mother to sit in the back row at my show, the way I sat in the front row at hers for eleven years, and not be allowed to move.”

Dr. Ho looked at her.

“And?”

“And I want her to see it anyway,” said Aurelia. Her voice went strange. “I want her to stand up at the end and walk round the plinths and turn them over and read the lines. I want her to read You can be angry in a coat. I want her to know who said it to me. And when. And why.” She looked at the window. “I want her to know that the worst night of my life was her toast, and that I turned it into the best thing I’ve ever made, and that she had nothing to do with it.”

Dr. Ho didn’t answer straight away.

“Those are two different things,” she said finally. “Wanting to punish her, and wanting her to see you.”

“I know.”

“Can you do both?”

Aurelia thought about it.

“Back row,” she said slowly. “And then she has to walk all the way to the front to see.”

Dr. Ho almost smiled.

“That,” she said, “sounds like something you would do.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She sent two tickets.

By courier. In a plain white envelope. No letter. Just two cards printed in gold on black, and on each, in Lily’s neat hand, the seat number.

Row R. Seats 1 and 2.

Row R was the last row. Seats 1 and 2 were on the end, by the fire door, behind a pillar.

She didn’t tell Chen Si until afterwards. He found the courier receipt on the hall table and looked at it and looked at her and said nothing. Then, at dinner, he said, very mildly, “Row R. Behind the pillar.”

“Qian checked the sightlines,” said Aurelia. “From R1 you can see about a third of the room. From R2, less.”

He put down his chopsticks.

“I wanted to be precise,” said Aurelia.

He looked at her across the table.

Then he laughed. Not quietly. Properly. With his head back. It made Zhao, who was at the other end of the table eating a fish with his hands, look up.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

“She put her parents behind a pillar,” said Chen Si. “In Row R. And had Qian check the sightlines.”

Zhao looked at Aurelia for four seconds.

Then he went back to his fish.

“Good,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the night, she did not look for them.

She had told herself she wouldn’t, and she didn’t. She stood at the back of the long glass hall at the museum, by the wall, in black, with no jewellery on except the plain wide bracelet on her left wrist, and watched two hundred people come in and find their seats, and she did not once look at Row R.

She looked at the front row.

Clause six. He was there. In a dark grey suit, in the centre seat, with his phone turned off and in his pocket, where Qian had watched him put it. Beside him, Serafina, in her team jacket, who had come from a race in Japan and refused to change. Beside her, Zhao, in black, with his hands on his knees, looking at the plinths as if they might attack someone. Beside him, Elowen, in green, who had given Aurelia a long, cool, appraising look at the door and said, “It’s good. I hate it,” and then squeezed her hand, very briefly, and gone to sit down.

Enzo. Lily. Mr. Lu and his tiny wife. Dr. Ma, who had not been invited and had come anyway and had said, at the door, “I wanted to see what the fuss was about,” and then gone very quiet in front of the third plinth.

The lights went down.

Eleven white plinths, under eleven narrow beams. Eleven pieces, turned inside out.

Two hundred people stood up and walked slowly round them, bending, reading, in silence.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not look at Row R.

She looked at the plinths. At the people bending over them. At the man from the provincial television channel reading Keep it as long as you like and turning to his wife. At Mrs. Leung’s daughter, who had worn yellow diamonds at her wedding, reading the long chain one link at a time, I thought whoever made it must know something about breaking, and crying again.

At the broken necklace, coat-coloured, on the eleventh plinth, at the front, by the window, with the harbour behind it and the line along the seam.

Don’t let them talk you into taking out the break.

Somebody was standing in front of it.

A man. Grey-haired. In a navy suit with a pocket square. Standing very still in front of the eleventh plinth, at the front of the room, with his hands at his sides, reading.

Her father.

He had walked from Row R. All the way. Past the pillar, past the press, past the buyers, past the bridesmaids, to the front of the room, to the last plinth, the one by the window. Alone.

Aurelia stood by the wall and could not move.

He read the line along the seam. He read it. Then he bent closer, and she saw him take his reading glasses out of his breast pocket and put them on, and bend closer still, and read the tiny cut characters again, the ones in a stranger’s hand, lifted at every turn.

Then he straightened up.

He took off his reading glasses. He put them back in his pocket. He stood in front of the plinth with his back to the room, a soft, tired, grey-haired man in a navy suit, looking at the harbour through the glass.

Then he turned round, and looked across the long glass hall, and found her by the wall.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came to her.

Across the room. Slowly. Through two hundred people, who stepped aside for him without knowing why. He came and stood in front of her at the back of the hall, by the wall, and looked at her.

“Tesoro,” said Song Weiren.

“Papà.”

“Row R,” he said.

She didn’t say anything.

“Behind a pillar.” Something moved at the corner of his mouth. It was very nearly a smile. “Your mother said it was an insult. She said we should leave. She is sitting there now, in R1, not moving, looking at the back of the ambassador’s head.”

Aurelia lifted her chin.

“It wasn’t an insult,” she said. “It was precise.”

“I know.” Her father very nearly smiled again. “I could see a third of the room from R1. Your mother had R2. She could see the pillar.”

Aurelia didn’t say anything.

“I got up,” said her father. “I said, Vittoria, I’m going to look at our daughter’s work. She said, Sit down, Weiren. I said no.” He looked down at his hands. “That’s twice. Twice in my life I’ve said no to someone. Once to Fu Jianguo, for my father, who never paid a bribe in his life. Once to your mother, tonight, for you.”

She stared at him.

“The line,” said her father. “On the necklace. At the front. Don’t let them talk you into taking out the break.” He looked up. “Who said that? Your husband?”

“On the balcony,” said Aurelia. Her voice had gone very small. “At your birthday. After the toast. He was standing at the end in the dark. He gave me his coat. And at the door, he said that.”

Her father was quiet.

“I stood up,” he said. “At my own birthday. I drank to what she said. I didn’t say anything.” His voice cracked. “I let them talk you into it. I let them try. For twenty-two years. And a man I had never met stood on my balcony in the dark and told you not to let them.” He looked at her. “I’m sorry, tesoro. I’m so sorry. I should have been the one on the balcony.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t cry.

She had learned, on Tuesdays, that she didn’t have to. That she could let a thing go through her and feel it all the way and not fall apart. She stood at the back of the long glass hall in black and let it go through her. Her father. I should have been the one on the balcony. Twenty-two years.

Then she did something she had not done since she was eleven, before Vienna, before the nine days, before rankings.

She put her arms round her father.

He went very still. Then his arms came round her, carefully, the way he used to hold her when she was very small, before her mother took her to the shows. He held her at the back of the hall, with two hundred people walking round eleven white plinths in the dark, and neither of them said anything.

Over his shoulder, she saw the front row.

Chen Si was standing. He had stood up when her father walked past, she realised; he had watched her father walk all the way from Row R to the front plinth and then all the way back to her, and he had stood up and was standing there in the front row, very still, watching, with an expression on his face that she could not see properly in the dark, and did not need to.

Beside him, Zhao had stood up too.

And Elowen, beside Zhao, in green, was looking at Aurelia across the room with an expression that was not cool, or appraising, or rivalrous at all. Just quiet. And very kind.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother did not come to the front.

Aurelia looked, finally, at the end of the evening, when the lights came up and people began to leave. She looked at Row R.

Seat 2 was empty.

Seat 1 was empty.

She went to the fire door at the end of Row R, behind the pillar, and opened it, and looked out. A corridor. Concrete. A side exit onto the harbour front.

On the floor by the door, as if someone had dropped it on the way out, there was a programme. A single folded sheet of black card, printed in gold, with the list of the eleven pieces, and the lines engraved inside them.

She picked it up.

Somebody had underlined one line. In pencil. Very faintly. The way you underline something you don’t want anyone to know you have read.

Not the necklace. Not the coat collar.

The open hand ring. The fourth piece. A tiny gold hand, palm up, offering, not insisting.

Keep it as long as you like.

✦ ✦ ✦

She showed it to Chen Si in the car.

He looked at it in the light from the passing street.

“Your mother,” he said.

“Her pencil. She always carries one. In her bag. For marking up catalogues.”

He was quiet.

“Keep it as long as you like,” he said. “That’s what I said about the coat.”

“I know.”

“Why would she underline that?”

Aurelia looked out of the window at the harbour going past.

“I think,” she said slowly, “because nobody ever said it to her.” She folded the programme very carefully and put it in her bag. “Nobody ever gave her anything without wanting it back. Not her father. Not the runways. Not the magazines. Not my father, even, at the start.” She was quiet. “I think she read it and thought, nobody ever said that to me. And underlined it. And couldn’t bear to keep it. So she dropped it by the door.”

He didn’t say anything for a while.

“Do you forgive her?” he said.

“No,” said Aurelia. “Not yet.” She looked at her bag, where the programme was. “But I’m going to keep this. For as long as I like.”

He took her hand off the bag and held it on his knee, and said nothing for two streets.

“For the record,” he said, “Row R was a masterpiece.” He pressed his thumb into the centre of her palm. “And if anyone ever puts you behind a pillar, I’ll have the pillar taken out.”

“It’s a load-bearing pillar.”

“I know,” said Chen Si mildly. “I had Qian check.”

She laughed, wet, against the window, all the way home.

chapters.title: Chen Si Takes a Day Off
chapters.desc: For the first time in eleven years, he switches off his phone at midnight and does not switch it back on. Nobody in the Syndicate knows what to do. She has planned the day. It involves a chess board, a bucket of ice, and rules.
chapters.epigraph: “Rule one. You lose a piece, you lose something else.” “That’s not chess.” “It is today.”
chapters.content:
He had not taken a day off in eleven years.

Qian told her. In November, two years after the boat, at his desk outside the office on the thirty-ninth floor, with his drawer of antacids open and a look of real distress. “Not one. Mrs. Chen. Not a Sunday. Not New Year. Not his birthday. Not after the hospital; he was working from bed on the third day, you remember, Dr. Ma took his laptop away.” He shut the drawer. “He took three days for the wedding. In Milan. He checked his phone in the toilets of the palazzo on the second day. I saw the messages come through.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“In the toilets?”

“Twice,” said Qian. “He told me not to tell you. I’m telling you now because it’s been two years and I think you’re going to do something about it.” He looked at her very seriously. “I would like it on the record that I approve of whatever it is.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She planned it for a month.

She planned it the way she planned a collection, at the bench at two in the morning, with a pencil and a sheet of cream paper. She cleared it with Mr. Pei, who ran the east coast and the airport now and was the most reliable man in the Syndicate. She cleared it with Mr. Lu. She cleared it with Zhao, who listened to the whole thing in silence in his office at the Docks, with a gun in pieces on a cloth on the desk, and at the end said, “Saturday?” and she said, “The fourth,” and he said, “I’ll answer his phone,” and she nearly kissed him, and didn’t, because he would have had to leave the country.

She did not clear it with Chen Si.

On the evening of Friday the third of December, at 11:58, she walked into his study on the forty-fourth floor, where he was sitting at his desk with his laptop and a list and a coffee he wasn’t drinking, in his shirtsleeves, and stood behind his chair, and reached over his shoulder, and closed the laptop.

He looked up at her.

She held out her hand.

“Phone,” she said.

“Aurelia—”

“Clause nine,” said Aurelia. “Phone.”

He looked at her. Then he took his phone out of his pocket and put it in her hand.

She switched it off. She watched the screen go dark. Then she took it to the kitchen and put it in the drawer with the tea towels and shut the drawer, and came back.

“Zhendong is answering it,” she said. “Mr. Pei has the routes. Mr. Lu has the shops. Qian has a list of everything that is allowed to interrupt you, and the list has one thing on it, and the thing is a fire.” She looked at the clock on his desk. 11:59. “In one minute, it’s Saturday. You don’t have a phone. You don’t have a laptop. You don’t have a list. You don’t have a meeting. You don’t have anywhere to be.”

He looked at her.

“For how long?” he said.
