“Until midnight tomorrow,” said Aurelia. “Twenty-four hours.” She smiled. “And I’ve made rules.”

The clock on his desk clicked over to midnight.

✦ ✦ ✦

He slept until ten.

He had not slept until ten in his adult life. He woke and looked at the clock and sat up so fast his heart skipped, and reached for the bedside table, for his phone, and found nothing there but his tablet and a glass of water and a note in her handwriting.

It’s Saturday. You don’t have a phone. Breakfast is on the table. Don’t get dressed.

He lay back down and looked at the ceiling.

After a while, he started to laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Breakfast was on the long table by the window. Congee, the way Zhao made it. Fried dough sticks from the stall at the edge of the Iron Docks where the crane drivers ate, which meant she had sent someone at five in the morning. Hot soy milk. A plate of oranges, peeled.

And beside his bowl, the jade chess board, set up.

She was sitting on the other side of it in his old grey jumper and nothing else, with her legs tucked up under her on the chair and her hair down and a cup of coffee in her hands that she was actually drinking.

“Sit,” she said.

He sat. In his pyjama trousers. No shirt. Because the note had said not to get dressed, and he found, sitting down, that he did not mind at all.

She looked at him across the board.

“Rule one,” she said. “We play all day. Every game, the loser chooses what happens next.”

“That sounds fair.”

“Rule two,” said Aurelia. “Every time you lose a piece, you lose something else.”

He looked at her.

“That’s not chess,” he said.

“It is today.” She put down her coffee. “Every piece I take off you, I get to take something. A thing you’re wearing. Or a thing you’re allowed to do. Or a word you’re allowed to say.” She looked at his bare chest. “You’re not wearing very much. You’re going to run out quite fast.”

“And if I take a piece off you?”

“Then you get to take something.” She looked down at the grey jumper. “I’m wearing one thing.”

He looked at the board.

He looked at her.

“Rule three?” he said.

“No phones,” said Aurelia. “No lists. No thinking about Fu Jianguo, or Rotterdam, or the judges’ fund, or the port.” She picked up a white pawn. “If I catch you thinking about work, I take a piece off the board. Any piece. My choice.”

“How will you know if I’m thinking about work?”

“Your face goes cold and far away,” said Aurelia. “Like a hall at six in the morning.” She put the pawn down on e4. “I always know.”

He looked at her across the jade board.

Then he picked up a black pawn.

“I’ve been playing chess since I was six,” he said. “I’ve beaten you forty-one times out of forty-six. You’ll be wearing nothing at all by noon.”

“I’m counting on it,” said Aurelia Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took his queen at 11:40.

He didn’t see it coming. Afterwards, he would not be able to say how it had happened; it had come out of a position he had thought was perfectly safe, a knight he had thought was pinned, a bishop on a long diagonal that he had not been watching because he had been watching her, sitting across the board in his jumper with her legs tucked up and her chin on her hand, biting her lip while she thought.

She lifted the black jade queen off the board and held it up between them.

“Mine,” she said.

He looked at the queen.

“That was a very good move,” he said, with real admiration.

“I know.” She put the queen down beside her coffee cup. “Rule two.”

He waited.

She looked at him, with her chin on her hand. At his bare chest. At his pyjama trousers. At his face.

“Your voice,” she said.

He went still.

“For the next game,” said Aurelia. “You’re not allowed to speak. Not one word. Whatever I do.” She smiled. “You lost your queen. You don’t get to talk.”

He opened his mouth.

She raised her eyebrows.

He closed it.

✦ ✦ ✦

He lost the game.

He lost it because she spent the whole of it, every one of her moves, doing something to him that made it impossible to think about anything except not making a sound.

It began with her foot. Under the table. On his ankle. Then higher. Very slowly. While she studied the board with an expression of total innocence and moved a rook. He moved a bishop, badly. She took it.

“Rule two,” she said sweetly, and got up, and came round the table, and stood behind his chair, and ran her hands down his bare shoulders and his chest, slowly, with her mouth against his ear, and said, “Your turn,” and went back to her seat.

He moved a knight. He did not know where. He did not care where.

She took that too.

She leaned across the board, the grey jumper falling forward, and kissed him, slowly, open-mouthed, with her hand on the back of his neck, and he made a sound in his throat that was not quite a word, and she pulled back an inch and said, “Was that a word?” and he shook his head, very fast, and she smiled and said, “I don’t think it was. I’ll allow it,” and sat back down.

He lost in nineteen moves.

He had not lost a game of chess in nineteen moves since he was eight.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Rule one,” said Aurelia. “You lost. I choose what happens next.” She looked at him. “And you still can’t talk.”

He looked at her across the wreck of the board, flushed, breathing hard, with his hands flat on the table because she had told him to keep them there for the last six moves.

She got up.

She went to the kitchen. He heard the freezer open. He heard ice.

She came back with a silver bucket, the one they used for champagne, full of ice, and put it on the table beside the chess board, and looked at him.

“Bedroom,” she said.

He stood up.

✦ ✦ ✦

What she did with the ice was not chess.

She told him to lie down. On his back, on the bed, with his hands above his head on the pillow, which she did not tie, because she didn’t need to; she just told him to keep them there, and he did. And she knelt beside him on the bed in his grey jumper with the silver bucket on the bedside table, and took a single cube of ice between her finger and thumb, and held it up so he could see it.

“Not a word,” she said.

He looked at the ice.

She touched it to the hollow of his throat.

He jerked. All of him. Off the bed. And made no sound at all, with his jaw locked so tight that she could see the muscle in it, and his hands, above his head, closing into fists in the pillow.

She smiled.

She drew the ice down. Slowly. Over his collarbone. Down the middle of his chest. Over his heart, where she paused, and held it, and felt his heart under her other hand going like something trapped, and said, “One hundred and four. I’m going to have to slow down,” and did not slow down at all. Down his ribs. Down his stomach, where his whole body went rigid. And then she took the ice away, and put her mouth where it had been, warm after cold, and followed the path of it all the way back up, slowly, and that was when he broke, and said her name, out loud, helplessly, the one word he was not allowed.

She lifted her head.

“That,” she said, “was a word.”

He looked up at her with his eyes black and his chest heaving and his hands still above his head on the pillow, where she had told him to keep them, and said, in a voice gone completely to gravel, “I know.”

“Rule two,” said Aurelia. “Every word costs.” She picked up another piece of ice. “I’ll start again from the top.”

“Then let it cost something worth it,” said Chen Si, hands still above his head. “Counter-offer. A few more words, and for them you give me thirty seconds with my hands. Your clock. You can say no.” He looked at her. “Do you want them on you?”

She held the ice over his heart and pretended to think. Then she looked at the clock on the bedside table.

“Thirty seconds,” she said. “Starting now.”

He used every one of them, and when she said time he put his hands back above his head on the pillow, exactly where they had been, and she had to sit back on her heels for a moment before she could pick up the ice again.

He closed his eyes.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four in the afternoon, they played again.

On the bed this time, with the board on the duvet between them, and the ice melted in its bucket, and the light going gold over the harbour outside the long window. She was wearing nothing at all. She had lost the grey jumper at about two, in a game he had won by playing with a ferocity that made her laugh out loud halfway through, and he had taken it off her very slowly, as his rule-two prize, and then thrown it across the room.

He was wearing nothing either. He had lost his pyjama trousers at 12:30, his voice at 11:40, the use of his hands at 1:15 for a whole game, and his dignity, he said, at some point around three, he wasn’t sure exactly when.

They had been playing all day.

She had won four. He had won five. It was the closest they had ever been.

“Your move,” she said, lying on her stomach with her chin on her hand, looking at the board.

He looked at the board. He looked at her.

He moved a pawn. Very deliberately. To a square where she could take it with her bishop.

She looked at it.

She looked at him.

“You did that on purpose,” she said.

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

She sat up on the bed.

“You told me, at the jade board on the thirty-ninth floor, three years ago,” she said. “If you lose on purpose, the game is over. There’s no point playing against someone who isn’t playing. So why—”

He reached across the board and laid his king down on its side on the duvet.

She stared at it.

“I don’t want to play any more,” said Chen Si. He looked at her, sitting on the bed in the gold light, with nothing on and her hair everywhere and her chin up and her face flushed, and his voice went very quiet. “In eleven years I haven’t once woken up without reaching for my phone. I haven’t eaten breakfast without reading something. I haven’t spent a whole afternoon without thinking about a hall at six in the morning.” He paused. “You didn’t take a single piece off the board all day for rule three.”

She thought about it.

“No,” she said slowly. “I didn’t.”

“Because I didn’t think about it,” said Chen Si. “Not once. Not Fu. Not the routes. Not the port. Nothing.” He reached out and pushed the chess board off the bed. It hit the floor with a crash, jade pieces everywhere, rolling across the pale wood. “I’ve been thinking about you since ten o’clock this morning. Only you.” He moved across the space where the board had been. “I don’t want to play against you any more. I want to lie down with you and not think about anything at all until midnight.”

She looked at him.

“That isn’t in the rules,” she said.

“Clause nine,” said Chen Si. “You make the rules. Unless you say otherwise.”

She looked at the jade pieces scattered across the floor. At the king lying on its side by the window. At the empty silver bucket. At his face, in the gold light, close to hers, with nothing cold or far away in it at all.

“Otherwise,” said Aurelia.

He did not move at once. He never did.

He took her wrist and turned it over and kissed the inside of it, where her pulse was, and kept his mouth there until he felt it climb. Then he laid her down in the warm gold light where the board had been, and lay beside her, not over her, with his head on his hand, and looked at her the way he had looked at the board all morning, as if there were nothing in the world he would rather work out.

“Rule one,” he said. “Nobody counts anything.”

“That isn’t a rule, that’s a—”

“Rule two,” said Chen Si, and kissed her, slowly, and she forgot what she had been going to say, and what came after rule two, and that she had ever in her life wanted to win.

They did not get up again until it was dark.

✦ ✦ ✦

He switched his phone back on at 12:04 on Sunday morning.

She was asleep. He got up very quietly, so as not to wake her, and went to the kitchen in the dark and opened the drawer with the tea towels and took it out and switched it on, and stood in the kitchen while it woke up.

Forty-four messages.

He scrolled through them. Mr. Pei: All quiet. Rotterdam clear. Mr. Lu: Shops fine. Wife sends regards to Mrs. Chen. Qian: No fires. Serafina, inexplicably: Did she make you play strip chess? She told me she was going to. Don’t tell her I told you.

And at the bottom, at 11:58 the night before, from Zhao.

Two words.

Was good?

He stood in the dark kitchen on the forty-fourth floor and read it three times.

Then he typed back, with his thumb, in the dark:

Yes. Same day next month.

And put the phone back in the drawer with the tea towels, and went back to bed, and lay down beside his wife, and was asleep in four minutes, which he had not been since he was fifteen years old.

chapters.title: The Necklace She Makes for Him
chapters.desc: It isn’t jewellery. It’s a tag. Plain gold, on a plain chain, with three lines engraved on it in her hand, for a man who has spent his whole life waiting to be taken down the stairs.
chapters.epigraph: “If anyone ever takes you anywhere, at six in the morning, in your pyjamas, they will find this on you. And they will know who to call.”
chapters.content:
The idea came to her at three in the morning, the way all her ideas came, but not at the bench.

In bed. In the dark. With his back against her chest and her arm round him, because he had woken from the dream again and she had turned him over and held him until his breathing slowed.

He had the dream twice a month. Sometimes less. Sometimes, in a bad month, every week. He never told her what it was. He didn’t have to. She had known since the first time, in the spring after the boat, when he had woken with a sound she had never heard from him and lain rigid in the dark with his eyes open and his heart going so hard she could feel it through his back, and she had put her hand flat on his chest and said nothing, and after a long while he had said, to the ceiling: six o’clock.

A hall. A staircase. A man in pyjamas going down it between two officers. Looking back at the door. Look after your mother. I’ll be home soon.

He never said any more than that.

She lay in the dark with her arm round him and felt his heart slow down under her palm, and thought: what did they take off his father, at the bottom of the stairs?

His watch, probably. His belt. His wallet. His wedding ring. Everything with a name on it. Everything that said who he was and who he belonged to. They would have put it in a plastic bag, the way the nurses had put Chen Si’s watch and necklace in a plastic bag on New Year’s Eve.

And then he had gone into a cell, with nothing on him that said who he was, and nobody had come.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the bench the next morning and drew a tag.

Not a necklace. She was very clear about that, even to herself. Not a pendant, not a charm, not jewellery. A tag. The kind soldiers wore. The kind they put on a man so that if anything happened to him, anyone who found him would know who he was and who to call.

A plain flat rectangle of gold, rounded at the corners, the size of the top joint of her thumb. On a plain chain. Not delicate. Strong. Box links, the kind that would not break if someone pulled.

No stones. No texture. No design. Nothing anyone would look at twice.

And on it, engraved, three lines.

She thought about the three lines for eleven days.

✦ ✦ ✦

“A dog tag,” said Enzo, holding up the drawing. “In twenty-two-carat gold.”

“A tag,” said Aurelia. “Yes.”

Enzo looked at the drawing over his magnifying glasses.

“Twenty-two carat is soft,” he said. “On a man who does what he does? It will scratch. It will dent. In a year it will look as if it has been to war.”

“Good,” said Aurelia. “Then I’ll be able to see where he’s been.”

Enzo grunted. “Then at least cut the chain in eighteen. Box links in twenty-two will stretch the first time someone pulls.”

“The chain in eighteen,” said Aurelia. “The tag in twenty-two.”

“It is the plainest thing you have ever designed,” he said. “A rectangle and a chain. A child could cut it.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “I’m going to cut it myself.”

Enzo put the drawing down.

“You haven’t cut a piece yourself since Numero Uno,” he said. “You design. I cut. That is how it is. That has been how it is since you were nineteen.”

“Not this one,” said Aurelia.

He looked at her over his glasses.

Then he got up from his bench, and went to the safe, and took out a small bar of gold, and put it on her bench, beside her saw and her files, and went back to his own bench, and did not say anything else at all for the rest of the day.

✦ ✦ ✦

She cut it over three weeks.

She did it at night. After the boutique closed. After the thirty-ninth floor. After dinner, after he had gone to bed, at eleven or twelve or one, she drove herself to Harbour Road and let herself in with her key and turned on the one light over her bench and sat down and cut.

She rolled the gold out herself, in the mill, to exactly the thickness she wanted. Thick enough that it would never bend. She cut the rectangle with a piercing saw, by hand, very slowly, following a line she had scribed with a needle. She filed the edges. She rounded the corners. She sanded it, and then polished it, and then sanded it again, because the first polish had left a faint ripple that nobody but her would ever have seen and that she could not bear.

She made the chain herself. Box links. Four hundred and twelve of them. She drew the wire, and rolled it flat into strip, and cut the strip into four hundred and twelve tiny blanks, and folded every one into its open square box with her pliers under the loupe, and fed each box through the last, and soldered them, one at a time, with the little torch, at two in the morning, in the one light, while the city slept. Last of all she took the tag to the wheel and gave it its final pass in rouge, until it held the lamp like water.

Enzo never asked.

Some mornings, she came in late and found a small plate on her bench with a pastry on it and a note in his old looping handwriting: Mangia. She ate them.

✦ ✦ ✦

The engraving took her four nights.

She had decided on the three lines on the eleventh day. She wrote them out on cream paper in her own hand, round and confident and red, and then wrote them out again, and again, a hundred times, the way she had once written his signature until the page was black, until her hand knew them without her.

She did not engrave them in his hand.

Everything else she had ever made for him, she had made with his words. Balcony, inside out. The lines from the balcony. His hand, lifted at every turn.

This one was hers.

She cut it in her own handwriting. Round. Confident. With the small flourish at the end of her A that her mother had tried to train out of her at six and failed. She cut it with a graver, by hand, under the loupe, one stroke at a time, so slowly that on the first night she managed only four characters and sat back at three in the morning with her hand aching and her eyes burning and looked at four characters on a tiny rectangle of gold and cried, for no reason at all, and then wiped her face and put the graver away and went home.

On the fourth night, she finished.

She sat at her bench and held it under the loupe.

Plain gold. Rounded corners. On a chain of four hundred and twelve links.

And on it, in her own hand:

CHEN SI.

Husband of Aurelia Chen.

If found, call her. She will come.

✦ ✦ ✦

She gave it to him on the morning of the sixth of January.

Not his birthday. Not an anniversary. Nothing. A Thursday in January, with rain on the long window, the kind of day nobody would ever think to remember. She wanted it that way. She wanted it to be a gift that wasn’t for anything except him.

She gave it to him at six in the morning.

On purpose. She woke before him, which she never did, at 5:40, and lay in the dark until the clock on the bedside table said six, and then she turned over and put it on his chest.

He woke.

He woke the way he always woke, all at once, his hand already moving toward the bedside table. Then he felt the weight on his chest, and stopped, and looked down.

A plain gold tag on a plain gold chain, lying on his bare skin in the grey light.

He picked it up.

He held it up above his face, where he could see it in the light from the window, and read it. She watched him read it. She watched him read it three times.

CHEN SI. Husband of Aurelia Chen. If found, call her. She will come.

He didn’t say anything.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It’s six o’clock,” said Aurelia.

He turned his head on the pillow and looked at her.

“I know about the dream,” she said. “You don’t have to tell me. I know what it is.” She put her hand flat on his chest, beside the tag. “A hall. A staircase. Six o’clock. Your father in his pyjamas. They took everything off him at the bottom of the stairs. His watch. His ring. Everything with a name on it. And they took him somewhere, and he had nothing on him that said who he was, or who loved him, and nobody came.”

He was very still.

“I can’t stop it happening,” said Aurelia. “I know that. You do what you do. Fu Jianguo is still out there. There are men in this city who would put you in a cell tomorrow if they could, and some of them have badges. One day, maybe, someone will come at six in the morning.” Her voice didn’t shake. She had practised. On Tuesdays. “I can’t stop it. But I can make sure that if anyone ever takes you anywhere, at six in the morning, in your pyjamas, they’ll find this on you. And they’ll know your name. And they’ll know whose you are.” She touched the tag. “And they’ll know who to call.”

He looked at the tag in his hand.

“She will come,” he said. His voice had gone very strange.

“I will,” said Aurelia. “Wherever it is. Whoever has you. I’ll come. With Ms. Fong, and Mr. Tan, and every judge we own, and Zhendong, and a laptop, and a gun, and your signature, which I can still do perfectly.” She lifted her chin. “I will sit in their chair until they give you back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was crying.

She had seen him cry three times. In a hospital bed, sideways into his hair, because he couldn’t get up. On the long grey sofa, once, telling her about his mother. And in the doorway of the workshop, when he came down thirty-nine flights of stairs and found her on the floor.

This was different.

He lay on his back in the grey light with the tag held up above his face in one hand and cried without any sound at all, with tears running out of the corners of his eyes into his hair, and his face perfectly still, and his chest rising and falling under her hand, and she understood that he was not crying about the tag.

He was crying about a man in pyjamas at the bottom of a staircase, thirteen years ago, with nothing on him that said who he was.

She didn’t say anything.

She took the tag out of his hand. She lifted the chain, four hundred and twelve links, and put it over his head, and he lifted his head off the pillow to let her, and she settled it round his neck, so that the tag lay on his chest, over his heart, beside the old broken necklace that he had worn every day since the proposal.

Two pieces of gold. One broken and mended. One plain.

She put her hand over both.

“There,” she said. “Now you have something with my name on it.”

He put his hand over hers.

“I’ve had something with your name on it since the balcony,” said Chen Si, through his tears. “I just didn’t have anywhere to wear it.”

She wiped his face with the heel of her hand, one side and then the other, carefully, the way you polish something you have made.

“It’s twenty-two carat,” she said. “It’s soft. It will show every knock. So if you ever come home with a dent in it, I’ll know exactly where you’ve been and who you were fighting, and I will be very cross.”

He laughed, wet, under her hand. “Then I’ll have to stop fighting.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “Then you’ll have to come home and let me look.” She bent and kissed the tag where it lay over his heart. “Every night. Under the lamp.”

He didn’t let her lift her head. He put his hand in her hair and held her there against his chest, against the gold, and then rolled them over in one movement, so that she was under him in the grey light and the new tag swung down and lay cool against her own throat. He kissed her the way he had not kissed her since the coast road: as if he had nearly lost something, and had only this second understood how much of it there was.

“You’ll come,” he said against her mouth. It was not a question. “And I will always, always come home. You have my word.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He wore it every day.

Under his shirt. Beside the broken necklace. He never took it off. Not to shower, not to sleep, not to swim, not when Dr. Ma listened to his heart every three months and looked at it, and read it, and looked at him, and said nothing at all, and put her stethoscope back on.

Not when he went into meetings on the thirty-ninth floor, where nobody knew it was there.

Not when, a year and a half later, at six in the morning, he stood in a hall in a house in the Western District, beside his wife, and watched two officers from the anti-corruption commission take a grey man in rimless glasses and a cardigan down a staircase in his pyjamas.

He touched it, then. She saw him. His hand went to his chest, under his coat, and stayed there, and he didn’t take his eyes off the staircase.

But that was later.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao found out about it at the end of January.

At New Year. At dinner. In the flat on the forty-fourth floor, where he came every New Year and every birthday and every time someone shot at one of them, and ate a whole fish with his hands, in silence, for two hours.

Chen Si leaned forward to reach the soy sauce, and the tag swung out of the open collar of his shirt.

Zhao looked at it.

He put down his fish.

He reached across the table, very slowly, and took the tag between his finger and thumb, and turned it to the light, and read it.

CHEN SI. Husband of Aurelia Chen. If found, call her. She will come.

Then he let it go, very carefully, so that it swung back against his brother’s chest.

He looked at Aurelia across the table.

He looked at her for a lot longer than four seconds.

Then he picked up his fish again.

“I want one,” said Zhao Zhendong.

There was a silence.

“Elowen can make it,” said Aurelia, after a moment. Her voice was not quite steady. “She’s very good with her hands. She cuts stems like a wound.”

Zhao looked at his fish.

“She can’t cut gold,” he said.

“No,” said Aurelia. “But I can teach her.”

Zhao didn’t say anything else. He finished his fish. But at the door, at midnight, when he was leaving, he stopped, and looked back at the two of them on the long grey sofa, and said, to the room in general:

“She will come.”

And then, after a pause, almost to himself, in a voice neither of them had ever heard him use:

“Mine would too.”

He went out.

The door closed.

Aurelia sat on the sofa with her mouth open.

“Did he just—about Elowen? Out loud?”

“Yes,” said Chen Si, and started to laugh, with his hand on the tag on his chest, and she started to laugh too, and they sat on the long grey sofa on the forty-fourth floor at midnight on New Year’s Eve laughing until they couldn’t breathe, about a man who had said three words, and meant every one.

chapters.title: Her Father Falls
chapters.desc: Shenzhen. Leverage. Four towers nobody will buy. Permits that won’t come. In eight weeks the Song Group goes from the second-richest family in the city to a story in the newspapers. Her father calls her at two in the morning. Her mother does not.
chapters.epigraph: “Tesoro. I don’t know who else to call.” — Song Weiren, 2:14 a.m.
chapters.content:
It started in Shenzhen.

Everything that year started in Shenzhen. Four towers, sixty storeys each, on the waterfront, that the Song Group had begun building three years before, with money borrowed from eleven banks against the value of everything the Song Group owned. They were supposed to be finished in the spring. They were supposed to be full by the summer.

In the spring, the market in Shenzhen fell over.

Not slowly. All at once. The way a tower falls if you take out the wrong floor. Prices dropped by a third in eight weeks. Buyers walked away from deposits. Developers twice the size of the Song Group went under in a fortnight. And four sixty-storey towers stood on the Shenzhen waterfront, half-finished, empty, worth less every morning than they had been the night before, and eleven banks looked at them, and then looked at the Song Group, and began, very politely, to ask for their money.

Aurelia read about it in the newspapers, like everyone else.

She did not call her father.

She told Dr. Ho, on the Tuesday, that she was not going to call him. That it was not her business. That the Song Group was her mother’s business and her father’s business and had never been hers, that they had closed her shop in January in front of two hundred people, that it was not her job to save them from Shenzhen.

Dr. Ho said, “You’ve said not my business four times in two minutes.”

Aurelia looked at the window.

✦ ✦ ✦

Then the permits stopped.

She heard about that from Chen Si. At dinner, in May. He put down his chopsticks and said, carefully, “The Song Group applied for an extension on the bridge. Harbour Bridge Two. They need it to keep the financing in place. The ministry hasn’t answered.”

She looked up. “Infrastructure?”

He nodded, and she went cold.

“Fu Jianguo.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si. “He signed the bridge in December, three and a half years ago, because you made his son sweat at Da Gianni. He’s never forgotten it. He’s been waiting.” He turned his glass on the tablecloth. “The bridge is the only part of the Song Group that still makes money. It’s three-quarters built. The banks are lending against it. If the extension doesn’t come, the banks call in everything. On the bridge, and on Shenzhen, together. On the same day.” He looked at her. “Fu knows that. He’s sitting on the extension the way he sat on the original. Waiting.”

“For what?”

“For your father to fall,” said Chen Si. “So that he can buy the pieces. Through a company in Macau with nobody’s name on it.”

She put her chopsticks down.

“Can you stop it?”

He took his time answering.

“Yes,” he said. “I could. I could write a letter. I could make a call.” He was quiet. “But you told me, three and a half years ago, in the back of a car, that you didn’t want me to. That you wanted your father’s bridge built properly, with no letter and no favour.” He held her eyes. “So I haven’t. I’m waiting for you to tell me.”

She looked at him.

“I don’t know,” she said.

“I know,” said Chen Si. “That’s why I’m waiting.”

He reached across the table and took her chopsticks out of her hand and laid them on the rest.

“You have moved the same piece of fish from one side of your bowl to the other five times,” he said. “I counted.”

He boned a piece of fish with his own chopsticks without looking down, and held it out across the table, the way she had once held out a spoon to him on a sofa. “Open.”

She stared at him. “I am not a child.”

“No,” he agreed. “A child would eat.”

She opened. And for the first time since the newspapers, she laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

It took eight weeks.

She watched it happen, in the newspapers, the way you watch a building come down on the news. The first bank called in its loan in June. Then a second. Then four in the same week. The Song Group sold the department store over the border. Then the one in Shanghai. Then the hotel in Macau. Then the art. Her mother’s art, the Morandis and the de Chirico from the drawing room at the Peak, at auction in Hong Kong in July, for less than her mother had paid for them, with the newspapers photographing the empty walls.

The Song Group shares fell by sixty per cent. Then seventy.

The extension did not come.

In the third week of July, there was a photograph on the front of the business section. The house on the Peak. From the road, through the gates. With a man in a suit standing at the door with a clipboard.

VALUERS AT SONG MANSION, said the headline.

She looked at it, at the counter of the boutique on Harbour Road, with the broken necklace in the window behind her.

She did not call.

✦ ✦ ✦

He called her.

At 2:14 in the morning on Tuesday the twenty-fifth of July. On her mobile. She was asleep. Chen Si was asleep. The phone buzzed on the bedside table and she reached for it in the dark and saw the name and sat straight up.

Papà.

She answered.

At first there was nothing on the line. Just breathing. Very uneven.

“Tesoro,” said her father.

His voice was not his voice. It was very old and very small and it was shaking.

“Papà,” said Aurelia. “What’s wrong? Where are you?”

“At the office.” A breath. “At the tower. On the fortieth floor. I couldn’t—I couldn’t go home. The valuers were at the house today. They’re coming back tomorrow. Your mother—” He stopped. “Your mother is at the house. She hasn’t spoken to me in four days.”

Beside her, in the dark, Chen Si was awake. She felt him sit up.

“The banks meet on Friday,” said her father. “All eleven. Together. If the extension doesn’t come by Friday, they call everything. The bridge. Shenzhen. The house. All of it. On Friday.” His voice broke. “Forty years. My father’s watches. The bridge he wanted. It’s all going on Friday, tesoro, and I don’t know what to do. I don’t know who to call. I’ve called everyone. Everyone I’ve ever known. Nobody answers. Nobody will even—” He stopped. “I’m sorry. I’m sorry. It’s two in the morning. I shouldn’t have called you. I shouldn’t. After everything. After the birthday. After I stood up and drank. I don’t have the right.” A long, ragged breath. “I just didn’t know who else to call.”

She sat in the dark with the phone against her ear.

Fifty floors across the harbour, through the window, she could see it. Song Group Tower. Forty storeys of gold glass. Her father’s name at the top, in letters three metres high, lit up. And on the fortieth floor, one window, at the top, still lit.

She looked at it.

“Papà,” she said. “Stay there. Don’t go anywhere. I’m coming.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went alone.

Chen Si offered. He was already getting up, reaching for his clothes. She put her hand on his arm.

“Not you,” she said.

He looked at her.

“If you come,” said Aurelia, “he’ll think you’re there to save him. He’ll think I brought you to write a letter to Fu. He’ll be grateful to you. He’ll owe you.” She got out of bed. “I don’t want him to owe you. I don’t want him to owe anyone. I want to see him first. Alone. Before I decide anything.”

He looked at her in the dark, and didn’t argue.

“Gun?”

“In my bag.”

“Zhendong will drive you.”

“Zhendong,” said Aurelia, “is asleep in a house on a hill with a florist, and if anyone wakes him at two in the morning she will cut them like a stem.” She pulled on a coat over her silk pyjamas. “I’ll drive myself.”

He caught her at the bedroom door. Not her arm: the coat. He turned the collar up for her, one side and then the other, as if it were the only thing in the world he was allowed to do.

“Text me when you get there,” he said. He kept hold of the lapels. “And when you leave. And if anyone in that building so much as looks at you—”

“Si. It’s my father.”

“I know.” He let go. “Go and get your father, my queen. I’ll be awake.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The tower was dark except for the lobby and the fortieth floor.

The night security guard knew her. He had known her since she was fifteen, when she came to the tower after school in her uniform to wait for her father, and sat in the lobby doing her homework at the reception desk. He looked at her coming through the revolving door at 2:51 in the morning in a coat over silk pyjamas, and his old face crumpled, and he said, “Miss Song,” and then, “Mrs. Chen,” and then, “He’s been up there since yesterday morning. He hasn’t come down.”

She took the lift to the fortieth floor.

Her father’s office was at the end of the corridor, behind a glass wall, with the whole harbour spread out below it. All the lights were off except one, a lamp on the desk.

He was sitting at the desk.

In his shirtsleeves. Tie gone. Grey hair standing up. He had his reading glasses on and there were papers all over the desk in front of him, hundreds of them, in piles, and a cold cup of tea, and a plate with a sandwich on it that had not been touched. He was holding a pen. He was not writing anything. He was looking at the window. At the harbour. At the far shore, where, three-quarters built, lit up at night with work lights, Harbour Bridge Two stood out over the water, unfinished, its last span missing, reaching for the other side and not getting there.

He didn’t hear her come in.

“Papà,” she said.

He turned round.

He looked at her in the doorway, in a coat over pyjamas, with her hair down and no gold on at all, and his face did something she would never forget.

He had always looked at her, all her life, the way you look at something precious that you are a little bit afraid of. A daughter who came first. A daughter who could be shown to ministers. A daughter her mother had made.

He did not look at her like that now.

He looked at her the way you look at the only light in a dark room.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat with him until five.

She didn’t say anything about the bridge. She didn’t say anything about Fu, or the banks, or Friday. She sat on the other side of his desk, in the chair where she used to sit at fifteen doing her homework, and made him eat the sandwich. All of it. While she watched. And then she made him drink a cup of tea, hot, which she made herself in the little kitchen at the end of the corridor, the way her grandmother had shown her, and he drank it with both hands round the cup, like a child.

Then she asked him to tell her.

Not the numbers. She knew the numbers. She had read them in the newspapers. She asked him to tell her what had happened. And he did. Shenzhen. The towers. The first bank, and the second. Selling the store in Shanghai, which his father had opened in 1979. Selling the art, and her mother standing in the drawing room at the Peak looking at the empty walls, and not speaking to him, for four days.

“She blames me,” he said. “She’s right. I built the towers. She told me not to. In 2020, she told me, Weiren, you are overextended, this is a mistake. I didn’t listen.” He looked at his tea. “The one time in thirty years she was trying to protect me, and I didn’t listen.”

Aurelia didn’t say anything.

“The bridge,” said her father. “If Fu signs the extension, the banks will wait. The bridge alone is worth enough to hold them. I could sell Shenzhen slowly. Keep the house, maybe. Keep the name.” He closed his eyes. “He won’t sign. I know he won’t. Not after Da Gianni. Not after what you did. He’s waiting for me to fall.” He opened his eyes. “I’m not asking you to ask your husband. I want you to know that. I would never ask that. I said that once, and I was wrong, and I won’t say it again.”

“I know, Papà.”

“I just—” His voice broke again. “I just wanted to hear your voice. Before Friday. Before it’s all gone. I wanted to hear one person say my name who didn’t want something.”

She looked at him across the desk. At her father, at four in the morning, in his shirtsleeves, with his reading glasses on and his grey hair standing up, in an office on the fortieth floor of a tower with his name on it that would belong to eleven banks by Friday.

She thought about Row R. About him walking all the way to the front, past the pillar, past the press, to read a line on a necklace.

Twice in my life I’ve said no to someone. Once for my father. Once for you.

“Papà,” she said. “Give me until Thursday.”

He looked at her.

“For what?”

Aurelia stood up.

“To read everything,” she said. “Every line. Every bank. Every loan. Every tower in Shenzhen and every bolt in that bridge.” She looked at the papers on his desk. “And then I’ll tell you what I can do. And what it will cost.” She lifted her chin. “Not Chen Si. Not a letter. Not Fu. Me.”

Her father looked up at her.

“What will it cost?” he said.

“I don’t know yet,” said Aurelia. “But I set the price.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She texted Chen Si from the lift at 5:12.

Coming home. He ate a sandwich. I need every bank file you have on the Song Group, and Ms. Fong at nine, and Mr. Tan on a call at ten, and coffee.

His reply came in four seconds.

All ready. Coffee’s on. Qian’s already here. He says he’s been waiting for this call for three years.

She stood in the lift going down forty floors in a coat over her pyjamas and laughed, once, out loud, and then put her hand over her mouth, because she was crying too, and didn’t know which it was.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother did not call.

Not that night. Not on the Tuesday, or the Wednesday. Aurelia did not expect her to. She sat on the thirty-ninth floor for three days and three nights with Ms. Fong and Qian and Mr. Lu and Mr. Tan on a screen from Singapore and read the Song Group, every line, the way she had once read four ledgers in a basement in the old town, and her mother did not call.

On the Thursday morning, at seven, an envelope came to the boutique on Harbour Road.

Cream. Dark blue initials. V.C.S.

There was no letter inside. Only an old brass key, heavy, with a tag tied to it with a faded ribbon, in her mother’s handwriting.

Morning room. Third drawer. Bureau.

Aurelia held it.

She knew the bureau. A small walnut writing desk from her great-grandmother’s house in Milan, in the corner of the morning room at the Peak, by the east window, that her mother sat at every morning from nine until ten with the newspapers and the day’s list, where nobody was allowed to disturb her. The third drawer had always been locked.

She had never once, in her whole life, seen it open.

chapters.title: Six in the Morning
chapters.desc: A locked drawer her mother never opened in front of anyone. A folder in her own safe, under the Geneva pieces. Eleven bankers around one table. And a hall in the Western District at six o’clock, where two people stand side by side and watch a grey man go down the stairs.
chapters.epigraph: “When it is done, she will be standing in the hall beside him at six in the morning. And then they will go and have breakfast.” — Clause 5
chapters.content:
The house on the Peak was very quiet.

The valuers had been and gone. There were little white stickers on the backs of things, on the dining chairs and the long sideboard and the pair of Venetian mirrors in the hall, with numbers on them in black ink. There were pale squares on the walls of the drawing room where the Morandis had hung. The great staircase, the one she had walked down at eighteen in a white dress for her debut with her mother’s hand flat between her shoulder blades, had a sticker on its newel post.

Nobody came to the door. There was no staff. Her mother had let them go, all but the old cook, who opened the kitchen door at the back, at nine on the Thursday morning, and looked at Aurelia standing on the step, and burst into tears.

“She’s upstairs,” said the cook. “She hasn’t come down.”

“I’m not here to see her,” said Aurelia. “I’m here for the morning room.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The morning room was at the east end of the house, on the ground floor, small and yellow, with a window that looked down the hill at the harbour. When she was a child, she had not been allowed in it between nine and ten. Nobody had. That was the hour her mother sat at the bureau with the newspapers and the list, and the door was shut, and if you knocked you were sent to your room.

The bureau was in the corner. Walnut. Small. From her great-grandmother’s house in Milan, with a sloping front and brass handles shaped like shells.

It had a sticker on it.

Aurelia stood in front of it with the brass key in her hand.

Then she knelt down and unlocked the third drawer.

✦ ✦ ✦

It was full of paper.

Two folders. One on top of the other.

The top one was thin. Brown card, the kind lawyers used, tied with a black ribbon. She untied it.

Letters. Six of them. On heavy ministry paper, with the crest at the top, in a hand she did not know, and all of them addressed to Mrs. Vittoria Conti Song. The first was dated September 2019. The last was January 2020.

She read them on her knees on the floor of the morning room.

The first one said, very politely, that the vice-minister had been delighted to meet Mrs. Song at the gala and had been thinking since about the Harbour Bridge Two application, and about how much he admired Mrs. Song’s elder daughter, who he understood had been married rather suddenly, abroad, to a man the vice-minister could not, in conscience, recommend.

The second one mentioned the vice-minister’s son, Fu Kang. Thirty. Unmarried. A fine young man.

The third one said that marriages abroad were not always recognised, and that some were easy to dissolve, and that the vice-minister had friends who could help, and that a family as distinguished as the Song family deserved a son-in-law who could sit at the ministry’s table in daylight.

The fourth mentioned a company in Macau. And a figure. Fifteen per cent.

The fifth said that the vice-minister was disappointed not to have had a reply.

The sixth said, in its entirety:

Mrs. Song, your daughter has embarrassed my son. I will not forget it. Neither, I think, will the ministry. — F.J.

Paperclipped to the sixth letter was a sheet of her mother’s cream notepaper, with the dark blue initials, in her mother’s tall slanting hand. A list of dates. Times. Places. The Mandarin Grill. A private room at the Jockey Club. The back seat of a car outside the opera house. And beside each, in her mother’s hand, a line.

Proposed F.K. for A. again. Declined.

Mentioned the 15%. Declined. Said Weiren would not.

Threatened the permits. Declined.

Asked me to bring A. to dinner without her husband. Declined.

And at the bottom, in January 2020, a week after the poisoning, a week after every newspaper in the city had run a photograph of Chen Si being carried off a boat on a stretcher:

He asked whether I would be very sorry if my son-in-law did not recover. I threw my drink at him. Kept these in case.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia sat back on her heels on the floor of the morning room.

She read the line again. I threw my drink at him.

Her mother. Vittoria Conti, who had never in her life raised her voice in public, who corrected the angle of a fork at a dinner for forty from the other end of the table with one look, who had stood up at her husband’s birthday and said second place is just the first of the losers into a microphone in front of two hundred people. Had thrown a drink at a vice-minister. For a son-in-law she had never once, to his face, called anything but Mr. Chen.

Kept these in case.

In case of what?

She opened the second folder.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second folder was thick. Very thick. Cream card, not brown. No ribbon. The corners soft from being handled.

Newspaper cuttings. Hundreds of them. Cut with scissors, very neatly, along the edges of the columns, and each one dated in pencil in the corner, in her mother’s tall slanting hand.

The first one was from 2015. A paragraph in the back of a local magazine, about a jewellery prize for students at the polytechnic, and the name of the girl who had come second.

Aurelia Song (19).

Underlined. In pencil. Very faintly.

The next one was the opening of the first boutique. Then the first review. Then a photograph of Numero Uno in a trade magazine nobody read. Then an interview she had forgotten she had ever given, to a student newspaper. Then the second boutique. Then the Milan wedding in Vogue, the most beautiful wedding of the year that nobody was invited to, with the photograph of her in her grandmother’s veil on the steps of the palazzo, and the edges of that one were softer than any of the others, as if it had been taken out and looked at, and put back, very many times.

Then Paris. Every review of Balcony. Le Monde. Le Figaro. The Financial Times. The piece in the New York Times that said she had turned the worst night of her life into the most important collection in a decade. Her mother had underlined the worst night of her life. Twice. And written beside it, in pencil, very small, one word.

Mine.

At the bottom of the folder, on its own, there was a programme. Black card, printed in gold. Balcony. The museum. June.

No. Not the one from the floor by the fire door. Aurelia had that one, in the drawer of her bench at the boutique.

This was a second one. Her mother must have taken two.

On this one, nothing was underlined. But on the back, in pencil, in her mother’s hand, very carefully, there was a list. The list of the eleven pieces, copied out. And beside each one, the line engraved inside it. All eleven. Word for word.

And at the bottom, alone:

He said them all to her. On my balcony. While I was inside, drinking to what I said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She stayed where she was, on the floor of the morning room.

The sun moved across the yellow carpet. Downstairs, in the kitchen, she could hear the old cook crying, quietly, and a radio playing opera. Through the window, down the hill, the harbour was very bright, and on the far shore, three-quarters built, Harbour Bridge Two stood out over the water, reaching for the other side.

She did not go upstairs.

She put both folders in her bag. She locked the drawer and left the brass key on top of the bureau, beside the valuer’s sticker, where her mother would find it. And she walked out of the morning room and down the hall past the Venetian mirrors and the great staircase and out of the front door, and did not look up at the windows.

In the car, she sat with her hands on the wheel for ten minutes.

Then she called Dr. Ho, who did not take calls on Thursdays, and Dr. Ho took it.

“I don’t know what to do with this,” said Aurelia.

“With what?”

“With knowing she was on my side,” said Aurelia. Her voice was perfectly steady and her face was wet. “The whole time. Behind my back. Throwing drinks at ministers. Cutting out my reviews. And never once telling me. Not once. Saying second place into a microphone with a folder of my reviews in a locked drawer.” She looked at the windows of the house. “I don’t know which is worse. That she was cruel. Or that she was cruel and loved me.”

Dr. Ho was quiet.

“You don’t have to decide today,” she said.

“I do,” said Aurelia. “I have eleven bankers at four o’clock.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the forty-fourth floor first.

He was in the study, at the desk, with Qian and Ms. Fong and a laptop, and three days of Song Group files spread across every flat surface, and when she walked in he looked up and saw her face and stood.

She put the brown folder on the desk.

He opened it. He read the six letters, one after another. He read her mother’s list. He read the line at the bottom.

He asked whether I would be very sorry if my son-in-law did not recover.

He went very still.

Ms. Fong, beside him, had taken off her enormous glasses and was reading over his shoulder with her face an inch from the paper.

“Mrs. Chen,” said Ms. Fong, in a voice like a door closing. “Where did these come from?”

“My mother’s desk.”

Ms. Fong put her glasses back on.

“A serving vice-minister,” she said, “soliciting a fifteen per cent interest in a public contract through a Macau shell, in writing, on ministry paper, signed with his initials, and threatening a citizen in connection with a pending permit.” She looked at Chen Si. “With contemporaneous notes from the citizen. With dates.” She looked at the folder. “And with what you already have.”

Chen Si didn’t say anything.

Aurelia went to the wall. To the painting of the harbour at night, which swung out on a hinge. To the safe behind it, which had been his and was now theirs. She opened it.

Under the Geneva pieces, the velvet trays of diamonds she had bought back from Monsieur Aubert, there was a single plastic sleeve.

One page. A trust deed. Liechtenstein. Seven companies deep.

Beneficiary: Fu Kang.

Second beneficiary: Fu Jianguo.

She took it out and put it on the desk beside her mother’s letters.

“Clause five,” she said. “He’s yours. You have the prior claim. I won’t interfere.” She looked at him. “But you told me once that you needed his name on a document. Now you have it on seven.”

He looked down at the desk. At a trust deed from her safe, and six letters from her mother’s drawer.

He put one finger on the plastic sleeve. Very lightly. The way you touch a photograph.

“Fourteen years,” he said.

“I know.”

“I was fifteen.” He didn’t look up. “I used to lie on the floor of my mother’s flat in the dark and think, one day I’ll have his name on a piece of paper. And I’ll take it somewhere where they can’t ignore it.” He was quiet. “I thought it would be a gun. For a long time, when I was sixteen, seventeen, I thought it would have to be a gun.”

“It isn’t,” said Aurelia.

“No.” He looked up at her. “It’s you. And your mother.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Ms. Fong took it to the commission that afternoon.

Not Chen Si. That was the point. Ms. Fong, in her enormous glasses, with a briefcase and a clerk, at two o’clock, through the front door of the Independent Commission, to a deputy commissioner she had been at law school with and who owed nobody in the city a single favour, least of all a man who owned docks. No letter. No call. No judge. Just paper.

“This is going to take a while,” said Ms. Fong, at the door. “They’ll want to verify every page. The bank in Liechtenstein. The handwriting. Mrs. Song will need to give a statement.” She looked at Aurelia. “Will she?”

Aurelia thought about the second folder in her bag. Mine.

“Yes,” she said. “She will.”

“Then they may move faster than you think,” said Ms. Fong. “He’s been on their list for years. They’ve been waiting for one piece of paper they could stand on.” She settled her glasses. “Now they have a floor.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At four o’clock, Aurelia walked into the boardroom on the fortieth floor of Song Group Tower in black, with gold on, every piece she owned, and sat down at the head of the table in her father’s chair.

Her father sat on her right. He had shaved. He was wearing a tie. He looked at her when she came in and his face did the thing again, the thing from the night, the only light in the room, and then he looked down at the table and didn’t look up for some time.

Around the table, eleven bankers.

Eleven men and two women, in grey and navy, with folders and tablets and the faces of people who have already decided. She knew four of them. One had come to her debut. One had sat at her mother’s table at the birthday and drunk to the toast.

On a screen at the far end, from Singapore, Mr. Tan.

“Good afternoon,” said Aurelia. “My name is Aurelia Chen. I have read every line of every loan you have made to the Song Group. I have read them twice. I would like to tell you what is going to happen.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not raise her voice once in three hours.

She did it the way she had done it in the Jade Hall, with eleven men round the table and a forged signature in her hand. She did it the way she did everything. She did the sums in her head.

Shenzhen would be sold. All four towers. Not in a fire sale; slowly, over eighteen months, to a consortium she had spent three nights assembling, on the phone, at two in the morning, in Italian and Cantonese and English: a pension fund in Milan that had known her grandfather; a family in Singapore that Mr. Tan had introduced her to over noodles; Mrs. Leung, whose daughter had been married in yellow diamonds and who had said on the phone at midnight, Aurelia, darling, I’ve wanted a tower for years. The price was a third below what the Song Group had hoped and a third above what the banks expected. She put the figure on the table.

The department stores were gone. They would stay gone.

The art was gone. It would stay gone.

The house on the Peak would go to auction. In the autumn. With everything in it that had a sticker.

Her father, on her right, closed his eyes.

And the bridge.

“The bridge,” said Aurelia, “is three-quarters built. It is the only thing the Song Group owns that is worth more every day. You know that. You are lending against it. You’re calling everything on Friday because the extension hasn’t come.” She looked round the table. “It will come.”

One of the bankers, the one who had drunk to the toast, smiled very slightly.

“Mrs. Chen,” he said, “with respect. The vice-minister has made his position very clear.”

“The vice-minister,” said Aurelia, “will not be in a position to sign anything for very much longer.” She did not smile. “I can’t tell you why. I can tell you that his deputy is a woman called Mrs. Ling, who has been trying to get Harbour Bridge Two extended for six months, and who has been told no by her superior eleven times, in writing, and kept copies.” She folded her hands. “I had tea with her yesterday.”

The banker stopped smiling.

“Until it comes,” said Aurelia, “you will not call anything. You will sign a standstill. Ninety days. In return, the Song Group will put up a guarantee.”

“What guarantee?” said the woman from the second-largest bank. “There’s nothing left.”

“Not the Song Group,” said Aurelia. “Me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The room went quiet.

On the screen, Mr. Tan took off his glasses.

“My boutiques,” said Aurelia. “All three. Harbour Road, the one in Central, and Singapore. The lease. The stock. Every stone in the safe. The workshop. The Balcony collection, all eleven pieces, which three museums have asked to buy and one has asked to borrow for a year. The name AURELIA, which is worth, I’m told, by a man from Paris who wants to buy it, rather more than four towers in Shenzhen.” She looked round the table. “Clause one of a contract I signed four years ago says every gram of gold I have ever cut is mine. I am putting it on this table. Behind the bridge. For ninety days.”

Her father turned in his chair.

“Tesoro,” he said. “No.”

“Papà.”

“No.” His voice cracked. “Not your shop. Not the shop. We closed it. Your mother and I. In January. In front of everyone. We—” He couldn’t finish.

“I know,” said Aurelia. “That’s why.”

She looked down the table at eleven bankers.

“My mother closed my first shop in front of two hundred people because I came second,” she said. “I would like it noted, in the minutes, that I am opening my last three as a guarantee for her husband’s bridge. In front of eleven.” She picked up her pen. “Now. Ninety days. Do we have a standstill, or do I take my gold and my consortium and go home, and you can all go to the Shenzhen waterfront on Friday and try to sell four empty towers by yourselves?”

On the screen, Mr. Tan put his glasses back on.

“Singapore signs,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

They all signed.

It took until seven. Nine of them signed at the table. Two went out into the corridor and made phone calls and came back and signed. The one who had drunk to the toast signed last, and when he had signed, he capped his pen and looked at her down the table and said, “Your mother never told us you could do this.”

Aurelia looked at him.

“No,” she said. “She never told anyone anything.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si had not come.

He had wanted to. He had stood in the hall of the forty-fourth floor at three o’clock in his dark grey suit, with his car keys in his hand, and she had stood in front of him and taken the keys out of his hand and put them in her own pocket.

“If you’re in that room,” she had said, “every banker at that table will think the guarantee is yours. They’ll sign because they’re afraid of you.” She had lifted her chin. “I don’t want them to sign because they’re afraid of you. I want them to sign because they’ve read the figures and they know I’m right.”

He had looked at her.

“And if they don’t sign?”

“Then they don’t,” said Aurelia. “And my father loses his bridge, and I lose my shops, and we start again. Both of us. With nothing. The way you did.” She had put her hand on his chest, on his shirt, over the tag. “But they’ll sign.”

They had signed.

He was in the car park underneath the tower, when she came down at 7:20. Leaning against the black car, in his shirtsleeves, with his jacket over his arm and Qian beside him eating antacids from the packet.

She walked across the concrete to him, in black, in heels, with every piece of gold she owned on.

He didn’t say anything. He just held out his arms.

She walked into them.

He held her against the black car with his jacket sliding off his arm onto the concrete, and Qian looked very hard at a pillar.

“They all signed,” he said into her hair. It wasn’t a question; Qian had had a text from Mr. Tan at 7:02.

He drew back far enough to look at her: every piece of gold she owned, chin up, eyes wet. His voice went low. “I’ve been down here for three hours being jealous of eleven bankers who got to watch you do that.” He picked his jacket up off the floor and put it round her shoulders, over the gold. “Next time you take my keys, take me with them. I’ll sit in the corridor. I won’t say a word. I just want to hear you win.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father’s guarantee lasted thirty-one days.

On the thirtieth day, a Friday, at four in the morning, Ms. Fong rang.

“Tomorrow,” she said. “Six o’clock. The commission. They’ve had the warrant since Wednesday. They’re going to the house.” A pause. “The deputy commissioner says that if Mr. and Mrs. Chen would like to be present in the hall, as the parties who supplied the evidence, he will raise no objection, provided they don’t speak.”

Aurelia sat up in bed in the dark.

Beside her, Chen Si was already sitting up. He had been awake. She realised he had probably been awake for every one of the thirty nights, and had not said.

She put the phone down.

She looked at him.

He was looking at the window. At the city, dark, all the way down to the harbour. His hand had gone to his chest, to the two pieces of gold under his T-shirt, and stayed there.

“Six o’clock,” he said.

She waited.

“I don’t know what to wear,” said Chen Si, and his voice did something very strange, and he put his face in his hands.

She had never seen him not know something.

She got up on her knees on the bed and took his wrists and drew his hands down from his face, and he let her, and the face under them was a boy’s face, fifteen, in a hall, waiting for someone to tell him what happens now. His eyes were dry. That was the worst of it. He had not cried at the top of a staircase either, she thought. There had been nobody to cry to.

“Look at me,” she said. “Si. Look at me.”

He looked at her.

“You don’t have to know,” said Aurelia. “That’s my job tomorrow. I’ll know what you wear and where you stand and when we leave. All you have to do is hold my hand and not let go.” She pressed his palms flat over her heart, so he could feel it going steady. “I sat in your chair. I can stand in a hall.”

He bent until his forehead was against hers, and stayed there, breathing, until the window went from black to grey.

✦ ✦ ✦

She chose for him.

The grey suit. The one from the first night. The one he had been wearing on the balcony, on the night of the birthday, when he had stood at the end of it in the dark and given her his coat. No tie. A white shirt, open at the throat, so that if she looked she could see the chain. No watch. She took it off his wrist herself and left it on the dresser. She wanted nothing on him in that hall that anyone could put in a plastic bag, except the gold she had made.

And she wore the coat.

His coat. The one from the balcony. Camel cashmere, too big for her, to her knees, that she had never given back and he had never asked for, keep it as long as you like, that had hung for five years in her wardrobe beside her silk and her gold and come out only on the nights that mattered.

She put it on at 5:20 in the morning in the dark bedroom, over a black dress, and turned round, and he looked at her in it and did not say anything at all.

✦ ✦ ✦

The house was in the Western District. On a quiet road on the slope above the university. White, three storeys, with a little garden in front with a lemon tree in it and a gate that the commission officers had already opened.

They stood in the hall.

Everything was very ordinary. A rack of coats. Umbrellas in a stand. A pair of slippers by the door, worn down at the heels. A framed photograph on the wall, of a younger man in a ministry suit shaking hands with someone important. A clock, ticking.

Six officers. Plain clothes. Very quiet. Two of them at the foot of the staircase.

Aurelia stood beside Chen Si by the coat rack, in his old coat, with her hand in his. His hand was perfectly steady. His face was perfectly still. He was looking up the stairs.

At 6:00, by the clock in the hall, the officers went up.

They heard a door. Voices, low. A woman, somewhere at the back of the house, crying out once and then not again. Footsteps.

And then he came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was smaller than she had thought.

That was what she would remember. That he was small. A grey man in rimless glasses, sixty-eight years old, in blue-striped cotton pyjamas and a beige cardigan buttoned wrong, with his hair flat on one side from the pillow. He came down the staircase between two officers, one step at a time, holding the banister, the way old men do.

He saw them at the bottom.

He stopped on the third stair.

He looked at Aurelia, in the coat. His eyes moved over her face and he didn’t know her. Then they moved to the man beside her, and stayed there, and she watched him not know him either. A man in a grey suit, twenty-nine, perfectly still. Nobody. A face in a hall.

Then something moved behind the rimless glasses.

Something very old. From fourteen years ago. A hall. A staircase. A boy of fifteen in pyjamas at the top of it, holding his mother’s hand, watching his father go down.

Fu Jianguo went very white.

Chen Si didn’t move. He didn’t speak. The deputy commissioner had said they should not speak, and he did not. He stood in the hall by the coat rack in his grey suit, with his wife’s hand in his, and looked at the old man on the third stair, and let him look back, for exactly as long as it took.

Then the officers moved, and Fu Jianguo came down the last three stairs, and at the bottom one of them reached out and took his watch off his wrist, and his wedding ring, and his glasses, and put them into a small plastic bag, and sealed it.

They walked him out of the front door, past the lemon tree, in his pyjamas.

He didn’t look back.

✦ ✦ ✦

They stood in the hall after he had gone.

The clock ticked. Somewhere at the back of the house, the woman was crying again, quietly. An officer was speaking to her in a low voice. Outside, a car door closed, and an engine started, and went away down the hill.

Chen Si stood by the coat rack and did not move.

She didn’t say anything. She held his hand. She stood beside him in the hall in his coat, which was clause five, and waited, which was clause ten without the word, for as long as he needed.

His hand had begun to shake.

Very slightly. Then more. She felt it start in his fingers and go all the way up his arm. He didn’t make a sound. His face didn’t change. He stood perfectly upright in his grey suit and looked at the empty staircase, and his whole body shook, very quietly, from the inside, like a building in an earthquake that does not fall down.

She turned and put both arms round him, inside the coat, so that the coat went round both of them.

He bent his head. Put his face down on her shoulder. In the wool. And stayed there.

“He didn’t look back,” said Chen Si, into the coat. Very muffled. Very young. “My father looked back. At the door. He looked back at us. Look after your mother. I’ll be home soon.” His breath went ragged. “He didn’t look back at anyone.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “Nobody’s waiting for him to come home.”

He didn’t say anything for a while.

“Thank you,” he said finally. “For coming.”

She put her hand on the back of his neck, under the collar of his grey suit, the way he had always held her.

“It’s on your chest,” she said. “In my handwriting. She will come.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Then they went and had breakfast.

That was the clause. That was what it said, on page four, in red ink, that he had read four times on a workshop floor and signed. And then they will go and have breakfast. She had written it at two in the morning in silk pyjamas in her flat, not knowing what it would mean, not knowing anything, except that whatever happened at the end, she wanted there to be breakfast after it.

She drove. In his coat. Down from the Western District, through the streets just waking up, the shutters going up on the shops and the old men coming out with their birdcages, all the way down to the old town, to the shop that sold funeral paper, and the stone steps so narrow you had to go sideways in heels.

Old Fan was at the wok.

He was always at the wok. Forty-five years, now. He looked up when they came down the steps at 7:10 on a Saturday morning, Mr. and Mrs. Chen, in a grey suit and a man’s coat, with their faces the way they were, and he looked at them, and didn’t say Princess, and didn’t say Mr. Chen.

He put down his ladle.

He came round from behind the wok, slowly, wiping his hands on his apron, and pulled out two plastic chairs at the corner table, the one where she had once read four ledgers in a single night, and stood beside them.

“Sit,” said Old Fan.

They sat.

He brought food without asking. Not the pork belly. Not the fish. Congee. Plain white congee, very hot, in two big bowls, with a little dish of salted egg and a little dish of pickled radish, and fried dough sticks, and hot soy milk with sugar. The breakfast you give someone who has been ill. The breakfast you give someone whose father has died.

He put it down in front of them and went back to his wok and did not look at them again.

Chen Si looked at the bowl.

Then he picked up his spoon, and ate. All of it. Slowly. Without stopping. In the white-tiled basement under the funeral shop, at a plastic table, at seven in the morning, in his grey suit, with his wife in his coat across from him. He ate a whole bowl of congee and two dough sticks and drank his soy milk and then he put the spoon down and sat back in the plastic chair and looked at her across the table.

He looked ten years younger.

No. That was wrong. He looked his age. Twenty-nine. For the first time since she had met him. Not older. Not carrying anything. A man of twenty-nine at a breakfast table.

“I’m hungry,” he said, sounding surprised.

Old Fan, at the wok, without turning round, put another bowl on the counter.

✦ ✦ ✦

The bridge extension was signed by Mrs. Ling on the following Tuesday.

The standstill became a restructuring. The guarantee was released on the ninetieth day, unused, and every gram of gold Aurelia had ever cut came back to her, the way it was always going to, because she had done the sums.

Fu Jianguo was charged in October. Eleven counts. The trial would take two years. His son, Fu Kang, left for Vancouver on a Thursday and was not seen in the city again.

And on the second Saturday of September, at eleven in the morning, in the boutique on Harbour Road, a car stopped outside.

Aurelia was at the counter. She looked up.

Her mother got out.

✦ ✦ ✦

Vittoria Conti Song came into the boutique in a navy coat that was three seasons old, and flat shoes, and no jewellery at all. Not a ring. Not a watch. Not the pearls, which had gone at auction in July with the Morandis. Her hair was grey at the roots. She had not had it done.

She stood in the middle of the floor, on the marble, under the soft lights, where she had once said, in January, in front of the staff, we are closing it.

She looked at the window. At the broken necklace, on its plinth, with its line along the seam.

Then she looked at her daughter.

Aurelia stood behind the counter and did not come out.

She had decided. On Tuesday, with Dr. Ho. She had decided what the price was. She had decided that she would not come out from behind the counter, and she would not speak first, and she would not make it easy, and she would not make it cruel either. She would stand there, and wait, and let her mother do the one thing that Vittoria Conti had never done in her life, to anyone, for anything.

Her mother came to the counter.

She put her hands on the glass. Her bare hands. No rings. Aurelia had never once in her life seen her mother’s hands without rings. They were thin and old and there was a pale band on the left one where the wedding ring had been for thirty years and had been sold.

“The commission took my statement,” said her mother. “On Wednesday. Four hours. I told them everything.” Her voice was low and perfectly controlled and her hands on the glass were shaking. “I told them about the drink.”

Aurelia said nothing.

“Your father told me what you did. At the table. With the bankers.” Her mother looked down at her hands. “Your shops. All three. Behind his bridge.”

Aurelia said nothing.

Her mother was quiet.

Then Vittoria Conti, who had said thank you all her life the way you sign a receipt, looked up at her daughter across the glass counter of the shop she had closed, and said it.

“Thank you.”

Two words.

Her voice broke on the second.

✦ ✦ ✦

Aurelia looked at her mother across the counter.

She thought of the folder. Mine. She thought of a pencil line under Keep it as long as you like, and a programme dropped by a fire door. She thought of second place is just the first of the losers, into a microphone, in front of two hundred people. She thought of nine days in Vienna and a rented room and a woman who corrected the angle of her fork from the other end of the table with one look, and who had thrown a drink at a vice-minister and never told anyone, and who had copied out eleven lines from the inside of eleven pieces of gold onto the back of a programme in pencil, very carefully, word for word.

She did not forgive her. Not yet.

But she came out from behind the counter.

She walked round the end of it, onto the marble, and stood in front of her mother, and they were the same height, she realised. She had always thought her mother was taller.

She took off the plain wide bracelet on her left wrist. The one piece of Balcony that had never been shown. The one engraved on the inside, in his hand, lifted at every turn: I’m more interested in what you do in the dark.

She took her mother’s bare left hand, the one with the pale band where the ring had been, and put the bracelet on her wrist, and closed it.

Her mother looked down at it.

“I don’t—” said Vittoria. “I can’t—”

“Keep it,” said Aurelia. “As long as you like.”

chapters.title: Number One, By Her Own Rules
chapters.desc: 2024. A collection called “Seconda”, made from every second place she ever came. A prize in Geneva that nobody from Asia has ever won. Her parents in the front row, and a daughter who does not look for them once. And afterwards, in a hotel suite above the lake, a medal on a ribbon and a man who is not allowed to touch it.
chapters.epigraph: “The winner sets the terms.” “You always set the terms.” “Tonight I set them in first place.”
chapters.content:
The idea came from a box.

A shoebox. Pale blue. From a shop in Milan that had closed twenty years ago. She found it in the autumn of 2023 at the back of her old wardrobe at the Peak, on the last day before the house went to auction, when she went back alone to take the few things that were hers, and the valuers had already been, and the wardrobe was empty except for that.

She sat on the bare floor of her childhood room, the room with the long mirror, and opened it.

Silver.

Medals. Ribbons. Certificates on thick card. A little plastic trophy of a girl on a pony. A brooch shaped like the number two. A silver plate engraved with the name of a school in Vienna.

Second place. Every one. From the age of six to the age of nineteen. Piano, ballet, riding, mathematics, debating, the regional science prize, the jewellery prize at the polytechnic. Every second place she had ever come, which her mother had taken off her in the car on the way home, every time, without a word, and which Aurelia had assumed for twenty years had been thrown away.

Her mother had kept them.

In a shoebox. In the back of her daughter’s wardrobe. Where her daughter would find them, one day, when the house was gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

She took the shoebox to the workshop and put it on Enzo’s bench.

He opened it. He looked inside without saying anything. He took out the silver plate from Vienna and turned it over and read the engraving, and put it back.

“Cara,” he said. “What do you want to do with these?”

“Melt them,” said Aurelia.

He looked at her over his magnifying glasses.

“Not to destroy them,” she said. “I don’t want to destroy them. I want to make them into something.” She picked up the little brooch shaped like a two. “I want to make a collection out of every time I came second. And I want to call it Seconda. And I want it to win.”

Enzo put the lid back on the box very slowly.

“The Prix de Genève,” he said. “Nobody from Asia has ever won it.”

“I know.”

“Your mother,” said Enzo, “entered you for it when you were twenty. You didn’t make the shortlist.”

“I came twelfth,” said Aurelia. She put the brooch back in the box. “She said that was worse than second. She said at least second was a number people remembered.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Seconda took her nine months.

Eleven pieces. Always eleven. She did not plan it that way; it simply always came out at eleven, and she had stopped fighting it, and Dr. Ho had said, on a Tuesday, mildly, “You know why, don’t you,” and Aurelia had said, “Forty-one sapphires, eleven clauses, eleven pages, eleven pieces of Balcony,” and Dr. Ho had said, “And?” and Aurelia had said, “And he took eleven seconds to answer, on the balcony, when I asked who he was,” and Dr. Ho had said nothing at all and written something down.

She melted the silver. All of it. The medals and the plate and the brooch and the little plastic trophy, which wasn’t silver at all but which she put in the crucible anyway, with the others, and watched go black and curl and vanish. Enzo would not let it near his gold until it had been to the refiner, because second-place medals, he said, are mostly lies about silver: a skin of plate over brass, a ribbon, some glue. Less than half came back. She said it was the most accurate thing anyone had ever told her about second place. And then she alloyed the silver with gold, very carefully, until the colour was something she had never seen before. Not yellow. Not white. A pale warm colour like the inside of a shell, like winter light on water. The colour of the second star you see at night, the one everyone forgets because they were looking for the first.

She made eleven pieces out of it.

A ring shaped like a podium, with the highest step left empty. A long necklace of links that were each a little different from the one before, so that no link was first and no link was last. A pair of earrings that didn’t match, on purpose. A cuff in the shape of a ribbon, twisted once, so that you couldn’t tell which side was the front. A brooch shaped like the number two, cut so finely that if you turned it in the light it became a swan.

And at the centre of the collection, on its own, a medal.

Round. Heavy. On a long silk ribbon, dark blue, the blue of her mother’s initials. Plain on the front. On the back, engraved, in her own handwriting, round and confident, with the flourish on the A:

Second is just the first of the ones who kept going.

✦ ✦ ✦

She entered Seconda for the Prix de Genève in February.

She entered it herself. Under her own name. On the form, where it said Sponsor or nominating house, she left the line blank. Where it said Previous entries, she wrote, 2016. Twelfth. Entered by my mother.

Lily, reading the form over her shoulder, said, “You can’t put that.”

“Why not?” said Aurelia. “It’s true.”

✦ ✦ ✦
