The shortlist came out in June. Six houses. Five from Paris and Geneva, houses that had been making jewellery since before the invention of the telephone. And one from Asia.

AURELIA. Seconda.

The ceremony was in October, in Geneva, in the great hall of the old hotel on the lake, under chandeliers, in front of four hundred people.

She sent her parents two tickets.

Front row.

She didn’t tell anyone she was doing it. Not Chen Si. Not Dr. Ho. She wrote the envelope herself, to the new flat in Mid-Levels where her parents lived now, three rooms and a view of a wall, and put two tickets in it, and on the back of one of them, in pencil, she wrote, very small: Seats A3 and A4. You can see everything from here.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the night, she did not look for them.

She had decided that too, on a Tuesday. Not out of revenge. She had done revenge, in Row R, behind a pillar, and found that it was not very satisfying, and that her father had walked to the front anyway. She did not look for them because she had finally understood, sitting on the floor of her old room with a shoebox, that she had spent twenty years looking at the front row to see if her mother was pleased, and she did not want to spend one more minute doing it. Not even tonight. Especially not tonight.

So when she walked into the great hall in Geneva at seven o’clock in a column of dark blue silk, with no gold on at all, only the pale shell-coloured metal of Seconda at her ears and wrists, she looked at one seat.

A1.

Clause six. Dark grey suit. Phone off, in Qian’s pocket, where Qian had watched him put it. Sitting very upright with his hands on his knees and his eyes on her, only on her, the whole length of the hall, as she walked.

She looked at him all the way to her seat. She sat down beside him in A2. He took her hand.

She did not turn her head to the right.

✦ ✦ ✦

Elowen was in the third row.

She had not been invited. She had bought a ticket. Aurelia found this out afterwards, from Zhao, who said it in five words: “She paid. Full price. Insisted.”

She was in green. Of course she was in green. She caught Aurelia’s eye across the hall during the speeches, and held it, coolly, appraisingly, for exactly four seconds, the way her husband did. And then, very slightly, so that nobody else in four hundred people could possibly have seen, she lifted one hand off her lap, and crossed two fingers.

Aurelia looked away very fast.

Her eyes were stinging.

Beside her, in A1, Chen Si squeezed her hand and said, without moving his lips, “Lin?”

“Shut up,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

They announced it in reverse order, the way they always did.

Sixth. Fifth. Fourth. Each time, a name she knew, a house from Paris, a polite storm of applause, someone in black walking up to the stage.

Third. A house from Geneva that had made the crown for a European queen. Applause.

She sat very still with her hand in his.

She found she was not doing sums. For the first time in her life, at a moment like this, she was not counting. She was not calculating the odds. She was not thinking about what her mother would say. She was not thinking about anything at all, except that his thumb was moving on the back of her hand, very slowly, in a small circle, the way it did, and that she could feel the pale warm metal of the medal, the real one, the one she had made for the collection and then made again, for herself, a second time, under her dress, against her breastbone.

“In second place,” said the woman on the stage, in French.

A name from Paris. An old name. A house that had been making jewellery since 1780.

Applause.

Aurelia closed her eyes.

“And the Prix de Genève, for the first time in its history, is awarded to a house from Asia.” The woman on the stage paused. “For a collection made, the designer tells us, from every second place she ever came. Seconda.” She smiled. “AURELIA.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t move.

She sat in A2 with her eyes closed and the sound of four hundred people coming at her like the sea, and could not move at all.

Then she felt him stand up.

He stood up beside her. Before anyone else. Before the applause had properly started. He stood up in A1 in his grey suit, and then, because he had stood, the whole front row stood, and then the second, and then the hall.

She opened her eyes.

She looked up at him.

He was not clapping. He was looking down at her with an expression she had seen exactly once before, on a balcony in October, in the dark, when she had turned round in a gold dress with her eyes wet and found him standing at the end of it.

“Go on,” he said. “First place.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She walked up to the stage.

She took the prize. A crystal, heavy, cut like a flame. She stood at the microphone in her dark blue silk with four hundred people standing in front of her, and the light in her eyes, so that she couldn’t see the front row properly at all, and that was fine.

She had written a speech. Two pages. On Tuesday, with Dr. Ho, and then again on the plane. She had it in her bag.

She didn’t take it out.

“When I was twenty,” said Aurelia, in French, and then again in English, and then again, very briefly, in Italian, “I was entered for this prize. I came twelfth. Someone I loved told me afterwards that twelfth was worse than second, because at least second was a number people remembered.”

The hall was very quiet.

“She was wrong,” said Aurelia. “Not about twelfth. About second.” She lifted her chin. “Second is not the first of the losers. Second is just the first of the ones who kept going. I know that because I’ve been second more times than anyone in this room, and I kept every one, and I melted them down, and I made them into this.” She touched the medal at her throat. “So this isn’t my first place. It’s all my second places. Together. Finally adding up.”

She paused.

“And I would like to thank one person,” she said, “who never once in six years asked me to win.”

She looked down at A1.

She still couldn’t see him properly. The light was in her eyes. But she knew exactly where he was.

“Thank you,” said Aurelia Chen, “for never asking.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not look for her parents.

Not when she came down from the stage. Not at the champagne afterwards, in the long gallery above the lake, with four hundred people wanting to shake her hand. Not when the man from the oldest house in Paris kissed her on both cheeks and said, “Merde, madame, I wanted to hate it.” Not when Elowen came past in green and said, not stopping, “Congratulations. Don’t get used to it,” and kept walking, and then, three steps later, turned round and came back and kissed her on the cheek, very quickly, and walked off again before anyone could see.

She found out afterwards what had happened, from Serafina, who had been in row C.

Her father had stood up when they said AURELIA. Before the hall. Before the front row. At the same moment as Chen Si, said Serafina; she had seen them, the two of them, standing up at the same second, at either end of the front row.

And her mother had not stood up.

Her mother had sat in A4, in her three-season-old navy coat, with her hands in her lap, and her head bowed, and stayed sitting, while four hundred people stood up around her. And Serafina had thought, of course, of course she won’t, and been so angry she couldn’t breathe.

And then she had seen her mother’s shoulders.

“She was crying,” said Serafina. “Aurelia. Mamma was crying. Sitting down. With her head down. Because she couldn’t stand up. Because her legs wouldn’t.” Serafina’s voice went strange. “Papà had to hold her arm. All the way through your speech. When you said second is just the first of the ones who kept going, she put her hand over her mouth.”

Aurelia didn’t say anything.

“I didn’t look,” she said finally.

“I know,” said Serafina. “I watched you not look. It was the most terrifying thing I’ve ever seen.” She was quiet. “Are you sorry?”

Aurelia thought about it. About A1. About a hand moving in small circles on the back of hers.

“No,” she said. “I was looking at the right seat.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The suite was on the top floor of the hotel, above the lake, with a long window and the lights of the city on the far shore and the great white plume of the fountain lit up in the dark.

She put the crystal on the table by the window.

He closed the door.

She turned round. Dark blue silk. No gold. And at her throat, on its long ribbon, under the silk, the second medal, the one she had made for herself. She reached up and drew it out, slowly, by the ribbon, so that it lay on the outside of her dress, pale and warm against the blue.

He looked at it.

“The winner,” said Aurelia, “sets the terms.”

He leaned back against the door.

“You always set the terms,” he said mildly. “Clause nine.”

“Tonight,” said Aurelia, “I set them in first place.” She came towards him across the carpet. Slowly. In bare feet; she had left her shoes by the window. “That’s different.”

“How?”

She stopped in front of him. Very close. Close enough to feel the warmth off him. Not touching.

“In first place,” she said, “I don’t have to win anything. I already have.” She looked up at him. “So I can take as long as I like.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took a very long time.

She told him to stand still, with his back against the door and his hands flat on it at his sides. And he did. And she undid his tie. Slowly. Pulling it through the knot an inch at a time, watching his face, and drew it off him, and dropped it on the floor. And unbuttoned his shirt, one button, and then stopped, and looked at him, and waited until his breathing changed, and then undid the next.

She did not kiss him.

That was the rule. She told him, with her mouth an inch from his. “Not yet. Not until I say. You don’t kiss me. You don’t touch me. You don’t move your hands from that door. If you move your hands, I stop, and go and sit by the window, and look at the fountain, for ten minutes, and then I start again from the first button.”

He looked down at her with his eyes gone black.

“And if I last?” he said.

“Then you get the medal,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

He lasted a very long time.

She took his shirt off. She ran her hands over his chest, very slowly, in the light from the city across the lake, over the two pieces of gold that lay there, the broken necklace and the plain tag, and over his heart, where she stopped, and counted, under her breath, out loud, ninety-six, ninety-seven, until he closed his eyes. She kissed the hollow of his throat, which was not his mouth and therefore allowed, and felt him swallow under her lips. She kissed the line of his collarbone, all the way across, and the scar on the inside of his left forearm, all the way up, from the wrist to the elbow, very slowly, while his hand stayed flat against the door beside her and shook.

She stood on her toes and put her mouth beside his, so close that he could feel her breath, and did not kiss him, and said, “Not yet,” and drew back.

He made a sound in his throat that she had never heard before.

His hands moved.

An inch. Off the door. Toward her.

She stopped, and stepped back, and looked at him.

He put them back on the door.

It was too late, and they both knew it.

Then she went and sat by the window, in her dark blue silk, with her bare feet tucked up under her on the chair, and looked out at the great white plume of the fountain in the dark.

Ten minutes.

She timed it on the clock on the wall. She did not look at him once. She could hear him breathing, behind her, against the door, very slowly and very carefully, the way a man breathes when he is trying not to do something.

At exactly ten minutes, she got up, and came back across the carpet, and stood in front of him.

“From the first button,” she said.

He laughed. Very low. Desperately. Against the door, with his head back.

“My queen,” he said, “you are going to kill me.”

“Not tonight,” said Aurelia. She picked his shirt up off the floor and held it out. “Put it back on.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He lasted the second time.

All of it. The shirt. Every button. The scar, wrist to elbow. Her mouth an inch from his, and not yet, and drawing back. He stood against the door with his hands flat on the wood and his eyes closed and his whole body trembling and did not move them, not an inch, not once, while she undid every button on his shirt again, and took it off him again, and kissed him everywhere except his mouth, slowly, all over again, from the beginning.

When she came up from kissing his ribs he spoke, without moving his hands, in his mildest and most dangerous voice.

“Aurelia. Let me kiss you. Please.” His eyes stayed on hers. “You can say no. I’ll stand here all night if you do.” A breath. “But tell me. Do you want it as much as I do?”

She didn’t answer at once. She didn’t need to. He could see it in her face.

And then she stopped, and stood in front of him, and lifted the medal off over her head by its long blue ribbon.

She put it round his neck.

It lay on his bare chest beside the other two. Three pieces of gold. One broken. One plain. One the colour of the second star.

He opened his eyes and looked down at it.

“First place,” said Aurelia. “You win.”

And then she took his face in both hands and kissed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He did not move his hands from the door.

Not for the first few seconds. He stood there and let her kiss him, slowly, deeply, with her hands on his face and her body against his, and kept his hands flat on the wood, shaking, because she had not said.

She drew back an inch.

“Otherwise,” she said, against his mouth.

He moved.

All at once. Off the door. His hands in her hair and on her back and at the zip of the dark blue silk, and his mouth on hers, hard, so that she gasped into it, and he turned them both round so that it was her back against the door now, and his hands on either side of her head, and the medal swinging between them on its ribbon, and he said into her mouth, in a voice like something breaking, “My turn.”

“Yes,” said Aurelia. “Yes.”

He made her wait, after that, exactly as long as she had made him.

Neither of them looked at the fountain again.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four in the morning, she woke.

The suite was dark. The fountain had been switched off. The lights on the far shore of the lake were very few. On the table by the window, the crystal caught what light there was and held it, like a small cold flame.

He was asleep beside her, on his back, with one arm flung up over his head and the other round her. Three pieces of gold on his chest. The medal on its blue ribbon had twisted round, so that the back was showing, the engraved side, in her handwriting, round and confident, with the flourish on the A.

Second is just the first of the ones who kept going.

She lay and looked at it.

Then she picked up her phone from the bedside table and turned it on, and there was one message on it, from a number she did not have saved, though she knew it by heart.

It had been sent at 11:14, while they were at the door.

I sat down because I could not stand. Not because I would not. Your father held my arm. I am very proud of you. I always was. I did not know how to say it, so I kept the box. — Mamma.

She read it four times.

I always was. She tried to set it beside everything else and it would not sit. Not beside second place is just the first of the losers. Not beside the car home from Vienna, a silver plate taken out of her hands without a word, nine days of silence. And then, all at once, it sat exactly, the way a stone drops into a setting you cut without knowing its size, and that was worse. Her mother had been proud of her the whole time, and had kept it in a box at the back of a wardrobe, where nobody could see it, like a second place.

Then she put the phone face down on the bedside table, and turned over, and put her face against her husband’s shoulder, beside the medal, and cried in the dark, in first place, without waking him.

He woke anyway. He always woke. He didn’t say anything. He just turned onto his side and gathered her in, and held her, for as long as she wanted to be held. He had not needed a clause for that in years.

chapters.title: Renewing the Contract
chapters.desc: Ten years to the day. Clause eleven says she may rewrite every clause. She has been drafting for a year. He has been preparing for longer, and he has a counter-offer, and a pen, and a book that cost a back-room doctor three days of stitches.
chapters.epigraph: “11. This agreement will be renewed after ten years, on the anniversary of its signing, at which point the Wife reserves the right to rewrite every clause.”
chapters.content:
She started drafting in March 2028, a year early, because she was Aurelia, and because the first time she had written it in four nights on the floor of a flat in silk pyjamas, terrified, and she wanted, this time, to take her time.

She did not tell him.

He knew anyway. He always knew. He found a sheet of cream paper in the bin in her study in April with CLAUSE 4 (REVISED?) written across the top in red and crossed out four times, and he did not say anything, and put it back in the bin exactly where it had been, at exactly the same angle. And she found it at exactly the same angle and knew he had read it, because nobody else on earth would have bothered to put it back like that, and she went and found him on the thirty-ninth floor and stood in the doorway in a temper and said, “You read my draft.”

He looked up from his desk.

“It was in the bin,” he said mildly.

“It was a private bin.”

“Clause three,” said Chen Si. “I won’t lie to you. I read it.” He leaned back. “For the record, I think revised is a mistake. Leave it as it is.”

She stared at him. “The one that says you won’t try to keep me somewhere safe?”

“I haven’t tried in ten years,” said Chen Si. “I’ve wanted to every single day. I’ve wanted to lock you in the flat and stand outside the door with a gun every time you’ve gone to the Iron Docks, or to a meeting with Mr. Kwan, or across the road for a coffee.” He picked up his pen. “But I haven’t. Because you’d leave me, and take the man in the cardigan. So it works. Leave it in.”

She threw a pen at him, because he was right and she had been about to cross it out a fifth time.

He caught it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The anniversary was a Monday. The twelfth of March, 2029. Ten years to the day since a Tuesday in March, at eleven in the morning, at the counter of her boutique on Harbour Road, exactly where he had first tried to rent it.

She closed the boutique for the day. She put a sign on the door in her own handwriting, CLOSED FOR A CONTRACT NEGOTIATION, and Lily took a photograph of it and put it on the boutique’s account, and it was shared eleven thousand times before lunch, and Zhao, who did not have a phone that did anything but ring, heard about it from Elowen and sent Chen Si a text that said only, Lawyer?, and Chen Si replied, No. Terrified, and Zhao replied, Good.

At eleven in the morning, the bell over the door rang.

She was standing behind the counter.

He came in. Grey suit. White shirt, no tie. A coffee in his hand that he wasn’t drinking. A leather folder under his arm.

Ten years. He had grey at his temples now, a little, which she liked very much and had told him so in clause nine circumstances, often. There were lines at the corners of his eyes that hadn’t been there on the balcony, from laughing, which he did now, which he had not done then. He was thirty-five.

He put the coffee down on the counter.

He looked at her. Behind the glass. In cream silk and gold, every piece, the broken necklace on its plinth in the window behind her, where it had always been.

“Good morning, Mrs. Chen,” he said. “I understand you have a commercial arrangement to discuss.”

She tried very hard not to smile.

She failed.

✦ ✦ ✦

Twelve pages, this time.

In red ink, on his cream paper, which Qian had given her without a single question, again, and which told her that Qian had not changed at all in ten years except that he now kept antacids in two drawers instead of one.

She slid it across the counter.

He took out the heavy black fountain pen. He uncapped it. He laid it on the glass beside the contract.

Then he read.

✦ ✦ ✦

She had kept most of them.

Clause one, unchanged. Her name, her boutiques, her designs, every gram of gold. His companies, his routes, his brother, his chess set. What is acquired together is held together.

Clause two, unchanged. All tables.

Clause three, unchanged. He read it and touched it with one finger and did not say anything.

Clause four, unchanged. He looked up at her. She looked back at him with her chin up. He went back to reading.

Clause five was struck through. A single clean red line, the way you strike out something that has been completed. And beside it, in the margin, in her handwriting:

Done. We had congee.

He looked at that for a while.

Clause six, unchanged. Front row. Phone off.

Clause seven, amended. The Wife will attend the Husband’s brother’s birthday every year and eat whatever he cooks, including fish with heads on, and will not, under any circumstances, let Elowen Lin win the argument about the centrepieces, which she has now won six years running.

He laughed out loud. In the empty shop.

Clause eight, unchanged.

Clause nine.

He read clause nine twice. She watched him read it twice. She had rewritten it eleven times over the year, and then, in the end, at two in the morning last week, had torn up all eleven drafts and written it again exactly as it was, word for word, with one sentence added at the end.

9. In private, the Wife sets the terms. She may tell the Husband to kneel, to wait, to take off his watch, to not move, to move, to beg, or anything else she likes, and he will do it, slowly, exactly as he did on the forty-fourth floor. Unless and until she says otherwise. When she says otherwise, he sets the terms, completely, until she says otherwise again. Both parties acknowledge that the Wife will say otherwise frequently and that this is not a contradiction. Both parties further acknowledge that, after ten years, the Husband has become very, very good at this, and that the Wife would like it noted in writing that she has no complaints whatsoever.

He looked up.

His face was doing something complicated.

“No complaints whatsoever,” he said.

“In writing,” said Aurelia. “If you sign it.”

He looked at her across the glass.

“I’d like an amendment,” he said.

“You always want an amendment.”

“Whatsoever,” said Chen Si, “is doing a great deal of work in that sentence, and I’d like it underlined.”

She picked up her red pen and underlined it. Twice.

✦ ✦ ✦

Clause ten, unchanged. The word was Milan.

Clause eleven, revised. This agreement will be renewed after ten more years, and every ten years after that, for as long as both parties are alive, at which point the Wife reserves the right to rewrite every clause, and the Husband reserves the right to read the drafts in the bin.

And then a new page.

Page twelve. The last page. With only one clause on it.

12. The Wife is not the Husband’s queen.

He stopped, and read it again.

He looked up at her, and his face had gone very still, and for one second she saw, behind it, a balcony, and a boy on a staircase, and a man in a hospital bed whispering my queen into the dark while the green line jumped.

“Keep reading,” said Aurelia.

He looked down.

12. The Wife is not the Husband’s queen. A queen sits beside a king. A queen is given a crown. A queen has a title, which can be taken away, and a throne, which belongs to somebody else. The Wife has none of these things and wants none of them. The Wife is the Husband’s equal, his partner, and the co-ruler of everything they have built, which is everything. She signs his name. He signs hers. When one of them falls, the other sits in the chair. When one of them is taken, the other comes. Neither of them, ever again, will stand at the end of a balcony alone.

The Husband may continue to say “my queen.” The Wife would be very upset if he stopped. But both parties acknowledge that it is not a title.

It never was.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

The shop was very quiet. Outside, on Harbour Road, the traffic went past, and somebody stopped to read the sign on the door, and laughed, and walked on.

He put both hands flat on the glass counter, either side of the contract.

“My queen is not a title,” he said. His voice had gone very low. “I said that. To your mother. In her drawing room. Nine years ago.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “I was standing behind you. In a gold-link dress. You didn’t know I could hear.”

“I knew,” said Chen Si. “I said it louder because you were standing there.” He looked down at page twelve. “I’ve been waiting nine years for you to put it in writing.”

She looked at him.

“Then sign it,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t pick up the pen.

He reached into the leather folder instead, and took out a single sheet of paper, and laid it on the glass on top of her twelve pages. Cream. His paper. In black ink. In his own precise hand.

COUNTER-OFFER.

She stared at it.

“You can’t make a counter-offer,” she said. “Clause eleven. The Wife reserves the right to rewrite every clause.”

“Every clause,” agreed Chen Si. “It doesn’t say anything about new ones.” He turned the sheet round so she could read it. “I’ve been drafting for two years. Before you. You’ve been sloppy with your bin. I’ve been very careful with mine.”

She looked at the sheet.

13. The Husband will, every year, on this date, give the Wife one thing she did not know she wanted. She is not allowed to refuse it, argue with it, set a price on it, or pay for it. She is only allowed to keep it, for as long as she likes.

She read it again.

“That’s not fair,” she said. Her voice had gone strange. “That’s—you can’t just—not allowed to set a price? I set the price. That’s what I do. That’s who I am—”

“Not on this,” said Chen Si.

He reached under the counter.

She hadn’t seen him put anything there. He must have done it when he came in, while she was trying not to smile. He put a box on the glass. Not a jewellery box. A plain wooden case, old, the size of a large book, with brass corners.

“The first one,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She opened it.

Inside, wrapped in a cloth of faded yellow silk, there was a book.

Very old. Bound in soft blue cloth gone grey at the edges, sewn with thread along the spine in the old way, the pages thin as skin and brown at the corners. On the cover, a narrow paper label, hand-lettered, in characters so old she had to bend close to read them.

Journey to the West.

She stopped breathing.

“No,” she said.

“Yes.”

“No. No, I—” Her hands were shaking. “I looked. For nine years. Since Zhendong told me. Every auction house in Europe and Asia. Every collector. Every library. I had Qian looking. I had Mr. Lu’s pawnbrokers looking. I had a man in Kyoto. I couldn’t find it—”

“I know,” said Chen Si. “You couldn’t find it because I already had it.”

She looked up at him.

“Since when?”

“Three years after the boat,” said Chen Si. He looked at the book. “I didn’t look for it. Not once. For ten years. I told myself I’d paid for something better with it, and that was true, and I didn’t want it back.” He was quiet. “Then you told Zhendong, outside the ICU, at four in the morning, that you were going to find it. And he told me. And I thought, she will. She’ll find it. She always finds everything.” He almost smiled. “And I couldn’t bear the idea of you paying for it.”

She stared at him.

“So I found it first,” said Chen Si. “A collector in Taipei. He’d bought it from a dealer in Guangzhou, who’d bought it from the doctor’s widow in 2014. He didn’t want to sell. I didn’t make him.” He touched the cloth. “I sat with him. Every month, for two years. Played chess with him. Told him about my father. About Block C. About the drains. About a boy who couldn’t read, and a book with pictures, and three days of stitches.” He looked at her. “In the end, he gave it to me. He wouldn’t take any money. He said he’d been looking after it for someone and hadn’t known who.”

She looked down at the book.

“I’ve had it for six years,” said Chen Si. “In the safe. Under the Geneva pieces. Under your diamonds. You’ve opened that safe a hundred times. You never once looked underneath.”

“I would never look under my own diamonds,” said Aurelia, through her tears, outraged.

“I know,” said Chen Si. “That’s why I put it there.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Why now?” she said. “Why not six years ago? Why not on the boat, or—”

“Because it isn’t for me,” said Chen Si.

She went very still.

“My father gave it to me when I was twelve,” he said. “He said, Si, this is the oldest thing our family owns. It isn’t worth anything to anyone but us. Keep it for whoever comes after you.” He looked at her. “There isn’t going to be anyone after me. We decided that. Both of us. And I don’t regret it, not for one second. I wouldn’t give one day of this life for anything.” He touched the cover of the book, very gently. “So there’s only you. You’re who comes after me. You’re who it’s for.”

She couldn’t speak.

“Clause thirteen,” said Chen Si. “You’re not allowed to refuse it. Or set a price. Or pay.” He picked up the heavy black pen. “You’re only allowed to keep it.”

She looked at him.

“For as long as I like,” she said.

He signed page twelve.

Then he turned back to page one and signed every page, one after another, the way he had ten years ago, in the same black ink, in the same precise hand.

When he had signed the last one, he capped the pen, and put it in his pocket, and slid the contract back across the counter.

She signed his counter-offer.

In red. In her own hand. Round and confident. With the flourish on the A.

✦ ✦ ✦

She reached past him and turned the sign on the door, which already said CLOSED, round to the blank side, so that it said nothing at all.

“Clause nine,” she said. “Starts now.”

He looked at her across the counter.

“Here?”

“The workshop,” said Aurelia. “Enzo’s gone to Milan. Lily’s at home. Nobody is coming back until tomorrow.” She came out from behind the counter, onto the marble, and walked past him, very close, without touching, and stopped at the door at the back of the shop. “Bring your tie.”

“I’m not wearing a tie.”

She looked at him over her shoulder.

“I know,” she said. “I put one in your pocket at breakfast. Left inside. Black silk.”

He put his hand in his left inside pocket and took out a black silk tie.

He looked at it, and then at her, and laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The workshop was the same.

Ten years. The same long benches, the same lamps on their jointed arms, the same smell of hot metal and polish and Enzo’s coffee. The same stool where women sat to try on rings. The same tiny scratched brass plaque on the wall by the door, where someone, a long time ago, had written in permanent marker under a hook: HIS COAT.

She pulled the blind down over the glass door to the shop.

She turned round.

He was standing in the middle of the workshop with the black tie in his hand, waiting.

She held out her hand.

He gave it to her.

“Kneel,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

He knelt.

Slowly. On the old wooden floor of the workshop, between the benches, in his grey suit, the way he had knelt ten years ago on the forty-fourth floor on the first night, when she had said the word for the first time and not known if he would.

He did not look away from her face.

She walked round him once. Slowly. In her heels, on the boards. She stopped behind him.

She drew the black silk tie across his eyes.

She felt him go still under her hands. She tied it at the back of his head, not tight, a single knot, the way she had tied it the first time, in this room, ten years ago, the night of the proposal, when he had said otherwise and she had said yes. And she bent, and put her mouth by his ear, and said:

“Ten years ago, in this room, I asked you to do as you were told. I asked you to trust me.” She let her breath move against his ear. “And you did. And you always have. Every single time.” She traced the edge of the silk over his cheekbone with one finger. “So tonight I’m not going to ask. Tonight I’m going to count.”

“Count what,” said Chen Si. His voice had already gone to gravel.

“Ten years,” said Aurelia. “One for every year. And on every one, I’m going to tell you something you did, that I never told you I noticed.” She straightened up. “And you can’t move. And you can’t speak. And you can’t touch me. Until I get to ten.”

He breathed out. Slowly.

“And then?” he said.

“And then I’ll say otherwise,” said Aurelia, “and you can do whatever you like to me, on Enzo’s bench, for as long as you like, and I’ll never be able to look him in the eye again.”

He laughed. On his knees. Blindfolded. Helplessly.

“One,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

“One,” she said, kneeling in front of him, on the boards, close, not touching. “The first year. In the summer. When I was sitting in the stands at the racetrack. Someone sent me an umbrella. Black. To my seat. With no card.” She leaned in. Her mouth very close to his. “It didn’t rain. It was for the sun. I was burning, and too proud to move, and you were on the thirty-ninth floor in a meeting with the Rotterdam people, and you saw it on the television, the pit-lane camera, and you sent an umbrella across the city in the middle of a meeting.” She brushed her lips, very lightly, across his jaw. Not his mouth. “I never told you I knew it was you.”

He didn’t move.

His throat moved.

“Two,” said Aurelia. She unbuttoned the top button of his shirt. Only the top one. “The first winter. On the boat. Before the glass. You put your hand on the small of my back when we went up the gangway, the way you always do. But on the boat you kept it there. All night. Every time I moved, your hand moved with me. Like you knew.” She kissed the hollow of his throat, where the button had been. “You didn’t know. You couldn’t have known. But you kept your hand there, all night. And afterwards, in the hospital, it was the thing I remembered.” Her voice wavered and steadied. “Your hand on my back. All the way to the end.”

His breath was coming unevenly now.

“Three,” said Aurelia. The second button. “You learned Italian.”

He went completely still.

“You think I don’t know,” she said. “You think I can’t tell. The third year. You started having lessons. On Wednesdays, at seven in the morning, before the thirty-ninth floor, with a woman from the consulate. Qian told me. Under duress.” She kissed his collarbone. “And you have never once spoken a word of Italian to me. In seven years of lessons. Not one. And I know why.”

His jaw was tight.

“Because I speak Italian when I’m angry,” said Aurelia. “And you wanted to know what I was saying. So you could fix it.” She put her forehead against his, over the black silk. “You learned a whole language so you could understand me shouting.”

He made a sound.

“That,” she said, “was very nearly a word.”

He shook his head, very slightly, blindfolded.

She smiled against his skin.

“Four.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She went slowly. She did not hurry once.

Four: the jumper. His old grey jumper, which she had taken in the first winter and never given back, and which he had replaced, quietly, every time it wore through at the elbows, with an identical one, from the same shop in Edinburgh, so that she would never notice it was gone. She had noticed. Three times. She kissed the inside of his wrist, below the scar, where his pulse was going like something trapped.

Five: the dream. That in the fifth year he had stopped waking up from it. That he hadn’t told her. That she had lain awake in the dark for a whole month waiting for it, and it hadn’t come, and she had cried, once, in the bathroom, with the taps running, from relief, and he had knocked on the door and said nothing, and waited outside it, sitting on the floor, until she came out. The fourth button.

Six: Geneva. That he had stood up first.

Seven: her mother. That every year, on her mother’s birthday, a box of white peonies arrived at the flat in Mid-Levels with no card, and her mother thought they were from Aurelia, and had written to thank her, and Aurelia had never corrected her. Because she had known, the moment she saw them, who had sent them, and why. So that she has something from you, even in the years you can’t. She kissed him on the corner of the mouth. Not quite the mouth. He shook.

Eight: the shoes. That he had never once in ten years walked into a room without checking where she was first, before anyone else, before the exits, before the guns. Not because he thought she was in danger. Because he wanted to know where to look.

By eight, his shirt was open, and her hands were on his chest, on the three pieces of gold, and his whole body was trembling under them, kneeling on the boards with his hands at his sides in fists and the black silk over his eyes and his head bowed, and he had not made a sound, not one, and she could hear his heart without needing to count it.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Nine,” said Aurelia.

She took his face in her hands. She put her thumbs along the edge of the black silk, at his cheekbones.

“You’ve never once,” she said, “in ten years, asked me to win.”

Her voice broke.

“Not once. Not at Paris. Not at Geneva. Not at the bankers. Not when my mother wrote. Not when I came twelfth, or second, or first. You never asked me to be first. You never asked me to be anything. You just stood at the end of a balcony with your coat and waited to see who I was.” She was crying, and didn’t stop, and didn’t care. “You don’t know what that is. You don’t know. To be twenty-two and have somebody look at you and want nothing. You don’t know what you did.”

He was crying too. Under the silk. She could feel it, wet, against her thumbs.

“Ten,” said Aurelia.

She leaned in.

“Ten,” she said, against his mouth, “is the balcony. You said, Don’t let them talk you into taking out the break. And I didn’t. I never did.” She pressed her lips to his, very lightly. Barely. “Ten years. I kept the break. I put it in a window. I made a collection out of it. I got married with it down my back. I wore it in an ICU. It’s on your chest right now.” She touched the broken necklace. “I never took it out. Because you told me not to. Because it was the first time anyone ever told me I could keep the broken part.”

He breathed in, raggedly, against her mouth.

“That’s ten,” said Aurelia.

She untied the silk.

She let it fall.

He opened his eyes. Wet. Black. On her face, an inch away.

“Otherwise,” she whispered.

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

He didn’t need to. He had been silent for ten years and ten counts on a workshop floor and he did not, now, need words. He put his hands up, slowly, both of them, shaking, and took her face, the way she had taken his. And he looked at her. Just looked. As though she were a balcony, and a ledger, and a necklace in a window, and every second place she had ever come, and he had been waiting ten years to see all of her at once.

Then he kissed her.

Not hard. Not the way he did when she said otherwise and he took the terms. Slowly. Deeply. With his whole mouth and his whole attention, until she was holding on to his open shirt in both fists and couldn’t breathe and didn’t want to.

He drew back an inch.

“My turn,” he said. Very low. Very rough. “My terms.”

“Yes.”

“Bench.”

She laughed. Wet. Shaky. “Chen Si. Enzo’s bench—”

“You said,” said Chen Si, getting up off the floor, lifting her with him as he came, “for as long as I like.” He set her down on the edge of the long bench, among the files and the pliers and the little drawers of stones, and stood between her knees, and looked at her.

He took the black silk tie off the floor. He held it up between them. He looked at her wrists, crossed in her lap, with the gold on them. He looked at her face.

“Yes?” he said.

She held out her wrists.

“Yes,” said Aurelia. “Always yes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was very thorough.

He was very, very good at it. After ten years. She had put it in writing.

He bound her wrists with the black silk, loosely, and lifted them over her head, and held them there against the old wooden pegboard where Enzo hung his saws, with one hand, while the other unfastened her gold, piece by piece, the way she had once taken off his watch, and laid each piece on the bench beside her, in a row, very carefully, without looking away from her face. Every bracelet. Every ring but one. The earrings, one at a time, with his mouth following each one down her neck. And he counted them. Out loud. In a low voice, against her skin, while she squirmed against the pegboard and said his name in two languages.

“Eleven,” he said, when the last one was on the bench. “Always eleven.”

And then he said something else, against her throat, in Italian, perfectly, with a Milanese accent he could only have got from a woman at the consulate at seven in the morning on Wednesdays for seven years.

She went completely still.

“You,” she said. “You said—you’ve never—”

“I was saving it,” said Chen Si, in Italian.

She didn’t say Milan.

She said a great many other things, in Italian, very loudly, that would have made Enzo cross himself. And he understood every single one of them, and did every single one of them, slowly, exactly, until she was saying nothing at all in any language, on the long bench, under the lamp, with her wrists in black silk above her head and his name in her mouth and her heels hooked round the back of his knees.

Afterwards, he untied her wrists, and kissed the inside of each one, and lay down with her on the floor of the workshop on his grey suit jacket, among the shavings, and held her, because she wanted to be held, and nobody had said the word.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What did you say,” she said, a long time later, into his chest. “At the start. In Italian. Against my neck.”

He was quiet.

“Ti ho aspettata tutta la vita,” said Chen Si. “Anche prima di sapere che stavo aspettando.”

She didn’t say anything.

I waited my whole life for you. Even before I knew I was waiting.

It was the amendment. The first one. In the margin of page one, ten years ago, in black ink. He would like it noted that he did not know, until this morning, that he had been waiting to be.

“You learned Italian,” she said finally, “for seven years, at seven in the morning, so that you could say your own amendment back to me. In my grandmother’s accent.”

“I asked the woman at the consulate for Milan,” said Chen Si. “Old Milan. She said there were only about four people left who talked like that.” He paused. “You’re one of them. When you’re very angry.”

She lifted her head and looked at him.

“Chen Si,” she said, “I am going to rewrite clause nine.”

He looked alarmed.

“Again?”

“Tomorrow,” said Aurelia. “To say that you are never, ever allowed to stop doing that.” She put her head back down on his chest, on the three pieces of gold. “Underlined.”

He laughed. Under her. On the floor of the workshop. And reached up without looking, and pulled his grey suit jacket down off the bench, and put it over both of them, because she was cold, and he always noticed.

On the wall by the door, under the hook, the brass plaque said HIS COAT.

The hook was empty. The coat was at home, in her wardrobe, where it had been for ten years.

She was keeping it.

For as long as she liked.

chapters.title: The Woman Who Sets the Price
chapters.desc: Epilogue. October. The house on the Peak, bought at auction by a woman who did not tell anyone she was bidding. A party for her father’s seventieth. The same balcony. A different coat. And the same man, standing at the end of it in the dark.
chapters.epigraph: “Who are you?” “Someone who doesn’t like lobster.” — the balcony, October 2018. “Who are you?” “The woman who sets the price.” — the balcony, October 2031
chapters.content:
She bought the house in the autumn of 2023, at auction, by telephone, under the name of a company in Singapore that Mr. Tan had set up for her over a bowl of noodles and that nobody in the city had ever heard of.

She did not tell anyone she was bidding.

Not her father, who sat in the back row of the auction room in a borrowed suit, because he could not bear not to be there, and watched his house go for less than he had paid for it, to a voice on a telephone, and went home to three rooms in Mid-Levels and sat in the dark. Not her mother, who did not go. Not Serafina. Not Dr. Ho.

Not Chen Si.

He found out anyway, of course. The next morning. From the bank statement, which he read every Thursday, all of it, every line, the way he read everything. He came into the kitchen on the forty-fourth floor where she was eating toast in his grey jumper and put the statement down beside her plate, folded open, with one line on it underlined in pencil.

She looked at it. She looked at him.

“Clause one,” she said. “Every gram of gold.”

“It’s a house,” said Chen Si mildly.

“It was mine first,” said Aurelia. “I grew up in it. I came second in every room of it.” She picked up her toast. “Clause one says I keep what’s mine.”

He looked at her over the bank statement.

“Clause three,” he said. “Are you going to tell them?”

“No,” said Aurelia. “Not yet.”

“When?”

She thought about it. About the balcony. About a gold dress and a microphone and a toast.

“His seventieth,” she said. “I’m going to give him a party.”

✦ ✦ ✦

It took her eight years.

She did not live in it. She did not sell it. She had it cleaned, and the roof mended, and the great staircase restored, and the yellow walls of the morning room painted again in exactly the same yellow. She bought back the Venetian mirrors from the dealer in Kowloon who had bought them at the auction, and the dining chairs, and the long sideboard. She could not buy back the Morandis, which had gone to a museum in Bologna; she sent the museum a letter, and a very large donation, and asked only that the label beside them should say formerly in the collection of Vittoria Conti Song, and the museum, slightly bewildered, agreed.

She bought the bureau back last.

It took her two years to find it. It had gone to a collector in Lucerne, who would not sell, and she flew to Lucerne four times, and the fourth time she brought with her the brass key, which her mother had given her, and which she had never returned, and showed it to the collector, and told him what had been in the third drawer.

He sold it to her that afternoon. For the price he had paid. And would not take a franc more.

She put it back in the corner of the morning room, by the east window.

She did not put anything in the third drawer.

That was for someone else.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her father turned seventy on the eleventh of October, 2031.

She sent the invitations herself. Cream card. Gold lettering. And on the front, in the place where the name of the house should go, nothing at all. Just the address. The Peak. And the date. And the time.

Seven o’clock. Black tie. Song Weiren is seventy.

Two hundred cards. Two hundred people. Her father’s old friends, who had stopped calling when the towers fell, and who had started calling again, cautiously, when the bridge was finished, and then more often, when it won a prize. The deputy minister, who was now the minister, Mrs. Ling, who had signed the extension on a Tuesday and had been promoted twice since and still had tea with Aurelia on the first Thursday of every month. Mrs. Leung, who owned a tower in Shenzhen now and said so to everyone. Mr. Tan, flown in from Singapore. Old Fan, who would not come, and sent a clay pot of braised pork belly with a cook’s apprentice, which was better.

Elowen and Zhao. In green and black.

Serafina, with Qin Haozhen, who had been holding her hand in public for six years now and still looked surprised every time she let him.

Enzo, seventy-six, who had retired twice and come back twice and was planning to retire a third time in the spring and nobody believed him.

And her parents.

She sent their invitation by courier, to the flat in Mid-Levels, in a plain white envelope, the way she had sent the tickets to Row R. On the back of the card, in pencil, very small, she wrote:

Papà. Mamma. Wear something you can stand on a balcony in.

✦ ✦ ✦

They didn’t know until the car turned up the hill.

She found that out afterwards, from her father, who told her with tears running down his face at the top of the great staircase, holding both her hands. He had thought it was a hotel. The Peak could mean twenty places. He had thought she had booked a restaurant, or a private room, or a terrace somewhere.

And then the car had turned off the Peak Road at the old stone gateposts, and gone up the drive, between the jacaranda trees that his own father had planted, and come round the last bend.

And the house had been lit.

Every window. Every one. Gold, from top to bottom, the way it had been lit on the night of his fifty-seventh, the way it had been lit every October for twenty-five years. The great front door standing open. The Venetian mirrors in the hall, in their places. The staircase, restored, with no sticker on the newel post.

“I thought I was dreaming,” said her father, at the top of the stairs. “I thought I had died.” He held her hands so hard it hurt. “Tesoro. Tesoro, what have you done.”

“I bought it,” said Aurelia. “In 2023. By telephone. While you were sitting in the back row.”

He stared at her.

“Eight years,” he said.

She lifted her chin. “I set the price. It was less than you paid. I thought you’d want to know.”

He laughed. With tears on his face. At the top of his own staircase, in black tie, seventy years old. He laughed until he had to hold on to the banister.

✦ ✦ ✦

Her mother did not cry.

Her mother walked into the hall in a dark blue dress, the colour of her own initials, with the plain wide bracelet on her left wrist, the one engraved on the inside, I’m more interested in what you do in the dark, which she had not taken off, Aurelia knew, in eight years, not once. And she stood in the middle of the hall under the chandelier and looked at the Venetian mirrors. And then she walked, very slowly, without a word to anyone, down the corridor to the east end of the house, to the morning room.

Aurelia followed her.

Her mother stood in the doorway of the yellow room and looked at the bureau in the corner, by the window.

She went to it. She put her hand on the sloping walnut front. She looked at the brass handles shaped like shells.

“Lucerne,” said Aurelia, from the door. “A collector. He wouldn’t sell. I went four times.”

Her mother didn’t turn round.

“The third drawer,” she said.

“It’s empty,” said Aurelia. “I didn’t put anything in it.” She held out her hand. In her palm, the old brass key, with its faded ribbon, and its tag in her mother’s handwriting. Morning room. Third drawer. Bureau. “It’s yours.”

Her mother turned round.

She looked at the key.

Then she took it. And put it in the pocket of her dark blue dress. And came across the yellow room to the doorway where her daughter was standing, and stood in front of her, and they were the same height, they had always been the same height, and Vittoria Conti Song put her arms round her elder daughter for the first time since Vienna.

She did not say anything.

She did not need to. She had said the two words, eight years ago, across a glass counter. She had written the rest in a text message at 11:14 in Geneva. I did not know how to say it, so I kept the box.

She held on.

When she let go, her face was perfectly composed, and her eyes were perfectly dry, and her hands, when she took them away from Aurelia’s shoulders, were shaking.

“Your hair,” said Vittoria, “is too long at the back.”

“I know, Mamma,” said Aurelia.

“It suits you.”

Aurelia looked at her.

It was, she thought, possibly the first compliment her mother had ever paid her without a number in it.

✦ ✦ ✦

At nine o’clock, her father gave a speech.

He stood at the top of the great staircase with a glass in his hand and two hundred people below him in the hall, where once, thirteen years before, he had stood beside his wife while she held the microphone.

He did not hold a microphone. He did not need one. The hall was very quiet.

“Thirteen years ago,” said Song Weiren, “in this hall, on my fifty-seventh birthday, my wife raised a glass to our daughter. To our elder daughter. Who had come second. And everyone in this room drank.” He looked down at the glass in his hand. “I drank.”

Silence. Nobody moved.

“I would like,” said her father, “to raise a different glass.”

He looked down the staircase. He found her. Standing in the middle of the hall, in the middle of two hundred people, in a dress of plain black silk with no gold on at all except the ring on her left hand and the necklace at her throat. The broken one. Coat-coloured. Out of the window, for one night. With a line of white along the seam.

“To my daughter,” said Song Weiren. “Who came first. And second. And twelfth. And who bought back her father’s house, at auction, by telephone, without telling anyone, for less than he paid. And who has never, in thirty-five years, been anything less than exactly herself.” His voice cracked. “I should have raised this glass when she was six. I’m raising it now. Late. In second place.” He lifted it. “To Aurelia. The woman who sets the price.”

Two hundred people raised their glasses.

Aurelia did not drink.

She stood in the middle of the hall and looked up at her father at the top of the stairs, and could not move.

Somebody, very quietly, put a hand on the small of her back.

She knew whose.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went out onto the balcony at ten.

Alone. The way she had gone out thirteen years ago, in a gold dress, shaking, doing sums in her head. The long stone balcony at the back of the house, overlooking the whole harbour, with the city spread out below it in a million lights and the water black and the boats on it like scattered stones.

On the far shore, lit up, finished, Harbour Bridge Two stood out over the water, and reached the other side.

It was October, and cold, the way it had been cold thirteen years ago. She was not wearing a coat.

She stood at the balustrade and looked at the bridge and did not do any sums at all.

After a while, she heard footsteps behind her. On the stone. Slow. Unhurried. A man’s.

He came to the end of the balcony and stood there, in the dark, where the light from the house did not reach.

She did not turn round.

“Cold,” he said mildly. “You’re shaking.”

“I am not shaking,” said Aurelia Chen, who was not shaking, and had not shaken on a balcony in thirteen years, “I am thirty-five years old and I own this balcony.”

“I know,” he said. “I read the bank statement.”

She laughed. Out loud. Into the dark, over the harbour.

✦ ✦ ✦

She heard him take something off.

Not his jacket; she knew the sound of his jacket. Something heavier.

He came up behind her, and put it round her shoulders.

She looked down.

Soft wool. Too big for her. To her knees. Smelling, very faintly, of cedar, and coffee he hadn’t drunk, and him.

It was not his coat.

It was new. She could tell from the weight, and the smell of the wool, and the stiffness of the collar. Charcoal, not camel. A different cut. A different coat. And when she put her hand into the pocket, the way she had thirteen years ago, she found a card.

She took it out.

Cream. His paper. In black ink. In his precise hand.

Clause thirteen. One thing you did not know you wanted. Not allowed to refuse it, argue with it, set a price on it, or pay. Only allowed to keep it.

The old one is yours. It always was. This one is mine.

I would like it back eventually. In about fifty years.

She read it in the light from the house.

She read it again.

Then she turned round.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was standing at the end of the balcony in the dark, the way he had stood thirteen years ago. In black tie, this time, not a grey suit. Grey at his temples. Lines at the corners of his eyes. His hands in his pockets.

He was looking at her the way he had looked at her then. As if she were a ledger, and a necklace in a window, and a woman doing sums in her head, and he wanted to read every line.

“Who are you?” said Aurelia.

It was what she had said. Thirteen years ago. On this balcony. In a gold dress, shaking, with her eyes wet.

He didn’t answer for eleven seconds.

She counted.

Then he smiled. The one that went all the way up.

“Someone who doesn’t like lobster,” said Chen Si. And then, because it was thirteen years later and he was allowed: “And the man who came to rent your shop. And stayed.”

She pulled his coat round her. His new coat. Charcoal. Too big. Hers now, for about fifty years.

“And who are you?” he said.

He had never asked. Not on this balcony. Not thirteen years ago. He had stood at the end of it in the dark and given her his coat and told her not to let them talk her into taking out the break, and he had never once, in thirteen years, asked her who she was. He had waited. To see.

She lifted her chin.

“The woman who sets the price,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came down the balcony to her.

He took her face in his hands, in the light from the house, with the harbour behind her and the bridge across the water and two hundred people inside drinking to her name.

“What’s the price?” he said. “For the shop. I never did pay rent.”

She looked up at him.

“You,” said Aurelia. “For about fifty years. Then we’ll renegotiate.”

“That’s very steep.”

“I know,” she said. “I always set it high. Nobody ever pays it.”

“I’ll pay it,” said Chen Si.

And he kissed her. On her own balcony. In his new coat. In the cold. Not mildly. He pulled her in by the lapels of the coat and kissed her the way he had on the forty-fourth floor at twenty-four, as if thirteen years had only made him hungrier, for a very long time, while inside, through the long windows, two hundred people pretended not to watch, and Elowen said something to Zhao that made him almost smile, and her father put his hand over his eyes, and her mother, standing very straight by the Venetian mirrors with a brass key in her pocket, watched through the glass, and did not look away.

✦ ✦ ✦

Much later, when everyone had gone, she sat on the balustrade of the balcony in the charcoal coat with her shoes off and her bare feet on the cold stone, and he stood between her knees with his arms round her, and they looked at the bridge.

“Fifty years,” he said. “And then?”

“And then I’ll rewrite every clause,” said Aurelia, “and you’ll read the drafts in the bin.” She put her head on his shoulder. “And then another fifty.”

He was quiet for a while.

“I don’t think people live that long,” he said.

“We will,” said Aurelia. “I’ll put it in writing.”

He laughed into her hair.

Below them, across the black water, the bridge reached the other side. Above them, the house was lit, every window, gold from top to bottom. And on the balcony, at the end of it, where thirteen years ago a man had stood alone in the dark and waited, there was nobody standing alone at all.

The End.

chapters.title: Floral vs. Jewelry, Round Forty-One
chapters.desc: A charity lunch. One centrepiece budget. Two women who were first and second at school, and who have not stopped keeping score. Their husbands sit at the end of the table and say nothing, which is the most dangerous thing either of them can do.
chapters.epigraph: “Forty-one.” “Forty. You can’t count the time I slapped you.” “I absolutely can.”
chapters.content:
The lunch was for the children’s hospital, and it was Mrs. Leung’s idea, and Mrs. Leung, Aurelia would later decide, should have been tried at The Hague.

“The centrepieces,” said Mrs. Leung, at the planning meeting, in the yellow drawing room of her house in Repulse Bay, beaming. “I thought, why choose? We have the two most talented women in the city on the committee. One of them does flowers. One of them does jewellery. Why not both?” She clasped her hands. “Twenty tables. Ten each. Let the guests decide.”

There was a silence in the yellow drawing room.

On one side of the coffee table, in cream silk and gold, Aurelia Chen.

On the other, in green, with her hair up and a pair of florist’s shears on a cord round her neck as if she might need them at any moment, Elowen Zhao.

They looked at each other.

“Decide what?” said Elowen pleasantly.

“Oh, nothing competitive,” said Mrs. Leung. “Just a little card on each table. Guests write down their favourite. For fun.”

“For fun,” said Aurelia, and Elowen said it at the same moment, in exactly the same voice.

✦ ✦ ✦

“She’s going to use peonies,” said Aurelia, that night, pacing the length of the flat on the forty-fourth floor in silk pyjamas with a pencil behind her ear. “White ones. Masses of them. It’s May, they’re at their best, she has a man in Yunnan who sends them overnight, she’s going to bury every table in white peonies and everyone is going to say oh, how fresh, how natural—”

“Come to bed,” said Chen Si, from the bed.

“—and I am going to be standing there with a jewellery box.” She turned at the window and paced back. “Gold doesn’t smell. Gold doesn’t grow. Nobody’s ever stood in front of a necklace and closed their eyes and breathed in.”

He put down his book.

“Aurelia,” he said. “Do you want help?”

She stopped pacing. She looked at him, propped up on the pillows, in his reading glasses, which he needed now and hated and which she found so attractive that she had once, in clause nine circumstances, made him keep them on for an entire evening.

“No,” she said. “You’d be cheating.” She narrowed her eyes. “Did Zhendong offer to help her?”

He picked his book back up.

“I couldn’t possibly say,” said Chen Si.

She threw a cushion at him.

He caught it, without looking up from the page, and tucked it behind his head. “Thank you,” he said. “I needed another one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhendong had not offered to help.

Aurelia found this out on the Tuesday, from Elowen herself, who rang at eleven at night, which she had never done before, and said without preamble:

“Does yours talk?”

Aurelia sat up in bed.

“I’m sorry?”

“When you’re working on something. At night. Does he talk to you about it?” Elowen sounded exhausted and furious. “I’ve been at the bench for six hours and he’s been sitting on a stool in the corner of the shop for six hours, sharpening my shears, every single pair, one after another, and he hasn’t said a word, and every time I put a stem in the wrong place he stops sharpening.”

Aurelia looked at Chen Si, who was asleep.

“The noise just stops. And I look round and he’s looking at the arrangement. And then I move the stem. And he starts sharpening again.” Elowen’s voice rose. “He’s right every time. Every time. He doesn’t know anything about flowers. He can’t tell a ranunculus from a cabbage. And he’s right.”

Aurelia lay back on the pillow.

“Mine does the same thing with coffee,” she said. “He holds a cup of coffee and doesn’t drink it, and when I put a stone in the wrong place, he puts the cup down.”

There was a silence on the line.

“They’re the same person,” said Elowen, appalled.

“They grew up in a drain together,” said Aurelia. “What did you expect?”

Another silence.

“Ninety-one per cent of me,” said Elowen, “wants to win this lunch so badly I can taste it.”

“And the other nine?”

“The other nine wants to know what you’re using,” said Elowen, and hung up before Aurelia could answer.

✦ ✦ ✦

She was using flowers.

That was the joke, and it took her a week to think of it, at the bench, at two in the morning, with his coffee going cold at her elbow. Gold flowers. Ten centrepieces of gold flowers, cut and chased by hand, every petal, every stamen, so fine they trembled when you breathed on them. Not peonies. She would not stoop to peonies. She did the flowers that grew in the cracks of the Walled City where Elowen had grown up, the ones nobody bought: dandelions, and wild violets, and the little white stars of chickweed, and a single thistle on every table, because Elowen had once called her a thistle in the rain when they were fifteen and Aurelia had never forgotten it.

Enzo, watching her solder a dandelion clock out of two hundred gold wires, said, “Cara, this is not a centrepiece. This is a declaration of war.”

“It’s a lunch,” said Aurelia. “For the children’s hospital.”

“It is a declaration of war for the children’s hospital,” said Enzo, and went back to his bench, shaking his head, and then, ten minutes later, came back with a finer gauge of wire and put it down beside her without a word.

✦ ✦ ✦

The lunch was on the third Saturday in May, at the Mandarin, in the ballroom, under the chandeliers.

Aurelia arrived at eleven to set up. Elowen was already there.

Of course she was there. She had been there since six. Ten tables on the left side of the ballroom were buried in flowers. Not white peonies.

Gold ones.

Aurelia stopped in the doorway.

Yellow peonies. Gold roses. Marigolds, and sunflowers, and long trailing sprays of something tiny and yellow she didn’t know the name of, and in the centre of every table, standing up out of the gold like a crown, a single stem of yellow orchid, the exact yellow, Aurelia realised, of twenty-two-carat gold.

Elowen was standing on a chair at table four, adjusting an orchid, in green, with her shears round her neck. She looked down and saw Aurelia in the doorway with ten crates of gold flowers on a trolley behind her, and her face did something complicated.

“You didn’t,” they said, at the same time.

They looked at each other across the ballroom. Elowen with ten tables of flowers that looked like gold. Aurelia with ten crates of gold that looked like flowers.

“How did you know?” said Elowen.

“I didn’t. How did you know?”

“I didn’t.” Elowen got down off the chair, slowly. She came across the ballroom. She looked in the first crate, at a gold dandelion clock trembling in its velvet, every seed a separate wire. She looked at it without saying anything.

“That’s chickweed,” she said. Her voice had gone strange. “Next to it. You did chickweed.”

“That grows by the steps. Outside our house in the Walled City. Nobody’s ever—” Elowen stopped. She looked at the thistle. “Is that a thistle?”

“You called me a thistle,” said Aurelia. “In the rain. When we were fifteen. After I slapped you.”

Elowen looked at the gold thistle.

Then she looked at Aurelia, and for one second, before she got it back under control, her face did something Aurelia had seen it do exactly once before, in the third row in Geneva, with two fingers crossed in her lap.

“That’s forty-one,” said Elowen. “The score. Since school.” Elowen lifted her chin. “I was winning, thirty-nine to forty. You just tied it.”

“I tied it?” said Aurelia, outraged. “I don’t tie. And it’s forty-one to thirty-nine. To me. You can’t count the eight-day library fight as three separate wins.”

“I absolutely can. They were three separate days.”

“Then I won the other five!”

They were standing very close together now, in the middle of the ballroom, between the flowers and the gold, both with their chins up, and the waiters setting the tables had stopped setting them.

✦ ✦ ✦

Their husbands came at twelve.

Together. They always came together, to these things, as if one of them might need the other at any moment and neither of them would admit it. Chen Si in grey. Zhao in black. They walked into the ballroom side by side and stopped at exactly the same moment, two steps inside the door, and looked at it.

Ten tables of flowers that looked like gold. Ten tables of gold that looked like flowers.

Their wives, in the middle of the floor, arguing about a library.

Zhao looked at the left side of the room for four seconds.

Chen Si looked at the right side of the room for four seconds.

Then they looked at each other.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

They went and sat down at the very end of the top table, side by side, with their hands on their knees, and said nothing at all for the entire lunch, which was, Aurelia said afterwards, the most passive-aggressive thing she had ever seen two men do.

✦ ✦ ✦

Two hundred guests. Twenty tables. A little card on every one.

Mrs. Leung counted them herself, at the end, at the top table, with her reading glasses on and an expression of enormous enjoyment.

“Well!” she said. “Isn’t this exciting.”

Nobody at the top table said anything.

Aurelia sat on one side of Mrs. Leung with her hands folded. Elowen sat on the other side with her hands folded. They did not look at each other. At the end of the table, their husbands did not look at anything.

“Ninety-nine,” said Mrs. Leung, putting down the last card on the left-hand pile. “For the flowers.” She put down the last card on the right. “And ninety-nine. For the gold.” She took off her reading glasses and beamed. “And two spoiled ballots! Isn’t that funny.”

Aurelia turned her head very slowly.

“Spoiled how?” she said.

Mrs. Leung held them up.

Two cards. On each one, in the space where you were supposed to write flowers or gold, there was something written in a hand Aurelia knew.

The first one, in a precise, angular black hand, lifted at every turn, said: Mine.

The second one, in a square, heavy hand, pressed so hard the pen had nearly gone through the card, said: Mine.

✦ ✦ ✦

Neither of them would admit it.

“You voted,” said Aurelia, in the car.

“I didn’t vote,” said Chen Si. “I spoiled my ballot. There’s a difference.”

“You were supposed to write gold!”

He looked out of the window, very mildly, at the harbour going past.

“I was asked,” he said, “which centrepiece I preferred. I didn’t prefer either centrepiece. I preferred the woman standing behind one of them, who had stayed up for three weeks soldering chickweed for someone she claims to hate.” He paused. “So I wrote that down. Briefly.”

She stared at him.

“Zhendong wrote the same thing,” she said.

“I know,” said Chen Si. “I watched him.” Something moved at the corner of his mouth. “He looked at me first. To see if I was going to. And I did. So he did.” He was quiet. “I think it’s the first time in fifteen years I’ve seen him copy somebody else’s homework.”

She looked at him across the back seat.

Then she leaned over and kissed him. Hard. On the mouth. With her hand on his jaw. And when she drew back, she was furious and pink and her eyes were wet.

“That,” she said, “is a tie. You made it a tie. I hate ties.”

“I know,” said Chen Si. “But she cried too. When Mrs. Leung read them out. Did you see?” He looked at her. “Behind the orchid. She thought nobody could see.”

Aurelia hadn’t seen.

She looked out of the window.

“Forty-one all,” she said finally.

He reached across the seat and pulled her into his side, and kept her there the rest of the way home, his mouth against her temple, as if a ballroom full of people had been looking at her all afternoon and he was taking her back.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Monday morning, a box arrived at the boutique on Harbour Road.

Inside, in wet moss, there was a single stem of something wild. Small, white, star-shaped. The kind of thing that grew in the cracks of steps.

Chickweed.

And a card, in green ink, in a quick, slanting hand.

It doesn’t count. Forty-one, thirty-nine. To me. — E.

P.S. Mine also wrote “mine.” You may tell yours he started it.

Aurelia put the chickweed in a glass of water on the counter, beside the window, beside the broken necklace.

It lasted eleven days.

She did not throw it away.

chapters.title: Chen Si Has Never Been Late. Today He Was Late.
chapters.desc: Seven o’clock. A dinner reservation he made himself. Seven-fifteen. Seven-thirty. His phone goes to voicemail. Zhao’s phone goes to voicemail. For forty minutes, Aurelia Chen finds out exactly how much of her is still sitting in a corridor outside an ICU.
chapters.epigraph: “You’re late.” “I know.” “You’re never late.” “I know. I’m sorry. I had to go and get something, and it fought back.”
chapters.content:
He was never late.

Not once. In eleven years. Not for a meeting, not for a dinner, not for the dentist. He arrived four minutes early, always, everywhere, and stood outside, and waited, and came in at exactly the time he had said, so that people who had worked with him for a decade had started to set their watches by the moment his hand touched the door.

The reservation was for seven. At Da Gianni. The table by the window on the sixty-first floor, where five years ago her father had laid out a bridge and a minister and she had ordered the risotto. He had made it himself, on the Monday, and told her on the Tuesday, very mildly, over breakfast: “Thursday. Seven. Wear the green.”

She did not own anything green. She owned nothing green on principle.

On Wednesday, a dress arrived at the flat. Green. Deep, dark, bottle-green silk, cut by someone in Milan who knew her measurements without being told, with a card in his hand that said, Lin doesn’t own the colour.

She put it on on Thursday at six and stood in front of the mirror, and decided, grudgingly, that he was right.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 6:56, she was at the table.

At 7:00, she looked at the door.

At 7:04, Carmine, the maître d’, who had been there since it opened and knew everyone by name and by order, came to the table with a glass of the white from Ningxia and put it down and said, “Mr. Chen is a little delayed, perhaps,” in the voice of a man who had never once had to say that sentence.

At 7:15, she called him.

Voicemail.

He did not have voicemail. That was the thing. He had never in eleven years let his phone go to voicemail. If he could not answer, it rang out. If he would not answer, Qian answered. It did not go to the woman’s voice saying the person you are calling is not available.

She put the phone down on the white tablecloth and looked at it.

At 7:17, she called Qian.

Qian answered on the first ring. “Mrs. Chen.”

“Where is he?”

A pause. A fractional pause. A pause she would think about afterwards, a great deal.

“He left the thirty-ninth floor at five,” said Qian. “With Mr. Zhao. He said he had an errand. He didn’t say what.”

“Qian.”

“He didn’t say, Mrs. Chen,” said Qian, and his voice was steady, and she had known Qian for six years, and she knew what it sounded like when he was telling the truth and very frightened at the same time. “He took the old car. Not the black one. He told me not to send anyone after him.”

She put the phone down.

At 7:19, she called Zhao.

Voicemail.

✦ ✦ ✦

The thing about being in a corridor outside an ICU, she would think afterwards, is that you never actually leave.

You think you do. You go home. You sleep in your own bed. You go to therapy on Tuesdays for four years and you learn to breathe and you learn to let things go through you and you learn that the body keeps the score but that you can, slowly, renegotiate the terms. You win a prize in Geneva. You put every gram of your gold on a table behind your father’s bridge, and get it all back. You have breakfast in a basement with a man who looks his age.

And then one night he is twenty minutes late, and his phone goes to voicemail, and you are back in the corridor. In a gold dress. On a plastic chair. At three in the morning. Not crying, because you will not cry until you know.

She sat at the table by the window on the sixty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel in a green silk dress and did not cry.

She did the sums.

Five o’clock. The old car. With Zhendong. An errand. No security. Told Qian not to follow. Two phones off, or out of signal, or—

She stopped that one.

She started again.

Five o’clock. Two hours and nineteen minutes. If he had gone to the airport, he would have been back. If he had gone to the Docks, he would have answered. If he had gone to the east coast, past the tunnel, there was no signal for eleven kilometres on the coast road, she knew that, she had driven it herself in the week he couldn’t get out of bed, and the lorry, the snake, the—

She stopped that one too.

Carmine came back to the table at 7:24 with a basket of bread nobody had asked for, and put it down, and looked at her face, and went away again without a word, and did not come back.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 7:31, she stood up.

She did not decide to. She was simply standing, with her bag in her hand, the gold clutch, and the small weight of what was in it. She had stood up the same way in the corridor, she remembered, at 3:12 in the morning, when Dr. Ma came through the double doors, before Dr. Ma had said a single word.

She would go to the car park. She would take her car. She would drive to the Docks, and then to the east coast, and she would drive the coast road with her headlights on full, past the tunnel, through the eleven kilometres with no signal, and she would find the old car, and—

Her phone rang.

On the table. Face up. Buzzing against the white cloth.

Chen Si.

She picked it up so fast she nearly dropped it.

“Where are you,” she said. It did not come out like a question. It came out of her like something being torn.

There was a pause. Breathing. Unsteady. And behind it, very faintly, a sound she did not understand at first. A high, thin, furious sound. Like a kettle. Like a—

“I’m in the lift,” said Chen Si. He sounded out of breath. “I’m so sorry. I’m so sorry, Aurelia. I’m coming up. I’m nearly there. I’m—” The high thin sound again, louder. “Ow. Zhendong, can you—”

“Hm,” said Zhao’s voice, somewhere near the phone.

“Chen Si,” said Aurelia, very slowly, “what is that noise.”

The lift doors opened.

She heard them on the phone, and she heard them across the restaurant at the same time, the soft chime, and she turned round, with her phone still at her ear.

✦ ✦ ✦

He came across the restaurant toward her.

In his grey suit. Which was torn. At the knee, and at the elbow, and the left sleeve was wet, and there was mud on his shoes, and a long red scratch down the side of his neck from his ear to his collar, and another across the back of his hand, and his hair was completely wrecked, and there was something on his shoulder that might have been a leaf.

He was holding a box.

A cardboard box. Not very big. With holes punched in the lid. And it was the box that was making the noise. The high, thin, furious noise, like a kettle, getting louder as he came across the restaurant, so that every single diner on the sixty-first floor of the Harbour Hotel stopped eating and turned to look.

Behind him, two steps behind, the way he always walked, came Zhao. In black. Also wet. Also muddy. With three long scratches across the back of his right hand, and an expression of profound and stoic suffering, and a second box.

This one was not making any noise at all.

Chen Si stopped in front of her. Out of breath. Torn and wet and scratched and holding a screaming box.

“I’m late,” he said.

She stared at him.

“I know,” he said. “I’m never late. I’m sorry. I had to go and get something.” The box screamed. He winced. “And it fought back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything.

She couldn’t. Her whole body was doing something she had no control over, a great flood of something hot and terrible and enormous going through her all at once, from the top of her head to the soles of her feet, so that she had to put her hand on the back of the chair.

He saw it. He always saw.

His face changed. All at once. The apology went out of it and something else came in, something stricken, and he put the screaming box down on the table, on the white cloth, beside the bread, without looking, and stepped toward her.

“Aurelia,” he said. “Aurelia. Hey. I’m here. I’m all right.” He took her face in both hands. His hands were cold and wet and one of them was bleeding very slightly. “I’m here. Look at me. It’s just scratches. I’m all right. I’m sorry. I didn’t think. The coast road, there’s no signal, and then the battery went, and Zhendong’s was in the car, and I didn’t—” His thumbs moved on her cheekbones. “I didn’t think. That you’d—I’m so sorry. I should have—”
