“Thirty-one minutes,” said Aurelia.

Her voice came out very small.

He went still.

“You’re never late,” she said. “Never. Six years. And you were thirty-one minutes late, and your phone went to voicemail, and Zhendong’s went to voicemail, and Qian said you took the old car and no one, and I was back—” She stopped. She couldn’t say it. She didn’t need to. She watched him understand it. Watched it go through his face. The corridor. “I was going to drive the coast road,” she said. “I was standing up. I had my bag. I was going to drive the coast road with the lights on and find the car.”

He looked down at her.

Then he put his forehead against hers. In the middle of the restaurant. With the box screaming on the table beside them and sixty diners watching and Carmine standing frozen by the kitchen door with a bottle in his hand.

“I’m sorry,” he said. Very low. Only to her. “I’m sorry. I won’t ever do that again. Not once. Not for anything. I swear it. Clause three.”

“You can’t swear to that.”

“I just did.”

She closed her eyes.

“What,” she said, “is in the box.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He let go of her face.

He turned round and lifted the lid of the box, very carefully, with the air of a man defusing something, and stepped back.

A head came up out of it.

Small. Grey. Flat-faced. With enormous round copper eyes and ears laid back flat with rage and a mouth open in a scream that went straight up through the chandeliers of Da Gianni and into the night sky over the harbour.

A kitten.

Perhaps eight weeks old. Soaking wet. Furious. Absolutely, comprehensively, magnificently furious, with every hair on its body standing on end, so that it looked twice its size, which was very small.

Aurelia stared at it.

The kitten stared back at her. And stopped screaming. Abruptly. As if it had run out. And looked up at her with its enormous copper eyes, and sneezed.

“You were thirty-one minutes late,” said Aurelia. “For a cat.”

“For your cat,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her at the table, after Carmine had brought towels, and a saucer of warm milk that the kitchen had sent out with enormous ceremony, and the kitten had been dried and wrapped in a napkin and was sitting on Aurelia’s lap in the green silk dress, purring like a small engine, with its claws hooked into her knee.

“Three weeks ago,” he said, “you said something. In your sleep.”

She looked up. She had not known she did that.

“Twice a year,” said Chen Si. “In Italian. Mostly about your mother’s dinner parties.” He turned his glass on the tablecloth. “Three weeks ago, you said, Pina, where is Topolino.”

She went very still.

Topolino.

She had not thought about Topolino in thirteen years.

“Signora Pina told me,” said Chen Si. “I rang her. In Bergamo. She retired there, after the house went. She cried on the phone for ten minutes. She said Topolino was a little grey cat you had in Milan, from when you were five. Flat face. Copper eyes. He slept on your bed every night. And when your mother moved the family here, when you were fifteen, she said there was no room for a cat in the new house, and he was given to the neighbours. And you didn’t cry. In front of anyone.” He looked at her. “Pina said you didn’t cry. You just asked her every night for a month where he was. In your sleep.”

The kitten on her lap stopped purring and looked up at her.

“There’s a breeder,” said Chen Si, “on the east coast. Past the tunnel. Past the eleven kilometres. She had one left. The same breed. The same colour.” He looked at his scratched hand. “She was supposed to have him in a carrier. She didn’t. He was in the barn. He did not want to come. It took Zhendong and me forty minutes and a ladder.”

Aurelia looked at Zhao.

Zhao, at the end of the table, eating bread, held up the back of his right hand. Three long red scratches.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

“He went up the ladder,” said Chen Si. “I held it. The cat went up the barn wall onto a beam. Zhendong went along the beam. The cat went down the other side into the water trough. I went into the water trough.” He indicated his wet sleeve. “Then it climbed me. All the way up. To my neck.” He touched the scratch from his ear to his collar. “Then it bit Zhendong.”

“Twice,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

She didn’t say anything.

She sat at the table by the window in her green dress with a grey kitten on her lap, and looked at her husband, torn and scratched and muddy and wet, at the most expensive restaurant in Asia, and she thought about a little grey cat on her bed in Milan when she was five. And about asking where he was. In her sleep. For a month. Thirteen years ago.

And a man who had heard her say it once, in the dark, in Italian, and had rung a retired maid in Bergamo, and driven past the tunnel with his brother, and gone into a water trough.

“What’s the other box?” she said finally. Her voice was wet.

Zhao, at the end of the table, put his hand flat on top of the second box.

It was silent. It had been silent the whole time.

“Mine,” said Zhao.

Chen Si looked at him.

“He took the sister,” said Chen Si. “I didn’t ask him to. He stood in the barn and looked at her for four seconds and picked her up and she didn’t scratch him at all. She went to sleep.” He paused. “He hasn’t told Lin yet.”

Zhao lifted the lid of his box half an inch.

Inside, curled in a nest of his black scarf, perfectly dry, fast asleep, there was a second kitten. Smaller. White. With one grey ear.

Zhao looked at it.

“She’ll be angry,” he said. To the kitten.

“She will not be angry,” said Aurelia, “and you know it.”

Zhao put the lid back down, very gently.

“No,” he agreed.

✦ ✦ ✦

At home, at one in the morning, the kitten was asleep on the pillow.

Her side. In the middle. As if it had been there for thirteen years. As if it had only gone out for a moment.

She lay on her side in the dark, very close to it, not touching, and watched it breathe.

He was behind her. His arm round her waist. His chest against her back. His scratched hand flat on her stomach, where she had put it, holding it there with her own.

“I’m sorry,” he said, into her hair. For the fourth time. “About the thirty-one minutes.”

“I know.” She was quiet. “I thought I was better. I thought I was finished with it. The corridor.” She watched the kitten breathe. “Four years of Tuesdays. And I was back in it in nineteen minutes.”

He held her tighter.

“You don’t have to be finished with it,” he said. “I’m not finished with a staircase. You’re not finished with a corridor.” He was quiet. “We just don’t have to sit in them alone any more.”

She turned her head on the pillow.

“Clause three,” she said. “The next time you’re going to be late, you call me first. From a phone that works. Even if it’s a surprise. Even if it’s a cat.”

He was quiet for a moment.

“What if it’s two cats?” he said.

She lifted her head and looked at him in the dark.

“Is there a second cat?”

“Not yet,” said Chen Si. “There was a brother. Grey. Copper eyes. He was very calm. He was asleep in the hay.” He paused. “Zhendong says the breeder is keeping him until Saturday.”

She put her face down in the pillow, beside the kitten, and laughed until she cried, and then cried until she laughed again, and he held her the whole time, and the kitten woke up, and looked at both of them with enormous copper eyes, and sneezed, and went back to sleep.

She named him Topolino.

The brother, who came on Saturday, she named Ritardo.

Late.

chapters.title: What the Don’s Assistant Puts Up With
chapters.desc: Qian has worked for Chen Si for twelve years. He has two drawers of antacids, a spreadsheet titled “Clause Nine Scheduling Conflicts”, and a theory that the most dangerous man in the city is completely, catastrophically, embarrassingly in love. A week in his life.
chapters.epigraph: Qian’s calendar, Monday, 9:00 a.m.: “Mr. Chen – Rotterdam call.” Qian’s calendar, Monday, 9:01 a.m.: “Mr. Chen – Rotterdam call (cancelled; Mrs. Chen came in).”
chapters.content:
Monday.

Qian arrived on the thirty-ninth floor at 7:15, as he had every working day for twelve years, and put his bag under his desk and opened the first drawer, the one with the antacids, and counted them.

Fourteen. He had bought a new packet on Friday. He took two, as a precaution, and closed the drawer.

At 7:42, the lift opened, and Mr. Chen came out.

Grey suit. Coffee he wasn’t drinking. The face. The calm, mild, perfectly still face that had made three ministers, a judge and the chairman of the port authority weep in that office over the past twelve years, and that Qian had seen, exactly once, crumple.

“Good morning, Qian.”

“Good morning, Mr. Chen. Rotterdam at nine. Mr. Pei at ten. The Macau people at eleven, they’re bringing the lawyer with the eyebrows.”

“Thank you.”

Mr. Chen went into his office. Qian heard the door close. He heard the chair. He heard the laptop open.

He heard, at 7:44, the faint and unmistakable sound of a man taking out his phone and looking at the same photograph he had looked at every morning at 7:44 for six years.

Qian did not know what the photograph was. He had never asked. He had a theory. The theory was that it was Mrs. Chen, asleep, in a grey jumper, with her mouth slightly open, and that Mr. Chen had taken it without her knowledge, and that if she ever found out she would throw something at him, and that he knew this, and kept it anyway, and looked at it every morning for exactly ninety seconds before Rotterdam.

At 7:45:30, the phone went back in the pocket.

Qian wrote 7:44–7:45:30 in the small black notebook he kept for no reason he could have explained to anyone, and turned on his computer.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 8:59, he put the Rotterdam call through.

At 9:01, the lift opened again.

Mrs. Chen came out. In cream. In gold. In heels that could be heard from the far end of the corridor, which Qian had long since concluded was deliberate, so that every man on the thirty-ninth floor had approximately eleven seconds of warning.

She did not stop at his desk. She never stopped at his desk. She said, “Morning, Qian, lovely tie,” without looking at it, which was how he knew she had looked at it, and went straight into the office without knocking.

Through the door, Qian heard the Rotterdam people say, in English, “Mr. Chen, regarding the third quarter—”

He heard Mr. Chen say, “I’m so sorry. Can I call you back?”

He heard the call end.

He sighed, and opened his calendar, and wrote cancelled; Mrs. Chen came in next to Rotterdam, and then rang Rotterdam himself, and apologised in his best English, and rescheduled for Thursday, and Rotterdam said, with weary understanding, “Is it the wife again?” and Qian said, “I couldn’t possibly comment,” and Rotterdam said, “It’s always the wife,” and hung up.

At 9:14, the door opened.

Mrs. Chen came out. Her lipstick was slightly less perfect than it had been at 9:01. She said, “Bye, Qian,” and went to the lift.

At 9:15, Mr. Chen came to his door.

His tie was very slightly crooked. He did not appear to have noticed.

“Qian,” he said, “call Rotterdam back.”

“I’ve rescheduled for Thursday, Mr. Chen.”

“Ah.” Mr. Chen looked at him. “Thank you.” A pause. “What did she want?”

Qian looked up.

“Mrs. Chen. Just now.” Mr. Chen frowned slightly, as though trying to remember. “She came in to tell me something. I don’t think she said it.”

Qian looked at his employer’s tie.

“I believe,” he said carefully, “that she may have come in to say good morning.”

Mr. Chen considered this.

“She said it at home,” he said. “At seven.”

“Perhaps,” said Qian, “she wanted to say it again.”

Mr. Chen stood in the doorway and thought about it.

Then something happened at the corner of his mouth, very small, that Qian had spent twelve years learning to read, and that meant, roughly translated, I am the happiest man in the province and I would kill anyone who said so.

He went back into his office.

He did not straighten his tie until after Mr. Pei had been and gone, and Mr. Pei, who had worked for him for eleven years, spent the entire meeting staring at it in silent terror.

✦ ✦ ✦

Tuesday.

Tuesday was therapy. Mrs. Chen’s, at nine, in Central.

Mr. Chen did not come in on Tuesdays until eleven. He drove her himself. He had done it every Tuesday for four years and he would do it, Qian suspected, until one of them died, and possibly afterwards.

Qian had once, in the first year, offered to have a driver take her.

Mr. Chen had looked at him.

Qian had not offered again.

On Tuesday mornings, therefore, the thirty-ninth floor was quiet, and Qian did the things that needed doing while nobody was watching. He reconciled the Macau accounts. He returned four calls from journalists. He rang the florist on the east side and confirmed the standing order: white peonies, every year, to a flat in Mid-Levels, no card. He rang the jeweller in Edinburgh, no, sorry, the woollens shop in Edinburgh, and confirmed that the grey jumper, medium, in the original weight, was still in production and that they would be informed immediately if it was ever discontinued.

“You ask us this every six months,” said the woman in Edinburgh.

“Yes,” said Qian.

“It’s a jumper.”

“It is not,” said Qian, “just a jumper.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 11:04, Mr. Chen came in.

He was quiet. He was always quiet on Tuesdays. He went into his office and closed the door, and Qian did not put anyone through for twenty minutes, because he had learned, in the first year, that on Tuesdays Mr. Chen sometimes needed twenty minutes.

At 11:24, the door opened.

“Qian.”

“Mr. Chen.”

“She laughed today.” Mr. Chen was standing in the doorway with his hand on the frame. “When she came out. She got in the car and she was laughing. She said Dr. Ho had told her she was the most stubborn patient she’d had in thirty years, and she said thank you, and Dr. Ho said it wasn’t a compliment, and she said it was to me.”

Qian looked at him.

“That’s very good, Mr. Chen.”

“Yes.” Mr. Chen looked at the floor. “Four years ago she couldn’t get out of the car.”

Qian didn’t say anything.

He remembered. He had been in the car park, that first Tuesday, by accident. He had seen Mrs. Chen sitting in the passenger seat, not moving, for eleven minutes, with Mr. Chen in the driver’s seat holding her hand, not saying anything, not making her go in. And at the eleventh minute she had opened the door.

“Put the Macau people back,” said Mr. Chen. “Half an hour.”

“Mr. Chen?”

“I want to sit for half an hour,” said Mr. Chen, “and think about her laughing.”

He went back into his office and closed the door.

Qian put the Macau people back half an hour. When they complained, he told them Mr. Chen was in a meeting of the highest importance, which was true.

✦ ✦ ✦

Wednesday.

At 6:58 in the morning, Qian’s phone rang.

“Qian,” said Mrs. Chen. “I need you to do something for me, and you can never, ever tell him.”

Qian closed his eyes.

There was a spreadsheet on his laptop. It had been there for nine years. It was titled Clause Nine Scheduling Conflicts, and it was password-protected, and the password was something he would take to his grave.

It recorded, as discreetly as he could manage, every occasion on which Mr. Chen’s calendar had been altered at short notice because Mrs. Chen had, in Qian’s careful phrasing, requested his presence. It had four hundred and twelve rows. It had a column for Reason Given to Third Party. The most common entry in that column was Family matter. The second most common was Urgent personal appointment. The third, which Qian had used only in desperation, was Dental.

Mr. Chen had, according to the spreadsheet, been to the dentist sixty-one times.

“Yes, Mrs. Chen,” said Qian.

“His birthday,” said Mrs. Chen. “It’s in three weeks. I want to give him something, and I need his calendar for the whole day, and the night, and the morning after, and I need you to tell everyone, everyone, including Zhendong, that he has a—”

“Dental appointment,” said Qian.

There was a pause.

“How did you know I was going to say that?”

“Instinct, Mrs. Chen.”

“Well, it’s—yes. A dental appointment. Twenty-six hours long.”

Qian opened the spreadsheet. He added row four hundred and thirteen.

“Mrs. Chen,” he said, “may I ask what you are giving him? So that I can prepare.”

There was a long silence on the line.

“No,” said Mrs. Chen. “No, Qian, you may not.”

He added, in the Notes column, Do not ask.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:30, Mr. Chen came to his desk.

“Qian,” he said, “I need you to do something for me, and you can never, ever tell her.”

Qian closed his eyes again.

There was a second spreadsheet. It was not on the laptop. It was in the small black notebook. It had no title. It recorded every occasion on which Mr. Chen had asked him to arrange something for Mrs. Chen in secret. It had, at last count, two hundred and ninety rows. It included forty-one umbrellas (the stands at the racetrack, the pit lane, the Paris shows, Geneva in the rain), six bowls of congee delivered to the workshop at four in the morning, two cats, one retired Italian maid’s phone number in Bergamo, a woman at the consulate who taught Milanese Italian on Wednesdays at seven, and an indefinite standing arrangement with a woollens shop in Edinburgh.

“Yes, Mr. Chen,” said Qian.

“Her birthday,” said Mr. Chen. “It’s in five weeks. I want—” He stopped. “I want to clear her calendar. The whole day. And night. And the morning after. And I need you to tell Lily, and Enzo, and anyone who asks, that she has a—”

He stopped.

Qian waited.

“What do people usually say?” said Mr. Chen.

“Dental appointment,” said Qian.

Mr. Chen looked at him.

“How long?” he said.

“Twenty-six hours, Mr. Chen,” said Qian, “is traditional.”

Mr. Chen looked at him without saying anything at all.

Then he went back into his office, and closed the door, and through it, quite distinctly, Qian heard the most dangerous man in the province laugh.

✦ ✦ ✦

Thursday.

Rotterdam, at nine. Rescheduled from Monday.

At 8:59, Qian put the call through.

At 9:00, the lift opened.

Qian looked up from his desk with the weary resignation of a man watching a train come down a track he has been tied to for twelve years.

But it wasn’t Mrs. Chen.

It was a delivery man, with a tray. On the tray, a bowl. Covered. Steaming.

“For Mr. Chen,” said the delivery man, who was in fact the doorman from the forty-fourth floor, looking very nervous. “From Mrs. Chen’s kitchen. It’s been on the stove since midnight. She said to say it’s the soup.”

Qian took the tray.

He knocked on the door. He went in.

Mr. Chen was at his desk, on the phone to Rotterdam, with his reading glasses on, saying, “—the third quarter, yes, I understand the concern—”

Qian put the tray down on the desk beside him and lifted the cover.

Clear soup. Dried scallops and pork and an old hen, ginger and red dates, simmered for eight hours until it was so clear you could read through it. Red dates floating on the top like small dark stones.

His mother’s soup.

Mr. Chen stopped speaking.

On the phone, Rotterdam said, “Mr. Chen? Mr. Chen, are you there?”

Mr. Chen looked at the soup.

There was a note tucked under the edge of the bowl. Cream paper. Red ink. Qian could see it from where he was standing, and did not try to read it, and read it anyway, because it was very short.

You skipped breakfast. I noticed. Eat this, or I’ll come up there and make you. And Rotterdam can wait. — A.

Mr. Chen picked up the note. He read it. He folded it once and put it in his inside pocket, on the left, where the two pieces of gold were.

He picked up the phone.

“I’m so sorry,” he said to Rotterdam, in a voice Qian had never heard him use on a business call. “I’m going to have to call you back. My wife has sent me soup.”

He put the phone down.

He picked up the spoon.

Qian went out and closed the door and sat down at his desk and wrote cancelled; soup in his calendar beside Rotterdam, and then rang Rotterdam, and before he could say a word, Rotterdam said, “Was it the wife?”

“It was soup,” said Qian. “From the wife.”

Rotterdam sighed. A long, heavy, defeated sigh, from the far side of the world.

“My wife,” said Rotterdam, “has not sent me soup in nineteen years.”

“I’m very sorry to hear that,” said Qian.

“Next Thursday,” said Rotterdam. “And tell him he’s a lucky bastard.”

“I couldn’t possibly,” said Qian.

✦ ✦ ✦

Friday.

On Friday, nothing happened.

Mr. Chen came in at 7:42. Looked at the photograph at 7:44 for ninety seconds. Took every meeting. Mrs. Chen did not come up. No soup arrived. No cats. No umbrellas. He went home at seven, exactly, the way he always did on Fridays, and said, “Good night, Qian,” and went to the lift.

At 7:02, Qian’s phone buzzed.

A text. From Mrs. Chen.

Qian. You’ve put up with us for twelve years. Look in your second drawer.

Qian looked at his phone.

He did not keep anything in his second drawer except the overflow antacids.

He opened it.

There was a small black box in it. Very plain. On top of the antacids.

He opened the box.

Inside, on black velvet, there was a pair of cufflinks. Gold. Very simple. Flat, round, the size of a fingernail. And on each one, engraved, very small, in two different hands, side by side: a round, confident one, with a flourish on the letter, and a sharp, precise one, lifted at every turn.

The left one said: Dental.

The right one said: Thank you.

Qian sat at his desk on the thirty-ninth floor at 7:03 on a Friday evening with a pair of gold cufflinks in his hand, and did not move for some time.

Then he took them out of the box and put them on.

He took the small black notebook out of his jacket and opened it to the last page, and wrote, very carefully, under row two hundred and ninety:

291. Received cufflinks. Both of them. Together. They knew about the spreadsheets.

They have probably always known.

He closed the notebook.

He opened the first drawer, and counted the antacids. Twelve, still. He had not needed one since Monday.

He closed the drawer, and turned off his computer, and went home. And on Monday, at 7:15, he came in, as he had every working day for twelve years, and put his bag under his desk, wearing the cufflinks.

At 7:42, Mr. Chen came out of the lift.

He looked at Qian’s wrists.

He did not say anything. He did not need to.

At 7:44, through the closed office door, Qian heard the faint and unmistakable sound of a man taking out his phone to look at a photograph.

He smiled, and wrote it down.

chapters.title: Blood Brothers Go Anniversary Shopping
chapters.desc: Two of the most feared men in the city. One shopping centre. Three hours before closing. Both their anniversaries are on the same week, and neither of them has bought anything, and one of them has never been inside a shop that sells things that aren’t guns.
chapters.epigraph: “What does she like?” “Me.” “That’s not a gift, Zhendong.” “Hm.”
chapters.content:
It was Zhao’s fault.

Chen Si said so afterwards, many times, to anyone who would listen, and nobody believed him, because Zhao had never been at fault for anything in his life, as far as anyone could tell, except possibly the Iron Docks fire of 2016, and nobody talked about that.

But it was.

It was a Wednesday in April. Chen Si was on the thirty-ninth floor at four in the afternoon, reading a contract, when the door opened without a knock, which meant one person, and Zhao came in and stood in front of his desk.

He stood there for four seconds.

“Friday,” said Zhao.

Chen Si looked up.

“Friday what?”

Zhao didn’t say anything. He looked at the window. He looked at the floor. He looked, for one second, at Chen Si, with an expression Chen Si had seen on his face exactly twice in fifteen years: once in a drain in the dark with the water at their chests, and once in a registry office, in a borrowed suit, waiting for a woman in green to walk through a door.

Panic.

“Zhendong,” said Chen Si slowly. “What’s on Friday?”

“Five years,” said Zhao.

Chen Si put down his pen.

“Your anniversary is on Friday,” he said. “And you haven’t bought anything.”

Silence.

“Zhendong. It’s Wednesday.”

“I know what day it is,” said Zhao, with enormous dignity.

“What did you get her last year?”

Zhao looked at the window.

“I asked her what she wanted,” he said. “She said nothing. So I got her nothing.”

Chen Si stared at him.

“She didn’t speak to me for two days,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si looked at the calendar on his desk.

Then he went very still, in a way that Zhao, who had known him since they were fifteen and sixteen, recognised at once, and his face went slightly grey.

“Hm,” said Zhao, with great interest.

“Be quiet.”

“When,” said Zhao.

Chen Si closed his eyes.

“Saturday,” he said. “Not the wedding. Not the proposal. The first time she called me by my name. Not Mr. Chen. Just my name. She proposed to me calling me Mr. Chen. Then three weeks later, at two in the morning, she rang to tell me a crate from Milan had come in early, and she said my name, and forgot to be embarrassed about it.” He rubbed his face. “She counts it. She counts everything. Last year she gave me a fountain pen engraved with the time. 2:14.” He opened his eyes. “I had something. I had something. I ordered it in January. From Kyoto. It was supposed to arrive last week.” He picked up his phone and looked at it as if it had betrayed him personally. “Qian. Qian rang me on Monday. It’s stuck in customs in Osaka.”

Zhao looked at him.

Then, very slightly, at the corner of his mouth, something happened that Chen Si had seen perhaps eleven times in fifteen years.

“Don’t,” said Chen Si.

Zhao didn’t say anything.

He didn’t need to. He just stood there, in front of the desk, with his hands in his pockets, almost smiling, for a full four seconds.

Chen Si got up and picked up his coat.

“Pacific Place,” he said. “It closes at ten.”

✦ ✦ ✦

They had never been shopping together.

That was the thing they both realised, about halfway down the escalator into the main atrium, at 6:20 on a Wednesday evening, with the crowds going past them in every direction and the great glass roof overhead and music playing from somewhere that was almost certainly designed to make people buy handbags.

Fifteen years. A drain, a back room behind a clinic, a basement in the old town, the Iron Docks, two weddings, a boat, an ICU. They had done everything together that two men could possibly do.

They had never once been inside a shop at the same time.

“Where do we start?” said Chen Si.

Zhao looked around the atrium. At the shops. Hundreds of them. Glass and light and marble, going up four floors, every one of them full of things he did not understand.

His hand went, very slightly, to his jacket. Where his gun was not, because Chen Si had made him leave it in the car.

“I don’t know,” he said.

It was the first time in fifteen years Chen Si had heard him say that.

✦ ✦ ✦

They started with jewellery.

This was a mistake.

“No,” said Chen Si, at the door of the first shop, a very grand one, from Paris, with a doorman in white gloves. “No, I can’t. I can’t buy her jewellery. She makes jewellery. She’d look at anything I bought here and tell me what was wrong with the setting.” He looked through the window. “She’d be right.”

“Elowen doesn’t make jewellery,” said Zhao.

“Then go in.”

Zhao went in.

He came out four minutes later. He had not bought anything. He had a slightly glazed expression.

“Well?” said Chen Si.

“The man asked me what her style was,” said Zhao. “I said green. He showed me emeralds. Many emeralds.” He was quiet. “She doesn’t wear jewellery. She cuts stems. It gets caught on the stems.” He looked back at the shop. “I told him that. He looked at me like I had shot someone.”

“Did you want to?”

“Hm,” said Zhao.

✦ ✦ ✦

They tried clothes.

They tried a very expensive shop on the second floor that sold cashmere, where Chen Si stood in front of a rack of coats, very still, and then said, “No. I already gave her a coat. The coat is—no. You can’t give the coat twice,” and walked out.

They tried a shop that sold scented candles, where Zhao picked up a candle, and smelled it, and put it down, and picked up another, and smelled it, and put it down, eleven times, in total silence, and then said, “They all smell like the inside of a florist’s,” and Chen Si said, “That’s the point, Zhendong, she’d like that,” and Zhao said, “She is the inside of a florist’s,” and Chen Si could not argue with that.

They tried a bookshop.

That was Chen Si’s idea.

Zhao stood in the doorway of the bookshop, looking at the shelves, and didn’t go in.

“I read out loud now,” he said.

Chen Si looked at him.

“You taught me the first words,” said Zhao. “In the canteen. With the pictures. The rest I did myself. At the Docks. With a dictionary. Shipping reports.” He looked at the books. “But I never read out loud. Not to anyone. Not once. In case I got a word wrong and somebody laughed.” His hand moved, very slightly, on the doorframe. “She made me. At night. In the shop. After closing. She said she liked my voice. She never once laughed when I got a word wrong.” He was quiet. “I read her a whole book last month. Out loud. In bed. All of it. She cried at the end.”

Chen Si didn’t say anything for a moment.

“What book?” he said.

Zhao looked at him.

“The monkey king,” he said. “The simple one. With pictures. The one you read me.” He looked away. “I found a copy. In a shop in the old town. It’s the same edition. I read it to her the way you read it to me.” His jaw moved. “I thought she should know. What you did. In the canteen.”

Chen Si stood in the doorway of a bookshop in a shopping centre on a Wednesday evening and could not speak.

Zhao looked at him for four seconds.

Then he cleared his throat, very loudly, and said, “Hm. Not books. She has books,” and walked away down the corridor, very fast, and Chen Si had to stand there for a minute before he could follow.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 8:40, they sat down on a bench.

In the middle of the atrium. By a fountain. With nothing.

Two of the most feared men in the city. The head of the Syndicate and his blood brother. Side by side on a bench in a shopping centre, with their hands on their knees, looking at a fountain.

A child went past with a balloon and stared at them.

Zhao stared back. The child fled.

“This is terrible,” said Chen Si.

“Hm.”

“I have negotiated with the port authority. I have negotiated with three ministers and a judge. I once got a man in Rotterdam to sell me a shipping company for a third of its value over a single lunch.” Chen Si looked at the fountain. “I cannot buy my wife a present.”

“You bought her a cat,” said Zhao.

“That was different. She said his name in her sleep.”

Zhao was quiet.

“Elowen talks in her sleep too,” he said.

Chen Si turned his head.

“What does she say?”

Zhao looked at the fountain.

“My name,” he said. “Mostly. Sometimes the names of flowers. Latin ones. She sorts them. In her sleep. Like she’s doing an order.” Something happened at the corner of his mouth. “Once she said Zhendong, the ranunculus are wrong, very angry, and then went back to sleep. I lay awake for an hour thinking about what I’d done to the ranunculus.”

Chen Si laughed. Out loud. On the bench. The child with the balloon, on the far side of the fountain, looked back in alarm.

“What does Aurelia say?” said Zhao.

Chen Si stopped laughing.

“Mostly Italian,” he said. “About her mother.” He was quiet. “Sometimes I’m not shaking.” He looked at his hands. “And once, about a month ago, she said, very clearly, in English, I want to go back to the beginning.”

Zhao looked at him.

“The beginning of what?”

“I don’t know,” said Chen Si. “I lay awake thinking about it. I thought maybe—” He stopped. “I thought maybe she meant she wanted to go back to before. Before me. Before all of it. The boat. The corridor.” His voice went very quiet. “I lay there for three hours, Zhendong, thinking my wife wanted to go back to before she met me.”

Zhao didn’t say anything.

“Ask her,” he said.

“I can’t ask her what she says in her sleep.”

“Clause three,” said Zhao.

Chen Si turned and looked at him.

“How do you know about clause three?”

“Everyone knows about clause three,” said Zhao. “Qian has it framed.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At 9:15, they found it.

They found it by accident, the way you find the important things. They had given up. They had got up off the bench and were walking back toward the car park, past a small shop at the end of the ground-floor corridor that neither of them had noticed on the way in. A narrow shop. Old-fashioned. With one window.

In the window, there was a map.

An old one. Framed. Hand-drawn, in faded ink, on paper gone brown at the edges. A map of the city as it had been in 1890. The harbour. The Peak. The old town. And in the corner, very small, a narrow road running along the waterfront, with a name on it in old-fashioned characters.

Chen Si stopped.

“Harbour Road,” he said.

Zhao stopped beside him.

They looked at the map in the window. At the narrow road along the water. At the little squares of buildings drawn along it, very carefully, by someone a hundred and thirty years ago.

“Her shop,” said Zhao.

“It wasn’t there in 1890.”

“The road was.” Zhao looked at it. “The beginning.”

Chen Si went very still.

I want to go back to the beginning.

He looked at the map.

Then he went into the shop.

✦ ✦ ✦

Zhao waited outside.

He stood by the window with his hands in his pockets and looked at the shop next door, which sold antique things, small ones, in cases. Netsuke. Snuff bottles. Old scissors. Old knives. Old tools.

He looked at the tools.

There was a pair of shears in the case. Very old. Iron, gone dark. With brass rings for the fingers and long narrow blades, and a little curl at the end of one handle, like a stem. A tag beside them in neat handwriting: Florist’s shears. Kyoto. c. 1880.

He looked at them for four seconds.

Then he went in.

✦ ✦ ✦

They met on the bench by the fountain at 9:51.

Chen Si had a long flat parcel under his arm, wrapped in brown paper. Zhao had a small box in his hand. Neither of them said anything for a while.

“Shears,” said Zhao eventually.

Chen Si looked at the box.

“Old ones?”

“Kyoto. 1880.” Zhao turned the box over in his hand. “The man said a woman used them for fifty years. In a flower shop in Gion. Every day. He said you could see her hand in the handles. Where she held them.” He was quiet. “Worn down. In the shape of her.”

Chen Si didn’t say anything.

“I want Elowen’s hand in them,” said Zhao. “Fifty years. In the shape of her.” He put the box in his pocket. “That’s the gift. Not the shears. Fifty years.”

Chen Si looked at his brother.

“That,” he said, “is the best gift I have ever heard of.”

“Hm,” said Zhao, and looked at the fountain, and his ears had gone red.

✦ ✦ ✦

He asked her on the Saturday.

At breakfast. On the long table by the window. With the map still in its brown paper beside his plate, and Topolino asleep on the chair beside her, and her hair down, in his grey jumper, eating toast.

“A month ago,” he said. “You said something in your sleep.”

She looked up, and waited.

“You said, I want to go back to the beginning.” He kept his voice very even. “Clause three. I need to know what you meant.”

She put down her toast.

She looked at him across the table, and he watched her understand, slowly, what he had been thinking for a month, and her face went through astonishment and outrage and something else, something very soft, all at once.

“You thought,” she said. “You thought I meant—before you?”

He didn’t say anything.

“Chen Si.” She got up. She came round the table. She took his face in both hands, the way she did. “Before you? Before you? Are you insane?”

“It was three in the morning.”

“I meant the balcony,” said Aurelia. “I was dreaming about the balcony. I was dreaming it was the beginning again, and you were standing at the end in the dark, and I hadn’t turned round yet, and I knew everything that was going to happen. Everything. The ledgers and the proposal and Milan and the boat and the corridor. All of it. And I wanted to go back. So I could turn round. And do it all again.” Her eyes were wet. “Every bit. The corridor too. I’d do it all again. I wanted to go back to the beginning so I could have all of it twice.”

He looked up at her.

He reached down beside his plate, without looking, and put the brown paper parcel in her hands.

She unwrapped it.

A map. The city, in 1890. The harbour. The Peak. The old town. And along the waterfront, very small, a narrow road.

Harbour Road.

She looked at it, and then at him.

“The beginning,” said Chen Si. “Before the shop. Before the balcony. Before either of us.” He was quiet. “I couldn’t give you the balcony twice. So I gave you the road. You can start wherever you like.”

She put the map down very carefully on the table.

She put her arms round his neck, and her face in his shoulder, and didn’t say anything at all for a while.

He stood up with her still holding on, so that her feet came off the floor, and kissed her, there by the breakfast table with the toast going cold and the cat watching, slowly and thoroughly, with a month of three-in-the-morning fear going out of him into it.

“All of it twice,” he said against her mouth. “I’d walk down Harbour Road for six years instead of six weeks. I’d take every glass on that boat.”

She leaned back in his arms and looked at him.

“Where’s the Kyoto thing?” she said.

He went still.

“What Kyoto thing?”

“The thing you ordered from Kyoto. In January. That’s stuck in customs in Osaka.” She smiled through her tears. “Qian told me. On Monday. Under duress.”

“Qian,” said Chen Si, with feeling, “is fired.”

“Qian has cufflinks that say Dental,” said Aurelia. “You can never fire him.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the Friday, at the florist’s shop on the edge of the Walled City, after closing, Zhao had given his wife a small box.

She had opened it.

She had looked at the shears. Old iron. Brass rings. The little curl at the end of one handle, like a stem. And in the brass, worn down, in the shape of a hand, the place where another woman had held them for fifty years.

She had put her hand into them.

They fitted. Almost. Not quite. Her fingers were a little longer.

“Fifty years,” Zhao had said. That was all.

And Elowen, who had once made a man who never read out loud read to her at night, in the shop, after closing, without ever once laughing at a wrong word, understood exactly what he meant.

She told Aurelia about it on the phone, three days later, at eleven at night, in a voice that was very nearly not cool at all.

“Forty-two,” said Aurelia, when she had finished. “To you. That’s the best anniversary present anyone’s ever been given. I can’t compete with that. You win.”

There was a long silence on the line.

“Mine copied yours,” said Elowen finally. “At the bookshop. He told me. He said your husband stood in the doorway and couldn’t speak, and it made him think of the shears.” She paused. “So it’s yours. Really. Forty-one, forty-one.”

Aurelia lay back on the pillow, with Topolino on her stomach and her husband asleep beside her and a map of 1890 on the bedside table.

“Lin,” she said. “Are you trying to give me a point?”

“I would never,” said Elowen. “Go to sleep. Your husband thinks you want to leave him when you talk in your sleep. It’s pathetic.”

“So does yours. About ranunculus.”

A pause.

“He told you about the ranunculus?”

“Forty-two,” said Aurelia, very happily, and hung up.

chapters.title: Aurelia Loses at Mahjong to Evangeline
chapters.desc: Aurelia Chen has not lost a game of mahjong since she was nineteen. Elowen’s quiet sister has not said more than eleven words to her in five years. One Lunar New Year, one table, four players, and a husband standing behind his wife’s chair who is enjoying this far too much.
chapters.epigraph: “Pung.” — Evangeline Lee, the only word she said for two hours
chapters.content:
Aurelia Chen did not lose at mahjong.

This was a fact, like the tides, and everyone in the Syndicate knew it. She had learned at fifteen, in the first year in the city, from the old cook at the Peak, in the kitchen, at night, when nobody was watching, because her mother thought mahjong was a game for servants. By nineteen she was playing in the back rooms of tea houses in the old town against men who had been playing for fifty years. By twenty-two, in the winter of the ledgers, she had taken eleven thousand dollars off Mr. Kwan and his tinted glasses in a single night, and Mr. Kwan had never entirely recovered.

She did the sums. That was all. She counted every tile that went down and every tile that didn’t and held the whole wall in her head, and by the third round she knew what everyone at the table was holding, and by the fourth they knew she knew.

“You can’t play with her,” Mr. Lu told a new man once, very kindly, in a pawnshop. “It isn’t a game. It’s an audit.”

✦ ✦ ✦

Lunar New Year was at the Lins’.

It had been at the Lins’ for three years now, ever since Elowen had said, at the end of a gala, coolly, “You might as well come. He’ll only sulk if you don’t,” and Aurelia had said, “Who will?” and Elowen had looked across the room at Zhao and Chen Si standing side by side by the wall with their hands in their pockets, not speaking, and said, “Both of them.”

So they went. Every year. To the tall old house in the Walled City with too many stairs, where every sound carried, and where the whole of Elowen’s family gathered on the first night: her father, Lin Jian, who had once been the most frightening man in the Walled City and was now mostly frightened of his daughters; her brother Raiden, who played the cheerful useless son so well that strangers believed it; Jia, the youngest, who had painted her nails black for New Year and looked at Aurelia’s gold with frank professional interest.

And Evangeline.

✦ ✦ ✦

Evangeline did not talk.

That was the thing everyone said about her, and it was true. She was the quiet one. The adopted one, though nobody in the family ever said so, and Aurelia, who had a sister she loved and fought with, understood exactly why. Evangeline was tall and very still and had a face like something carved, and she married a man called Lee Jun Hyuk, who was kind and enormous and talked enough for both of them, and in five years of galas and lunches and New Years, she had said, by Aurelia’s count, eleven words to her.

Hello. Five times.

Thank you. Twice, which was four words.

And once, at a wedding, when Aurelia had stood beside her at the bar for a full minute in silence, Evangeline had looked down at the broken necklace at Aurelia’s throat, and said, very quietly:

Good mend.

Aurelia had thought about that for a week.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Mahjong,” said Lin Jian, after dinner, rubbing his hands. “Four players. Who’s in?”

“Me,” said Aurelia.

There was a silence round the long table.

“Ah,” said Lin Jian, who had heard about Mr. Kwan.

“I’ll play,” said Raiden cheerfully. “I love losing money. It’s my hobby.”

“I’ll play,” said Elowen, coolly. “Somebody has to keep her honest.”

“I’m always honest,” said Aurelia. “I just count.”

Lin Jian looked round the table for a fourth. At Jia, who held up her black nails and said, “Not with these, they’re still wet.” At Zhao, who said “Hm,” in a tone that meant absolutely not. At Chen Si, who smiled mildly and said, “I couldn’t possibly. I’d have to play against my wife, and clause nine doesn’t cover it.”

Elowen choked on her tea.

“Evie?” said Lin Jian.

Evangeline looked up from the end of the table, where she had been sitting very still, the way she always did, with her hands folded around a cup.

She looked at Aurelia across the room.

Then she stood up, and went to the table by the window where the tiles were, and sat down in the east seat, and began, without a word, to turn the tiles face down.

✦ ✦ ✦

Chen Si stood behind his wife’s chair.

He always did, when she played. Not too close. Not looking at her tiles; he never once looked at her tiles, in five years, because he said it would be cheating, and because, he said, he liked her better when he didn’t know what she was going to do. He stood behind her with a cup of tea he wasn’t drinking and his free hand resting on the back of her chair, so lightly she could only feel it when she leaned back.

She leaned back a great deal.

“You’re distracting me,” she said, without turning round, in the first round, building her wall. “You’re breathing.”

“I can stop,” said Chen Si, “if you’d like. For a short time.”

She reached back without looking and pinched the back of his hand, hard, and he made a small sound that made Raiden, across the table, look up in delight.

“Is he allowed to stand there?” said Raiden. “Isn’t that—he could be signalling. He could have a whole system. Taps on the chair. Very slight coughs.”

“He doesn’t look at my tiles,” said Aurelia sweetly. “If he did, I would know, and I would make him sleep in the study, and he hates the study. He’s been in the study twice in five years. Once for losing on purpose at chess. Once for buying me a second cat without telling me.”

“There’s a third cat?” said Jia, from the sofa, interested.

“There will never be a third cat,” said Aurelia, and behind her, very quietly, Chen Si coughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

The first round, she won.

Of course she did. She counted. By the twelfth tile she knew Raiden was going for a flush, by the twentieth she knew Elowen was holding two dragons, and by the thirtieth she had the whole table in her head, the way she held a ledger, and she went out on a self-drawn tile and turned her hand face up and said, pleasantly, “Pay me.”

Raiden paid her, cheerfully. Elowen paid her, coolly, with an expression of deep personal grievance.

Evangeline paid her without a word.

Aurelia looked across the table at her.

Evangeline had not won anything. She had not declared anything. She had not said a single word, all round. She had sat in the east seat with her back very straight and drawn and discarded and drawn and discarded, quickly, without hesitating, without looking at anyone, and her face had not changed once.

And her discards had been very strange.

Aurelia had counted them. Every one. They did not make sense. They were not the discards of someone building a hand. They were scattered, random, a bamboo here, a circle there, a wind she should have kept.

She doesn’t know how to play, Aurelia thought.

And then, more slowly: Or.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second round, Evangeline won.

On the eighth turn.

Aurelia had never seen anyone win on the eighth turn. Not in the tea houses. Not against Mr. Kwan. Not anywhere. She was still building her hand, three tiles from anything, counting, when Evangeline reached out a long still hand and took Raiden’s discard and laid down her tiles.

A perfect hand. All one suit. Circles. Every one.

Raiden stared at it.

“Evie,” he said.

Evangeline said nothing. She held out her hand to be paid.

Aurelia looked at the tiles.

Then she looked at Evangeline. At the carved, still face. At the eyes, which were looking back at her, very calmly, with something in them that Aurelia had seen once before, in a mirror, at twenty-two, on the night she took eleven thousand dollars off Mr. Kwan.

She counts too.

“The first round,” said Aurelia slowly. “Your discards. They didn’t make sense.”

Evangeline said nothing.

“You were letting me count you,” said Aurelia. “You were giving me things to count. Things that were wrong. So I’d think I had you.”

Evangeline picked up her cup of tea and drank from it, very slowly, without taking her eyes off Aurelia’s face.

Behind Aurelia’s chair, Chen Si made a sound that he turned, at the last second, into a cough.

“Don’t,” said Aurelia, without turning round.

“I was only going to say,” said Chen Si, very mildly, “that in five years I have never once seen you look at anyone the way you are looking at your sister-in-law’s sister right now.” He paused. “I’m a little jealous.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She lost the third round.

And the fourth.

And the fifth.

She did not lose them badly. She lost them by one tile, by two, by a single turn. Every round, she counted. Every round, she held the whole table in her head. And every round, at some point between the tenth turn and the twentieth, she would look across the table at Evangeline’s discards and realise that the picture in her head was wrong. That she had been given a picture. That she had built it herself, out of tiles Evangeline had put down for her, precisely, like breadcrumbs, and walked straight into it.

It was the most beautiful thing she had ever seen.

“Pung,” said Evangeline, in the fifth round, taking a tile.

It was the first word she had said in two hours.

Raiden looked up as if he had heard a ghost.

Elowen, beside him, had put down her tiles altogether and was watching the two of them, Aurelia and Evangeline, across the table, with an expression of enormous, unholy delight that she was not even trying to hide.

“Forty-two,” she said, under her breath. “Forty-three. Forty-four.”

“Lin,” said Aurelia, without taking her eyes off Evangeline, “if you count my losses to your sister as points to you, I will set your shop on fire.”

“Family points,” said Elowen serenely. “They count.”

✦ ✦ ✦

By the sixth round, Aurelia had stopped counting.

She didn’t decide to. It just happened. She was sitting at the table in the tall old house in the Walled City with her husband’s hand on the back of her chair and three of the Lins around her and the firecrackers going off in the street outside, and she realised that she was not counting anything at all. She was watching Evangeline’s hands. The long, still, careful hands. Drawing and discarding. Building a hand that was also a lie that was also, somehow, a kind of conversation.

Good mend, Evangeline had said. Once. At a wedding. Looking at a broken necklace.

Aurelia thought: she has been watching me for five years. The way I watch everything.

She thought: nobody has ever watched me back.

She leaned back in her chair. Into his hand.

He moved his thumb, very slightly. Once. On her shoulder.

She lost the sixth round by a single tile, and laughed out loud, and could not stop.

✦ ✦ ✦

At two in the morning, the game broke up.

Raiden had lost two thousand dollars, cheerfully. Elowen had lost one thousand, coolly, and spent the last round sitting sideways in her chair with her feet in Zhao’s lap, where he had come and sat beside her and put his hand round her ankle without a word. Lin Jian had gone to bed. Jia was asleep on the sofa with her black nails curled under her chin.

Aurelia had lost three thousand four hundred dollars.

To Evangeline.

It was the most she had lost at a mahjong table in her life. It was the first time she had lost at a mahjong table since she was nineteen.

She counted it out. In cash. In red envelopes, because it was New Year. She put the envelopes in a neat pile on the table in front of the east seat.

Evangeline looked at them.

Then she looked at Aurelia.

And then she did something that made Elowen sit straight up in her chair and Zhao’s hand go still on her ankle, and Raiden, at the door, turn round.

She pushed the pile back across the table.

All of it.

“Keep it,” said Evangeline.

Aurelia stared at her.

“I don’t—you won it. It’s yours. I lost.”

“Yes,” said Evangeline.

It was the longest conversation they had ever had.

She looked at Aurelia across the table, very still, with her carved face. Then she looked, very briefly, at the man standing behind Aurelia’s chair, with his hand on the back of it, who had not looked at a single tile in six rounds.

“I wanted to see,” said Evangeline, very quietly, “what you were like when you lost.” She stood up. “You laughed.” She picked up her cup. “Good mend.”

She walked out of the room and up the stairs, and every one of them carried the sound, and nobody said a word until she had gone.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the car, Aurelia did not speak for twenty minutes.

He drove. Himself. The black car. Through the Walled City and out along the harbour, with the last of the firecrackers going off in the streets and the red paper blowing in the gutters.

She sat in the passenger seat with three thousand four hundred dollars in red envelopes in her lap and looked out of the window.

“Thirteen words,” she said finally.

“Hm?”

“Evangeline. She said thirteen words tonight. Pung. Keep it. Yes. I wanted to see what you were like when you lost. You laughed. Good mend.” She counted again. “No. Nineteen.” She was quiet. “Nineteen words. In five years, eleven. Tonight, nineteen.”

He didn’t say anything.

“She was testing me,” said Aurelia. “All night. Five rounds. She was beating me on purpose to see what I did.” She looked down at the red envelopes. “My mother would have—if I had lost five rounds in a row at my mother’s table. In front of people.” She stopped.

“I know,” said Chen Si.

“I laughed,” said Aurelia. Her voice had gone very strange. “I didn’t know I was going to. I just—it was so beautiful, what she was doing, and I couldn’t count it, and I didn’t want to, and I laughed.” She looked at him. “When did I start laughing when I lose?”

He didn’t answer straight away. He kept his eyes on the road.

“I think,” he said carefully, “it was about the time you stopped needing to win.”

She looked at him.

“And when was that?”

He took his hand off the gear stick and held it out, palm up, on the seat between them, without looking at her.

She looked at it.

She put her hand in it.

“About eleven seconds after you asked me who I was,” said Chen Si, “on a balcony, and I didn’t say.”

✦ ✦ ✦

At home, at three in the morning, she sat on the edge of the bed in her New Year red with the envelopes in her lap and did not take her dress off.

He came and knelt in front of her.

Not because she had told him to. Because he wanted to. He took the envelopes out of her lap and put them on the bedside table. He took off her shoes, one at a time, and set them side by side on the floor. He took her hands in his.

“You’re still thinking about it,” he said.

“I’m thinking about how she did it,” said Aurelia. “The discards. The fake picture. I want to learn it. I want to do it to you.”

“You do it to me every day,” said Chen Si.

She looked down at him.

“Do I?”

“You let me think I know what you’re going to do,” he said, “and then you do something else. You walk into my office in cream at nine in the morning and I think it’s about Rotterdam, and it isn’t. You send me soup when I think you’re angry. You switch off my phone at midnight and take my queen before lunch.” His thumbs moved on her knuckles. “You’ve been beating me at a game I didn’t know I was playing for six years. And I lose every single time. And I don’t count. And I laugh.” He looked up at her. “That’s how I know it’s working.”

She looked down at him, kneeling in front of her in the dark, at three in the morning, on the first night of the year.

“Get up,” she said.

He got up.

She pulled him down onto the bed by the front of his shirt, and kissed him, slowly, the way you kiss someone at the start of a year, and he laughed into her mouth, and she laughed into his, and somewhere in the middle of it, while he was looking for the zip of the red dress and not finding it because there wasn’t one, it was buttons, forty-one of them, down the back, because she had made it herself, she said, against his ear:

“Pung.”

He stopped.

He lifted his head.

“What did you just say?”

“Pung,” said Aurelia. “I’m taking a tile. Yours. The one you just discarded.” She smiled up at him in the dark. “Your whole plan for the next hour. I’m taking it.”

He looked down at her.

“And what are you going to do with it?” he said.

“Make it a perfect hand,” said Aurelia Chen. “All one suit.” She reached up and undid the first button of his shirt. “Mine.”

He did not count the buttons on her dress. For the first time in his life, he lost track at nine.

She laughed.

✦ ✦ ✦

On the third day of New Year, a parcel arrived at the boutique on Harbour Road.

Small. Wrapped in plain brown paper. No card.

Inside, there was a single mahjong tile. Old. Ivory gone yellow with age. Hand-carved.

The one circle. The dot in the middle cut so deep that it had cracked, long ago, straight through, and been mended, with a thin seam of gold.

Aurelia looked at it.

She put it in the window. Beside the broken necklace.

It has been there ever since.

chapters.title: The Sewer, Nineteen Years Ago
chapters.desc: Chen Si has told this story once, to nobody, in his head, every night for nineteen years. Tonight his wife asks about the scar on his arm, and he tells it out loud. Block C. The riot. A boy who came down off the top bunk without deciding to. And half a kilometre of freezing water in the dark.
chapters.epigraph: “You don’t leave them behind you. Not ever. Everything you leave behind you comes back.”
chapters.content:
She asked on a Sunday, in bed, in the afternoon, with the rain on the long window.

She was lying on her stomach beside him with her chin on his chest, idly, the way she did on Sundays when neither of them had anywhere to be, tracing the scar on the inside of his left forearm with one fingertip. Wrist to elbow. A long, pale, puckered line, shiny in places, like wax that had run and set.

She had traced it a thousand times. She had kissed it, in Geneva, wrist to elbow, very slowly, while his hand shook against a door. She had never asked.

“How,” she said.

He looked down at her.

She did not look up. She kept tracing it. Wrist to elbow. Elbow to wrist.

“Zhendong told me about the drain,” she said. “Outside the ICU. At four in the morning. The riot, and the blade, and carrying him. He told it his way. All of it, in fewer words than anyone else would have needed.” She paused at the elbow. “He didn’t tell me this.”

“He didn’t see it,” said Chen Si.

She looked up then.

He was looking at the ceiling. At the rain moving on the window, and the grey light. His face had gone the way it went on the thirty-ninth floor, still and far away, and she nearly said never mind, nearly let it go.

She didn’t.

“Tell me,” she said. “Your way.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her.

✦ ✦ ✦

He was sixteen.

He arrived at Block C in October, in the back of a van with no windows, with a plastic bag of clothes and his father’s watch on his wrist, which they should have taken and didn’t, because the officer who processed him was lazy, and a book.

The book was wrapped in a shirt. At the bottom of the bag. He had wrapped it himself, the night before, in his mother’s flat, in the dark, among her things, which nobody had come to take away. Her reading glasses were still folded on the arm of her chair. Her slippers were still by the door. He had not turned on the light, because if he turned on the light he would see that the chair was empty, and he could not bear to see it one more time. Blue cloth gone grey. Sewn at the spine. Paper like skin. Journey to the West. The oldest thing his family owned. His father had given it to him when he was twelve and said keep it for whoever comes after you, and his father had gone down a staircase at six in the morning and died in a cell eight months later, before his trial, with nothing on him that said who he was, and his mother had died the next winter of a heart that simply stopped.

So he took the book. And the watch. They were all that was left of anyone.

He did not read the book in Block C. It was too valuable, and too fragile, and there were too many hands. He kept it wrapped in the shirt, inside his pillowcase, and slept with his head on it. He read other books. From the library trolley that came round on Thursdays. Falling-apart paperbacks with the covers torn off. A history of a war between two generals. A children’s book about the monkey king, with pictures, the simple version, the kind you give to a boy of seven.

He read the simple one because it was the same story. Because if he closed his eyes while he read it, he could almost hear his father’s voice.

✦ ✦ ✦

The older boys didn’t like him.

He understood why. He talked like the television. He held his chopsticks properly. He said please to the guards. He was thin and pale and had soft hands and had been, until a year and a half ago, the son of a deputy provincial governor, and every boy in Block C had been on the other end of someone like his father at some point in their lives, and they could smell it on him.

They waited for him. In the showers. In the corridor to the laundry. In the corner of the yard where the cameras didn’t reach.

He learned very fast. He learned where to stand and how not to flinch and how to come back from the showers with a split lip and sit down on his bunk and open a book and keep reading as if nothing had happened, because the moment you let them see it hurt, it got worse. He learned that the guards would not help. He learned that nobody would help.

And on his second day, before any of that, he bribed a guard with his father’s watch.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You gave away his watch,” said Aurelia.

“For the drawings,” said Chen Si.

He was quiet for a moment.

“The office had the maintenance plans. From when the building was a factory. I saw them through the window when they processed me, rolled up on a shelf. I knew what they were. My father used to bring plans home. Bridges. Roads. He used to spread them on the dining table and show me where the water went.” He looked at the ceiling. “I gave the watch to a guard called Liu, on the second night, and he let me sit in the office for an hour while he smoked outside. I memorised every drain in the building. Every pipe. Every vent.” His voice didn’t change at all. “I was sixteen. My father was dead. My mother was dead. Nobody was coming. I decided on the second night that I wasn’t going to die there.”

She put her hand flat on his chest.

“I didn’t know about the riot,” he said. “I didn’t plan for a riot. I planned for spring. When the water was lower. I had a list in my head. I was going to go alone.”

He stopped.

“I was always going to go alone,” he said. “Until the laundry.”

✦ ✦ ✦

There was a boy in the laundry.

Fifteen. Bigger than him. Gap-toothed. With a face like a shut door. He worked the press, folding the uniforms, and nobody went near him, ever, not the older boys, not Gao, not anyone, because of something that had happened in his first week that nobody would talk about.

He folded the uniforms before he put them in the press.

Every one. Carefully. Corner to corner. So that they came out with a crease. Nobody had asked him to. Nobody noticed. Chen Si noticed, on the first day, standing in the doorway with a basket, and stayed there, watching a boy nobody went near fold a stranger’s shirt corner to corner as though it mattered.

“You fold them first,” he said.

The boy didn’t answer.

So the next day, in the canteen, Chen Si sat down at the end of his table.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Why?” said Aurelia.

He thought about it.

“Because nobody else in that building did anything carefully,” he said finally. “Nothing. Not the guards. Not the food. Not the way they hit you. Everything was thrown. And there was one boy, in the laundry, folding shirts for people who would never know.” He was quiet. “I thought, that’s someone who still believes things should be done properly. And I thought, I’d like to sit near that.”

She didn’t say anything.

“I sat at the end of his table for a week,” said Chen Si. “I didn’t say anything. I read. Nobody came near me, all week, at meals, because nobody went near him.” Something moved at the corner of his mouth. “I knew that. It wasn’t only because I liked the folding.”

“You used him,” said Aurelia, with interest.

“For a week,” agreed Chen Si. “And then on the seventh day he said, without looking up from his tray, What’s the book?” He was quiet. “And I looked at him. And I saw his face, looking at the page. And I understood that he couldn’t read it.”

Her finger stopped on his arm.

“And he was ashamed,” said Chen Si. “Fifteen. Bigger than anyone. Nobody went near him. And he was ashamed, in front of me, the rich boy, because he couldn’t read the words on a page.” His voice went very quiet. “So I said, it’s about a war, two generals, one of them wins because he’s stronger, the other wins because he knows where the river goes. And I said, I’ll read it to you, if you want.”

“And he said yes.”

“He said nothing,” said Chen Si. “He didn’t say no.” He almost smiled. “That’s yes, with Zhendong. You’ve learned that.”

She had.

✦ ✦ ✦

That night, he read to him.

From the bunk below. Quietly. In the dark. The war book, and then, the next week, the monkey king, the simple one, with the pictures, because the boy on the top bunk had asked, in four words, what the pictures were, and Chen Si had held the book up to the light from the corridor and shown him. Sun Wukong. The stone monkey. Born out of a rock on a mountain, with no father and no mother, who learned seventy-two transformations and fought heaven itself and was trapped under a mountain for five hundred years, and then let out, and given a teacher, and a road, and companions, and a long way to walk.

The boy on the top bunk said nothing at all while he read. Not once.

But on the third night, when Chen Si stopped, the boy said, out of the dark, “Again.”

So he read it again.

✦ ✦ ✦

The riot was in January.

He told her the rest the way it had happened, as far as he could. The heating in Block A. The shouting through the walls. Smoke coming under the door in a grey line. The guards locking the blocks and walking out into the yard and standing in the snow and smoking. Sixty boys in Block C understanding, all at once, that nobody was coming.

Gao.

Three of them. Coming down the aisle between the bunks through the smoke. Gao in front, seventeen, with a slat from a bed frame in his hand, sharpened against the concrete for weeks.

He had been on his bunk with the book. His father’s book. He had taken it out of the pillowcase that night, for the first time, because the smoke was coming and he thought, if this is the end, I want to have held it. And he looked up and saw them coming, and he did not run, because there was nowhere to run, and he did not shout, because nobody would come. He closed the book and put it down very carefully on the blanket.

The way you put down something you want to come back to.

And then the boy came down off the top bunk.

✦ ✦ ✦

He stopped, and for a while he didn’t go on.

She lay with her hand on his chest and felt his heart under it, and it was going very fast, faster than she had felt it since Geneva, and his face had not changed at all.

“He didn’t decide to,” said Chen Si. “I saw his face. He didn’t decide anything. One second he was on the top bunk against the wall, and the next he was standing in the aisle between me and Gao. In the smoke. With his fists closed. Fifteen.” His voice cracked, very slightly, and steadied. “Nobody had ever done that. My whole life. Not my father’s friends, when he was arrested. Not my mother’s family. Not the teachers at my school. Not one person, when it mattered, had ever stood between me and anything.”

He was quiet.

“And a boy who couldn’t read,” he said, “whose name I didn’t know, who I’d been using for a week to keep people away from my table, came down off his bunk and stood in front of me. Because I read him a book.”

Aurelia put her face down on his chest.

✦ ✦ ✦

He told her about the slat.

He did not tell it well. He had never told it. He told it in pieces, the way he remembered it: the sound it made. Zhendong not making any sound at all. Zhendong pulling it out, himself, and looking at Gao, and Gao backing away. Zhendong hitting him until Chen Si got both arms around him from behind and held on and said his name, over and over, and he stopped.

Zhendong sitting down in the aisle. All red. His shirt and his trousers and the floor.

“Si,” Zhendong had said. The first time he ever said it. “You should go.”

He had knelt in front of him with his own shirt pressed against the wound, both hands, as hard as he could, and the blood coming through it, warm, between his fingers, and he had understood, very clearly, kneeling there in the smoke, that this was the moment. That everything in his life had been leading to this. That he could go. Alone. The way he had planned. Through the drain, under the yard, to the road. That he could make it on his own.

And that if he did, he would be his father’s friends, and his mother’s family, and everyone who had ever looked at him in the street after the staircase and crossed to the other side.

“Go where?” he had said. “The doors are locked.”

“Go anyway,” said Zhendong.

And he had laughed. He didn’t know why. He was sixteen and covered in someone else’s blood and he laughed.

“Zhendong,” he said. “I know where the river goes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“The shower block,” said Chen Si. “There was a grate in the floor. Old iron. From the factory. It went down into the main drain.” He looked at his arm. At her finger, resting on the scar. “The boiler room was underneath. Under the showers. Somebody had set fire to the mattresses in Block B, and the fire had got into the boiler room, and the pipes under the floor were—”

He stopped.

“The grate was hot,” said Aurelia.

“Yes,” he said, very mildly. “I didn’t know. I didn’t think. I got the end of a bed slat under it and lifted, and it wouldn’t come, it was rusted in, and I needed more weight. So I put my arm on it.” He turned his arm over on the sheet, so that the scar faced the ceiling. “Wrist to elbow. Leaned on it. All my weight. Until it moved.”

She stared at him.

“How long?” she said. Her voice had gone very thin.

“I don’t know. Ten seconds. Fifteen.” He looked at the scar. “I didn’t feel it until the drain. The water was freezing. When I went into it, it felt like someone was pulling my arm off.” He was quiet. “Zhendong was half unconscious. He never saw. I never told him. He thinks it happened in the ditch. Against the road. He asked me once and I said it was the road.”

“You lied to him.”

“For nineteen years,” said Chen Si. “I didn’t want him to know that getting him out cost anything. He’d already paid. With his side.” He looked at her. “Clause three doesn’t cover Zhendong.”

She sat up.

She sat up on the bed in the grey Sunday light and looked down at him, and her face was wet and furious, and she took his left arm in both her hands and held it, the scar, wrist to elbow, as if she could take the heat out of it nineteen years late.

“Ten seconds,” she said. “On a hot grate. At sixteen.”

“Fifteen, maybe.”

“Chen Si.”

“It moved,” said Chen Si, simply. “That was the point. It moved.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The drain.

He did not tell her very much about the drain, because he did not remember very much about it. Darkness. Water to his chest, so cold it stopped his breath. The smell. Zhendong’s weight on his shoulder, more and more of it, until it was all of it. His own arm, screaming.

He counted. Out loud. Forty, forty-one, forty-two, keep going, Zhendong, keep going. He counted because if he counted, Zhendong had something to follow. And when Zhendong stopped, and sat down in the water, and said leave me, go, you can make it on your own, he crouched in front of him in the dark and found his face with his hands.

“You don’t leave them behind you,” he said. “Not ever. Everything you leave behind you comes back.”

He had said it about his father. About the staircase. About every man who had crossed the street. He had been saying it to himself for eight months, every night, on his pillow, on his book.

It was the first time he had said it about someone he wanted to keep.

“And you are not something I am leaving behind,” he said. “Get up.”

Zhendong got up.

And somewhere in the second half, when Zhendong was so heavy that Chen Si was carrying him, all of him, fifty kilos carrying eighty, and his voice had gone, and he couldn’t count any more, he started telling the story instead. The monkey king. The simple one. From memory. All of it. The stone and the mountain and the seventy-two transformations and the five hundred years. Out loud. In the dark. Through the water. So that Zhendong would have something to listen to.

So that he wouldn’t fall asleep.

✦ ✦ ✦

“You told him the monkey king,” said Aurelia. “In the drain.”

“All of it,” said Chen Si. “Twice. I got to the end and started again.” He was quiet. “When we came out, I was at the bit where the monk takes him out from under the mountain. Where he’s been trapped for five hundred years, alone, and someone comes and lets him out and gives him a road.” He looked at the ceiling. “It was snowing. It was the most beautiful thing I had ever seen. Snow coming straight down out of a black sky and no wind at all. And I laid him down in the ditch and he looked up at it and said, if I’m dying, don’t take me to a hospital, let me go.”

“And you said no.”

He nodded.

✦ ✦ ✦

The next town. A clinic. A back room. A doctor who looked at two boys in the snow at two in the morning, one bleeding out and one with an arm that was black and blistered from wrist to elbow, and did not ask any questions.

Brothers, he had said. Our name is Wang.

And when the doctor named a price, he went to his plastic bag, which he had carried through the drain on his back, tied with a sleeve, the whole half kilometre, and took out a shirt, and unwrapped a book.

Blue cloth. Paper like skin.

The doctor turned it over in his hands. He was an educated man. He had been something else, once, before he was a doctor in a back room. He knew what it was.

“This is worth more than the clinic,” said the doctor. “More than the town.”

“I know,” said Chen Si.

The doctor looked at him. At the boy on the table. At his arm.

“Are you sure?” said the doctor.

And Chen Si, who was sixteen, and had lost everything, and had held on to one thing, looked at the boy on the table who had come down off the top bunk, and said:

“I’ve paid for something better with it.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Three days,” said Chen Si. “He woke up on the third day. I was asleep in the chair. When I woke up he was looking at me.” He was quiet. “He didn’t say thank you. He’s never said thank you. Not once in nineteen years.”

“No,” said Aurelia. “He said Mine would too. At New Year. About Elowen.” She wiped her face with the back of her hand. “That’s the same thing.”

He looked at her.

“The doctor had a knife,” he said. “For the stitches. On the tray. When Zhendong could sit up, on the fourth day, he picked it up. And looked at me. And held out his left hand.” He turned his own left hand over on the sheet. The palm. The thin white line across it, from the base of the first finger to the heel. “He didn’t say anything. He just held it out. And I took the knife. And I did mine. And he did his. And we put them together.”

She looked at the line on his palm.

“He’s never said what it meant,” said Chen Si. “I’ve never asked.”

“You don’t need to ask,” said Aurelia. “It means I came down off the bunk.” She put her own left hand on his, palm to palm, over the line. “And you said I know where the river goes.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He didn’t say anything.

Neither did she.

They lay in the grey Sunday light with the rain on the window and her palm on his palm, and outside, forty-four floors down, the city went on, and somewhere in it, on the edge of the Walled City, in a florist’s shop with the shutters down, a man with a scar from his ribs to his hip was probably sitting on a stool in the corner, sharpening shears, while his wife finished an order.

“I’m going to tell him,” said Aurelia.

He went still.

“About the grate,” she said. “Not today. Not soon. But one day. When he’s old, and you’re old, and he’s sitting on a stool somewhere being insufferable, I’m going to tell him what it cost. Ten seconds. Wrist to elbow.” She lifted her chin. “Because he should know. Because you lied to him for nineteen years so he wouldn’t think he owed you, and he doesn’t owe you, and you don’t owe him, and that’s the point, Si. Neither of you owes anybody. You just came down off the bunk for each other.”

He looked at her.

Si. She said it the way his mother had said it. And his father, at the top of the staircase. And a boy in a drain, once, bleeding, for the first time.

“Say that again,” he said.

“Which part?”

“You just came down off the bunk for each other.” His voice had gone very rough. “Say it again. Slowly. I want to hear what it sounds like when somebody else says it.”

She said it again. Slowly. With her palm on his palm.

He was quiet.

Then he reached up and pulled her down onto his chest, and put his arms round her, both of them, the scarred one too, and held her so tightly she couldn’t breathe, and didn’t say anything at all while the rain came down.

✦ ✦ ✦

At four o’clock, she got up.

She went to the bookshelf in the study. To the plain wooden case with brass corners, on the top shelf, where it had lived since the twelfth of March, 2029, in its faded yellow silk.

She took it down and brought it back to bed.

She unwrapped it. Blue cloth gone grey. Paper like skin. She opened it, very carefully, to the first page, and held it so he could see.

“Read it to me,” she said.

He looked at her.

“It’s in classical Chinese,” he said. “From 1592. It’s very hard. Half the characters aren’t used any more.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “I won’t understand it.” She lay down beside him with her head on his shoulder and the book open on his chest, over the two pieces of gold. “I want to hear what it sounded like. When your father read it to you.”

He looked down at the page.

Then he began to read.

Slowly. In a low voice. In the grey light, with the rain. The stone on the mountain. The monkey born out of it, with no father and no mother. She didn’t understand a word. She lay with her eyes closed and her hand on his scar and listened to his voice go up and down, the old rhythm of it, the way his father’s must have gone, in a flat in the Western District, before the staircase.

At the end of the first chapter, he stopped.

She opened her eyes.

“Again,” she said.

He looked down at her. His face did something she had seen it do on a balcony and a staircase and a workshop floor and nowhere else.

He turned back to the first page.

He read it again.

chapters.title: Aurelia’s Rules for Galas
chapters.desc: The Shen Foundation gala, December 2025, from the other side of the room. Eleven rules, written on cream paper in red ink and slipped into her husband’s pocket at six o’clock. He has annotated every one. In black. In the car.
chapters.epigraph: Rule 1. Arrive after Elowen. (Annotation, in black: “You have arrived after Elowen at every event for seven years. She has started arriving later on purpose. One day you will both arrive at midnight.”)
chapters.content:
She wrote them at the bench at four in the afternoon, the way she wrote everything, and folded them twice, and slipped them into the inside pocket of his dinner jacket while he was doing up his cufflinks in the bedroom mirror, and kissed him on the jaw, and walked out of the room.

He found them in the car.

He read them under the light in the back seat, while she sat beside him in black velvet doing her lipstick in the little mirror of her gold clutch, very carefully not looking at him.

Then he took out his pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

AURELIA’S RULES FOR GALAS (The Shen Foundation Winter Gala, Harbour Hotel, 20 December. Non-negotiable.)

1. Arrive after Elowen.

He wrote underneath, in black, small:

You have arrived after Elowen at every event for seven years. She has started arriving later on purpose. Last month at the Leungs’ you both sat in your cars outside for forty minutes. Zhendong texted me “Hm”. One day you will both arrive at midnight and the party will be over.

She read it over his shoulder.

“She was early at the Leungs’,” she said. “She was hiding behind the van.”
