“She was in the van,” said Chen Si. “With Zhendong. Waiting for you. It’s a tie. Again.”

She snatched the pen.

✦ ✦ ✦

They arrived at 7:29.

Elowen’s car was already there. Aurelia saw it from the end of the drive, parked under the portico, empty, with Zhao’s driver leaning on the bonnet, and made a small sound of triumph that she would deny for the rest of her life.

“After her,” she said. “Rule one.”

He looked at his watch.

“By two minutes,” he said. “She’s still in the cloakroom. I can see Zhendong through the window. He’s holding her coat.” He paused. “And looking at us.”

Aurelia looked.

In the lit window of the cloakroom, Zhao Zhendong, in black, holding a green coat over one arm, was looking straight at their car with an expression of profound, unhurried judgement.

He raised one hand. Two fingers.

Chen Si said nothing at all, which was worse.

✦ ✦ ✦

2. Do not stand beside me for the first hour. Circulate. People are afraid of you. It’s bad for business. Mine, not yours.

Annotation: I will circulate. I will be standing four metres behind you the entire time. You will not see me. You will know I am there. This is the compromise we reached in 2019 and I see no reason to revisit it.

✦ ✦ ✦

She circulated.

She was very good at it. She had been doing it since she was eleven, on her mother’s arm, in Milan, at parties where the men were three times her age and the women were watching her shoes. She moved through the ballroom of the Harbour Hotel like water, like gold silk, with a word for everyone and a hand on an arm and the exact amount of laughter each person required, and by eight o’clock she had sold two necklaces, booked a private commission from a woman from Shanghai, and made the deputy chairman of a bank blush down to his collar.

She did not see him once.

She knew exactly where he was.

Four metres behind her. By a pillar, or a palm, or the end of the bar. With a glass of something he wasn’t drinking. Watching. Not her face. Never her face, in public; he said that was hers. He watched the people who came near her. Their hands. Their eyes. Their glasses. The waiters with trays.

She knew because every time a man stood too close, he moved away again, quite soon, for no reason he could explain. And every time a waiter came toward her with champagne, the waiter changed direction at the last moment and went somewhere else.

She did not drink champagne at galas. Not since the boat.

Nobody had ever asked her why. Nobody had needed to. He had simply arranged, since the first gala after the hospital, that no glass would reach her that had not come from his own hand.

At 8:12, she turned round, very suddenly, in the middle of a conversation about Swiss watches, and looked straight at the pillar four metres behind her.

He was there. Exactly there.

He did not pretend he wasn’t. He looked back at her, mildly, over a glass of something he wasn’t drinking, and inclined his head, very slightly.

I see you seeing me.

She turned back round and finished her sentence about Swiss watches, and her face was warm, and the man from the bank asked if she was feeling all right, and she said she had never been better in her life.

✦ ✦ ✦

3. Find Miles Wei. Fix his bow tie. He will be wearing it wrong. He always wears it wrong. He wore it wrong at the reunion in 2020 and I fixed it in three movements and Elowen pretended not to watch.

Annotation: I have never met Miles Wei. I have heard about Miles Wei for seven years. You pursued him for two years at school and lost to Elowen and slapped her in the rain. You told me this on our second date. You have told me this approximately forty times since. I would like it recorded that I am not jealous.

Second annotation, below, in red, in her hand: You are SO jealous.

Third annotation, in black: I am not jealous. I am curious about a man who was apparently so attractive at sixteen that the most intelligent woman I have ever met spent two years doing calculus she didn’t need to be near him.

Fourth, red: That IS jealous. That is the definition.

Fifth, black: Fix his tie.

✦ ✦ ✦

She found Miles Wei at 7:31, actually, before she had even taken off her coat, standing alone at the far end of the ballroom by a window with a glass of water in his hand and a bow tie that had been tied, very confidently, by a man who understood the Navier–Stokes equations and not knots.

She walked up behind him.

“Hold still,” she said.

He jumped.

She did it in three movements. Exactly as before. Untie, cross, fold. While he stood there, rigid, staring straight ahead with the expression of a man who had just been ambushed by a past he had spent five years trying not to think about. When she finished, she patted the knot, once, and stepped back, and looked at him.

He was taller than at school. Leaner. With a little grey in his hair at the front that would be more in ten years, and a face that had been, at sixteen, beautiful and closed, like a door, and was now only beautiful, and not closed at all, because somebody had opened it.

She knew who.

She could see Elowen across the room, by the pillar, in green, with her husband. She could see Elowen not looking at them.

“There,” said Aurelia. “Now you look like someone who’s allowed to be here.”

Miles Wei looked down at her.

“Aurelia Song,” he said. A little faintly.

“Chen,” she said. “Aurelia Chen.” She turned. “And this is my husband, who has heard a great deal about you.”

He had materialised behind her. She hadn’t heard him come. She never did.

He held out his hand to Miles Wei.

“Mostly unprintable,” said Chen Si pleasantly.

✦ ✦ ✦

4. Do not, under any circumstances, let Zhao Zhendong glare at Miles Wei all night. It is embarrassing for everyone.

Annotation: I cannot stop Zhendong glaring at anyone. Nobody has ever been able to stop Zhendong glaring at anyone. The last person who tried was in Rotterdam and now lives in Portugal.

Second annotation: He is not glaring at Miles Wei. Watch him. He is glaring at everything that comes within two metres of Lin. Miles Wei is just the thing that has been within two metres of her the longest.

Third annotation, red, very small: …oh.

Fourth, black: Yes.

✦ ✦ ✦

She watched.

From the bar. At 7:54. While Miles Wei, at the far end of the room, with his newly perfect bow tie, stood very still under the most terrifying stare in the city, and tried to look as though he did not know that it was happening.

Zhao stood by a pillar.

Elowen was beside him. In green. Talking to a woman from the Shen Foundation about wedding flowers, very calmly, with a green stain on her thumb, because she had cut three hundred white roses that morning and come straight here.

And Aurelia, who had spent seven years watching her husband watch every waiter, every tray, every man within four metres of her, watched Zhao Zhendong.

He was not glaring at Miles.

He was glaring at everything.

A waiter came toward Elowen with a tray of champagne. Zhao did not move. He did not do anything. He simply looked at the waiter, for perhaps one second, and the waiter discovered urgent business at the other end of the ballroom.

A man from a shipping company came to say hello to Elowen and stood a little too close. Zhao moved. Half a step. No more. Half a step closer to his wife.

The man from the shipping company remembered he had left something in his car.

Aurelia stayed at the bar and watched him do it twice more.

Then she turned round and looked at the pillar four metres behind her, where her husband was standing, watching every waiter with a tray who came within reach of her.

“It’s the same,” she said. Not loudly. He was four metres away. He heard anyway.

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

“You do exactly the same thing.”

“We learned it in the same place,” said Chen Si. “From the same people. In a building where nobody came.” He looked at her. “So now we stand by the pillar. And everything that comes near you goes through us first.”

She looked at him.

Then she raised her voice. Not much. Just enough to carry to the far end of the room, to a man by a pillar in black.

“Zhendong,” she said, very sweetly, “Elowen has three hundred white roses to do for a wedding tomorrow, and you’re driving her to the flower market at half past three in the morning to carry the buckets.”

Zhao turned his head.

He looked at her across the ballroom for four seconds.

Elowen, beside him, had gone very slightly pink.

“Hm,” said Zhao.

And moved half a step closer.

✦ ✦ ✦

5. Whisper to my husband, at least once, that he is still jealous. He will pretend not to hear. He will have heard.

Annotation: I always hear.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did it at 7:36, actually, standing between him and Miles Wei, with Miles Wei shaking his hand and Chen Si saying mostly unprintable.

She leaned back, very slightly, against his shoulder, and said, without turning her head, in a voice too low for anyone else:

“You’re still jealous.”

He did not react. At all. His face did not move. He went on shaking Miles Wei’s hand, pleasantly, for exactly as long as was polite.

Then he let go. And put his hand on the small of her back. Where it always went. And left it there.

And, under cover of a passing waiter, against her hair, said:

“I am not jealous. I have simply never forgotten that there was a time, before the balcony, when you wanted something that wasn’t me. And I would like him to know that I know.”

She went very still.

“That,” she said, under her breath, “is the most jealous thing I have ever heard.”

“Clause three,” said Chen Si. “I’m not allowed to lie.”

She turned her head and looked up at him.

His face was perfectly mild. His eyes were not.

She was going to be thinking about that, she realised, for the rest of the evening. In the middle of conversations. In the middle of selling necklaces. She was going to be thinking about the look in his eyes when he said I would like him to know that I know, and losing her place in sentences.

He knew that.

That was why he had said it.

✦ ✦ ✦

6. No champagne. Not from a tray. Not ever. Only from your hand.

Annotation: Yes.

That was all. One word. Underlined twice.

✦ ✦ ✦

7. If I look at you across the room and touch my left earring, it means come and get me, I am bored. If I touch my right earring, it means come and get me, I am about to say something I will regret to someone important. If I touch both, it means come and get me now, take me home, and I will explain in the car.

Annotation: You have never once in seven years touched your left earring. Or your right. You have touched both, every time, at every gala, at approximately ten-thirty. I have started arriving at ten-twenty-five to stand where you can see me.

Second annotation, red: That’s because I am never bored and I never regret anything. I just want to go home with you.

Third, black: I know.

✦ ✦ ✦

At 10:22, standing by the window with the woman from Shanghai, talking about emeralds, she reached up with both hands, very casually, and touched both earrings.

She did not look across the room.

She didn’t need to. By the time she lowered her hands, he was there. At her elbow. Saying something very charming to the woman from Shanghai in Mandarin about the weather in Hangzhou, and taking Aurelia’s coat from the cloakroom attendant who had appeared beside him as if summoned, and putting it round her shoulders.

“You’re early,” said Chen Si, as they walked to the door. “It’s 10:23.”

“I couldn’t wait.”

He looked down at her.

“Neither could I,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

8. Say goodbye to Elowen. Politely. With no score.

Annotation: You will not manage this.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not manage this.

They passed Elowen and Zhao at the door. Elowen was putting on her green coat, which Zhao was holding, and Aurelia stopped, and Elowen stopped, and they looked at each other.

“Lovely evening,” said Aurelia.

“Wasn’t it,” said Elowen.

“Your flowers were very good.”

“Your necklace,” said Elowen, “was very slightly crooked. On the left. All night.”

Aurelia’s hand went to her throat before she could stop it.

Elowen smiled. Very slightly. And walked out of the door on her husband’s arm into the December night.

“Forty-three,” said Elowen, over her shoulder.

“It wasn’t crooked!” said Aurelia, to the empty doorway.

Beside her, Chen Si laughed.

“It wasn’t,” he said. “I would have told you.”

“I know it wasn’t.”

“She knew that too.” He held the car door open. “That’s why it worked.”

✦ ✦ ✦

9. In the car, do not say anything clever. Just hold my hand.

Annotation: Agreed.

10. In the lift, say something clever.

Annotation: Agreed. I have been preparing since Thursday.

11. At home, you set the terms. All night. Unless and until I say otherwise.

Annotation:

He hadn’t written anything beside eleven.

She noticed that in the car, holding his hand, not saying anything clever, looking down at the cream paper in her lap in the light from the street.

Ten annotations. Neat black lines. And beside eleven, nothing.

She looked at him.

He was looking out of the window, at the harbour going past, with his thumb moving on the back of her hand in small circles.

“You didn’t annotate eleven,” she said.

“Rule nine,” said Chen Si, not looking round. “Nothing clever in the car.”

She looked at the blank space beside eleven for the rest of the drive.

✦ ✦ ✦

In the lift, going up forty-four floors, he said something clever.

He turned to her. He took the cream paper out of her hand, very gently, and folded it, and put it back in his inside pocket, on the left, beside the gold.

“Rule eleven,” he said. “I didn’t annotate it because you got it wrong.”

She looked up at him.

“I never get the rules wrong.”

“Rule eleven,” said Chen Si, “says that at home, I set the terms. All night.” The lift went past thirty. “But that’s clause nine backwards. Clause nine says you set the terms, unless and until you say otherwise. Rule eleven says I set them, unless and until you say otherwise.” He looked down at her. “Which means you’ve already said otherwise. In writing. In red ink. At four o’clock this afternoon.”

She stared at him.

“Which means,” said Chen Si, very mildly, as the lift went past forty, “that I have been setting the terms since four o’clock this afternoon. You just didn’t know.” He leaned down until his mouth was beside her ear. “Who do you think told Qian to have the champagne kept away from you? Who do you think told the cloakroom attendant to be standing by at ten-twenty? Who do you think sent the waiter away from Lin?”

“That was Zhendong.”

“That was me,” said Chen Si. “I texted him. At 7:53. One word.” He straightened up. “He did it because I asked.”

She opened her mouth.

She closed it.

“What word?” she said.

The lift doors opened on the forty-fourth floor.

He took her hand, and led her out, into the dark hall, and stopped, and turned round, and looked at her in her black velvet and her gold and her necklace, which was not crooked at all.

“Mine,” said Chen Si.

Then, before she could find anything clever to say, he set the terms.

“Shoes,” he said. “Off. Here.” He watched her step out of them, one and then the other, and did not help. “Now the necklace. Slowly. I want to watch you take off the thing Lin said was crooked.”

“It wasn’t crooked.”

“I know. Take it off anyway.” He held out his hand, and when it lay warm in his palm he put it in his pocket, with her rules, beside the gold. “Leave the earrings.”

“Why the—”

“Because,” said Chen Si, against her ear, “at some point tonight you’re going to touch both of them, and I want to find out what it means when we’re already home.”

She didn’t say anything clever.

She didn’t say anything at all, which, she would point out to him much later, around three in the morning, was a breach of rule ten, and therefore technically a loss, and therefore the first gala in seven years she had come home from without winning.

“I don’t mind,” she said, into his shoulder, in the dark.

“I know,” said Chen Si. “You touched both earrings at 10:22.”

“Is that a rule?”

“It is now,” he said. “Rule twelve. I’ll annotate it in the morning.”

chapters.title: Chen Si Reads Her Reviews
chapters.desc: Every review. Every one. Since 2018. In a folder on his laptop called “Rotterdam (Q3)” so that nobody will ever open it. And one night she finds out that he does not only read them. He answers them. Under a name she would recognise anywhere.
chapters.epigraph: “Who is LiftedAtEveryTurn?” “I have no idea.” “Clause three.” “…Ah.”
chapters.content:
She found out because of a man called Desmond Holt.

Desmond Holt wrote about jewellery for a magazine in London that everyone in the trade read and nobody admitted to reading, and he had disliked her since 2021, since Balcony, in the particular way that men who write about beautiful things sometimes dislike women who make them. He called Balcony “a therapy session with a hallmark.” He called Seconda “an expensive tantrum about Mummy.” He called her, in a review of the new Singapore boutique, in a sentence that was quoted in four other magazines and that she read once and never read again, “a gangster’s wife playing at haute joaillerie with her husband’s money.”

She did not respond. She never responded. She had decided that at twenty-one, after the first bad review, sitting on the floor of her first shop with the magazine in her lap: you never respond. You make the next thing better. That’s the only answer.

So she didn’t.

But on a Wednesday night in February, at eleven, Lily rang her, and said, in a strange voice, “Mrs. Chen, have you seen the comments under Desmond Holt’s piece?”

“I never read the comments.”

“I think,” said Lily carefully, “you might want to read these ones.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She read them in bed.

On her tablet. In the dark. With Topolino asleep on her feet and Ritardo asleep on her husband, who was asleep, on his back, with his reading glasses still on and a contract open on his chest.

Desmond Holt’s piece was about the new collection. A short one, eight pieces, a winter collection, rings and cuffs in white gold and black enamel that she had called Inverno and that he had called “joyless, which is at least a change from her usual hysteria.”

Underneath, there were two hundred and eleven comments.

Most of them were what comments always were. People agreeing. People disagreeing. People saying things about her that she had learned, at twenty-one, not to read.

And then, on the fourth one down, a reply.

From a user called LiftedAtEveryTurn.

Mr. Holt describes the Inverno pieces as joyless. He appears not to have turned them over. Each piece is engraved on the inside surface, where it lies against the skin, with a single line. The cuff (Inverno III) reads “The first snow I ever saw was through a drain.” The ring (Inverno VI) reads “Somebody came.” Perhaps Mr. Holt finds these lines joyless. I would suggest that he has confused joy with noise. The pieces are quiet because what they are about is quiet. That is not the absence of feeling. It is its most precise expression.

She sat up in bed.

She read it again.

Nobody knew about the engravings on Inverno. Not yet. They had not been in the press release. They had not been in the photographs. She had told Enzo, and Lily, and one other person, at the bench, at two in the morning, with his coffee going cold at her elbow, and he had read every line and said nothing at all and then kissed the inside of her wrist.

She scrolled down.

✦ ✦ ✦

LiftedAtEveryTurn had replied to a great many comments.

Not angrily. Never angrily. Calmly, precisely, at length, in perfect English and occasionally in perfect French, with references. To a man who said her work was derivative, a three-paragraph history of the broken-and-mended motif in East Asian metalwork, with dates, ending: The difference is that Mrs. Chen does not hide the mend. She cuts it in white gold, so you cannot miss it. If that is derivative, it is derivative of something nobody else has had the courage to do. To a woman who said she only got where she was because of her husband, a single sentence: Her husband has never paid for a gram of her gold; clause one of their marriage contract forbids it, which you would know if you had read the profile in the Financial Times, which I recommend.

To someone who said the Balcony collection was self-indulgent, a long, quiet paragraph about the line Don’t let them talk you into taking out the break, that ended: I was there when it was said. I can confirm that it was not self-indulgent. It was the truth, said by someone who had waited six weeks to say it, to someone who needed to hear it more than anyone in the house.

She stopped scrolling.

She looked at the account name.

LiftedAtEveryTurn.

She clicked on it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The account was seven years old.

It had been opened in March 2019. The week after a Tuesday at the counter of a boutique on Harbour Road.

It had posted two thousand, four hundred and six comments. Every single one of them was under a review of her work.

Every review. Every magazine. Every newspaper. Every blog, every forum, every trade journal she had ever been mentioned in, in four languages, for seven years. The good ones too. Under the New York Times piece about Balcony, the one that had made her mother write mine in the margin, there was a comment from LiftedAtEveryTurn that said only:

Yes. Exactly this. Thank you for seeing it.

Under a tiny paragraph in a local magazine about the opening of her second boutique, in 2019, a paragraph so small she had forgotten it existed, a comment:

I was outside. In the rain. She didn’t see me. She cut the ribbon herself, with her own shears, and then she went back inside and cried for one minute behind the counter, and then she came back out and sold a ring. I have never seen anyone so brave about something so small. I hope she opens a hundred more.

She put the tablet down on the duvet.

She sat in the dark.

Beside her, on his back, with his reading glasses on and a contract on his chest and a grey kitten asleep on his stomach, her husband breathed slowly and evenly, and did not know that she knew.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not wake him.

She lay down beside him in the dark and looked at the ceiling and thought about two thousand, four hundred and six comments.

Seven years.

She thought about him on the thirty-ninth floor at seven in the morning, before Rotterdam, reading a review of her work in a trade journal from Antwerp in Dutch, which he did not speak, with a dictionary open on his laptop. She thought about him in the back of the car between meetings, typing a three-paragraph history of East Asian metalwork with his thumb. She thought about him in the ICU, in the six weeks he couldn’t get out of bed, when she had been running the Syndicate from his armchair, and he had been lying in a hospital bed with nothing to do—

She sat up again. She picked up the tablet.

She scrolled to January 2020.

He had posted forty-one comments in January 2020. From a hospital bed. With a tube in his arm and Dr. Ma taking his laptop away every afternoon. Forty-one. Under every review of the AURELIA winter collection, which she had launched, alone, in December, the week before the boat, and which she had not thought about since, because her husband had been dying.

Under the worst one, from Desmond Holt, the first time Holt had ever written about her, which called it “pretty, shallow, and a little desperate,” there was a comment, posted at 3:14 in the morning on the ninth of January 2020.

She made this collection in the same month she was learning to run four hundred people’s livelihoods, and she made it beautifully, and then she sat in a corridor for nine nights and did not cry, and she is out there tonight, the tenth. Mr. Holt, you have never in your life been as brave as the woman you are describing, and you never will be. I have nothing else to say to you. I am going to sleep now, because she has asked me to, and I do what she asks.

✦ ✦ ✦

She cried.

She did not mean to. She sat up in bed in the dark at one in the morning with the tablet on her knees and cried, silently, the way he had once cried in the grey light with a gold tag above his face, and Topolino woke up on her feet and looked at her with his enormous copper eyes and came up the bed and sat on her lap and purred, very loudly, which did not help at all.

The sound woke him.

Not the crying. She was very quiet. Topolino purring, which was like a small engine.

He opened his eyes. He took off his reading glasses. He looked at her sitting up in bed in the dark with a cat on her lap and her face wet and the tablet glowing on her knees.

He went very still.

He looked at the screen.

“Ah,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Who,” said Aurelia, “is LiftedAtEveryTurn?”

He looked at her.

“I have no idea,” he said.

“Clause three.”

He closed his eyes.

“Ah,” he said again.

She waited.

He opened his eyes and looked at the ceiling.

“It was meant to be once,” he said. “The first one. March 2019. The week after the proposal. There was a review in a magazine in Shanghai that said her spring collection was derivative and overdesigned, and I read it on the thirty-ninth floor, and I—” He stopped. “I wanted to have the man killed.”

“Chen Si.”

“I didn’t,” he said. “Obviously. Clause four. You’d have left me. And taken the man in the cardigan.” He was quiet. “But I wanted to. Very much. For about an hour. And then I thought, she wouldn’t want me to do anything. She’d want me to just read it, and know it was wrong, and say nothing.” He looked at her. “And I couldn’t say nothing. I tried. For a whole day. And at eleven at night I made an account and wrote three paragraphs about the history of the solitaire setting, very politely, and explained exactly why the man was wrong, and posted it, and went to bed, and slept for the first time in a week.”

She stared at him.

“It was meant to be once,” said Chen Si again. “And then the next review came. And I thought, well, I have the account now.”

“Two thousand four hundred and six times,” said Aurelia. “I counted. In the dark, just now, with a cat on me.”

✦ ✦ ✦

“Why didn’t you tell me?” she said.

He took a while to answer.

“Because you told me,” he said, “the first night in the basement under the funeral shop, over the ledgers, with chilli oil on your chin, that you never respond. You said, you never respond. You make the next thing better. That’s the only answer.” He looked at her. “And I thought that was the bravest thing I’d ever heard. And I didn’t want you to think I thought you needed help.” He paused. “You don’t. You never have. You’d have been fine without one single comment. You’d have made the next thing better.”

“Then why—”

“Because I’m not brave,” said Chen Si simply. “Not about you. I can sit in a room with a man who’s trying to take my port and not blink. I can walk into a hall at six in the morning and watch Fu Jianguo go down the stairs. I can’t read a stranger in London calling you a gangster’s wife and do nothing.” He looked at the screen, at Desmond Holt’s piece, at the comment four down. “So I don’t do nothing. I do the smallest thing I can. I write down the truth, very politely, under the lie. And then I go to sleep.”

She looked at him.

“You wrote that he’d never been as brave as me,” she said. “From the ICU. At three in the morning.”

He went very still.

“You read that one.”

She nodded.

“I was on a lot of morphine,” said Chen Si, with dignity.

“You said I do what she asks.”

“That,” said Chen Si, “was not the morphine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She put the tablet down on the bedside table, face down.

She put Topolino on the floor, gently, where he sat and looked offended and then went and got on the chair.

She lay down beside her husband, on her side, facing him, very close, in the dark.

“Seven years,” she said. “Every review. Even the ones in Dutch.”

“Especially the ones in Dutch,” said Chen Si. “They’re very blunt, the Dutch. I had to use a dictionary. It took me forty minutes once to find out whether a man in Antwerp had called you bold or loud.”

“Which was it?”

“Bold,” said Chen Si. “I wrote to thank him.”

She laughed. Wet. Into his shoulder.

“Do you read the good ones too?” she said. “Or only the bad ones?”

“All of them.” He was quiet. “The good ones I read twice.”

She lifted her head.

“Twice?”

“Once for the review,” said Chen Si. “And once to imagine your face when you read it.” He looked at her in the dark. “I don’t usually get to see you read them. You read them at the bench, alone, at two in the morning. So I imagine it. I imagine you reading the New York Times about Balcony. I imagine you reading Geneva.” His voice went very low. “I’ve imagined your face reading good reviews of your work about two thousand times, Aurelia. It’s my favourite thing to imagine. Better than Fu Jianguo on the stairs.”

She didn’t say anything.

Then she reached over him, and picked the tablet up off the bedside table, and turned it on.

“What are you doing?” he said.

“Reading you a review,” said Aurelia. “Out loud. So you don’t have to imagine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She found the New York Times. The one about Balcony. From 2021.

She lay on her back, beside him, with the tablet held up above her face in the dark and his arm under her neck, and read it to him. All of it. Every word. Slowly. In her own voice. The part about the worst night of her life. The part about the most important collection in a decade. The part about the line along the seam.

He didn’t look at the tablet.

He looked at her face.

She could feel him looking. The whole time. She didn’t look back. She read. And when she got to the end, to the last line, which said that she was the only designer working today who understood that a mend could be more beautiful than the thing that broke, her voice went, and she couldn’t finish it, and she put the tablet down on her chest and turned her face into his shoulder.

“Well?” she said, muffled. “Was it like you imagined?”

He was quiet for a while.

“No,” said Chen Si. “Much better.”

✦ ✦ ✦

In the morning, she logged on to Desmond Holt’s piece about Inverno.

She scrolled to the fourth comment. LiftedAtEveryTurn. He appears not to have turned them over.

She clicked reply.

She had never once, in nine years, responded to a review. She had decided at twenty-one, on the floor of her first shop, that she never would.

She typed, with her thumb, in the kitchen on the forty-fourth floor, in his grey jumper, at seven in the morning, while he made coffee he wasn’t going to drink and pretended not to watch:

Thank you. I think you might be the only person in the world who has read everything I’ve ever made. I would like to meet you. I’m free tonight, at eight, in the basement under the funeral shop in the old town. I’ll be the one with chilli oil on her chin. — A.C.

She posted it.

She put the tablet down.

He was standing at the counter with the coffee pot in his hand, very still, looking at her.

“You responded,” he said.

“Once,” said Aurelia. “It’s meant to be once.”

He looked at her.

Then he put down the coffee pot, and crossed the kitchen, and took her face in his hands, and kissed her, slowly, in the grey morning light, while two cats watched from the windowsill.

“Eight o’clock,” he said, against her mouth.

“Don’t be late.”

“I’ll be four minutes early,” said Chen Si, “and stand outside, and wait.”

“I know,” said Aurelia. “I’ve always known. I used to watch you through the window.”

✦ ✦ ✦

He was four minutes early.

He came down the stone steps sideways at 7:56, in a grey suit, with a coffee cup in his hand that he wasn’t drinking and a folder under his arm.

She was at the corner table. The one where she had read four ledgers in a single night.

He sat down across from her.

He opened the folder. Inside, printed out, two thousand, four hundred and seven pages. One for every comment. And on top, the last one, the two thousand four hundred and seventh, her reply, in her own words, I would like to meet you.

Under it, in his precise black hand, lifted at every turn, he had written his response.

Hello. I’m the man who came to rent your shop. I’ve read everything you’ve ever made. I would like to read everything you ever make, for the rest of my life. Please don’t stop.

Old Fan, at the wok, without being asked, put down a plate of pork belly in chilli oil so red it was almost black.

She ate it. All of it. With chilli oil on her chin.

He watched her. The whole time.

He didn’t have to imagine.

chapters.title: Milan in August
chapters.desc: The city is empty. Everyone who matters has gone to the lakes. The palazzo where they were married is closed for the summer and she has the only key. There is a problem, though, and it is clause ten: the safe word is the name of the city they are standing in, and every waiter in Milan keeps saying it.
chapters.epigraph: “Clause ten. Temporary rider. While physically present in the city of Milan, the word is ‘Rotterdam’.” “Why Rotterdam?” “Because nothing about Rotterdam has ever been sexy.”
chapters.content:
The problem became apparent at the airport.

“Benvenuti a Milano,” said the woman at passport control, cheerfully, stamping their passports, and Chen Si, who had been looking at his wife’s mouth instead of the queue, stopped dead in the middle of the hall at Linate as if he had walked into a wall.

Aurelia, three steps ahead, turned round.

“What?”

He looked at her. He looked at the woman at passport control, who was now stamping someone else’s passport, still saying it, to every single person, Milano, Milano, benvenuti a Milano.

“Clause ten,” he said, faintly.

She looked at him blankly.

Then she understood, and put her hand over her mouth, and laughed so hard in the middle of the arrivals hall that two carabinieri turned round to look.

✦ ✦ ✦

“It doesn’t count,” she said, in the car, still laughing. “It doesn’t count if a woman at passport control says it.”

“The clause says if either party says it,” said Chen Si. “It doesn’t say anything about passport control. But it also says in any room, in any circumstances.” He looked out of the window, at the city going past, the yellow trams and the shuttered shops and the heat coming up off the stones. “Every sign says it. Every bus. Every newspaper. Every waiter. Benvenuti a Milano. Milano centrale. Il Corriere di Milano.” He turned and looked at her. “We are going to spend five days in a city whose name means everything stops.”

She looked at him.

He looked back.

She was still laughing. But there was something else in her face, too, under it, that he had been watching for eleven years and knew very well.

“Then I’ll write a rider,” said Aurelia.

✦ ✦ ✦

She wrote it on the back of the hotel registration card, at the desk of the small old hotel on the Via Bigli, in red, while the night porter watched in mild bewilderment.

Clause ten. Temporary rider. While either party is physically present in the city of Milan, the word is “Rotterdam”. On departure, the word reverts. Signed A.C.

She turned it round and held out the pen.

He read it.

“Why Rotterdam?” he said.

“Because,” said Aurelia, “nothing about Rotterdam has ever been sexy. Nobody has ever said Rotterdam in a moment of passion. You could say it in the middle of anything and it would stop at once.” She tilted her head. “It’s the least sexy word in the world.”

He looked at the card.

“I have a call with Rotterdam on Thursday,” he said.

“Not any more,” said Aurelia. “Qian cancelled it. I asked him.” She smiled. “He wrote dental in the calendar. Five days.”

He signed the card.

The night porter, who spoke no Chinese and very little English, but who had been working at a hotel in Milan for thirty years and knew exactly what he was looking at, took the card back with enormous gravity and put it in a drawer and handed them the key and said, “Buona permanenza, signori,” and did not say the name of the city once.

✦ ✦ ✦

Milan in August was empty.

That was why she had brought him. She told him on the first morning, at seven, walking through the Quadrilatero with the shops all shuttered and the streets silent and the light coming down gold between the buildings like something poured. Everyone who mattered had gone. To the lakes. To the sea. To the mountains. The city emptied out in August like a theatre after the last act, and the people who stayed behind were the ones who had nowhere else to go, or nothing to prove.

“My grandmother used to bring me,” she said. “Every August. When I was small. Before Vienna. Before rankings.” She looked up at a balcony, high up, with geraniums on it. “My mother was always at the sea. Being photographed. My grandmother stayed in the city, because she said the city was only honest in August, and she took me everywhere. To the market. To the Duomo roof. To a little bar in Brera where the old men played cards.” She was quiet. “She was the only person in my family who never asked me to win.”

He took her hand.

“Show me,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She showed him everything.

The roof of the Duomo, at eight in the morning, when the cleaners were the only people there, and the marble was already warm under their hands, and the whole city lay out under them like a map. The market at Papiniano, half shut, where a woman selling peaches recognised her, after twenty-four years, and shrieked, and kissed her on both cheeks, and looked at Chen Si, and said something very fast in dialect that made Aurelia go pink to the roots of her hair.

“What did she say?” he asked, walking away, with a bag of peaches.

“She said,” said Aurelia, through her teeth, “that he looks at you like a man looking at bread after Lent.”

He considered this.

“That’s accurate,” he said mildly. “I fasted for twenty-two years. I think I’m entitled to look at bread.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The bar in Brera was still there.

The same one. Small and dark, with a zinc counter and a television in the corner showing cycling, and four old men at the back playing cards, who looked up when she came in, and one of them, the oldest, with a white moustache and hands like roots, put down his cards very slowly.

“La piccola Conti,” he said.

Aurelia stopped in the doorway.

He was ninety-seven, perhaps. He had been seventy when she was seven. He had taught her a card game called scopa at this table, on a summer afternoon, while her grandmother drank a coffee at the counter, and he had let her win, every time, and she had known he was letting her win, and had loved him for it, because nobody else in her life had ever let her.

“Signor Bruno,” she said.

He looked at her. At the gold. At the face. At the man beside her.

Then he said, in the old Milanese dialect, the one there were only about four people left who spoke, something long and slow and rough, and the other three old men laughed, and Aurelia went pink again and opened her mouth to translate.

She didn’t get the chance.

Chen Si answered him.

In dialect. In the old Milanese. Slowly, carefully, with the accent of a woman at the consulate on Wednesdays at seven in the morning, and the grammar of a man who had practised every single word in the car on the way to the thirty-ninth floor for nine years.

There was a silence at the back of the bar.

Signor Bruno stared at him.

Then he threw back his head and laughed, a great cracked laugh like a door coming off its hinges, and banged the table so hard the cards jumped, and pulled out a chair, and said, in Italian now, wiping his eyes, “Siediti. Siediti, cinese. Giochiamo.”

Sit down. Sit down, Chinese. We’ll play.

✦ ✦ ✦

“What did he say?” she demanded, an hour later, outside, in the heat, while he walked beside her with an expression of profound and complicated satisfaction. He had lost eleven games of scopa to four men with a combined age of three hundred and forty, and they had let him lose, every time, and he had known, and had loved them for it. “What did he say? The first thing? The thing they laughed at?”

“He said,” said Chen Si, “that the little Conti girl had brought home a man who looked like he could kill a horse with his bare hands, and did I intend to, and if so, could I start with the horse in the next street, which was very loud at night.”

She stared at him.

“And what did you say?”

He looked straight ahead. His ears had gone very slightly red.

“I said I only kill things that try to hurt her,” said Chen Si, “and that I’d leave the horse alone, unless it looked at her wrong.”

She stopped walking.

In the middle of the Via Brera, in the August heat, with the shutters down all along the street and nobody there at all.

She looked up at him.

“You realise,” she said, very slowly, “that by tonight every old person in Milan who still speaks that dialect, all four of them, will know that the little Conti girl’s husband said he only kills things that hurt her.”

“Yes,” said Chen Si.

“My grandmother would have—” She stopped. Her face did something. “She would have loved you.”

He looked down at her.

“I know,” he said. “You told me. On the forty-fourth floor. The first winter. You said, she would have liked you, because you never ask me to win.” He took her hand. “I learned her language so I could say it back.”

✦ ✦ ✦

The palazzo was on the Naviglio Grande.

The canal was low and green in the August heat, and the cafés along it were shuttered, and the only sound was a single bicycle somewhere, ticking past on the stones.

She had the only key.

She had bought it. Not the palazzo; the key. In 2019, after the wedding, from the old contessa who owned the building and lived in Switzerland and let out the ground-floor rooms for weddings and parties. The contessa had looked at the young woman in ivory silk who had been married that morning in her courtyard, with a gold chain down her bare back, and asked what on earth she wanted with a key to a building she would never own.

For August, Aurelia had said. When it’s closed. I want to come back.

The contessa had looked at her, and then at the man beside her. And then she had taken the key off her own ring and given it to her for nothing, and said, The courtyard is cooler at night. Bring wine. Don’t break the mirrors.

✦ ✦ ✦

The mirrors were in the long room on the first floor.

Eight of them. Old. Venetian. On every wall, in gilt frames gone soft and dark with two hundred years of candle smoke, facing each other, so that if you stood in the middle of the room you were reflected into the distance forever, smaller and smaller, a thousand times, in the old silvered glass that made everything gold.

She had been married downstairs. In the courtyard. In ivory, with her grandmother’s veil. And afterwards, at midnight, she had brought him up here, to this room, and stood him in the middle of the floor, and looked at him in eight mirrors, and not been able to speak.

She had never told anyone what happened in this room on the night of her wedding.

She unlocked the door.

She turned on one lamp, very low, in the corner. She opened the long windows onto the canal, so that the warm air came in and the shutters moved.

She turned round.

He was standing in the doorway in his shirtsleeves. White linen, open at the throat. The heat had got into everything; his hair was damp at the temples and his shirt was creased and he had peach on his fingers, still, from the market, and gold on his chest, three pieces, and he was looking at her in eight mirrors at once.

“Middle of the room,” said Aurelia.

He came to the middle of the room.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Rotterdam,” she said.

He looked at her.

“Just checking you remember the word,” said Aurelia. “Say it if you need it.”

“I won’t need it.”

“You don’t know that,” said Aurelia. “You don’t know what I’m going to do.”

He looked at her, in the low gold light, standing in front of him in a white silk slip dress and bare feet and nothing else at all except the gold.

All of it. Every piece. She had put it on at the hotel at six o’clock, in front of him, slowly, piece by piece, while he sat on the end of the bed and was not allowed to help. Eleven bracelets. Nine rings. The earrings. The long chain from the wedding, the one that went down her back. The broken necklace at her throat. She was wearing, he had calculated in the car, approximately three kilos of gold, and it moved when she moved and caught the lamp in every one of the eight mirrors so that the whole room was full of small gold lights.

“No,” he said. “I never do.”

She came round behind him. Slowly. He could see her in the mirrors. Every mirror. Eight of her, moving round him, and behind them a thousand more, getting smaller and smaller into the old glass, all of them coming toward him.

She stopped behind him.

She put her mouth by his ear.

“Count them,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

“Count what?” said Chen Si.

“The pieces,” said Aurelia. “The gold. Everything I’m wearing.” She put her hands on his shoulders, from behind, and he felt the cold of nine rings through his shirt. “I’m going to take them off. One at a time. And put them on you. And you’re going to count, out loud. And you’re not allowed to move, or turn round, or touch me, or look anywhere except the mirror in front of you.” She let her breath move against his neck. “And if you lose count, I start again. From the first one. And put them all back on me.”

He closed his eyes.

“Open them,” said Aurelia. “Mirror. In front of you. Watch.”

He opened them.

In the mirror in front of him, in the old gold glass, his wife stood behind him with her chin on his shoulder and her eyes on his, and reached down, slowly, and took off the first bracelet.

“One,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

She put it on his wrist.

Not quickly. She took his left hand in hers, from behind, and lifted it, and slid the bracelet over his knuckles, very slowly, and let it fall down onto his wrist, onto the scar, and then put her mouth on the inside of his wrist, just above it, where his pulse was.

“Two,” he said. It came out rougher than he meant.

The second bracelet. The other wrist. Her mouth on that one too.

“Three.”

She took off a ring. The plain one, on her right hand. She put it on his little finger, where it only went halfway, and kissed his knuckle, and left it there.

“Four.”

He watched it in the mirror. In eight mirrors. In a thousand. A thousand of her, taking the gold off herself and putting it on him, piece by piece, and her mouth following every piece, and her eyes, every time she lifted her head, finding his in the glass.

By eleven he was not standing very steadily.

By fifteen his voice had gone completely.

By eighteen, when she reached up behind her own neck, slowly, in the mirror, and unfastened the long chain from the wedding, the one that had gone down the bare length of her back in the courtyard downstairs in front of eleven guests, and drew it off, link by link, warm from her skin, and stood on her toes behind him and fastened it round his neck, so that it lay against his back under his shirt, the whole length of his spine, he lost count.

He didn’t know what came next.

He stood in the middle of the room with eighteen pieces of her gold on him and her breath on the back of his neck and his heart going so hard he could see it in the mirror, in his throat, and he could not remember the next number.

She waited.

“You’ve lost count,” she said.

“No.”

“You have.” Her hands came round his chest from behind, flat, over the three pieces of gold that had always been there. “What’s next? After eighteen?”

He opened his mouth.

He closed it.

“Nineteen,” said Aurelia. Very gently. In his ear. “It’s nineteen. Say it.”

He said it.

“That doesn’t count,” said Aurelia, “if I tell you.” She kissed the back of his neck, below his hair, where the chain had just been fastened. “From the first one.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She took it all back.

Every piece. In reverse. Off him and onto herself again, the chain and the rings and the bracelets, with her mouth on every place she took one from. In the mirror. In eight mirrors. Slowly. While he stood in the middle of the room and made a sound, about halfway through, that she had heard exactly twice before in eleven years and had written down, both times, afterwards, at the bench, on cream paper, in red, so that she would never forget it.

And then she came round in front of him.

For the first time. Not in the mirror. In front of him. Close. In white silk and three kilos of gold, with her face flushed and her eyes very dark and her mouth an inch from his.

“Again,” she said. “From one.”

He looked down at her.

“Aurelia,” he said. His voice was a ruin. “I am not going to make it to nineteen.” He didn’t move his hands from his sides. “Let me touch you. Just your waist. Please. I’ll still count.”

“Then say the word,” said Aurelia sweetly.

He looked at her.

“Rotterdam,” he said.

She stopped at once, completely, the way the clause said. No questions. Her hands went still on his chest and her face changed, all at once, the teasing going out of it, and she looked up at him, searching, ready to hold him, ready to sit on the floor with him for as long as he wanted.

“Are you—”

“I’m fine,” said Chen Si. “I just wanted to see if it worked.”

She stared at him.

“It works,” he said. “Thank you.” And then, before she could say anything at all: “Otherwise.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She had forgotten.

Clause nine. When she says otherwise, he sets the terms. It said when she says otherwise. It did not say what happened if he said it first, in her own accent, and then waited, with his eyes on hers, until she heard herself say it back before she had decided to. Otherwise, she had said, faintly, to the canal. She had written it eleven years ago on the floor of her flat at two in the morning and had read it a thousand times and had never once noticed.

He had.

He picked her up.

All of her. Three kilos of gold and white silk and outrage. He lifted her off the floor as if she weighed nothing, and she said that is not how the clause works, and he said read it again, and she said I wrote it, and he said then you should have been more careful, and carried her to the long window over the canal where the shutters were moving in the warm night air, and set her down on the wide stone sill with her back against the frame and the whole of Milan behind her, dark and silent and empty and gold.

He stood between her knees.

He looked at her.

“My turn,” he said. “Count.”

She looked at him.

“Count what?”

He took her left hand, and lifted it, and very slowly, without taking his eyes off her face, slid the first bracelet off her wrist.

“One,” said Aurelia Chen.

✦ ✦ ✦

She lost count at seven.

She had always known she would. She had calculated it, in the car, the way she calculated everything. She had calculated that she would last until about twelve, if he went slowly, and that he would go slowly, because he always did, because he had learned from her.

She had not calculated his mouth.

She had not calculated that he would take off each piece and then, instead of putting it on himself, put it on the stone sill beside her, in a row, very carefully, in order, the way he had once laid out her gold on Enzo’s bench in the workshop, and then say something against the place he had taken it from. In dialect. In the old Milanese. Things she had not heard anyone say since her grandmother died. Not words of love. Not exactly. Old words. Words for the light on the Duomo at eight in the morning, and the sound of the trams, and the smell of peaches in August, and a little girl at a card table in Brera being let win.

At seven, he said, against the inside of her elbow, la piccola Conti.

She forgot what came after seven.

She forgot what numbers were.

“You’ve lost count,” he said, lifting his head.

She couldn’t answer.

He smiled. The one that went all the way up. In the dark, in the window, with the canal below.

“From the first one,” said Chen Si.

✦ ✦ ✦

At three in the morning, they sat in the courtyard.

Downstairs. On the stone bench under the old fig tree where, eleven years before, eleven guests had sat in the sun and watched a woman in ivory walk toward a man in grey. The contessa had been right. It was cooler at night. They had brought wine. They had not broken the mirrors.

She was wearing his shirt, the white linen one, and nothing else, and no gold at all. It was all upstairs, on the window sill, in a long row of twenty-four pieces, in order.

He was wearing his trousers and the three pieces of gold that never came off.

She had her head on his shoulder. He had his arm round her. Neither of them had said anything.

“Rotterdam,” she said.

He went still.

She lifted her head.

“No,” she said quickly. “No, I don’t—I’m fine. I just wanted to say it. Here. In the courtyard.” She looked up at the fig tree, at the dark sky over the palazzo, at the single lit window upstairs where the gold was. “Because I’ll never be able to hear it again without thinking about tonight. A boring port in Holland. And I’ll be sitting in a meeting with Mr. Pei and someone will say Rotterdam and I’ll have to leave the room.”

He was quiet for a moment.

Then he started to laugh.

Helplessly, into her hair, with his whole body shaking against hers on the stone bench.

“What?” she said. “What?”

“I have a call,” said Chen Si, “with Rotterdam. Every Thursday. At nine. For the rest of my life.”

She stared at him.

Then she put her face in his shoulder and laughed until she couldn’t breathe, in the courtyard where she had been married, at three in the morning, in August, in the only city in the world whose name meant everything stops.

✦ ✦ ✦

On Thursday, the twenty-second of August, at nine in the morning, back on the thirty-ninth floor, Qian put the Rotterdam call through.

At 9:02, he heard Mr. Chen say, in a voice he had never heard him use on a business call, “I’m so sorry. Could you say that again?”

And then, a moment later, in a very strange tone: “No. No, nothing’s wrong. Please go on.”

At 9:04, the call ended.

At 9:05, Mr. Chen came to his door.

His ears were red.

“Qian,” he said, “I need you to reschedule all calls with Rotterdam. Permanently. Until further notice.”

Qian looked up.

“May I ask why, Mr. Chen?”

Mr. Chen looked at him.

“Dental,” said Chen Si, and went back into his office, and shut the door.

Qian opened the spreadsheet. He added row five hundred and two.

In the Notes column, after a very long pause, he wrote: Do not ask. Ever.

chapters.title: The Ring She Designed Herself
chapters.desc: For three weeks, her husband gets out of bed at two in the morning and comes back at five smelling of polish. Aurelia Chen does not do jealousy. Aurelia Chen follows him anyway, in silk pyjamas and a coat, with a gun in her bag, and finds him somewhere she never expected: at her own bench.
chapters.epigraph: Sketchbook, age fifteen, first page, in pencil: “A ring for someone who is loved without having to win. (Mamma says: sentimental. Second-rate. Don’t waste the paper.)”
chapters.content:
The first night, she thought nothing of it.

She woke at 2:10 in the morning because the bed was cold on his side, and she lay in the dark and listened, and heard the front door close very softly, and the lift, and then nothing. She thought: Rotterdam. She thought: the port. She thought: something has happened at the Docks and he has gone without waking me because I have the Leungs at nine.

She went back to sleep.

He was there when she woke at seven, asleep on his back, with his arm flung over his head. She kissed his shoulder and got up.

His shoulder smelled of polish.

Not soap. Not cologne. Polish. The red rouge they used on the wheel in the workshop for the last pass on gold. She would have known it anywhere. She had smelled of it every day of her life since she was nineteen.

She stood by the bed, looking down at him.

Then she went and had a shower, and decided she had imagined it.

✦ ✦ ✦

The second night, 2:04.

The third night, 1:58.

By the end of the first week, she had stopped sleeping at all after midnight. She lay in the dark with her eyes closed and her breathing slow, the way she had learned to fake sleep at eleven in her mother’s house so that nobody would come in and check whether she was practising. And at some point between 1:55 and 2:10, every night, she felt him get up. Very carefully. An inch at a time, so as not to move the mattress. She heard him dress in the dark without turning on a light. She heard the front door.

And at some point between 4:50 and 5:10, every night, he came back. And got into bed. An inch at a time. And smelled of polish.

He did not say anything about it in the mornings. He was exactly the same. He read the newspaper at breakfast. He kissed her at the door. He went to the thirty-ninth floor at 7:42 and looked at a photograph on his phone at 7:44.

He looked tired.

She noticed that on the eighth day. A faint greyness under his eyes. A slowness, once, in reaching for his coffee. A cut on the side of his left index finger, small, healing, that had not been there before.

She looked at the cut across the breakfast table.

“What happened to your finger?” she said.

He looked down at it as if surprised to find it there.

“Paper,” he said.

✦ ✦ ✦

She did not do jealousy.

She had told Dr. Ho this, on the Tuesday, very firmly. She did not do jealousy. She had never in her life been jealous of anyone except Elowen Lin, and that wasn’t jealousy, that was a sporting rivalry with a fifteen-year history and a running score. She did not do jealousy about men. Men were not worth it. Men came second, at best, and usually lower.

“And your husband?” said Dr. Ho.

Aurelia looked at the window.

“He doesn’t lie,” she said. “Clause three. In eight years he has never lied to me. Not once.”

“Then ask him.”

“If I ask him,” said Aurelia, “and he says I can’t tell you this yet, which is what clause three says he has to say if he can’t tell me something, then I’ll know there’s something. And I’ll have to wait. And I’m very bad at waiting.” She folded her hands. “If I don’t ask him, there’s nothing. Yet.”

Dr. Ho looked at her over her glasses.

“And the polish?” she said.

Aurelia did not say anything.

“Who do you think it is?” said Dr. Ho gently.

“It isn’t a who,” said Aurelia. “He wouldn’t. He couldn’t. He’s—” She stopped. “I know it isn’t a who. I know that. I know it the way I know gold. It isn’t a who.” Her voice went very small, and very young. “But he smells of a workshop, Dr. Ho. And it isn’t mine.”

✦ ✦ ✦

On the twenty-first night, at 2:01, she followed him.

She got up as soon as the front door closed. She was already dressed, under the duvet: silk pyjamas, the black ones, and over them his old camel coat, the one from the balcony, which she had put on at midnight in the bathroom without knowing why. Bare feet in flat shoes. Her hair in a knot. The gold clutch, with the small black gun in it, because she always took the clutch, and because if it was a who, she wanted to be holding something.

She took the stairs. Forty-four floors. In flat shoes. Faster than the lift, the way he had once come down thirty-nine.

She came out into the car park just in time to see the old car pull out of its space.

Not the black one. The old one. The one he had taken to the east coast for a cat.

No driver. No Zhao. No security car behind.

She got into her own car and followed him.

✦ ✦ ✦

He drove along the harbour.

Not toward the Docks. Not toward the port. Not toward the airport, or the old town, or the east coast, or any of the places her mind had been taking her at three in the morning for three weeks. He drove along the harbour front, slowly, under the street lights, with the water black on his left and the towers dark on his right, and she followed four cars behind, with her lights off when she dared, and her heart going so hard she could hear it.

He turned onto Harbour Road.

She nearly drove into a lamppost.

He parked outside her boutique.

Her boutique. The first one. With the broken necklace in the window, lit up on its plinth all night the way it had been for eight years.

She stopped her car at the end of the road and sat with her hands on the wheel and watched him get out of the old car, and look up and down the empty street, and take a key out of his pocket, and let himself in through the side door, the staff door, the one that went straight back to the workshop.

A light came on at the back of the shop.

The workshop light. The one over her bench.

✦ ✦ ✦

She sat in the car.

She didn’t understand. She thought about every possibility, very fast, the way she did sums, and none of them added up. Not a who. Obviously not a who. Not in her own workshop, at her own bench. A robbery? With a key? A deal? In her shop, without telling her, in breach of clause two? Something to do with the necklace? With the safe? With—

She got out of the car.

She walked down Harbour Road in the dark in black silk pyjamas and a camel coat with a gold clutch in her hand, and let herself in through the side door with her own key, very quietly, and stood in the short dark corridor that went back to the workshop, and listened.

Voices.

Two of them.

One was her husband’s, low. The other was old, and Italian, and very irritable.

“No. No, no, no. Così la rovini. Piano. Piano, Si.”

No. No, no. You’ll ruin it like that. Gently. Gently, Si.

Enzo.

She stood in the dark corridor with her mouth open.

✦ ✦ ✦

She went to the door of the workshop. She looked through the gap.

Enzo was sitting on the stool where women sat to try on rings. In his cardigan. With his magnifying glasses on his forehead and a cup of espresso in his hand and an expression of profound, theatrical suffering.

And at her bench, under her lamp, in his shirtsleeves, with her loupe screwed into his right eye and her ring clamp in his left hand and a tiny file in his right, bent over the bench with the total, rigid, furious concentration of a man defusing a bomb, sat her husband.

Filing a ring.

Very badly.

She could see from the door that he was doing it badly. The angle was wrong. He was holding the file like a pen, which everyone did the first time, and pressing much too hard, which everyone also did, and his whole shoulder was locked, and there was a plaster on the side of his left index finger and another, new, on his thumb.

“Piano,” said Enzo again, with enormous patience, and took a sip of espresso. “You file gold like you are angry with it. Gold does not respond to anger. Gold responds to time. Twenty-one nights, and you still file like a man in a fight.”

“I am in a fight,” said Chen Si, through his teeth, not lifting his eye from the loupe. “With this ring.”

“And the ring is winning,” said Enzo serenely.

✦ ✦ ✦

She must have made a sound.

She didn’t know what sound. Something. A breath. Because both of them turned round at the same moment and looked at the door.

Enzo nearly dropped his espresso.

Chen Si took the loupe out of his eye very slowly.

He looked at her, standing in the doorway of her own workshop at 2:40 in the morning, in black silk pyjamas and his old camel coat, with her hair coming down and her gold clutch in her hand and her face—

He saw her face.

He was off the stool before Enzo could speak.

“Aurelia,” he said. “Aurelia. Hey.” He crossed the workshop in three steps and stopped in front of her and didn’t touch her, because of whatever was in her face, and his own face had gone white. “What are you—how long have you—you followed me? From the flat? Alone?”

“You got up,” she said. Her voice came out very strange. “Every night. For three weeks. At two o’clock. And came back at five.” She looked at his shirt. “Smelling of polish.”

He went completely still.

He understood. She watched him understand. Watched it go across his face, every single thing she had thought for twenty-one nights, lying in the dark, faking sleep, all at once.

“Oh,” said Chen Si.

It was barely a sound.

“Oh, no. No. Aurelia. No.” He took her face in his hands, the way he did, and his hands had plasters on them and smelled of rouge and were shaking. “You thought—for three weeks—you’ve been lying there—” He couldn’t finish. “Why didn’t you ask me?”

“Because you’d have said I can’t tell you this yet,” said Aurelia. Her eyes were wet. “Clause three. And then I’d have known there was something. And I’d have had to wait.”

“I would have said I can’t tell you this yet,” he agreed, his voice cracking. “And then I would have said, but it’s for you, and it’s in your shop, and Enzo is being very rude to me about it.” His thumbs moved on her cheekbones. “And you’d have known. In one second. And slept.”

She stared at him.

“It’s for me,” she said.

✦ ✦ ✦

Behind him, from the stool, Enzo cleared his throat.

“Cara,” he said. “Before you kill him. Which I would understand. Come and look.”

She looked past her husband’s shoulder at the bench.

At the clamp. At what was in it.

A ring.

Small. Gold. Not finished; she could see that from the door, the way you can see that a cake isn’t done, the shank still rough on one side, the top not yet set. A narrow band, very plain, rising at the front into two tiny gold hands. Not clasped. Not holding anything. Just resting together, palm to palm, side by side, the way two people sit on a bench. And between the hands, in the space where they almost touched, a setting. Empty. Waiting for a stone.

She knew it.

She knew it the way you know your own handwriting.

She walked past him, to the bench, slowly, as if it might go away, and stood over it, and looked down.

Beside the clamp, held flat under a steel rule so that it wouldn’t curl, there was a page. Old. Torn out of a sketchbook. The paper gone soft and yellow at the edges. A drawing in pencil, very careful, very young, with a lot of rubbing out. Two small hands on a band. Palm to palm.

And at the top of the page, in a round, confident, fifteen-year-old hand, with the flourish on the A that had not yet been trained out of her:

A ring for someone who is loved without having to win.

And underneath, in a different hand. Tall. Slanting. Dark blue ink.

Sentimental. Second-rate. Don’t waste the paper. — Mamma.

✦ ✦ ✦

For a while she didn’t say anything.

She stood at her own bench at 2:45 in the morning and looked at a drawing she had made at fifteen, in her first winter in the city, in the room with the long mirror at the Peak, on the night after her first ranking. She had come second. In the regional mathematics olympiad. To a boy from Shanghai who had not even seemed to be trying. And she had gone home and sat on her bed and drawn a ring. For no one. For a girl who might, one day, somehow, be loved without having to win.

And her mother had come in, at eleven, to check that she was studying, and seen it, and taken the fountain pen off the desk, and written, in dark blue ink, so that it could never be rubbed out. Aurelia had tried anyway. With an eraser, and then with her thumb, until the paper went thin and soft and the ink did not move at all.

And Aurelia had torn the page out and put it in the back of the sketchbook and never looked at it again. Never made it. Never drawn anything like it. Never once, in fifteen years and four hundred engagement rings for other women, designed a single ring for herself.

“Where,” she said. Her voice wouldn’t work. “Where did you—”

“Your old room,” said Chen Si, behind her. “At the Peak. Last summer, when the restorers were doing the window seat. Under the cushion there was a board that lifted. You must have put them there when you were fifteen. A box of sketchbooks.” He was quiet. “You were in Paris. The foreman rang Qian. Qian rang me. I went up to the house on my own and sat on the floor of your old room in front of the long mirror and opened the first one, and it fell open at the back.”

“You never said.”

“You’d just come back from Paris,” said Chen Si. “You’d been crying about the shoebox for a year, on and off. The silver one. With the medals.” He paused. “I didn’t want to give you another thing to carry. So I put the page in my pocket, and the sketchbooks in the safe, under your diamonds, where you never look. And I took the page to Enzo.”

She turned round.

“And Enzo said?”

“Enzo said,” said Enzo, from the stool, with dignity, “that he would make it. In a week. In his sleep. That it was a simple piece, and a very good one, and that her mother was a fool.” He sniffed. “And your husband said no.”

She looked at Chen Si.

“You said no to Enzo?”

“I said I wanted to make it myself,” said Chen Si.

He said it very simply. Standing in the middle of her workshop in his shirtsleeves with plasters on two fingers and red rouge on his cuffs and grey under his eyes from three weeks without sleep.

“You don’t know how,” said Aurelia.

“No,” he agreed. “I don’t. Enzo has been teaching me. For twenty-one nights.” He looked at the ring in the clamp. “I’m very bad at it. I’ve cut myself four times. I melted the first one completely. The second one cracked. Enzo threw the third one in the bin and wouldn’t let me take it out.” Something moved at the corner of his mouth. “This is the fourth.”

“Why?” said Aurelia.

Her voice broke on it.

“Why would you—you have the best goldsmith in Asia sitting right there. He could have made it in a week. Perfectly. You don’t have to—you didn’t have to cut your hands and get up at two in the morning for three weeks and make me think—” She stopped. She couldn’t. “Why?”

He looked at her.

“Because someone wrote on it,” said Chen Si.

She went still.

“Someone took a pen,” he said, “when you were fifteen, and wrote on the thing you made, second-rate, don’t waste the paper. And you believed her. For fifteen years. You never made it. You never made yourself a ring.” His voice went very low. “Four hundred rings for other women. And not one for you. Because the one time you tried, someone told you it wasn’t worth the paper.”

He came across the workshop to her. He stopped in front of her.

“I didn’t want the best goldsmith in Asia to make it,” he said. “I wanted someone who loves you to make it. Badly. Slowly. With his hands. Because he thinks it’s worth more than the paper. Because he thinks it’s worth everything. Because he would get up at two in the morning for the rest of his life to file a ring that a fifteen-year-old girl drew for herself and was told not to.” He took her hands. “I wanted it to be made by someone who doesn’t care if it’s second-rate. Because it’s yours.”

✦ ✦ ✦

She cried.

She stood in her own workshop in his old coat and cried, properly, with her face in his chest and her fists in his shirt, the way she had cried on the floor of this room once with her back against her bench and no air in her lungs. Not like that. The opposite of that. She cried until his shirt was wet through and Enzo had got up off the stool and gone out of the room, very quietly, muttering in Italian, and shut the door.

He held her. He didn’t say anything.

When she could breathe, she lifted her head.

“It’s not finished,” she said. “The shank’s rough. On the left. And you’ve filed the top too thin; the hands will bend if anyone knocks them.”

He looked down at her.

“I know,” he said.

“And the setting’s empty.”

“I know. I was going to ask Enzo which stone.” He paused. “He said I had to ask you.”

She looked at the ring in the clamp.

“No stone,” she said.

He looked at her.

“I left it empty,” said Aurelia. “When I was fifteen. On purpose. Look at the drawing.” She pointed with a shaking finger. “There’s nothing in the setting. I didn’t draw one. I didn’t know what went there.” She looked at him. “I didn’t know what it looked like. Being loved without having to win. So I left the space.”

He looked at the drawing.

He looked at her.

“And now?” he said.

She thought about it.

She thought about a balcony, and a coat held out, not round her shoulders. A cup of coffee he didn’t drink. A man at the front row with his phone off. Soup on the thirty-ninth floor. Two cats in a water trough. Two thousand four hundred and six comments. Eleven seconds of silence when she asked him who he was. Every single time he had not asked her to win.

“Still nothing,” she said. “Leave it empty.”

He frowned, very slightly.

“Why?”

“Because,” said Aurelia, “it isn’t a thing. It doesn’t look like anything. It’s just the space. Where you stand.” She looked up at him. “Leave it empty. So I can see through it. So every time I look at it I can see what’s on the other side.”

He didn’t say anything for a while.

Then he let go of her hands, and went back to the bench, and sat down on her stool, and picked up the loupe, and screwed it into his eye, and picked up the file.

“Show me,” he said. “The shank. On the left. Where it’s rough.”

She came and stood behind him.

She put her hand over his, on the file. The way Enzo had once put his hand over hers, when she was nineteen.

“Piano,” she said, into his ear. “Gently. You file like you’re in a fight.”

“I am in a fight.”

“Not any more,” said Aurelia. “Gold responds to time.”

She guided his hand.

✦ ✦ ✦

They finished it at 5:40 in the morning.

Together. His hands and hers. At her bench, under her lamp, with the street outside going from black to grey and the first tram going past on Harbour Road and Enzo asleep in an armchair in the shop with his espresso cold beside him.

It was not perfect.

It was a little thick on one side, where he had been angry with it, and a little thin on the other, where she had overcorrected. The two small hands did not quite match. One of them had a tiny mark on the palm where his file had slipped on the fourth night and he had refused to let Enzo polish it out.

“That’s mine,” he had said. “That stays.”

She held it under the lamp.

He took it out of her fingers.

He did not kneel. He had knelt a thousand times, under clause nine, on a forty-fourth floor and a workshop floor and in Geneva and in Milan. He did not kneel now. He stood in front of her in his shirtsleeves with plasters on his fingers and rouge on his cuffs, and took her right hand, the one without the wedding ring, and held it.

“I’m not asking you anything,” he said. “You asked. In this shop. Eleven pages. I said yes.” He looked at the ring. “I’m just giving you this. Clause thirteen. You can’t refuse it, or set a price on it, or pay for it. You can only keep it.”

“For as long as I like,” said Aurelia.

He put it on her finger.

It fitted. Of course it fitted. He had measured her ring finger in her sleep, he would tell her later, on the second night, with a strip of paper, in the dark, and nearly woken her, and frozen for four minutes with the paper round her finger until she stopped moving.

She held up her hand.

Two small gold hands, palm to palm, side by side, on her finger. And between them, a space. Empty. And through it, when she lifted it to the light, she could see him.

He did not let her look for long. He took the hand with the ring on it and kissed the two small gold hands, and then pulled her in by it and kissed her mouth, hard and long, with plasters on his fingers and rouge on his cuffs and Enzo snoring in the next room, like a man who had spent twenty-one nights wanting to tell her and could finally stop holding it in.

✦ ✦ ✦

At the bottom of the old sketchbook page, under her mother’s writing, there was a space.

She found a pen. Red. On the bench.

She wrote, in her own hand, round and confident, with the flourish on the A:

Made, 2026. By someone who loves her. Badly, slowly, with his hands. Worth more than the paper.

And under that, in black, in a sharp, precise hand, lifted at every turn, he wrote one word.

Mine.

She had the page framed. It hangs in the workshop, on the wall by the door, beside the brass plaque that says HIS COAT.

Customers sometimes ask about it. A torn page from a child’s sketchbook. A drawing in pencil, two hands on a ring. Three different handwritings.

She tells them it’s the most valuable thing in the shop.

Nobody believes her.

Enzo does.
